title: Design of Structures — practice questions
$comment: Answer positions were distributed while authoring, per the discipline recorded after the chapter 1 bank was found to key 55% of its questions to option (b). Numerical items were recomputed independently before keying.

questions.stem: In computing the DEAD LOAD of a reinforced concrete member, the unit weight of reinforced concrete is taken as:
options: 20 kN/m³
22 kN/m³
25 kN/m³
28 kN/m³
questions.solution:
**25 kN/m³.**

**The unit weights used in dead load calculations:**

| Material | Unit weight |
|---|---|
| **REINFORCED concrete** ← | **25 kN/m³** ← |
| **PLAIN concrete** ← | **24 kN/m³ — the reinforcement accounts for the extra 1 kN/m³** ← |
| **Brick masonry** | **19 to 20 kN/m³** ← |
| **Stone masonry (coursed rubble)** | **24 to 26 kN/m³** ← |
| **Cement mortar / plaster** | **20 kN/m³** ← |
| **Cement concrete flooring** | **24 kN/m³** ← |
| **Steel** | **78.5 kN/m³** ← |
| **Timber (seasoned sal)** | **8 to 10 kN/m³** ← |
| **Water** | **9.81 kN/m³, taken as 10** ← |
| **Soil (moist)** | **18 to 20 kN/m³** ← |

> **THE 25 AGAINST 24 DISTINCTION IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS SMALL BUT IT IS THE ONE THE QUESTION TURNS ON, and the reason is straightforward: steel weighs about three times as much as concrete, and reinforcement occupies roughly half a per cent of the volume in an ordinary member.**

> **That adds approximately 1 kN/m³, which is why reinforced concrete is taken at 25 and plain concrete at 24.**

> **The figures are given in IS 875 Part 1, which is the code of practice for dead loads.**

**WHAT COUNTS AS DEAD LOAD, WHICH IS WHERE ERRORS ACTUALLY ARISE:**

| Item | Dead or imposed? |
|---|---|
| **Self weight of the slab, beam, column, wall** ← | **DEAD** |
| **FLOOR FINISH — screed, tiles, marble** ← | **DEAD — and commonly taken as 1.0 to 1.5 kN/m², which is not negligible** ← |
| **CEILING plaster and services below the slab** ← | **DEAD, about 0.3 to 0.5 kN/m²** ← |
| **PARTITION walls in a fixed position** ← | **DEAD** ← |
| **PARTITIONS whose position may change** ← | **Taken as an equivalent IMPOSED load, commonly 1.0 kN/m² — because they may be moved** ← |
| **Water in a tank** ← | **IMPOSED, since the tank may be emptied** ← |
| **Fixed plant and machinery** | **DEAD if permanently fixed** |
| **People, furniture, stored goods** | **IMPOSED** |

> **THE FLOOR FINISH IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE ITEM MOST OFTEN UNDER-ESTIMATED AND IT IS WORTH TAKING SERIOUSLY: a 50 mm screed plus 20 mm of marble weighs about 1.7 kN/m².**

> **On a 125 mm slab whose own weight is 3.1 kN/m², that is more than half again, and an imposed load of 2 kN/m² for a residential room is of the same order as the finish.**

> **So a designer who allows a token 0.5 kN/m² for finishes has made an error comparable in size to omitting a third of the live load — and the error is permanent, because unlike live load the finish is always there.**

> **THE MOVABLE PARTITION IN THE FIFTH ROW IS A GOOD ILLUSTRATION OF WHY THE DEAD-OR-IMPOSED QUESTION IS DECIDED BY PERMANENCE RATHER THAN BY THE NATURE OF THE OBJECT: a brick partition is unambiguously a heavy fixed object, yet if its position is liable to change it must be treated as an imposed load.**

> **The reason is that a dead load is applied where the drawing shows it, and the design can exploit that — a beam directly beneath a wall is sized for it and the slab beside it is not.**

> **A load that may be moved must be assumed capable of standing anywhere, which is a quite different and more onerous requirement, and treating it as a uniformly distributed imposed load is the way that is done.**

examTip.trick: **RCC 25 kN/m³, plain concrete 24** — the reinforcement is worth the extra 1 kN/m³. Brick masonry 19-20, steel 78.5.
examTip.trap: **Floor finishes are 1.0-1.5 kN/m², comparable to the residential imposed load itself** — and unlike live load they are always present. A token 0.5 is a serious under-estimate.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dead or imposed is decided by PERMANENCE, not by weight** — a movable brick partition is taken as an equivalent imposed load, because it must be assumed capable of standing anywhere.

questions.stem: As per IS 875 (Part 2), the IMPOSED (live) load to be taken on the floor of a RESIDENTIAL room in a dwelling is:
options: 2.0 kN/m²
3.0 kN/m²
4.0 kN/m²
5.0 kN/m²
questions.solution:
**2.0 kN/m².**

**The imposed floor loads most commonly needed:**

| Occupancy | Imposed load |
|---|---|
| **RESIDENTIAL rooms in a dwelling** ← | **2.0 kN/m²** ← |
| **Residential BALCONIES** ← | **3.0 kN/m² — higher than the rooms, because people crowd onto them** ← |
| **OFFICE rooms, above the ground floor** | **2.5 kN/m²** ← |
| **Office floors with filing and storage** | **4.0 kN/m² or more** ← |
| **CLASSROOMS** | **3.0 kN/m²** ← |
| **ASSEMBLY halls with FIXED seating** ← | **4.0 kN/m²** ← |
| **Assembly areas WITHOUT fixed seating** ← | **5.0 kN/m² — the crowd can pack more densely when it is not seated in rows** ← |
| **CORRIDORS, staircases, lobbies in a dwelling** | **3.0 kN/m²** ← |
| **Corridors and stairs in public buildings** | **4.0 kN/m²** ← |
| **Flat ROOFS with access** | **1.5 kN/m²** ← |
| **Flat roofs WITHOUT access** ← | **0.75 kN/m²** ← |
| **SHOPS and warehouses** | **4.0 kN/m² upward, by the goods stored** ← |

> **THE PATTERN RUNNING THROUGH THE TABLE IS WORTH NOTICING BECAUSE IT MAKES THE WHOLE LIST RECOVERABLE INSTEAD OF MEMORABLE: the load rises with the DENSITY OF PEOPLE the space invites.**

> **A bedroom holds a few people and their furniture. A corridor and a staircase channel everyone in the building through a small area. An assembly hall packs people deliberately. A warehouse stacks goods to the ceiling.**

> **So 2 for rooms, 3 for circulation and balconies, 4 for public circulation and seated assembly, 5 for standing crowds — and the sequence follows the occupancy rather than needing to be looked up each time.**

**THE BALCONY IN THE SECOND ROW AND THE STANDING CROWD IN THE SEVENTH ARE BOTH WORTH DWELLING ON, BECAUSE BOTH REFLECT HARD-WON EXPERIENCE:**

| Case | Note |
|---|---|
| **A balcony carries a HIGHER load than the room it opens off** ← | **Because when something happens outside, everyone goes out onto it at once** ← |
| **Balcony and cantilever failures are a recurring cause of casualties** ← | **And they fail suddenly, being cantilevers with no redundancy** ← |
| **A STANDING crowd is denser than a SEATED one** ← | **Fixed seating limits the density; an open floor does not** ← |
| **Which is why removing fixed seating from a hall changes its design load** ← | **A real consideration when a building is altered or its use changes** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A PRACTICAL WARNING THAT ARISES CONSTANTLY IN PRACTICE AND SELDOM IN TEXTBOOKS: a change of USE can overload a structure that was perfectly adequate for its original purpose, without a single alteration to the building.**

> **A residential floor designed for 2 kN/m² and later used as a records store at 5 kN/m² is loaded to two and a half times its design imposed load.**

> **Nothing has been built or removed; only the occupancy has changed, and the structure has no way of announcing that it is now overloaded until it cracks or deflects visibly.**

> **So a change of use requires a structural assessment, and an engineer asked to approve one must establish what the floor was designed for rather than observing that it has stood for twenty years — which it did under a quite different load.**

**And the LOAD REDUCTION allowance, which follows naturally:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A COLUMN supporting many floors may be designed for a REDUCED imposed load** ← | **10 per cent reduction per floor supported, down to a maximum reduction of 50 per cent** ← |
| **The justification is probabilistic** ← | **It is very unlikely that every floor in a tall building carries its full imposed load simultaneously** ← |
| **No reduction is allowed on a single floor's beams and slabs** ← | **One floor may well be fully loaded** ← |
| **And none where the imposed load is a fixed, certain load** ← | **A warehouse's stored goods, or plant** ← |

> **The distinction in the third row is the one to hold: the reduction is a statement about SIMULTANEITY across floors, so it applies only to members collecting load from several floors, and never to the member carrying one floor.**

examTip.trick: **2 for residential rooms, 3 for corridors and balconies, 4 for public circulation and seated assembly, 5 for standing crowds.** The load follows the density of people invited.
examTip.trap: **A BALCONY carries more than the room it opens off (3 against 2)** — because everyone goes out at once, and a cantilever fails suddenly with no redundancy.
examTip.mnemonic: **A CHANGE OF USE can overload a sound structure with no alteration at all** — a 2 kN/m² residential floor used as a 5 kN/m² store. Standing 20 years proves nothing about the new load.

questions.stem: As per IS 875 (Part 2), the reduction in imposed load permitted in the design of a COLUMN supporting several floors is:
options: No reduction is permitted under any circumstances
A flat 25 per cent reduction irrespective of the number of floors
50 per cent for every floor supported, without limit
10 PER CENT for each floor supported, subject to a MAXIMUM reduction of 50 per cent
questions.solution:
**10 PER CENT for each floor supported, subject to a maximum reduction of 50 per cent.**

**The rule as applied:**

| Floors carried by the column at that level | Reduction | Imposed load taken |
|---|---|---|
| **1 (the roof, or the topmost floor)** ← | **NIL** ← | **100 per cent** |
| **2** | **10 %** ← | **90 %** |
| **3** | **20 %** ← | **80 %** |
| **4** | **30 %** | **70 %** |
| **5** | **40 %** | **60 %** |
| **6 or more** ← | **50 %, the CEILING** ← | **50 per cent, and no further reduction however many floors** ← |

> **THE JUSTIFICATION IS PROBABILISTIC AND IT IS WORTH STATING PROPERLY, because the rule looks like an unprincipled discount if its basis is not understood.**

> **The imposed load prescribed for a floor is a value that a single floor may credibly reach — a room genuinely crowded with people and furniture.**

> **But a column at the base of a ten-storey building carries ten floors, and the probability that ALL TEN are simultaneously loaded to that full value is extremely small.**

> **Designing the column for ten times the full floor load would therefore be designing for an event that will not occur, and the reduction corrects for that.**

> **The 50 per cent ceiling exists because the argument, extended indefinitely, would eventually reduce the load to nothing — and beyond a certain number of floors the code declines to press the statistics further.**

**WHERE THE REDUCTION MAY NOT BE APPLIED, WHICH IS AS IMPORTANT AS THE RULE ITSELF:**

| Case | Reason |
|---|---|
| **BEAMS and SLABS of a single floor** ← | **One floor may certainly be fully loaded — there is no simultaneity argument to make** ← |
| **Where the imposed load is a FIXED, CERTAIN load** ← | **Stored goods in a warehouse, fixed plant, water in a tank that is normally full — these do not vary independently** ← |
| **Where the loading is specified as a definite quantity by the client** ← | **The client's stated load is a requirement, not a statistical estimate** ← |
| **On the roof's own imposed load** ← | **Which is counted as one floor and gets no reduction** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE EXCEPTION MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND IT MATTERS BECAUSE IT IS EXACTLY WHERE THE CONSEQUENCE OF ERROR IS GREATEST: a warehouse's imposed load is not a probabilistic crowd, it is pallets of goods that sit there permanently.**

> **A ten-storey warehouse may genuinely be full on every floor at once — that is what a warehouse is for.**

> **Applying a 50 per cent reduction to the columns of such a building halves the design load on a structure whose load will actually be present in full, which is not a conservative approximation but a straightforward error of a factor of two.**

> **So the character of the imposed load must be examined before the reduction is applied, and the reduction belongs to buildings whose occupancy varies — dwellings, offices, hotels — rather than to those whose load is placed and left.**

**A note on the SIMILAR reduction for beams, for completeness:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **A beam carrying a large FLOOR AREA may also take a reduced imposed load** ← | **The same simultaneity argument applied horizontally rather than vertically** ← |
| **5 per cent for every 50 m² of floor area supported, up to 25 per cent** ← | **Applying to a beam or girder, not to a slab** ← |
| **The two reductions are not compounded arbitrarily** ← | **The code's provisions are to be applied as written rather than multiplied together** ← |

> **The third row is worth a caution: reductions of this kind are code provisions with defined scope, and stacking several of them because each is individually justified produces a total reduction that no code intended and that no probabilistic argument supports.**

examTip.trick: **10 % per floor, ceiling of 50 %** — so from six floors down, the column takes half the imposed load. The topmost floor gets no reduction.
examTip.trap: **Never on a single floor's beams and slabs, and never where the load is FIXED** — a warehouse really can be full on every floor at once, so the reduction there is an error of a factor of two.
examTip.mnemonic: **The reduction is a statement about SIMULTANEITY** — it belongs to occupancies that vary (dwellings, offices, hotels), not to loads that are placed and left.

questions.stem: The BASIC WIND SPEED given in the wind maps of IS 875 (Part 3) and NBC 104 is defined as the:
options: Annual average wind speed at the site
PEAK GUST speed averaged over about 3 SECONDS, at 10 m above mean ground level in open terrain, with a 50-year mean return period
Maximum wind speed ever recorded at the nearest meteorological station
Hourly mean wind speed at the top of the proposed structure
questions.solution:
**The PEAK GUST speed averaged over about 3 SECONDS, at 10 m above mean ground level in open terrain, with a 50-year mean return period.**

**Every element of that definition is doing work:**

| Element | Why it is specified |
|---|---|
| **PEAK GUST, averaged over 3 seconds** ← | **A short gust is what loads a small structure — the averaging time must match the size of the thing being loaded** ← |
| **At 10 m above ground** ← | **A standard reference height, because wind speed increases with height** ← |
| **In OPEN terrain (category 2)** ← | **A standard exposure, because roughness reduces the speed near the ground** ← |
| **50-year mean return period** ← | **The probability level — a speed exceeded on average once in 50 years** ← |

> **THE 3-SECOND AVERAGING IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE POINT MOST WORTH UNDERSTANDING, and it explains why wind codes specify an averaging time at all.**

> **Wind is gusty: the speed fluctuates continuously about its mean.**

> **A small element — a window pane, a cladding panel, a signboard — is fully engulfed by a brief gust and must be designed for the peak.**

> **A very large structure is not: a gust of a few seconds' duration does not cover the whole of a large building at once, so the load averaged over the whole structure is less than the peak gust everywhere simultaneously.**

> **Hence a code based on a 3-second gust is directly applicable to small elements, and larger structures are treated with size and dynamic factors — and a code based on an hourly mean, as some are, needs a gust factor applied instead.**

**From the basic wind speed to the design pressure:**

| Step | Expression |
|---|---|
| **1. Basic wind speed** | **V_b, from the map** ← |
| **2. Design wind speed at height z** | **V_z = V_b · k₁ · k₂ · k₃ (and k₄ where cyclones apply)** ← |
| **3. Design wind PRESSURE** ← | **p_z = 0.6 V_z² in N/m², with V_z in m/s** ← |
| **4. Wind FORCE on the element** | **F = (C_pe − C_pi) · A · p_z, or F = C_f · A · p_z** ← |

**The modifying factors:**

| Factor | Represents |
|---|---|
| **k₁ — RISK coefficient** ← | **The return period appropriate to the structure — higher for important structures and long design lives, lower for temporary works** ← |
| **k₂ — TERRAIN, height and size factor** ← | **Roughness of the surroundings and the height above ground — the wind is slower near a rough surface and faster higher up** ← |
| **k₃ — TOPOGRAPHY factor** ← | **Speed-up over hills, ridges and escarpments — never less than 1.0** ← |
| **k₄ — importance factor for CYCLONIC regions** | **Coastal areas; not applicable inland** ← |

> **THE k₃ FACTOR IN THE THIRD ROW DESERVES PARTICULAR ATTENTION IN NEPAL AND IS ROUTINELY IGNORED: wind accelerates as it is forced up and over a ridge, and the speed-up at the crest can be substantial.**

> **A building on a hilltop or on the shoulder of a ridge is therefore exposed to a higher wind than the map's value, and k₃ can reach 1.36 in the worst geometry.**

> **Since the pressure varies as the SQUARE of the speed, a k₃ of 1.36 increases the pressure by 85 per cent — which is not a refinement but a near-doubling.**

> **In a country where a great many buildings sit on ridges and hill shoulders because that is where the flat land is, taking k₃ as 1.0 by default is a real and systematic under-design.**

> **THE SQUARE RELATIONSHIP IN THE THIRD STEP IS THE REASON EVERY ONE OF THESE FACTORS MATTERS MORE THAN IT APPEARS: pressure goes as V², so a 20 per cent error in speed is a 44 per cent error in pressure.**

> **Wind speed estimates therefore deserve more care than their apparent precision suggests, and the habit of taking every k factor as unity — which quietly assumes flat open ground, ordinary importance and a 50-year life — should be a conscious decision rather than a default.**

examTip.trick: **3-second peak gust, at 10 m, in open terrain, 50-year return period.** Every clause of that definition is a standardisation the code needs.
examTip.trap: **k₃ (topography) can reach 1.36 on a ridge crest, and pressure goes as V², so that is an 85 % increase in pressure.** Taking it as 1.0 by default under-designs hilltop buildings systematically.
examTip.mnemonic: **p_z = 0.6 V_z², with V_z = V_b·k₁·k₂·k₃.** Because pressure goes as the square, a 20 % speed error is a 44 % pressure error.

questions.stem: The design wind speed at a certain height on a building works out to 47 m/s. The design wind PRESSURE at that height is:
options: 0.88 kN/m²
1.10 kN/m²
1.33 kN/m²
2.21 kN/m²
questions.solution:
**1.33 kN/m².**

**The relation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **p_z = 0.6 V_z², giving p_z in N/m² for V_z in m/s** ← | ← |
| **V_z²** | **= 47² = 2,209** ← |
| **p_z** | **= 0.6 × 2,209 = 1,325.4 N/m²** ← |
| **In kN/m²** | **= 1.325, that is about 1.33 kN/m²** ← |

> **So the design wind pressure is about 1.33 kN/m².**

**WHERE THE COEFFICIENT 0.6 COMES FROM IS WORTH KNOWING, BECAUSE IT MAKES THE FORMULA RECOVERABLE AND SHOWS WHAT IT ASSUMES:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The stagnation pressure of a moving fluid is ½ρV²** ← | **Bernoulli's result — the pressure when the flow is brought to rest** ← |
| **For air, ρ ≈ 1.2 kg/m³ at standard conditions** ← | ← |
| **So ½ρ = ½ × 1.2 = 0.6** ← | **Which is exactly the coefficient in the code's formula** ← |
| **The 0.6 is therefore ½ρ for air, not an empirical constant** ← | **The formula is simply the dynamic pressure of the airstream** ← |

> **THAT DERIVATION HAS A PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE THAT MATTERS IN NEPAL AND IS RARELY MENTIONED: air DENSITY falls with altitude.**

> **At 3,000 m the density is roughly 0.9 kg/m³ against 1.2 at sea level, so the true coefficient is nearer 0.45 than 0.6.**

> **A structure at high altitude therefore experiences about 25 per cent less wind pressure than the formula gives for the same speed — a conservative error, and one that codes generally leave uncorrected for simplicity.**

> **It is worth knowing chiefly because it explains why the formula is a convention rather than a physical law, and because the same reasoning in reverse warns against applying a sea-level coefficient to a fluid other than air.**

**And what the pressure is then used for, which is where the design work lies:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The pressure p_z is the DYNAMIC pressure of the wind, not the load on the surface** ← | **The load depends on the shape and on which surface is considered** ← |
| **F = (C_pe − C_pi) · A · p_z for a building's cladding or roof** ← | **External pressure coefficient minus internal, times the area, times p_z** ← |
| **C_pe is NEGATIVE (suction) over much of a roof and on the leeward wall** ← | **So the load is often outward, lifting the roof off** ← |
| **C_pi depends on the OPENINGS in the building** ← | **A building with a large opening on the windward side is internally pressurised, which adds to the roof uplift** ← |
| **F = C_f · A · p_z for a lattice tower, a signboard or a chimney** ← | **Using a force coefficient for the whole body** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS TOGETHER EXPLAIN THE COMMONEST WIND FAILURE IN THE REGION AND IT IS WORTH SEEING HOW THE TWO COMBINE: light roofs are blown OFF, not pushed down.**

> **The flow separating over a roof's windward edge creates strong suction on the upper surface — the roof behaves like a wing.**

> **If the building also has a large windward opening — an open shutter, a broken window, an open door — the interior is pressurised, and that internal pressure pushes the roof upward from below at the same moment.**

> **The two effects add, and a light corrugated sheet roof on inadequate holding-down straps departs entirely.**

> **The practical consequences are that the HOLDING DOWN of a light roof is the critical design item rather than its strength in bending, and that closing a building's openings in a storm is not superstition but a genuine reduction of the internal pressure coefficient.**

examTip.trick: **p_z = 0.6 V_z² = 0.6 × 47² = 1,325 N/m² = 1.33 kN/m².** Answer in N/m² when the speed is in m/s.
examTip.trap: **The 0.6 is ½ρ for air (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³)** — it is dynamic pressure, not an empirical constant. At 3,000 m the density is lower, so the formula is conservative there.
examTip.mnemonic: **Light roofs are blown OFF, not pushed down** — roof suction plus internal pressure from a windward opening, adding together. So HOLDING DOWN is the critical design item.

questions.stem: SNOW LOAD on a roof, as treated in IS 875 (Part 4) and in Nepali practice, is characterised by the fact that it:
options: INCREASES with altitude, and is greater on a FLAT or shallow roof than on a steep one — since snow slides off a steep slope but accumulates on a flat one
Is independent of the roof's slope, being taken as a fixed intensity everywhere
Is greater on a steep roof, because the snow is retained by the greater surface area
Need never be considered in Nepal, snow being confined to uninhabited altitudes
questions.solution:
**It INCREASES with altitude, and is greater on a FLAT or shallow roof than on a steep one** — since snow slides off a steep slope but accumulates on a flat one.

**How the snow load is arrived at:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The GROUND snow load s₀ is established for the location** ← | **From records or from the altitude, in kN/m² — it increases with elevation** ← |
| **A SHAPE coefficient μ converts it to a roof load** ← | **s = μ s₀** ← |
| **μ = 0.8 for a roof slope up to 30 degrees** ← | **The snow stays on** ← |
| **μ reduces linearly from 0.8 to ZERO between 30 and 60 degrees** ← | **Snow progressively slides off** ← |
| **μ = 0 for slopes above 60 degrees** ← | **No snow is retained at all** ← |

> **THE SLOPE DEPENDENCE IN THE THIRD TO FIFTH ROWS IS THE PRACTICAL HEART OF SNOW DESIGN AND IT POINTS DIRECTLY AT THE REMEDY: a steep roof is the simplest defence against snow load.**

> **This is why traditional buildings in snowy regions everywhere have steeply pitched roofs — a form arrived at by experience long before any code, and correct for exactly the reason the code gives.**

> **Conversely a flat roof in a snowy area carries the full ground snow load and must be designed for it, which is a heavy load and one that can be increased further by drifting.**

**DRIFTING AND UNBALANCED LOADING, WHICH IS THE CASE THAT ACTUALLY CAUSES FAILURES:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Wind redistributes snow, piling it in the LEE of obstructions** ← | **Against parapets, walls, plant rooms, and in valleys between roofs** ← |
| **The drift load can be SEVERAL TIMES the uniform load locally** ← | ← |
| **A MULTI-SPAN roof accumulates snow in its VALLEYS** ← | **Which is why north-light and multi-bay roofs are particularly vulnerable** ← |
| **UNBALANCED loading — snow on one slope only, having slid or blown off the other** ← | **Which loads a symmetrical truss or portal asymmetrically, a condition it may not have been designed for** ← |
| **A STEP in roof level creates a drift against the higher wall** ← | **A classic failure location** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE CASE MOST OFTEN MISSED AND IT IS WORTH BEING EXPLICIT ABOUT WHY IT MATTERS: a symmetrical structure loaded symmetrically develops one set of forces, and the same structure loaded on one half develops quite another.**

> **A three-pinned or two-pinned arch, a portal frame or a truss may have far larger moments under half-span loading than under full-span loading, even though the total load is less.**

> **So checking only the uniform full-load case is not conservative — the unbalanced case must be checked separately, and it frequently governs.**

> **This is the same principle as the pattern-loading requirement for continuous beams under imposed load, where alternate spans loaded gives larger moments than all spans loaded.**

**WHERE SNOW MATTERS IN NEPAL, SINCE OPTION (d) IS A REAL MISCONCEPTION AND WORTH ANSWERING:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Substantial permanent settlements sit above 2,500 m** ← | **In Mustang, Manang, Dolpa, Humla, Solukhumbu and the northern belt generally** ← |
| **Snow loads there are real and can be severe** ← | **And a heavy snowfall year loads roofs that ordinary years do not** ← |
| **Trekking lodges, schools, health posts and army and police posts are built at such altitudes** ← | **Often with imported light steel roofs designed for the Terai** ← |
| **A light roof designed for wind uplift may be quite inadequate for snow's DOWNWARD load** ← | **The two governing cases act in opposite directions, and satisfying one does not satisfy the other** ← |

> **The last row is a genuine and easily-made error: a light sheet roof's design in the hills is usually driven by wind UPLIFT, and the members and fixings are sized for a net outward force.**

> **Snow imposes a large DOWNWARD load on the same members, and the purlin spacing, sheet thickness and truss that were adequate against uplift may buckle or deflect badly under it — so both cases must be checked, in both directions.**

examTip.trick: **μ = 0.8 up to 30°, falling linearly to zero at 60°.** A steep roof sheds snow — which is why traditional snowy-region roofs are steeply pitched.
examTip.trap: **UNBALANCED snow (one slope only) can govern over full uniform load** — a symmetrical truss or portal develops larger moments under half-span loading. Check it separately.
examTip.mnemonic: **Wind uplift and snow act in OPPOSITE directions** — a light roof designed against uplift in the hills may buckle under snow. Both cases, both directions.

questions.stem: In the SEISMIC COEFFICIENT method, the design base shear on a building is obtained as:
options: The building's total weight multiplied by the peak ground acceleration in g
The building's total weight divided by the response reduction factor
The imposed load on the building multiplied by the zone factor
V_B = A_h · W, where A_h is the design horizontal seismic coefficient and W the SEISMIC WEIGHT of the building
questions.solution:
**V_B = A_h · W**, where A_h is the design horizontal seismic coefficient and W the SEISMIC WEIGHT of the building.

**The two quantities:**

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **A_h — the design horizontal seismic coefficient** ← | **A fraction of g, obtained as Z I (S_a/g) / (2R) in the IS 1893 formulation** ← |
| **W — the SEISMIC WEIGHT** ← | **The full dead load PLUS a specified FRACTION of the imposed load** ← |

**The seismic weight, which is where errors are made:**

| Component | Included in W? |
|---|---|
| **Full DEAD load of the structure and all finishes** ← | **YES, entirely** ← |
| **IMPOSED load up to 3 kN/m²** ← | **25 per cent of it** ← |
| **Imposed load above 3 kN/m²** ← | **50 per cent of it** ← |
| **Imposed load on the ROOF** ← | **NONE — the roof's imposed load is not counted** ← |
| **Weight of permanent plant, tanks and their contents** | **Included as dead load** ← |

> **THE PARTIAL INCLUSION OF IMPOSED LOAD IN THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS IS THE FEATURE THAT DISTINGUISHES SEISMIC WEIGHT FROM GRAVITY LOAD, AND ITS LOGIC IS SPECIFIC: an earthquake force is an INERTIA force, proportional to the MASS that is actually present and actually attached to the structure.**

> **The full imposed load is a value a floor may reach occasionally; the mass usually present is much less, and the probability of a design earthquake coinciding with a fully loaded building is small.**

> **Furthermore, some imposed load is not attached to the structure at all — loose furniture and people slide and do not fully participate in the inertia.**

> **Hence a fraction, and hence a larger fraction (50 per cent) where the imposed load is heavy and therefore likely to be goods in storage, which are present continuously and do move with the building.**

> **THE ROOF EXCLUSION IN THE FOURTH ROW FOLLOWS THE SAME REASONING TAKEN TO ITS CONCLUSION: a roof's imposed load is a notional allowance for maintenance access, not a real mass that sits there, so none of it is counted.**

> **A designer who includes it has added a mass at the TOP of the building, where it contributes most to the base shear and most to the overturning moment — so the error is in the conservative direction but is disproportionately large.**

**Where the base shear then goes:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **V_B is the TOTAL horizontal force at the base** ← | ← |
| **It is DISTRIBUTED up the height in proportion to W_i h_i²** ← | **So the force is concentrated toward the TOP — reflecting the first mode's shape** ← |
| **Each storey's share is applied at that floor level** ← | ← |
| **The floors act as DIAPHRAGMS, distributing their force to the vertical elements** ← | **In proportion to stiffness, with a torsional component if the centres of mass and rigidity do not coincide** ← |
| **Each vertical element then carries its share down to the foundation** | ← |

> **THE h² IN THE SECOND ROW IS WORTH NOTING BECAUSE ITS EFFECT IS LARGE: the force at a level goes with the SQUARE of its height, so the top storey of a ten-storey building receives far more than a tenth of the base shear.**

> **The distribution is roughly triangular in effect — small forces low down, large forces high up — which is why the upper storeys of a building whip during an earthquake and why appendages at roof level, such as water tanks and parapets, are so vulnerable.**

> **A parapet or a tank at the top of a building experiences accelerations several times the ground acceleration, and its anchorage must be designed for that rather than for the base value.**

> **Failures of roof-level water tanks, parapets and mumty walls are among the commonest earthquake damage in Nepal and among the easiest to prevent, and they follow directly from this distribution.**

examTip.trick: **V_B = A_h · W**, with W the seismic weight: full dead load plus 25 % of imposed up to 3 kN/m², 50 % above it, and NONE on the roof.
examTip.trap: **Earthquake force is an INERTIA force, so only real attached MASS counts** — that is why imposed load enters only partly, and why the roof's notional imposed load is excluded entirely.
examTip.mnemonic: **Distribution goes with W_i h_i², so the force piles up at the TOP** — which is why roof tanks, parapets and mumty walls fail so often, and why their anchorage needs the amplified acceleration.

questions.stem: The RESPONSE REDUCTION FACTOR (R) in the seismic design of a building represents:
options: The reduction in the design load permitted because an earthquake is unlikely during the building's life
The structure's capacity to DISSIPATE energy through DUCTILE inelastic deformation and its overstrength
The reduction in the seismic weight because imposed loads are only partly included
The ratio of the design earthquake's return period to the building's design life
questions.solution:
**The structure's capacity to DISSIPATE energy through DUCTILE inelastic deformation, together with its overstrength** — allowing the design force to be a fraction of the elastic demand, on the understanding that the structure will be DAMAGED but will not collapse.

**What R actually does in the calculation, and what it means:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A_h = Z I (S_a/g) / (2R), so R DIVIDES the design force** ← | **A larger R means a smaller design force** ← |
| **The force calculated WITHOUT R is the ELASTIC demand** ← | **What the structure would have to resist if it were to remain undamaged** ← |
| **That elastic demand is enormous and uneconomic to resist** ← | **A building designed to remain elastic in a severe earthquake would be extraordinarily expensive** ← |
| **So the code permits design for a REDUCED force** ← | **Accepting that the structure will yield and be damaged** ← |
| **In exchange, the structure must be DETAILED for ductility** ← | **So that it can deform far beyond yield without losing its load-carrying capacity** ← |

> **THE BARGAIN IN THE LAST TWO ROWS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT IDEA IN EARTHQUAKE-RESISTANT DESIGN AND IT MUST BE UNDERSTOOD AS A BARGAIN: the code gives a reduced force and demands ductile detailing in return.**

> **The reduction is not a discount, it is a payment for a capability that has to be built into the structure.**

> **A designer who takes the reduced force and neglects the ductile detailing has taken the benefit without providing the capability — and the resulting structure has neither the strength to resist the earthquake elastically nor the ductility to survive it inelastically.**

> **That is the single most dangerous error in seismic design, and it is invisible in the calculations: the numbers add up perfectly, and the building collapses.**

**The values of R, which show what is being rewarded:**

| System | R (IS 1893) |
|---|---|
| **Ordinary RC moment resisting frame (OMRF)** ← | **3.0** ← |
| **SPECIAL RC moment resisting frame (SMRF), ductile detailed to IS 13920** ← | **5.0** ← |
| **RC shear walls, ductile** | **4.0 to 5.0** ← |
| **Steel moment frame with ductile detailing** | **5.0** ← |
| **UNREINFORCED masonry, load bearing** ← | **1.5 — the lowest, because it has almost NO ductility** ← |
| **Reinforced masonry** | **2.5 to 3.0** ← |

> **THE COMPARISON BETWEEN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST IN PRACTICE AND IT IS A LARGE INCENTIVE: ductile detailing to IS 13920 earns R = 5 instead of R = 3, which is a design force forty per cent lower.**

> **The extra cost of the detailing — closer stirrups in the plastic hinge zones, proper anchorage, confinement at joints, stronger columns than beams — is a few per cent of the structure's cost.**

> **The saving in the design force is far larger, so ductile detailing pays for itself directly, quite apart from being the thing that keeps the building standing.**

> **THE UNREINFORCED MASONRY ROW IS THE UNCOMFORTABLE ONE FOR NEPAL AND IT SHOULD BE READ PLAINLY: unreinforced masonry has an R of 1.5 because it is BRITTLE.**

> **It cracks and it fails; it does not yield and absorb energy.**

> **So it must be designed for a force more than three times that of a ductile frame — a requirement that most existing unreinforced masonry buildings in the country do not come close to satisfying.**

> **This is precisely why the NBC's mandatory rules of thumb for masonry construction concentrate on bands, corner reinforcement and vertical bars at openings: they are ways of introducing a measure of ductility and integrity into a material that has none, so that the wall cracks and holds rather than cracking and falling.**

> **The distinction between a masonry building that has seismic bands and one that does not is, in earthquake terms, the difference between damage and burial — and it costs a small fraction of the building.**

examTip.trick: **R divides the design force, paying for ductility and overstrength** — the structure is accepted as damaged but not collapsed. Without R the force is the full elastic demand.
examTip.trap: **Taking the reduced force WITHOUT the ductile detailing is the most dangerous error in seismic design** — neither strong enough to stay elastic nor ductile enough to survive. The numbers still add up.
examTip.mnemonic: **OMRF 3, SMRF 5, unreinforced masonry 1.5.** Ductile detailing cuts the design force 40 % for a few per cent of cost — and masonry's R of 1.5 is exactly why NBC bands exist.

questions.stem: For a building in seismic zone V (Z = 0.36) of ordinary importance (I = 1.0), with a spectral acceleration ratio S_a/g of 2.5 and a response reduction factor R of 5.0, the design horizontal seismic coefficient A_h is:
questions.solution:
**0.090.**

**The formula and the substitution:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **A_h = Z · I · (S_a/g) / (2 R)** ← | **The IS 1893 expression** ← |
| **Numerator** | **0.36 × 1.0 × 2.5 = 0.90** ← |
| **Denominator** | **2 × 5.0 = 10** ← |
| **A_h** | **= 0.90 / 10 = 0.090** ← |

> **So A_h = 0.09, meaning the design base shear is 9 per cent of the seismic weight.**

**The four quantities, and what each represents:**

| Symbol | Meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Z — ZONE factor** ← | **The expected peak ground acceleration for the region, as a fraction of g** ← | **0.10, 0.16, 0.24 and 0.36 for zones II to V** ← |
| **I — IMPORTANCE factor** ← | **1.0 ordinarily; 1.5 for hospitals, schools, fire stations, monuments and other critical buildings** ← | **A deliberate increase in safety for buildings that must survive** ← |
| **S_a/g — SPECTRAL acceleration ratio** ← | **From the response spectrum, depending on the fundamental PERIOD and the SOIL type** ← | **Maximum 2.5 for medium soil in the plateau of the spectrum** ← |
| **R — response reduction factor** ← | **The ductility and overstrength credit** ← | **3 to 5 for the usual systems** ← |

> **THE FACTOR OF 2 IN THE DENOMINATOR IS THE PART OF THE FORMULA THAT LOOKS MYSTERIOUS AND IT HAS A SPECIFIC MEANING WORTH KNOWING: Z is defined as the zone factor for the MAXIMUM CONSIDERED EARTHQUAKE, and the 2 halves it to the DESIGN BASIS EARTHQUAKE.**

> **The design basis earthquake is taken as half the maximum considered earthquake, on the reasoning that a structure designed for the smaller event and detailed for ductility will survive the larger one with damage but without collapse.**

> **So the 2 is not a factor of safety and not an arbitrary constant — it is the ratio between two defined levels of earthquake, and the whole two-level design philosophy is embedded in it.**

> **A candidate who remembers the formula as Z I S_a / (2Rg) without knowing what the 2 is will get the arithmetic right, and will also miss the fact that the code has quietly stated its entire performance objective in that one digit.**

**THE S_a/g TERM IS THE ONE THAT REQUIRES ACTUAL WORK IN A REAL DESIGN, AND IT IS WORTH SEEING WHY:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The fundamental PERIOD T must be estimated first** ← | **From an empirical formula such as T = 0.075 h^0.75 for a bare RC frame, or from an analysis** ← |
| **S_a/g is then read from the response spectrum for the SOIL type at that period** ← | **Hard rock, medium soil and soft soil have distinctly different spectra** ← |
| **The value 2.5 is the PLATEAU — the maximum, for short-period structures** ← | **Which is why 2.5 is so often used in examples: most low-rise buildings sit on the plateau** ← |
| **For longer periods S_a/g falls off** ← | **So a tall, flexible building attracts a lower coefficient — though its displacements are larger** ← |
| **SOFT soil raises the spectrum and extends the plateau** ← | **Which is why soil type matters so much, and why Kathmandu's basin sediments are a serious concern** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE LOCAL POINT AND IT DESERVES EMPHASIS: the Kathmandu valley is a thick basin of soft lacustrine sediment, which AMPLIFIES ground motion and lengthens its period.**

> **A building on such a deposit experiences stronger and longer-period shaking than the same building on rock a few kilometres away, and the response spectrum for soft soil accordingly gives a higher S_a/g over a wider band of periods.**

> **So taking the rock spectrum, or ignoring the soil classification, systematically under-estimates the demand in exactly the place where most of the country's building stock stands — which is why the soil type is not a detail to be assumed but a determination to be made.**

examTip.trick: **A_h = Z·I·(S_a/g)/(2R) = 0.36 × 1.0 × 2.5 / 10 = 0.090** — a base shear of 9 % of the seismic weight.
examTip.trap: **The 2 in the denominator halves the MAXIMUM CONSIDERED earthquake to the DESIGN BASIS earthquake** — the code's whole two-level performance objective sits in that one digit.
examTip.mnemonic: **Z: 0.10/0.16/0.24/0.36 for zones II-V. I = 1.5 for hospitals and schools. S_a/g plateau = 2.5.** And SOFT SOIL amplifies — which is the Kathmandu basin problem.

questions.stem: Using the empirical relation T_a = 0.075 h^0.75 for a bare reinforced concrete moment-resisting frame, the fundamental natural period of a building 20 m high is about:
questions.solution:
**About 0.71 second.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **h^0.75 with h = 20** | **20^0.75** ← |
| **Evaluating** | **= 9.46** ← |
| **T_a = 0.075 × 9.46** | **= 0.709 s, about 0.71 s** ← |

> **So the fundamental period is approximately 0.71 second.**

**The empirical period formulae, which differ by system:**

| Structure | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Bare RC moment resisting frame, no infill** ← | **T_a = 0.075 h^0.75** ← |
| **Bare STEEL moment resisting frame** ← | **T_a = 0.085 h^0.75 — longer, steel being more flexible** ← |
| **RC or steel frame WITH brick INFILL panels** ← | **T_a = 0.09 h / √d, where d is the base dimension in the direction considered** ← |
| **RC frame with shear walls** ← | **Shorter still, the walls being very stiff** ← |

> **THE INFILL FORMULA IN THE THIRD ROW GIVES A MUCH SHORTER PERIOD THAN THE BARE FRAME FORMULA, AND THAT DIFFERENCE IS NOT A TECHNICALITY: brick infill STIFFENS a frame very substantially.**

> **A designer who computes the period from the bare-frame formula for a building that will in fact be fully infilled with brickwork has over-estimated the period.**

> **And since S_a/g generally FALLS as the period lengthens, over-estimating the period UNDER-estimates the seismic coefficient — an error in the unsafe direction.**

> **So the infill must be accounted for even though it is treated as non-structural, which is one of several respects in which infill walls refuse to be ignored.**

**WHY THE PERIOD MATTERS AT ALL, WHICH IS THE POINT OF COMPUTING IT:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **S_a/g is read from the response spectrum AT the fundamental period** ← | **So the period determines the design acceleration directly** ← |
| **A SHORT-period (stiff) building sits on the spectrum's PLATEAU** ← | **Attracting the maximum coefficient of 2.5 — stiff buildings take large forces** ← |
| **A LONG-period (flexible) building attracts a lower coefficient** ← | **But suffers much larger DISPLACEMENTS, and the drift limit then governs** ← |
| **RESONANCE with the ground's own predominant period is to be avoided** ← | **A building whose period matches the site's amplifies the motion severely** ← |

> **THE RESONANCE POINT IN THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE AND IT HAS A DEVASTATING PRECEDENT: the Mexico City earthquake of 1985 destroyed buildings of a particular height range while leaving shorter and taller ones nearby largely intact.**

> **The city's soft lake-bed clay had a natural period near 2 seconds, and buildings of roughly 6 to 15 storeys shared that period.**

> **Those buildings resonated with the ground and were shaken to destruction; stiffer low-rise and more flexible high-rise buildings did not.**

> **The lesson is that seismic vulnerability is not simply a matter of height or of strength but of the MATCH between the structure's period and the site's — which is why soft-soil sites require the soil's own characteristics to be considered and not merely a spectrum read off a table.**

> **It is a lesson with direct application to the Kathmandu valley, whose deep soft sediments have a long predominant period, and it argues for real site response study rather than a nominal soil classification when a significant building is designed there.**

examTip.trick: **T_a = 0.075 × 20^0.75 = 0.075 × 9.46 = 0.71 s.** Steel bare frame uses 0.085; infilled frames use 0.09h/√d.
examTip.trap: **Infill STIFFENS the frame, shortening the period** — using the bare-frame formula on a building that will be infilled over-estimates T, which UNDER-estimates S_a/g. Unsafe direction.
examTip.mnemonic: **Stiff buildings sit on the 2.5 plateau and take big forces; flexible ones take less force but drift more.** And avoid resonance with the site — the lesson of Mexico City 1985.

questions.stem: In limit state design to IS 456, the load combination used for the ULTIMATE limit state under dead load (DL) and imposed load (LL) alone is:
questions.solution:
**1.5 DL + 1.5 LL.**

**The load combinations for the ultimate limit state:**

| Combination | Partial factors |
|---|---|
| **DL and LL only** ← | **1.5 DL + 1.5 LL** ← |
| **DL, LL and WIND or EARTHQUAKE together** ← | **1.2 (DL + LL + WL or EL)** ← |
| **DL with WIND or EARTHQUAKE, no imposed load** ← | **1.5 (DL ± WL or EL)** ← |
| **DL opposing WIND or EARTHQUAKE — the OVERTURNING case** ← | **0.9 DL ± 1.5 WL or EL** ← |

**And for the SERVICEABILITY limit state, where deflection and cracking are checked:**

| Combination | Partial factors |
|---|---|
| **DL and LL** ← | **1.0 DL + 1.0 LL** ← (which is option a) |
| **DL, LL and WL or EL** | **1.0 DL + 0.8 LL + 0.8 WL** ← |
| **DL with WL or EL** | **1.0 DL + 1.0 WL** ← |

> **THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE TWO TABLES IS THE ESSENCE OF LIMIT STATE DESIGN AND IT IS WORTH STATING EXPLICITLY: the ULTIMATE limit state asks whether the structure will COLLAPSE, and applies factors above unity to guard against under-estimated loads and understrength materials.**

> **The SERVICEABILITY limit state asks whether the structure will be UNSATISFACTORY IN USE — deflecting visibly, cracking, vibrating — and applies the loads at their actual expected values, because the question is what the structure will really do in service rather than what it might just survive.**

> **So option (a) is not wrong in itself; it is the serviceability combination, applied to the wrong limit state.**

**THE 1.2 IN THE SECOND ROW OF THE FIRST TABLE IS THE FACTOR MOST OFTEN QUERIED AND ITS LOGIC IS PROBABILISTIC:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **When THREE loads act together, each is factored LESS than when it acts alone** ← | **1.2 rather than 1.5** ← |
| **Because the probability that dead load, full imposed load AND the design wind or earthquake all reach their extreme values SIMULTANEOUSLY is very small** ← | **Each factor guards against one load being under-estimated; all three being under-estimated at once is far less likely** ← |
| **This is the same simultaneity reasoning as the live load reduction and the partial seismic weight** ← | **A recurring principle rather than three separate rules** ← |

> **THE 0.9 DL IN THE FOURTH ROW OF THE FIRST TABLE IS THE COMBINATION MOST OFTEN OMITTED AND IT IS THE ONE THAT GOVERNS OVERTURNING AND UPLIFT, so it deserves a separate word.**

> **Where the dead load RESISTS the effect being checked — holding down a light roof against wind uplift, stabilising a retaining wall or a tall slender frame against overturning, keeping a footing in compression — the dead load is a FAVOURABLE load.**

> **A favourable load must be factored DOWN, not up, because the danger is that there is LESS of it than assumed rather than more.**

> **Hence 0.9: the dead load is reduced by 10 per cent while the wind or earthquake is increased by 50 per cent, giving the worst credible combination for stability.**

> **Using 1.5 DL in that case would make the structure appear far more stable than it is, and it is exactly the sort of error that produces a footing in tension or a roof that departs — the calculation showing an ample margin throughout.**

> **The general principle is worth carrying beyond this table: a partial safety factor is applied in the direction that makes the situation WORSE, and whether that is above or below unity depends on whether the load helps or hinders.**

examTip.trick: **1.5(DL + LL) for ultimate; 1.2(DL + LL + WL/EL) with three loads; 1.5(DL ± WL/EL) with two.** Option (a) is the SERVICEABILITY combination.
examTip.trap: **0.9 DL ± 1.5 WL/EL is the OVERTURNING and UPLIFT case** — where dead load HELPS, it must be factored DOWN, because the danger is having less of it than assumed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Three loads together get 1.2 each, because all three reaching their extremes at once is improbable** — the same simultaneity logic as live load reduction and partial seismic weight.

questions.stem: A structure is being checked for STABILITY AGAINST OVERTURNING under wind load. In this check, the DEAD LOAD of the structure should be:
options: Multiplied by 1.5, as in every other ultimate limit state combination
Factored DOWN, typically to 0.9 of its characteristic value
Ignored entirely, since only the overturning forces matter
Multiplied by 1.2, as when three loads act together
questions.solution:
**Factored DOWN, typically to 0.9 of its characteristic value** — because it is a FAVOURABLE (stabilising) load, and the danger lies in there being LESS of it than assumed.

**The principle, stated generally:**

| Situation | Direction of the factor |
|---|---|
| **A load whose increase makes the situation WORSE** ← | **Factored UP — 1.5, or 1.2 in combination** ← |
| **A load whose DECREASE makes the situation worse** ← | **Factored DOWN — 0.9, or in some codes 1.0** ← |
| **The test to apply** ← | **Ask what would be dangerous: too much of this load, or too little?** ← |

> **THE TEST IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE WHOLE OF IT AND IT REMOVES THE NEED TO MEMORISE ANY OF THIS: a partial safety factor exists to guard against the load being different from the assumed value in the DANGEROUS direction.**

> **For a beam's bending, more load is dangerous, so the factor is above unity.**

> **For a wall's stability against overturning, LESS self-weight is dangerous, so the factor is below unity.**

> **The same load, in the same structure, is therefore factored differently in different checks — which surprises people but follows directly from what a partial factor is for.**

**Where the favourable-load reduction governs, in practice:**

| Case | Note |
|---|---|
| **A LIGHT ROOF against wind UPLIFT** ← | **The roof's own weight resists the suction; if it is lighter than assumed, the roof lifts** ← |
| **A RETAINING WALL against overturning about its toe** ← | **The wall's weight and the earth on its heel are stabilising** ← |
| **A TALL SLENDER building or tower against overturning** ← | ← |
| **A footing checked for NO TENSION at its base** ← | **The column load holds it down; less load means tension develops sooner** ← |
| **A GRAVITY DAM's stability, where the concrete's weight resists water thrust** ← | **The same reasoning appears there as the no-tension criterion** ← |
| **A buried tank or basement against FLOTATION when the water table rises** ← | **An empty tank with a high water table can float, and its own weight is what prevents it** ← |

> **THE FLOTATION CASE IN THE LAST ROW IS WORTH SINGLING OUT BECAUSE IT IS SO OFTEN DISCOVERED THE HARD WAY: an empty underground tank or a basement is a boat.**

> **Its resistance to floating is its own dead weight plus whatever soil sits on it, and the uplift is the full buoyant force of the displaced groundwater.**

> **Basements and empty tanks have genuinely floated and lifted out of the ground during construction — usually when dewatering is stopped before the structure has been backfilled and loaded.**

> **The check is a straightforward one and the sequence of construction is part of it: the structure must be safe against flotation at every stage, not merely when complete, and the temporary condition immediately after the dewatering stops is usually the critical one.**

> **THE DEEPER POINT, WHICH IS WORTH CARRYING BEYOND THIS PARTICULAR CLAUSE, IS THAT STABILITY CHECKS ARE STRUCTURALLY DIFFERENT FROM STRENGTH CHECKS:**

> **A strength check compares an internal action with a member's capacity, and more load is always worse.**

> **A stability check compares two OPPOSING actions — an overturning moment against a restoring moment, an uplift against a weight — and the answer depends on both.**

> **So a stability check requires each load to be examined for which side it is on, and factored accordingly.**

> **A designer who applies 1.5 to everything in a stability check has increased both the overturning and the restoring effect, and the factor largely cancels — producing an answer that appears safe and carries no margin whatever.**

It is a FAVOURABLE (stabilising) load and the danger lies in there being LESS of it than assumed.

examTip.trick: **Ask what would be dangerous: too much of this load, or too little?** Dead load stabilises here, so it is factored DOWN to 0.9.
examTip.trap: **Applying 1.5 to everything in a stability check cancels out** — both the overturning and the restoring moment grow, so the answer looks safe with no real margin.
examTip.mnemonic: **An empty basement or tank is a BOAT** — check flotation at every construction stage, especially the moment dewatering stops before backfill.

questions.stem: TORSIONAL response of a building during an earthquake arises when:
options: The building is symmetrical in both plan directions
The building's fundamental period is very short
The floor slabs are too thin to act as rigid diaphragms
The CENTRE OF MASS and the CENTRE OF RIGIDITY of a storey do NOT COINCIDE
questions.solution:
**The CENTRE OF MASS and the CENTRE OF RIGIDITY of a storey do NOT COINCIDE** — so the inertia force, acting through the centre of mass, exerts a moment about the centre of rigidity.

**The mechanism:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **The CENTRE OF MASS is where the storey's inertia force effectively acts** ← | **Determined by the distribution of weight** ← |
| **The CENTRE OF RIGIDITY is the point about which the storey twists** ← | **Determined by the distribution of STIFFNESS — the columns and walls** ← |
| **If they coincide, the storey translates without twisting** ← | **Every vertical element takes load in proportion to its stiffness** ← |
| **If they are offset by a distance e, a TORSIONAL MOMENT of (force × e) acts** ← | **Twisting the storey in plan** ← |
| **The twist ADDS displacement at the elements FARTHEST from the centre of rigidity** ← | **Which are usually the corner columns** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHY TORSION IS SO DAMAGING AND IT IS WORTH SEEING THE GEOMETRY: the extra displacement from twisting is proportional to the distance from the centre of rigidity.**

> **So the corner columns of a torsionally irregular building move much more than the average, and being displaced more they are strained more.**

> **They fail first, and once a corner column fails the stiffness distribution changes, the centre of rigidity shifts further, and the twist increases — a progressive mechanism.**

> **Corner column failures are a recognisable signature of torsional response in earthquake damage surveys.**

**How the offset comes about in real buildings:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **A shear wall or a stair core placed at ONE END or in ONE CORNER** ← | **The commonest cause — the core is enormously stiffer than the frame, so the centre of rigidity moves to it while the mass stays central** ← |
| **An L, T, U or cruciform PLAN** ← | **Re-entrant corners give an inherently eccentric geometry** ← |
| **Infill walls on two sides only** ← | **A building open on the street frontage and walled at the back and sides — extremely common in commercial buildings** ← |
| **Heavy elements concentrated on one side** ← | **A water tank, a library, a strongroom, a plant room** ← |
| **Setbacks and irregular column layouts** | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT AND THE MOST FIXABLE, AND THE REMEDY IS PURELY A MATTER OF LAYOUT: shear walls and cores should be placed SYMMETRICALLY, and as far as possible toward the PERIMETER.**

> **Two walls on opposite sides are vastly better than one wall at one end, and cost no more.**

> **Placing them at the perimeter also maximises their lever arm, so they resist torsion effectively as well as not causing it — a wall near the centre of the plan resists translation but does little against twist.**

> **This is one of the very few seismic improvements that is free: it is a decision about WHERE to put the same quantity of material.**

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE VERSION OF THE PROBLEM THAT DOMINATES NEPALI COMMERCIAL BUILDINGS AND IT IS USUALLY UNINTENTIONAL: a shop or showroom is left open at the front for display and access, while the other three sides are filled with brick.**

> **The designer treats the infill as non-structural and ignores it, but the walls are stiff and they are on three sides only — so the real centre of rigidity is well behind the geometric centre, while the mass is central.**

> **The building is therefore torsionally irregular in fact although the analysis showed it as symmetrical, and it will twist about a point the calculation never identified.**

> **This is the second respect in which infill refuses to be ignored, alongside its effect on the period — and both errors arise from the same habit of treating a stiff, heavy, structurally significant material as though it were not there.**

> **The code's response is to require a DESIGN ECCENTRICITY that is larger than the calculated one — commonly 1.5 times the static eccentricity plus an allowance of 5 per cent of the plan dimension — precisely because the real eccentricity is never quite what the drawing implies.**

examTip.trick: **Mass acts at the centre of MASS, twist occurs about the centre of RIGIDITY** — offset them and the inertia force exerts a torsional moment.
examTip.trap: **Infill on three sides only makes a 'symmetrical' building torsionally irregular** — the walls are stiff and off-centre, so the real centre of rigidity is not where the analysis put it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Corner columns fail first**, moving most from the twist. And the fix is free: place walls and cores SYMMETRICALLY and near the PERIMETER — same material, different location.

questions.stem: An OPEN GROUND STOREY (soft storey) in a reinforced concrete building — a ground floor left free of infill walls for parking or shops while the upper storeys are fully infilled — is hazardous in an earthquake because:
options: The SUDDEN drop in stiffness and strength at that level concentrates the whole building's drift and inelastic demand into the ground storey columns
The ground storey carries the least vertical load and is therefore the weakest
The absence of walls increases the building's total seismic weight
The columns at ground level are shorter than those above
questions.solution:
**The SUDDEN drop in stiffness and strength at that level concentrates the whole building's drift and inelastic demand into the ground storey columns**, which then fail while the stiff upper storeys move almost as a rigid block.

**The mechanism, step by step:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The upper storeys are infilled with brickwork, which is very STIFF in its own plane** ← | **The infilled frame is many times stiffer than the bare frame** ← |
| **The ground storey has no infill, so it is a BARE frame — far more flexible** ← | ← |
| **Under lateral load, the flexible storey deforms while the stiff ones barely do** ← | **Deformation goes where the stiffness is not** ← |
| **Essentially the WHOLE building's lateral displacement occurs in that one storey** ← | **The upper part translating almost as a rigid body on top of it** ← |
| **The ground storey columns must absorb ALL the inelastic rotation** ← | **Demanding a ductility they cannot supply** ← |
| **They form hinges at both ends and collapse, and the building comes down bodily** ← | **The upper storeys often arriving intact on the ground** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER EXPLAIN THE DISTINCTIVE APPEARANCE OF THIS FAILURE AND IT IS UNMISTAKABLE IN DAMAGE PHOTOGRAPHS: the upper floors are found sitting on the ground, largely undamaged, with the ground storey crushed to nothing beneath them.**

> **The upper structure was never seriously strained, because it never deformed — all the deformation was taken by the storey that could not sustain it.**

> **It is among the most lethal of all structural failures, since the whole building descends by a full storey height and the ground floor's occupants have no chance at all.**

> **It was a prominent cause of collapse and death in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, and it remains extremely common in newly built commercial and residential buildings throughout the country.**

**Why it is built so persistently, which has to be understood before it can be addressed:**

| Driver | Note |
|---|---|
| **PARKING must go somewhere, and the ground floor is the obvious place** ← | ← |
| **SHOPS and showrooms want open frontage** ← | **Walls are commercially undesirable at street level** ← |
| **The upper floors want partitioned rooms, so they are infilled** ← | **The irregularity therefore arises from the building's USE, not from carelessness** ← |
| **And the infill is treated as non-structural, so the analysis does not show the problem** ← | **A bare-frame model of the building is perfectly regular and gives no warning** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE CRUX AND IT IS WHY THE PROBLEM PERSISTS DESPITE BEING WELL KNOWN: if the infill is omitted from the model, the building analysed is a uniform bare frame, and a uniform bare frame has no soft storey.**

> **The analysis is then not merely inaccurate but actively misleading — it certifies as regular a building that is severely irregular in reality.**

> **The irregularity is created by the walls, and a model without walls cannot see it.**

**The remedies, in order of effectiveness:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **Provide SHEAR WALLS continuous from foundation to roof** ← | **The proper solution — the walls carry the lateral load at every level, so the infill's presence or absence ceases to matter** ← |
| **Design the ground storey columns for AMPLIFIED forces** ← | **IS 1893 requires the ground storey's members to be designed for 2.5 times the forces from a bare frame analysis — a code recognition that the storey will take the whole demand** ← |
| **Stiffen the ground storey with braced bays or stub walls** ← | **Placed symmetrically, or torsion is introduced instead** ← |
| **Model the infill explicitly as diagonal STRUTS and design accordingly** ← | **The analytically honest approach** ← |
| **Avoid the configuration altogether** ← | **Put the parking outside or below ground** ← |

> **The 2.5 factor in the second row is worth remembering precisely because it is so large: the code is not applying a small correction, it is saying that the ground storey of such a building carries two and a half times what a regular analysis suggests.**

> **A factor of that magnitude is a warning about the configuration rather than a routine adjustment — and where a designer finds it uneconomic to satisfy, that is the code indicating that the configuration should be changed rather than the columns enlarged.**

examTip.trick: **Deformation goes where the stiffness is not** — the whole building's drift concentrates in the one bare storey, whose columns cannot supply that ductility.
examTip.trap: **A bare-frame model shows no soft storey at all** — the irregularity is created by the infill, so a model without walls cannot see it and certifies the building as regular.
examTip.mnemonic: **IS 1893 demands 2.5 times the bare-frame forces in the ground storey** — a factor that large is a warning about the configuration, not a routine adjustment. Continuous shear walls are the real fix.

questions.stem: The STRONG COLUMN — WEAK BEAM principle in the seismic design of a moment resisting frame requires that:
options: Columns be made of higher grade concrete than beams
Beams be designed to remain elastic while the columns yield
At every beam-column joint, the sum of the columns' moment capacities EXCEED that of the beams
Columns be larger in cross-section than beams in every case
questions.solution:
**At every beam-column joint, the sum of the COLUMNS' moment capacities must EXCEED that of the beams** — so that plastic hinges form in the BEAMS rather than in the columns.

**Why the location of the hinges is decisive:**

| Hinges in the BEAMS | Hinges in the COLUMNS |
|---|---|
| **A beam hinge is a LOCAL failure** ← | **A column hinge threatens the whole structure** ← |
| **The floor above is still supported** ← | **The columns carry the gravity load — a hinged column can no longer carry it reliably** ← |
| **Many hinges must form before a mechanism develops** ← | **Hinges at the top and bottom of every column in one storey is a complete MECHANISM — that storey collapses** ← |
| **Energy is dissipated at many locations** ← | **Energy is concentrated at a few, so the demand at each is extreme** ← |
| **Repairable after the event** ← | **Usually not** ← |
| **The building may be damaged but stands** ← | **The building comes down** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CONTAINS THE STRUCTURAL ARGUMENT AND IT IS WORTH SEEING IN TERMS OF MECHANISMS: a frame collapses when enough hinges form to make a mechanism.**

> **If hinges form in the beams, a great many are needed — one at each end of every beam over several floors — before the frame can move as a mechanism, and each hinge absorbs energy on the way.**

> **If hinges form at the top and bottom of the columns of a single storey, that storey alone becomes a mechanism immediately, and the building above it descends.**

> **So the beam-hinge mechanism distributes the damage over the whole frame and requires an enormous amount of energy to complete, while the column-hinge mechanism is local, sudden and fatal.**

> **Designing for the first rather than the second is what CAPACITY DESIGN means, and this principle is its clearest application.**

**How it is achieved in practice:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **The code requires ΣM_column ≥ 1.4 ΣM_beam at each joint** ← | **IS 13920's requirement — the columns must be 40 per cent stronger in flexure than the beams framing into the joint** ← |
| **Columns are therefore made LARGER and more heavily reinforced than the beams demand for gravity load alone** ← | ← |
| **Beams are deliberately NOT over-reinforced** ← | **Adding steel to a beam 'for safety' RAISES its capacity and can defeat the hierarchy — one of the few cases where extra reinforcement is harmful** ← |
| **The SLAB reinforcement adjacent to the beam counts toward the beam's capacity** ← | **A commonly overlooked contribution that makes the beam stronger than intended** ← |
| **Joints are designed and detailed to remain intact** ← | **A joint failure defeats the whole hierarchy, since neither member can then develop its capacity** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS GENUINELY COUNTER-INTUITIVE AND IT DESERVES EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT INVERTS AN ORDINARY HABIT: in capacity design, making a member STRONGER can make the structure WORSE.**

> **A beam given generous extra reinforcement is stronger, so it does not hinge; the demand then goes to the column, which hinges instead; and the intended hierarchy is reversed.**

> **So the beam's capacity is a designed quantity to be achieved rather than a minimum to be exceeded, and adding steel without rechecking the joint hierarchy is a real error.**

> **The same reasoning applies to the slab steel in the fourth row: reinforcement in the slab within a certain width of the beam acts with the beam in negative bending and increases its true capacity above the value computed from the beam section alone.**

> **The overall lesson is that seismic design is concerned with the ORDER in which things fail as much as with whether they fail — and an element's strength has to be considered relative to its neighbours rather than in isolation.**

> **That is a different habit of mind from gravity design, where every member is simply made adequate for its own actions, and it is the habit that capacity design exists to instil.**

examTip.trick: **ΣM_column ≥ 1.4 ΣM_beam at every joint** — hinges in beams are local and repairable; hinges top and bottom of one storey's columns is an immediate collapse mechanism.
examTip.trap: **Adding steel to a beam 'for safety' can DEFEAT the hierarchy** — a stronger beam does not hinge, so the column does instead. Slab steel near the beam counts toward its capacity too.
examTip.mnemonic: **Capacity design cares about the ORDER of failure, not just whether things fail** — strength must be judged relative to neighbours, which is the opposite habit from gravity design.

questions.stem: The CHARACTERISTIC value of a load, as used in limit state design, is defined as the value:
options: Obtained by averaging all recorded values of that load
Which has a 95 PER CENT probability of NOT BEING EXCEEDED during the life of the structure
Equal to the maximum value ever measured for that type of load
Obtained by multiplying the working load by the partial safety factor
questions.solution:
**The value which has a 95 per cent probability of NOT being exceeded during the life of the structure** — that is, only a 5 per cent chance of being exceeded.

**The definitions, which must be kept apart:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **CHARACTERISTIC LOAD** ← | **The value with only a 5 per cent chance of being exceeded in the structure's life — this question** ← |
| **CHARACTERISTIC STRENGTH of a material** ← | **The value BELOW which not more than 5 per cent of test results are expected to fall** ← |
| **DESIGN LOAD** ← | **Characteristic load × partial safety factor for load (γ_f) — larger** ← (option d describes this) |
| **DESIGN STRENGTH** ← | **Characteristic strength ÷ partial safety factor for material (γ_m) — smaller** ← |

> **THE SYMMETRY BETWEEN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS ELEGANT AND WORTH NOTICING, BECAUSE IT MAKES BOTH DEFINITIONS ONE IDEA: in each case the characteristic value is the 5 per cent point of a distribution, taken on the UNFAVOURABLE side.**

> **For a LOAD, the unfavourable side is high, so the characteristic value is high in the distribution — the 95th percentile.**

> **For a STRENGTH, the unfavourable side is low, so the characteristic value is low — the 5th percentile.**

> **The same probability level, applied to the tail that matters in each case, which is why the definitions look opposite while expressing an identical principle.**

**For strength, the definition gives the well-known relation:**

| Relation | Note |
|---|---|
| **f_ck = f_m − 1.65 σ** ← | **Characteristic strength = mean strength minus 1.65 standard deviations** ← |
| **Where 1.65 is the standard normal value for the 5 per cent lower tail** ← | ← |
| **So the TARGET MEAN strength for a mix design is f_ck + 1.65 σ** ← | **The mix must be designed for MORE than the characteristic strength** ← |
| **And σ depends on the QUALITY CONTROL achieved** ← | **Good control gives a small σ, so a smaller margin suffices** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS TOGETHER CONTAIN A COMMERCIALLY IMPORTANT CONSEQUENCE THAT IS EASY TO MISS: better quality control makes concrete CHEAPER.**

> **A plant with poor control has a large standard deviation, so it must aim at a much higher mean strength to be confident of achieving the characteristic strength — which means more cement in every cubic metre, for ever.**

> **A plant with tight control aims closer to the characteristic value and uses less cement to reach the same specified grade.**

> **So the investment in weighing equipment, moisture correction, trained operators and regular testing is repaid directly in reduced cement consumption, quite apart from the improvement in reliability.**

> **This is the strongest practical argument for quality control and it is an economic one, which makes it more persuasive on a site than an appeal to good practice.**

**Why the 5 per cent level rather than some other, which is the closing point:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A load or strength has no absolute maximum or minimum** ← | **Distributions have tails, so any 'guaranteed' value is unattainable** ← (which is why option c is not a workable definition) |
| **The MEAN would be exceeded half the time** ← | **Useless as a design value** ← (option a) |
| **So a defined PROBABILITY level must be chosen** ← | **And 5 per cent is the convention, being small enough to be safe and large enough to be economic** ← |
| **The remaining risk is then covered by the PARTIAL SAFETY FACTORS** ← | **Which is what they are for — the characteristic value is not itself the design value** ← |

> **The last row is the point that ties the system together: the characteristic value is deliberately NOT a safe value, it is a defined statistical value.**

> **Safety is introduced afterwards and separately, through partial factors chosen for the load type and the material — which is precisely the improvement that limit state design made over working stress design, where a single factor of safety had to cover every uncertainty at once and could not be adjusted to reflect which uncertainty was large.**

examTip.trick: **5 per cent chance of being exceeded** for a load; 5 per cent of results falling below it for a strength. Same probability level, applied to the unfavourable tail in each case.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) is the DESIGN load** — characteristic × γ_f. The characteristic value is a statistical value, deliberately not a safe one; safety comes from the partial factors afterwards.
examTip.mnemonic: **f_ck = mean − 1.65σ, so target mean = f_ck + 1.65σ** — and better quality control shrinks σ, which means LESS CEMENT for the same grade. Quality control pays for itself.

questions.stem: In the design of a building, WIND LOAD and EARTHQUAKE LOAD are:
options: Always added together, since both are lateral loads
Combined at half their respective values in every lateral load case
Taken as one load whose value is the greater of the two, multiplied by 1.5
NOT considered to act SIMULTANEOUSLY
questions.solution:
**NOT considered to act SIMULTANEOUSLY** — each is combined separately with the gravity loads, and the design is governed by whichever combination proves more severe.

**The reasoning:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Both are extreme, RARE events** ← | **A design wind and a design earthquake each have a long return period** ← |
| **They are also INDEPENDENT of one another** ← | **There is no physical mechanism by which an earthquake causes a storm or vice versa** ← |
| **So the probability of both reaching their design values at the same moment is the PRODUCT of two small probabilities** ← | **Which is negligible** ← |
| **Designing for their sum would therefore be designing for an event that will not occur** ← | ← |
| **Each is instead paired with the gravity loads and the worse case governs** ← | **Which is the code's requirement** ← |

> **THE INDEPENDENCE IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE ESSENTIAL CONDITION AND IT IS WORTH STATING EXPLICITLY, because the rule does not extend to loads that are physically linked.**

> **Wind and earthquake are unrelated phenomena, so their coincidence is a matter of pure chance and the product rule applies.**

> **Where two loads ARE linked — a flood and the scour it causes, an earthquake and the liquefaction or landslide it triggers, a cyclone's wind and its accompanying rain — they MUST be considered together, because one causes the other and their coincidence is certain rather than improbable.**

> **So the question to ask of any two loads is not merely whether both are rare, but whether they are INDEPENDENT — and a great many serious failures have followed from combining loads probabilistically that were in fact causally connected.**

**Which of the two governs, in practice:**

| Building type | Usually governed by |
|---|---|
| **LOW-RISE, heavy construction — masonry, RC** ← | **EARTHQUAKE, because seismic force is proportional to MASS and a heavy building attracts a large force while presenting little sail area** ← |
| **TALL, SLENDER buildings** ← | **Often WIND, because wind pressure acts on a large exposed area with a long lever arm** ← |
| **LIGHT structures — steel sheds, roofs, hoardings, towers** ← | **WIND, and usually wind UPLIFT, since there is little mass to attract seismic force** ← |
| **Heavy structures in high seismic zones** ← | **EARTHQUAKE, decisively** ← |

> **THE CONTRAST BETWEEN THE FIRST AND THIRD ROWS IS THE MOST USEFUL THING IN THIS ANSWER AND IT FOLLOWS FROM WHAT EACH LOAD IS PROPORTIONAL TO: seismic force goes with MASS, wind force with AREA.**

> **So making a building heavier increases its earthquake demand and does nothing for its wind demand, while making it larger in exposed area increases its wind demand and not its seismic demand.**

> **A light steel shed has almost no seismic force but a large sail area, and it is designed against wind uplift.**

> **A squat masonry building has an enormous seismic force and hardly notices the wind.**

> **This is one of the strongest arguments for LIGHT construction in a seismic region — reducing mass reduces the demand at source, which is a more fundamental improvement than strengthening to resist it.**

> **It is why light roofs, hollow blocks and lightweight partitions are seismically beneficial, and why a heavy stone-and-mud building in a high seismic zone is inherently disadvantaged before any question of its strength arises.**

> **In Nepal both loads must nevertheless be checked, because the country is in a high seismic zone AND experiences strong winds — and the light structures that are seismically favourable are precisely the ones for which wind then governs.**

> **A designer who checks only the earthquake case on a light steel-roofed building in the hills, on the reasoning that Nepal is a seismic country, has omitted the case that actually governs.**

examTip.trick: **Never together** — each is paired with gravity loads separately and the worse governs. Two independent rare events coinciding has a negligible probability.
examTip.trap: **The rule needs INDEPENDENCE** — an earthquake and the landslide it triggers, or a flood and its scour, MUST be combined, because one causes the other.
