examTip.mnemonic: **Seismic force goes with MASS, wind force with AREA.** Heavy squat buildings: earthquake. Light sheds and roofs: wind uplift. Which is why light construction is seismically good — and then wind governs.

questions.stem: For a MASS CONCRETE pour such as a large raft or a gravity dam block, the most appropriate cement is:
options: Ordinary Portland cement of grade 53, for its high early strength
PORTLAND POZZOLANA CEMENT or a low-heat cement, because the HEAT OF HYDRATION is lower and is released more slowly
Rapid hardening Portland cement, so the formwork can be struck early
White Portland cement, for its uniform appearance
questions.solution:
**PORTLAND POZZOLANA CEMENT or a low-heat cement** — because the heat of hydration is lower and is released more slowly, limiting the temperature rise and the thermal cracking that follows.

**The problem in mass concrete:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cement hydration is EXOTHERMIC** ← | **Releasing of the order of 300 to 500 kJ per kg of cement** ← |
| **In a thin member the heat escapes to the surroundings** ← | **And the temperature rise is modest** ← |
| **In a THICK member the interior cannot lose heat** ← | **Concrete being a poor conductor, so the core temperature can rise 30 to 50 °C above the placing temperature** ← |
| **The core EXPANDS while the surface, which has cooled, does not** ← | **Creating tension at the surface — SURFACE cracking** ← |
| **Later the core cools and contracts against a restraint** ← | **Creating tension in the core — INTERNAL cracking, and cracking against the foundation restraint** ← |
| **Neither has anything to do with the load** ← | **These are purely thermal cracks, and they occur before the structure is ever loaded** ← |

> **THE TWO DISTINCT CRACKING MECHANISMS IN THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS ARE WORTH SEPARATING, BECAUSE THEY OCCUR AT DIFFERENT TIMES AND CALL FOR DIFFERENT REMEDIES:**

> **The EARLY problem is the temperature DIFFERENCE between the hot core and the cooler surface — a gradient, which cracks the surface. Insulating the surface, or keeping it warm, reduces it.**

> **The LATER problem is the total temperature DROP as the whole mass eventually returns to ambient, restrained by the foundation or by previously placed concrete — which cracks the body. Reducing the peak temperature is the only real remedy for that.**

> **So covering a young pour to keep the surface warm addresses the first and does nothing for the second, and the two must be considered separately.**

**The measures available, in order of effectiveness:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Use a LOW-HEAT cement, or PPC or PSC with a high replacement level** ← | **Fly ash and slag hydrate more slowly and release less heat — this question** ← |
| **Reduce the CEMENT CONTENT** ← | **Fewer kilograms of cement means less heat; achieved with a larger maximum aggregate size, good grading and plasticisers** ← |
| **Use the largest practicable MAXIMUM AGGREGATE SIZE** ← | **Up to 150 mm in dam concrete — aggregate generates no heat, so displacing paste with stone displaces heat** ← |
| **PRE-COOL the ingredients** ← | **Chilled water, ice replacing part of the mixing water, cooled or shaded aggregate stockpiles** ← |
| **POST-COOL with embedded pipes** ← | **Circulating chilled water through pipes cast into the mass — used on major dams** ← |
| **Place in LIFTS with a delay between them** ← | **Allowing each lift to shed its heat before the next is placed** ← |
| **Place at NIGHT or in the cool season** | **Reducing the placing temperature directly** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MEASURE MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND THE MOST ECONOMICAL, AND ITS LOGIC IS SIMPLE: only the CEMENT PASTE generates heat.**

> **Aggregate is inert. So the more of the volume that is aggregate and the less that is paste, the less heat is produced per cubic metre.**

> **A larger maximum aggregate size reduces the total surface area to be coated with paste, so less paste is needed for the same workability — which is why dam concrete uses stones that would be inconceivable in a beam.**

> **The same reasoning explains why PLUM concrete, in which large stones are embedded in the mass, is used in thick unreinforced foundations: it reduces the cement per cubic metre, and therefore both the cost and the heat.**

**AND OPTION (a) IS WORTH ADDRESSING DIRECTLY, BECAUSE THE INSTINCT BEHIND IT IS EXACTLY BACKWARDS:**

> **A high-grade or rapid-hardening cement gains strength quickly because it hydrates quickly — and it hydrates quickly because it releases its heat quickly.**

> **Early strength and low heat are therefore in direct opposition: the property that makes OPC 53 or rapid-hardening cement attractive for a hurried column is precisely what makes it wrong for a mass pour.**

> **Choosing a cement is thus a matter of matching its rate of hydration to the member, and the fastest cement is the worst choice for the thickest member.**

examTip.trick: **Low heat, released slowly** — PPC or PSC. The core of a thick pour can rise 30-50 °C, and the cracking is purely thermal, before any load is applied.
examTip.trap: **Early strength and low heat are OPPOSED** — OPC 53 and rapid-hardening cement hydrate fast because they release heat fast. The fastest cement is worst for the thickest member.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only the PASTE makes heat; aggregate is inert** — so a larger maximum aggregate size and plum concrete cut both cement and heat per cubic metre.

questions.stem: Among the Bogue compounds of Portland cement, the one principally responsible for the EARLY strength gain in the first few days is:
options: TRICALCIUM SILICATE (C₃S)
Dicalcium silicate (C₂S)
Tricalcium aluminate (C₃A)
Tetracalcium aluminoferrite (C₄AF)
questions.solution:
**TRICALCIUM SILICATE (C₃S).**

**The four principal compounds and what each does:**

| Compound | Proportion | Rate | Contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C₃S — tricalcium silicate (alite)** ← | **About 45 to 50 %** ← | **FAST** ← | **EARLY strength, in the first days and weeks; substantial heat** ← |
| **C₂S — dicalcium silicate (belite)** ← | **About 25 to 30 %** ← | **SLOW** ← | **LATER strength, developing over months and years; little heat** ← |
| **C₃A — tricalcium aluminate** ← | **About 8 to 12 %** ← | **VERY FAST** ← | **Flash set if uncontrolled; the MOST heat; and the compound VULNERABLE TO SULPHATE attack** ← |
| **C₄AF — tetracalcium aluminoferrite** ← | **About 6 to 10 %** ← | **Moderate** ← | **Little strength; gives cement its GREY colour** ← |

> **THE C₃S AGAINST C₂S CONTRAST IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS THE ONE THAT EXPLAINS CEMENT GRADES, AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL THING IN THIS TABLE: both are calcium silicates and both produce the same strength-giving product, but at very different rates.**

> **A cement ground finer and richer in C₃S gains strength fast — that is what an OPC 53 is.**

> **A cement richer in C₂S gains strength slowly but continues to gain it for a long time, and generates less heat doing so — which is what a low-heat cement is.**

> **So the grade of a cement is largely a statement about the C₃S to C₂S balance and the fineness of grinding, and the choice between grades is a choice about the RATE at which strength and heat arrive rather than about the ultimate strength.**

**C₃A IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE TROUBLESOME COMPOUND AND IT ACCOUNTS FOR SEVERAL SEPARATE FACTS:**

| Fact | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **GYPSUM is added to cement during grinding** ← | **To control C₃A's violent early reaction; without it the cement would FLASH SET on contact with water** ← |
| **SULPHATE RESISTING cement is defined by a LOW C₃A content** ← | **Because sulphate attack works by reacting with the hydrated C₃A to form expansive ettringite** ← |
| **C₃A generates the most heat per kilogram** ← | **So low-heat cements limit it as well as favouring C₂S** ← |
| **C₃A contributes little to strength** ← | **It is present because it lowers the kiln's clinkering temperature, not because it is wanted in the product** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE OBSERVATION THAT MAKES SENSE OF THE WHOLE COMPOUND: C₃A is essentially a manufacturing convenience whose presence in the finished cement is a nuisance.**

> **It acts as a flux in the kiln, allowing the clinker to form at a lower temperature and saving a great deal of fuel.**

> **Having served that purpose it remains in the cement, where it contributes almost no strength, generates the most heat, must be restrained with gypsum to prevent flash set, and provides the point of attack for sulphates.**

> **Which is why sulphate resisting cement — with C₃A held below about 5 per cent — costs more: the kiln must work harder without the flux.**

> **THE GYPSUM POINT IN THE FIRST ROW ALSO EXPLAINS A DISTINCTION WORTH KEEPING CLEAR: FLASH SET is C₃A reacting uncontrolled, and it is prevented by gypsum.**

> **FALSE SET is a different phenomenon — a premature stiffening caused by the dehydration of gypsum in an over-heated grinding mill, which can be overcome by further mixing without adding water.**

> **The two look similar on site and call for opposite responses: false set needs remixing, while a true flash set means the batch is lost.**

examTip.trick: **C₃S fast and early, C₂S slow and late, C₃A fastest with the most heat, C₄AF the grey colour and little else.**
examTip.trap: **C₃A is a kiln FLUX, not a wanted product** — no strength, most heat, needs gypsum to prevent flash set, and is the point of sulphate attack. Sulphate resisting cement keeps it below about 5 %.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cement grade is really the C₃S:C₂S balance plus fineness** — a statement about the RATE strength and heat arrive, not about ultimate strength.

questions.stem: Increasing the WATER-CEMENT RATIO of a concrete mix, all else being equal:
options: Increases both the workability and the strength
Reduces the workability and increases the strength
Increases the WORKABILITY but REDUCES the strength and the durability
Has no significant effect on either workability or strength
questions.solution:
**Increases the WORKABILITY but REDUCES the strength and the durability** — because the excess water leaves capillary pores in the hardened paste when it evaporates.

**The mechanism, which is the whole of concrete technology in miniature:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cement needs only about 0.23 to 0.25 of its own weight of water to hydrate FULLY** ← | **Chemically, that is all that is required** ← |
| **A further 0.10 to 0.15 is held in the gel pores** ← | **So about 0.38 is the theoretical minimum for complete hydration** ← |
| **Mixes are made at 0.40 to 0.60 for WORKABILITY** ← | **The extra water is there only to make the concrete placeable** ← |
| **That extra water occupies SPACE in the fresh paste** ← | ← |
| **When it later evaporates or is consumed, the space remains as a CAPILLARY PORE** ← | **A void where there was water** ← |
| **Strength and impermeability both depend on the paste being DENSE** ← | **So the pores reduce both, and they do so steeply** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS ARE THE ESSENTIAL INSIGHT AND IT IS WORTH FIXING FIRMLY: every litre of water added beyond what hydration needs becomes a litre of VOID in the finished concrete.**

> **Water is not an ingredient that disappears — it is a temporary space-filler, and its space is inherited by air.**

> **Which is why Abrams stated the relation as strength being a function of the water-cement ratio alone, largely independent of the mix's other proportions: it is a statement about how porous the paste will end up.**

**THE DURABILITY CONSEQUENCE IS MORE SERIOUS THAN THE STRENGTH CONSEQUENCE AND IS OFTEN GIVEN LESS WEIGHT:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Capillary pores are CONNECTED, forming a path through the concrete** ← | **Above about w/c 0.5 the capillary system becomes continuous** ← |
| **Water, chlorides, sulphates and carbon dioxide can then MIGRATE inward** ← | ← |
| **Reaching the reinforcement, they cause CORROSION** ← | **Which is the dominant durability failure in reinforced concrete** ← |
| **A strength deficiency can be assessed and lived with; a permeability deficiency cannot be corrected** ← | **The concrete is porous for its whole life** ← |
| **Hence codes limit the MAXIMUM w/c by exposure condition** ← | **A durability limit, quite separate from the strength requirement** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE POINT THAT DECIDES HOW SERIOUSLY TO TREAT AN EXCESS OF WATER ON SITE: a low cube result can be investigated, cored, and often accepted with a reduced load.**

> **Porous concrete cannot be made dense afterwards. It will admit chlorides and carbon dioxide for the rest of the structure's life, and the reinforcement will corrode on a schedule set the day the concrete was placed.**

> **This is why adding water at the point of discharge — to make a stiff mix easier to place, a universal temptation — is far more damaging than it appears.**

> **A few extra litres per cubic metre may cost a modest amount of strength, and may cost the structure decades of its service life.**

**WHAT TO DO INSTEAD, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL RESOLUTION:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Use a PLASTICISER or SUPERPLASTICISER** ← | **Which increases workability with NO extra water — this is precisely the problem admixtures were invented to solve** ← |
| **Improve the aggregate GRADING and shape** ← | **Well-graded rounded aggregate needs less water than gap-graded angular aggregate for the same workability** ← |
| **Use a larger maximum aggregate SIZE where the section permits** ← | **Less surface to coat, so less paste and less water** ← |
| **Improve the compaction rather than the flow** ← | **Proper vibration places a stiff mix that could not be placed by hand** ← |

> **The first and last rows together are the correct answer to a stiff mix on site: increase the vibration or add a plasticiser — never the water.**

> **The relation between these two remedies is worth noting: a plasticiser and a vibrator do the same job by different means, both making a low-water mix placeable, and the availability of either removes the only legitimate reason anyone ever had for a high water-cement ratio.**

examTip.trick: **Workability up, strength and durability down** — the extra water is a temporary space-filler whose space is inherited by air as capillary pores.
examTip.trap: **The DURABILITY loss is worse than the strength loss** — a low cube can be investigated and accepted; porous concrete admits chlorides and CO₂ for the whole of its life and cannot be densified later.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hydration needs only about w/c 0.38; everything above that is for placing.** So the answer to a stiff mix is a plasticiser or a vibrator — never water.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, the SLUMP appropriate to concrete being placed in a lightly reinforced beam or slab, compacted by vibration, is of the order of:
options: 0 to 25 mm
150 to 200 mm
Above 200 mm
25 to 75 mm
questions.solution:
**25 to 75 mm.**

**The slump ranges for different work:**

| Type of work | Slump |
|---|---|
| **Mass concrete, lightly reinforced sections, ROAD pavements — vibrated** ← | **10 to 25 mm** ← |
| **Lightly reinforced beams and slabs, vibrated** ← | **25 to 75 mm** ← |
| **Heavily reinforced sections, columns and thin walls, vibrated** ← | **50 to 100 mm** ← |
| **Slip-formed work, PUMPED concrete, congested sections** ← | **100 to 150 mm, achieved with plasticisers** ← |
| **Tremie concrete and heavily congested piles** ← | **150 to 200 mm, self-compacting or near it** ← |
| **Hand compacted, lightly reinforced** | **80 to 150 mm — much higher, because there is no vibration to place it** ← |

> **THE PATTERN IS CONSISTENT AND MAKES THE TABLE RECOVERABLE RATHER THAN MEMORABLE: the slump required rises with the CONGESTION of the section and falls with the COMPACTIVE EFFORT available.**

> **A mass pour with no reinforcement can take a nearly dry mix, because the vibrator can work it into place.**

> **A column with dense reinforcement and a 40 mm cover needs a mix that will flow between the bars.**

> **And hand compaction, having so little effort behind it, demands a much wetter mix than a vibrator does for the same section — which is the comparison in the last row.**

**THE LAST ROW DESERVES PARTICULAR ATTENTION BECAUSE IT IS WHERE THE HIGH WATER-CEMENT RATIOS ON SMALL SITES COME FROM:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Hand compaction cannot place a stiff mix** ← | **Rodding and tamping deliver a fraction of a vibrator's energy** ← |
| **So a hand-compacted mix must be WETTER to be placeable** ← | **80 to 150 mm slump against 25 to 75** ← |
| **Which means a HIGHER water-cement ratio, and therefore lower strength and higher permeability** ← | **Unless a plasticiser is used** ← |
| **A vibrator is therefore not a labour-saving device but a QUALITY device** ← | **It permits a lower water content, which is the single most effective improvement available** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE ARGUMENT WORTH MAKING ON ANY SITE THAT DOES ITS CONCRETING BY HAND: a needle vibrator is inexpensive, and its real value is not that it saves labour but that it allows the same cement to produce substantially better concrete.**

> **A mix at 0.45 water-cement ratio placed with a vibrator is a different material from the same cement at 0.60 placed by hand, and the difference shows in strength, in permeability and in the reinforcement's service life.**

**And the other workability tests, for the distinction:**

| Test | Suited to |
|---|---|
| **SLUMP cone** ← | **Medium to high workability — the standard site test; INSENSITIVE at low slumps** ← |
| **COMPACTING FACTOR** ← | **LOW workability mixes, where slump gives no useful reading** ← |
| **VEE-BEE consistometer** ← | **VERY low workability, very dry mixes — measures the time to remould under vibration** ← |
| **FLOW TABLE** ← | **HIGH workability and flowing concrete, where slump has collapsed** ← |
| **SLUMP FLOW and J-ring** | **SELF-COMPACTING concrete** ← |

> **THE RANGE LIMITATION IN THE FIRST ROW IS WHY THESE OTHER TESTS EXIST AND IT IS THE PRACTICAL POINT: a slump cone reading of zero tells you nothing beyond that the mix is dry — a very dry mix and a moderately dry mix both give zero.**

> **At the other extreme, a mix that has collapsed entirely also gives an uninformative reading.**

> **So the slump test is a good test over the range of ordinary structural concrete and a poor one outside it, and choosing the workability test to match the mix is part of specifying it properly.**

examTip.trick: **10-25 mass, 25-75 lightly reinforced beams and slabs, 50-100 columns and heavily reinforced, 100-150 pumped.** Slump rises with congestion, falls with compactive effort.
examTip.trap: **Hand compaction needs 80-150 mm** — far wetter than vibrated work, hence a higher w/c. A vibrator is a QUALITY device, not a labour-saving one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Slump is useless below about 25 mm and above collapse** — use the compacting factor for dry mixes, Vee-Bee for very dry, flow table for flowing.

questions.stem: The COMPACTING FACTOR of a fresh concrete is defined as the ratio of the:
options: Volume of the compacted concrete to the volume of the mould
WEIGHT of the PARTIALLY compacted concrete to the weight of the FULLY compacted concrete in the same cylinder
Height of the slumped concrete to the height of the cone
Weight of the coarse aggregate to the total weight of the mix
questions.solution:
**The WEIGHT of the PARTIALLY compacted concrete to the weight of the FULLY compacted concrete in the same cylinder.**

**The test:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Concrete is placed in the UPPER hopper and released** ← | **Falling into the lower hopper under gravity alone** ← |
| **It is released again from the lower hopper into the CYLINDER** ← | **A standard drop, giving a standard amount of compactive work** ← |
| **The excess is struck off and the cylinder's contents WEIGHED** ← | **This is the PARTIALLY compacted weight** ← |
| **The cylinder is then refilled and FULLY compacted by vibration or rodding, and weighed again** ← | **The FULLY compacted weight** ← |
| **Compacting factor = partially compacted weight ÷ fully compacted weight** ← | **Always less than 1.0** ← |

**Interpreting the value:**

| Compacting factor | Workability |
|---|---|
| **0.78** | **VERY LOW** ← |
| **0.85** | **LOW** ← |
| **0.92** | **MEDIUM** ← |
| **0.95** | **HIGH** ← |

> **THE FACT THAT THE RESULT IS A WEIGHT RATIO RATHER THAN A DIMENSION IS THE FEATURE THAT MAKES THIS TEST WORK WHERE SLUMP FAILS, and it is worth understanding why.**

> **The slump test measures how far concrete SUBSIDES under its own weight. A dry mix does not subside at all, so it gives zero regardless of how dry it is, and the test cannot discriminate.**

> **The compacting factor instead measures how much concrete a standard amount of falling work manages to compact into a fixed volume.**

> **A dry mix arrives loose and full of voids, so it weighs less; a wetter mix compacts better under the same fall and weighs more.**

> **Since even a very dry mix has SOME density, the test yields a meaningful and discriminating number right down to the driest practical mixes — which is exactly the range where slump is blind.**

**THE NARROWNESS OF THE SCALE IS THE TEST'S PRACTICAL DRAWBACK AND IT IS WORTH NOTING:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The whole useful range lies between about 0.78 and 0.95** ← | **A span of 0.17 covering everything from very low to high workability** ← |
| **So the weighings must be ACCURATE** ← | **A 1 per cent weighing error is a significant fraction of the range** ← |
| **The apparatus is bulky and not well suited to site use** ← | **Which is why slump, for all its limitations, remains the site test** ← |
| **And the test is really a LABORATORY test** ← | **Used in mix design and in research rather than for routine site control** ← |

> **THE DIVISION OF LABOUR IN THE LAST TWO ROWS IS THE REALISTIC POSITION AND IT IS WORTH STATING RATHER THAN PRETENDING OTHERWISE: the slump cone survives as the universal site test because it is cheap, quick, portable and needs no balance.**

> **The compacting factor and the Vee-Bee test are better tests over their ranges but require apparatus and care that a site pour cannot spare.**

> **So a designer specifying a very dry mix — for a road pavement, a mass pour, or precast work — should expect its workability to be controlled by compacting factor or Vee-Bee in the laboratory, and should not specify a slump limit that the test cannot meaningfully measure.**

> **Specifying 'slump 0 to 25 mm' for a roller-compacted or a very dry mix is a common instance of a requirement that cannot in practice be verified, and it is better replaced by the test that suits the material.**

examTip.trick: **Partially compacted weight ÷ fully compacted weight**, in the same cylinder. Always below 1.0: 0.78 very low, 0.85 low, 0.92 medium, 0.95 high.
examTip.trap: **It works where slump is blind** — a dry mix gives zero slump whatever its dryness, but always has a measurable density, so the weight ratio still discriminates.
examTip.mnemonic: **The whole scale is 0.78 to 0.95** — only 0.17 wide, so the weighings must be accurate. That, plus bulky apparatus, keeps it a laboratory test while slump stays on site.

questions.stem: The grade designation M25 for concrete signifies that the concrete has a:
options: CHARACTERISTIC COMPRESSIVE STRENGTH of 25 N/mm² at 28 days, measured on 150 mm CUBES
Mean compressive strength of 25 N/mm² at 28 days on cubes
Characteristic compressive strength of 25 N/mm² at 7 days
Mix proportion of 1 part cement to 2 of sand to 5 of coarse aggregate
questions.solution:
**A CHARACTERISTIC COMPRESSIVE STRENGTH of 25 N/mm² at 28 days, measured on 150 mm CUBES.**

**Every element of that definition matters:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **M stands for MIX, and the number is the strength in N/mm²** ← | ← |
| **CHARACTERISTIC, not mean** ← | **The value below which not more than 5 per cent of results are expected to fall — so the MEAN must be higher** ← (which is why option b is wrong) |
| **At 28 DAYS** ← | **The standard age; concrete continues to gain strength beyond it** ← (option c) |
| **On 150 mm CUBES** ← | **The Indian and Nepali convention; cylinders are used in American and European practice and give a LOWER figure** ← |
| **It is a STRENGTH, not a proportion** ← | **A nominal mix such as 1:2:4 is a different way of specifying concrete** ← (option d) |

> **THE 'CHARACTERISTIC RATHER THAN MEAN' DISTINCTION IN THE SECOND ROW HAS A DIRECT CONSEQUENCE FOR MIX DESIGN AND IS WORTH FOLLOWING THROUGH: M25 does NOT mean the concrete will average 25 N/mm².**

> **It means 25 is the 5 per cent lower fractile, so the mix must be designed for a TARGET MEAN of f_ck + 1.65σ.**

> **With a standard deviation of 4 N/mm² for M25, the target mean is 25 + 1.65 × 4 = 31.6 N/mm² — some 26 per cent above the grade.**

> **A producer who designs the mix to average exactly 25 will find half his results below the specified grade, and will fail the acceptance criteria consistently while believing he has met the specification.**

**The grades and their common uses:**

| Grade | Typical use |
|---|---|
| **M5, M7.5** | **Lean concrete, blinding, levelling course** ← |
| **M10, M15** | **Plain concrete, non-structural fill; M15 is the minimum for PCC work** ← |
| **M20** ← | **The MINIMUM grade permitted for reinforced concrete under IS 456** ← |
| **M25, M30** ← | **Ordinary structural work — beams, slabs, columns, footings** ← |
| **M35 to M50** | **Higher-strength columns, prestressed work, severe exposure** ← |
| **Above M60** | **High-strength concrete, requiring special materials and control** ← |

> **THE M20 MINIMUM IN THE THIRD ROW IS A DURABILITY REQUIREMENT RATHER THAN A STRENGTH ONE, WHICH IS THE POINT WORTH GRASPING: reinforced concrete of lower grade would often be strong enough for the loads in a lightly loaded member.**

> **It is prohibited because a weak mix is a POROUS mix — the two go together, both being consequences of a high water-cement ratio and a low cement content.**

> **A porous cover admits carbon dioxide and chlorides to the reinforcement, and the steel corrodes.**

> **So the minimum grade protects the REINFORCEMENT rather than guaranteeing the member's capacity, and it rises with the severity of the exposure: M20 for mild exposure, M25 for moderate, M30 for severe, M35 for very severe and M40 for extreme.**

> **That progression is the clearest illustration in the code that concrete grade is a durability parameter as much as a structural one, and it explains why a designer cannot simply choose a low grade on the grounds that the stresses are small.**

**And the CUBE against CYLINDER point in the fourth row, which causes real confusion when foreign literature is used:**

> **A cylinder of 150 mm diameter and 300 mm height gives about 0.8 times the strength of a 150 mm cube of the same concrete.**

> **The difference is a testing artefact: the cube's platens restrain its ends by friction, confining the specimen and raising the apparent strength, and the cube's squat shape means that restraint affects the whole height.**

> **The slender cylinder has a mid-height region free of that restraint, so it fails at a lower stress that is closer to the material's true uniaxial strength.**

> **Hence a concrete described as C25/30 in European notation has a cylinder strength of 25 and a cube strength of 30 — the same material stated both ways, and a source of serious error if one figure is read as the other.**

examTip.trick: **Characteristic (5 % fractile) compressive strength at 28 days on 150 mm cubes.** Not the mean, not 7 days, not a proportion.
examTip.trap: **M25 must be designed for a target MEAN of f_ck + 1.65σ ≈ 31.6 N/mm²** — aiming at 25 puts half the results below grade while appearing to meet the specification.
examTip.mnemonic: **M20 is the RCC minimum for DURABILITY, not strength** — weak concrete is porous concrete, and the grade minimum rises with exposure: 20/25/30/35/40 for mild to extreme.

questions.stem: The compressive strength of a standard concrete CYLINDER (150 mm × 300 mm) is generally taken as approximately what fraction of the strength of a 150 mm CUBE of the same concrete?
options: 1.25 times the cube strength
Equal to the cube strength
0.80 times the cube strength
0.50 times the cube strength
questions.solution:
**About 0.80 times the cube strength.**

**So for a concrete of 30 N/mm² cube strength, the cylinder strength is about 24 N/mm².**

**Why the two differ, which is entirely a matter of the TEST rather than the material:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **The loading PLATENS restrain the specimen's ends by FRICTION** ← | **Concrete tries to expand laterally under compression (Poisson effect); the steel platen prevents it at the contact surface** ← |
| **That restraint puts the end regions into a CONFINED state** ← | **And confined concrete is much stronger than unconfined concrete** ← |
| **The restraint's influence extends about one specimen-width inward** ← | ← |
| **A CUBE is only as tall as it is wide, so the restrained zones from both ends MEET** ← | **The whole cube is confined to some degree, and its apparent strength is raised** ← |
| **A CYLINDER has a height-to-diameter ratio of 2, so its MID-HEIGHT is free of restraint** ← | **It fails there, at a stress much closer to the true uniaxial strength** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER ARE THE WHOLE EXPLANATION AND THEY LEAD TO A CONCLUSION WORTH STATING PLAINLY: the CYLINDER gives the more honest measure of the material's strength, and the cube gives a flattering one.**

> **The cube is not measuring a different property; it is measuring the same property with a systematic error caused by its own proportions.**

> **The cube nevertheless persists in Indian, Nepali and British practice because it is easier to cast, easier to handle, needs no capping to give a plane loading face, and stands stably in the machine on any face.**

> **A cylinder must be capped or ground flat, which is an extra operation and a source of error in itself, and it is more awkward to demould and carry.**

> **So the choice between them is one of convenience against fidelity, and both conventions are internally consistent provided the two figures are never confused.**

**WHERE THE CONFUSION ACTUALLY BITES, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL WARNING:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **European notation C25/30** ← | **Means CYLINDER 25 and CUBE 30 — the same concrete, stated both ways** ← |
| **American practice quotes f'_c as a CYLINDER strength** ← | **So an American 4,000 psi (27.6 MPa) concrete is about M35 in cube terms, not M27** ← |
| **Eurocode formulae use f_ck as a CYLINDER strength** ← | **While IS 456 formulae use f_ck as a CUBE strength — the same symbol for different quantities** ← |
| **Reading a cylinder value as a cube value UNDER-estimates the concrete by 20 per cent** ← | **Conservative, and wasteful** ← |
| **Reading a cube value as a cylinder value OVER-estimates it by 25 per cent** ← | **Which is unsafe** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST DANGEROUS AND IT ARISES WHENEVER FORMULAE ARE MIXED BETWEEN CODES: f_ck means a cylinder strength in Eurocode and a cube strength in IS 456, and the symbol gives no warning.**

> **An expression such as the Eurocode's tensile strength or elastic modulus formula, applied with an IS cube strength substituted for f_ck, over-estimates the property by a substantial margin.**

> **The rule to follow is that a formula must be used with the strength definition of the code it came from, and any transfer between codes requires the 0.8 conversion to be applied deliberately and noted.**

> **Mixing code provisions is generally unwise for exactly this class of reason: the symbols are shared but their definitions are not, and the incompatibility is silent.**

**And the size effect, for completeness:**

> **Larger specimens give LOWER strengths, cubes and cylinders alike, because a larger volume is more likely to contain a critical flaw — the weakest-link statistics that govern all brittle materials.**

> **This is why the specimen size is part of the standard and not a matter of convenience: a 100 mm cube gives a slightly higher result than a 150 mm cube of the same concrete, and comparing results from different sizes without correction is not valid.**

examTip.trick: **Cylinder ≈ 0.80 × cube.** The cube's squat shape lets platen friction confine its whole height, flattering the result; the slender cylinder's mid-height is unrestrained.
examTip.trap: **f_ck is a CYLINDER strength in Eurocode and a CUBE strength in IS 456** — the same symbol, different quantities, and no warning. Mixing code formulae over-estimates by 25 %.
examTip.mnemonic: **C25/30 means cylinder 25, cube 30** — one concrete, two conventions. And larger specimens give lower strengths: weakest-link statistics.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, NOMINAL MIX concrete (proportions such as 1:2:4 by volume) may be used only:
options: For any grade of concrete, provided the site is properly supervised
For grades above M25 only
Never — every concrete must be a design mix
For grades UP TO M20, and even then design mix concrete is PREFERRED
questions.solution:
**For grades UP TO M20** — and even then design mix concrete is preferred, because a nominal mix takes no account of the actual materials and therefore wastes cement while giving less reliable strength.

**The two ways of specifying a concrete:**

| Approach | Basis |
|---|---|
| **NOMINAL MIX** ← | **Fixed PROPORTIONS by volume — 1:3:6 for M10, 1:2:4 for M15, 1:1.5:3 for M20** ← |
| **DESIGN MIX** ← | **Proportions determined by TRIAL to achieve a target strength with the ACTUAL materials** ← |

**Why the design mix is superior:**

| Consideration | Nominal mix | Design mix |
|---|---|---|
| **Accounts for the actual aggregate GRADING and shape** ← | **NO** ← | **YES** ← |
| **Accounts for the actual cement's strength** ← | **NO — a 43 grade and a 53 grade cement are treated alike** ← | **YES** ← |
| **Accounts for the standard deviation achievable on site** ← | **NO** ← | **YES, through the target mean** ← |
| **Cement content** ← | **Generous, since the proportions must be safe with poor materials** ← | **Optimised — commonly 10 to 20 per cent less cement for the same strength** ← |
| **Reliability of the strength achieved** | **Variable** ← | **Demonstrated by trial** ← |
| **Effort required** | **None** | **Trial mixes, testing, a competent laboratory** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW CONTAINS THE ARGUMENT THAT SETTLES THE MATTER ON ANY JOB OF SIZE AND IT IS AN ECONOMIC ONE: a nominal mix must be safe with the WORST materials it might encounter, so it carries a margin for materials the site may not actually have.**

> **With good aggregate and a 53 grade cement, a 1:1.5:3 mix will substantially exceed M20 — the extra strength being surplus, paid for in cement that was not needed.**

> **A design mix identifies that surplus and removes it, so the saving in cement typically exceeds the cost of the trials many times over on any pour of consequence.**

> **Which is why the nominal mix survives only for small quantities and low grades, where the cost of designing the mix would exceed the cement saved.**

**THE 'BY VOLUME' BASIS IS THE NOMINAL MIX'S DEEPER WEAKNESS AND IT IS WORTH BEING EXPLICIT ABOUT WHY, because it is a genuine measurement problem rather than merely an approximation:**

| Problem | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sand BULKS when damp** ← | **Moist sand occupies 20 to 30 per cent more volume than the same dry sand, because water films hold the grains apart** ← |
| **So a box of damp sand contains substantially LESS sand than the same box of dry sand** ← | ← |
| **A 1:2:4 mix batched by volume with damp sand is therefore RICHER in cement than intended** ← | **Wasteful, though not unsafe** ← |
| **And the WATER carried in by the sand is unmeasured** ← | **Which raises the water-cement ratio by an unknown amount — this is the unsafe consequence** ← |
| **Bulking is greatest at about 4 to 6 per cent moisture and disappears when the sand is saturated** ← | **So the error varies with the weather, which makes it impossible to allow for by a fixed adjustment** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE SERIOUS ONE AND IT DEFEATS THE ENTIRE PURPOSE OF SPECIFYING A GRADE: the strength of concrete depends chiefly on the water-cement ratio, and volume batching with damp sand leaves the water content genuinely unknown.**

> **The mixer operator adds water until the mix looks right, without knowing how much the sand already contributed, so the actual water-cement ratio varies from batch to batch with the sand's moisture and the operator's judgment.**

> **This is why WEIGH BATCHING with a moisture correction is required for design mixes, and why it is the single most effective quality control measure on a concreting site.**

> **It is also why the bulking test — measuring the volume of a sample of the sand loose and then inundated — is worth doing on any site that must batch by volume: it at least quantifies the error, and the sand allowance can be adjusted for the day's condition.**

examTip.trick: **Up to M20 only, and design mix is preferred even there.** 1:3:6 for M10, 1:2:4 for M15, 1:1.5:3 for M20.
examTip.trap: **Damp sand BULKS 20-30 %**, so a volume-batched mix is richer in cement than intended AND carries unmeasured water — which makes the water-cement ratio, and hence the strength, genuinely unknown.
examTip.mnemonic: **A nominal mix must be safe with the WORST materials it might meet**, so with good ones it wastes 10-20 % of the cement. Weigh batching with a moisture correction is the real fix.

questions.stem: IS 456 prescribes a MINIMUM CEMENT CONTENT and a MAXIMUM water-cement ratio for each EXPOSURE CONDITION, in addition to the strength requirement, because:
options: DURABILITY depends on the concrete's IMPERMEABILITY, which the strength requirement alone does not guarantee
The strength requirement is too difficult to verify on site
Cement content has no effect on strength and must therefore be specified separately
The exposure condition determines the loads on the structure
questions.solution:
**DURABILITY depends on the concrete's IMPERMEABILITY, which the strength requirement alone does not guarantee** — a mix can reach its strength with too little cement or too much water and still be porous.

**The requirements by exposure, which come as a set of three:**

| Exposure | Min. grade | Max. w/c | Min. cement (kg/m³) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MILD** ← | **M20** | **0.55** | **300** |
| **MODERATE** ← | **M25** | **0.50** | **300** |
| **SEVERE** ← | **M30** | **0.45** | **320** |
| **VERY SEVERE** ← | **M35** | **0.45** | **340** |
| **EXTREME** ← | **M40** | **0.40** | **360** |

> **(For reinforced concrete; the cover requirement rises with exposure in the same way, from 20 mm for mild to 75 mm for extreme.)**

**THE REASON ALL THREE ARE NEEDED, AND NOT MERELY THE GRADE, IS THE HEART OF THE QUESTION:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Strength and impermeability USUALLY go together, both depending on the water-cement ratio** ← | **So a strong mix is generally a dense mix** ← |
| **But they can be DECOUPLED** ← | **A mix with a low water-cement ratio and very little cement — a harsh, lean, well-graded mix — can reach a respectable strength while having too little PASTE to fill the aggregate voids** ← |
| **Such a mix is strong and PERMEABLE** ← | **Because the voids between the aggregate particles are not all filled with paste** ← |
| **Hence a MINIMUM CEMENT requirement, independent of strength** ← | **To ensure there is enough paste to produce a continuous impermeable matrix and to coat and protect the steel** ← |
| **And a MAXIMUM water-cement ratio, independent of strength** ← | **To limit the capillary porosity of whatever paste there is** ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS DESCRIBE THE SPECIFIC LOOPHOLE THAT THE MINIMUM CEMENT REQUIREMENT CLOSES, and it is worth understanding because it is not obvious: strength is not a complete proxy for quality.**

> **A concrete can pass its cubes and still be unfit for its exposure, and the cube test gives no warning of it — which is why durability is specified prescriptively rather than left to be inferred from a performance test.**

**THERE IS ALSO A MAXIMUM CEMENT CONTENT, WHICH SURPRISES PEOPLE AND IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **IS 456 limits cement to 450 kg/m³** ← | **A ceiling, not a floor** ← |
| **Because a very rich mix SHRINKS more** ← | **Shrinkage is a property of the paste, so more paste means more shrinkage cracking** ← |
| **And generates more HEAT** ← | **With the thermal cracking consequences discussed for mass concrete** ← |
| **And creeps more** ← | ← |
| **So more cement is not simply better** ← | **Beyond a point it makes the concrete worse in service while still passing its cubes** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW OF THIS TABLE PUTS THE WHOLE DURABILITY PROVISION IN PERSPECTIVE AND IS THE RIGHT NOTE TO CLOSE ON: cement content has an optimum rather than a direction.**

> **Too little and the concrete is porous and the steel unprotected. Too much and it shrinks, cracks, heats and creeps.**

> **The code's minima and maximum together define a band, and a durable concrete is one that sits inside it with an appropriate water-cement ratio — not simply one with as much cement as the budget allows.**

> **This is a useful corrective to a common site instinct that an extra bag of cement can do no harm: it can, and the crack pattern of an over-rich slab is the evidence of it.**

examTip.trick: **Durability needs IMPERMEABILITY, which strength alone does not guarantee** — a lean, harsh, low-w/c mix can be strong yet have too little paste to fill the aggregate voids.
examTip.trap: **Mild/moderate/severe/very severe/extreme: M20/M25/M30/M35/M40, w/c 0.55/0.50/0.45/0.45/0.40.** And the cover requirement rises the same way, 20 mm to 75 mm.
examTip.mnemonic: **There is also a MAXIMUM of 450 kg/m³** — too much cement shrinks, heats and creeps. Cement content has an optimum, not a direction.

questions.stem: Under the acceptance criteria of IS 456 for concrete of grade M20 and above, the compressive strength is accepted if the mean of any FOUR consecutive test results is not less than f_ck + 0.825σ (or f_ck + 3 N/mm², whichever is greater) AND every individual result is not less than:
options: f_ck
f_ck − 3 N/mm²
f_ck + 3 N/mm²
questions.solution:
**f_ck − 3 N/mm².**

**The two conditions, both of which must be satisfied:**

| Condition | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **On the MEAN of four consecutive samples** ← | **≥ f_ck + 0.825 σ, or f_ck + 3 N/mm², whichever is GREATER** ← |
| **On EVERY INDIVIDUAL sample** ← | **≥ f_ck − 3 N/mm²** ← |

> **THE TWO CONDITIONS DO DIFFERENT JOBS AND BOTH ARE NECESSARY, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE PAIR:**

> **The MEAN condition controls the AVERAGE QUALITY of the concrete being supplied. It ensures the producer is aiming high enough — that the population's mean sits above the characteristic value by the statistically required margin.**

> **The INDIVIDUAL condition controls the WORST BATCH. It ensures that even while the average is satisfactory, no single batch is grossly deficient.**

> **A producer with an excellent mean and terrible consistency would pass the first test and fail the second, and rightly so — a structure contains individual batches, not averages, and one very weak batch may be sitting in a critical member.**

> **Conversely a producer whose every result is just above f_ck − 3 but whose mean is too low fails the first test, because the population is centred too low and future batches will fall below.**

**Why the tolerance of 3 N/mm² below the grade on an individual result is not a license:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The CHARACTERISTIC strength is defined as the 5 per cent fractile** ← | **So by definition about 1 result in 20 is EXPECTED to fall below f_ck** ← |
| **A criterion demanding every result to reach f_ck would therefore contradict the definition** ← | **It would reject concrete that exactly met the specification** ← |
| **Hence a defined allowance below f_ck for individual results** ← | **Which accommodates the expected scatter without accepting genuinely bad concrete** ← |
| **A result below f_ck − 3 is a FAILURE and must be investigated** ← | **Not averaged away** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE LOGICAL NECESSITY BEHIND THE ALLOWANCE AND IT IS WORTH GRASPING, because the allowance otherwise looks like a concession: if concrete is specified as a 5 per cent fractile, then results below the fractile are part of the specification being met, not evidence of it being missed.**

> **Rejecting a batch for a single result below f_ck would mean that no concrete could ever comply, which is a specification that cannot be satisfied.**

**What happens when concrete FAILS the criteria, which is the practically important part:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Check the TESTING first** ← | **Cube making, curing, capping, machine calibration and the test itself are all sources of spurious low results — and a testing error is much commoner than genuinely bad concrete** ← |
| **2. Re-examine the batching records for that day** ← | **Water added, cement weighed, admixture dose** ← |
| **3. NON-DESTRUCTIVE testing of the affected member** ← | **Rebound hammer and ultrasonic pulse velocity, to locate the extent** ← |
| **4. CORE tests cut from the structure** ← | **The definitive evidence of the in-situ strength, since it tests the actual concrete in place** ← |
| **5. LOAD TEST of the member, if necessary** ← | **The final resort, testing the member's actual performance rather than the material's strength** ← |
| **6. Strengthen, or accept with a reduced capacity, or demolish** ← | **In that order of preference** ← |

> **THE FIRST STEP DESERVES ITS PLACE AT THE TOP AND IS ROUTINELY SKIPPED IN THE ALARM THAT FOLLOWS A LOW RESULT: badly made or badly cured cubes give low results from perfectly good concrete.**

> **A cube cured in the sun rather than in water, insufficiently compacted, tested with unplaned faces, or tested in an uncalibrated machine can read many newtons per square millimetre below the truth.**

> **So the first question is whether the CUBE is representative of the concrete, and only when the testing is confirmed sound does the concrete itself come under suspicion.**

> **The core test in step 4 is the arbiter precisely because it bypasses the cube entirely and interrogates the structure — and its result, corrected for the core's shape, moisture and the presence of reinforcement, is what a dispute over acceptance ultimately turns on.**

examTip.trick: **Mean of four ≥ f_ck + 0.825σ (or f_ck + 3, whichever is greater); every individual ≥ f_ck − 3.** Two conditions, both mandatory.
examTip.trap: **The mean condition controls average quality; the individual condition controls the worst batch.** A good mean with bad consistency passes one and fails the other — and should.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check the TESTING before the concrete** — poorly made or sun-cured cubes give low results from sound concrete. The CORE test is the arbiter because it bypasses the cube entirely.

questions.stem: The principal purpose of CURING concrete is to:
options: Cool the concrete so that thermal cracking is avoided
Wash away the laitance from the surface
RETAIN sufficient MOISTURE in the concrete for HYDRATION to continue
Compact the surface layer so that it becomes wear-resistant
questions.solution:
**To RETAIN sufficient MOISTURE in the concrete for HYDRATION to continue** — since hydration ceases if the relative humidity within the pores falls below about 80 per cent.

**The mechanism:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cement gains strength by HYDRATION, a chemical reaction with water** ← | **Not by drying — which is the misconception curing exists to correct** ← |
| **The reaction continues for MONTHS if water is available** ← | **Most of the strength arrives in the first 28 days, but gain continues well beyond** ← |
| **If the concrete DRIES, hydration STOPS** ← | **Below about 80 per cent internal relative humidity the reaction ceases** ← |
| **And it does not fully resume when water is restored** ← | **The gel structure has been disrupted, so strength lost to early drying is permanently lost** ← |
| **Curing therefore protects the SURFACE ZONE above all** ← | **Which dries first, and which is the cover protecting the reinforcement** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS WHY CURING CANNOT BE POSTPONED AND IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL POINT: the damage from early drying is not recoverable.**

> **A slab left to dry for its first two days and then watered diligently for a fortnight does not end up where it would have been — the hydration that failed to occur in those first days is not made up later.**

> **So curing is urgent in a way that few site activities are: it must begin as soon as the surface can bear it and must not be interrupted.**

> **THE FIFTH ROW EXPLAINS WHY POOR CURING IS SO DAMAGING OUT OF PROPORTION TO THE STRENGTH IT COSTS: the concrete that dries is the SURFACE, and the surface is the cover.**

> **A member whose core is well hydrated and whose outer 30 mm is under-hydrated has nearly its full structural capacity and a badly compromised cover — porous, weak and permeable exactly where the reinforcement needs protection.**

> **The cubes, being fully cured in a tank, show none of this. So poor curing is a defect that the standard testing regime cannot detect, and it manifests years later as corrosion.**

**The minimum curing periods:**

| Cement | Minimum period |
|---|---|
| **Ordinary Portland cement** ← | **7 days** ← |
| **BLENDED cements — PPC, PSC, and mineral admixture mixes** ← | **10 to 14 days — LONGER, because the pozzolanic reaction is slower** ← |
| **In hot and dry weather** ← | **Extended, and the surface protected from wind and sun as well as watered** ← |

> **THE LONGER PERIOD FOR BLENDED CEMENTS IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE PROVISION MOST OFTEN VIOLATED AND IT MATTERS INCREASINGLY, since PPC has largely displaced OPC in the market.**

> **The pozzolanic reaction consumes the calcium hydroxide released by cement hydration and is inherently slow — it needs both time and moisture.**

> **A PPC concrete cured for 7 days as though it were OPC has been denied the very reaction that gives it its long-term strength and, more importantly, its refined pore structure and low permeability.**

> **The irony is direct: PPC's principal advantage is durability, and inadequate curing removes precisely that advantage while leaving the slower early strength gain as a pure disadvantage.**

**The methods, and their relative merit:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **PONDING — a retained pool of water on a slab** ← | **The best method for flat surfaces; full saturation, no drying** ← |
| **Wet HESSIAN or jute, kept continuously damp** ← | **Effective for vertical surfaces and beams — but if it dries it becomes a WICK and draws moisture OUT** ← |
| **Continuous SPRINKLING or fogging** | **Effective, wasteful of water, and must not be intermittent** ← |
| **MEMBRANE curing compounds** ← | **Sprayed on to seal the surface — convenient where water is scarce, though it retains only the water already present rather than supplying more** ← |
| **Polythene SHEETING** | **Prevents evaporation; must be sealed at the edges or it ventilates** ← |
| **STEAM curing** | **For precast work, accelerating strength gain** ← |

> **The warning in the second row is worth taking seriously because it inverts the intention: hessian applied and then allowed to dry out is worse than no hessian at all.**

> **Dry fabric in contact with damp concrete draws water from it by capillary action and delivers it to the air — so intermittent curing, which is what happens when a site waters once a day and forgets at weekends, can actively accelerate the drying it was meant to prevent.**

examTip.trick: **Concrete gains strength by HYDRATION, not by drying** — below about 80 % internal RH the reaction stops, and strength lost to early drying is lost permanently.
examTip.trap: **7 days for OPC but 10-14 for PPC and blended cements** — the pozzolanic reaction is slow. Curing PPC for 7 days removes the durability that was the reason for choosing it.
examTip.mnemonic: **The concrete that dries is the COVER** — cubes cured in a tank never show it, so poor curing is invisible to testing and appears years later as corrosion. And dry hessian is a WICK.

questions.stem: BLEEDING in fresh concrete is:
options: The separation of the coarse aggregate from the mortar during handling
The loss of workability with time after mixing
The formation of a weak, dusty layer of fine material on the surface after finishing
The upward migration of MIXING WATER to the surface as the solids settle
questions.solution:
**The upward migration of MIXING WATER to the surface as the solids settle** — leaving water-filled channels, weakened zones beneath aggregate particles and reinforcement, and a laitance on the surface.

**The related defects, which are distinct and are constantly confused:**

| Defect | Definition |
|---|---|
| **BLEEDING** ← | **WATER rising to the surface as the solids settle — this question** ← |
| **SEGREGATION** ← | **Separation of the COARSE AGGREGATE from the mortar, so the mix is no longer uniform** ← (option a) |
| **SLUMP LOSS** ← | **Progressive stiffening with time after mixing** ← (option b) |
| **LAITANCE** ← | **The weak, dusty layer of fine material left on the surface — a CONSEQUENCE of bleeding, carried up by the rising water** ← (option c) |
| **PLASTIC SETTLEMENT cracking** ← | **Cracks over reinforcement, where the concrete settles and the bar does not** ← |

> **THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THE FIRST AND FOURTH ROWS IS THE ONE TO GET RIGHT, since option (c) describes a real thing that is not the answer: laitance is what bleeding LEAVES BEHIND, not bleeding itself.**

> **The rising water carries the finest particles — cement fines and silt — to the surface, where the water evaporates and the fines remain as a weak dusty film.**

> **So laitance is the visible evidence of bleeding, and its presence on a construction joint is why such joints must be scabbled, wire-brushed or green-cut before the next lift is placed.**

**The damage bleeding does, which is more than cosmetic:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **CHANNELS are left where the water rose** ← | **Continuous vertical paths of high permeability through the concrete** ← |
| **Water accumulates UNDER coarse aggregate particles and UNDER reinforcing bars** ← | **Leaving a void or a weak porous zone there when it is consumed or evaporates** ← |
| **The BOND between concrete and reinforcement is weakened on the UNDERSIDE of horizontal bars** ← | **Which is a genuine structural consequence, particularly for top steel in a deep member** ← |
| **LAITANCE forms a weak plane at the surface** ← | **Poor wear resistance on a floor, and a poor bond at a construction joint** ← |
| **The top of a deep lift becomes richer in water and therefore WEAKER than the bottom** ← | **A strength gradient through the pour** ← |
| **PLASTIC SETTLEMENT cracks appear over the bars** ← | **Where the settling concrete is locally restrained** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE CONSEQUENCE MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND IT IS A REAL STRUCTURAL ONE: a horizontal bar high in a deep pour has bleed water collecting beneath it, so its lower half is bonded to porous, weak, water-formed concrete.**

> **The bar's bond strength on that side is substantially reduced, which matters most for the top reinforcement of a deep beam — where the top steel is the tension steel over a support.**

> **This is one reason codes limit the depth of a single lift and require deep members to be placed in layers with an interval, and it is why the phenomenon has a name of its own — 'top bar effect'.**

**How bleeding is controlled:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Reduce the WATER content** ← | **The direct cause is excess water; less water means less to bleed** ← |
| **Increase the FINES — cement, fly ash, or finer sand** ← | **Fine particles hold water by surface area and impede its upward flow** ← |
| **Use AIR ENTRAINMENT** ← | **The tiny bubbles obstruct the bleed channels remarkably effectively** ← |
| **Avoid over-vibration** ← | **Prolonged vibration drives the solids down and the water up, causing both bleeding and segregation** ← |
| **Place in shallower LIFTS** ← | **Less depth of solids to settle, so less water expelled** ← |
| **Delay the FINISHING until bleeding has ceased** ← | **Finishing while bleed water is still on the surface works that water back into the top layer, which is the classic cause of a dusting, crazed floor** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE COMMONEST WORKMANSHIP ERROR IN SLAB FINISHING AND IT IS ENTIRELY AVOIDABLE: trowelling a surface while bleed water stands on it mixes that water into the very layer that must be hardest and densest.**

> **The result is a top few millimetres of extremely high water-cement ratio — soft, dusty, permeable and liable to craze and wear.**

> **The correct practice is to wait for the bleed water to disappear by evaporation or to remove it, and only then to float and trowel — and never to sprinkle dry cement on a wet surface to absorb the water, which produces exactly the same defect in a more concentrated form.**

examTip.trick: **WATER rises as the solids settle.** Segregation is the coarse aggregate separating (a); laitance is what bleeding leaves behind (c), not bleeding itself.
examTip.trap: **Bleed water collects under horizontal bars, weakening bond on their underside** — the 'top bar effect', worst for the tension steel over a support in a deep beam.
examTip.mnemonic: **Never finish while bleed water stands on the surface** — trowelling works it into the top layer and gives a soft, dusty, crazing floor. And never sprinkle dry cement to soak it up.

questions.stem: A SUPERPLASTICISER (high range water reducer) is used in concrete principally to:
options: Achieve a large increase in WORKABILITY at the same water content, or the same workability at a much REDUCED water content
Delay the setting time in hot weather
Entrain fine air bubbles to improve frost resistance
Accelerate the strength gain so that formwork can be struck early
questions.solution:
**To achieve a large increase in WORKABILITY at the same water content, or the same workability at a much REDUCED water content** — a water reduction of 15 to 30 per cent being typical.

**How it works:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cement particles carry surface charges and FLOCCULATE in water** ← | **Clumping together into loose aggregations** ← |
| **Those flocs TRAP water inside them** ← | **Water that is therefore unavailable to lubricate the mix** ← |
| **A superplasticiser adsorbs onto the particles and DISPERSES them** ← | **By electrostatic repulsion, and in the newer polycarboxylate types also by steric hindrance** ← |
| **The trapped water is RELEASED and the particles slide past one another freely** ← | **So the mix flows without any extra water having been added** ← |
| **Dispersal also exposes more cement surface to water** ← | **Which slightly improves hydration as well** ← |

> **THE SIGNIFICANCE OF THIS IS LARGER THAN A CONVENIENCE AND IT IS WORTH STATING PROPERLY: the superplasticiser breaks the link between WORKABILITY and WATER CONTENT that otherwise governs concrete.**

> **Before admixtures, a placeable mix required a high water-cement ratio, and a low water-cement ratio meant a mix that could barely be placed — the two requirements were in direct conflict, and every concrete was a compromise between them.**

> **A superplasticiser removes the conflict: a mix can be both fluid and lean in water.**

> **Which is why the entire family of modern high-performance concretes — high strength, self-compacting, low permeability — depends on them.**

> **A water-cement ratio of 0.30 with a 200 mm slump is unattainable without a superplasticiser and routine with one, and concretes of 80 or 100 N/mm² simply could not be placed otherwise.**

**The admixture families, for the distinction:**

| Admixture | Effect |
|---|---|
| **PLASTICISER (water reducer)** ← | **5 to 12 per cent water reduction — lignosulphonate based** ← |
| **SUPERPLASTICISER (high range)** ← | **15 to 30 per cent — naphthalene, melamine or polycarboxylate based; this question** ← |
| **RETARDER** ← | **DELAYS setting — for hot weather, long hauls, and large pours that must remain workable** ← (option b) |
| **ACCELERATOR** ← | **HASTENS setting and early strength — for cold weather and early stripping** ← (option d) |
| **AIR ENTRAINING agent** ← | **Introduces stable microscopic bubbles — FROST resistance and improved workability** ← (option c) |
| **WATERPROOFING / integral permeability reducer** | **Reduces capillary absorption** ← |
| **MINERAL admixtures — fly ash, slag, silica fume** ← | **Pozzolanic materials, added in quantity, not chemical admixtures at all** ← |

> **THE AIR ENTRAINING AGENT IN THE FIFTH ROW DESERVES A NOTE BECAUSE ITS ACTION IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE: it deliberately puts AIR into concrete, which reduces its strength by roughly 5 per cent for each 1 per cent of air.**

> **That is accepted because the bubbles provide expansion room for water freezing in the pores, without which freeze-thaw cycling spalls the concrete apart.**

> **In a high-altitude Nepali context — a bridge deck or a canal lining in Mustang or Solukhumbu — freeze-thaw is a genuine mechanism and air entrainment is appropriate; in the Terai it is an unnecessary loss of strength.**

> **THE FINAL ROW IS A DISTINCTION WORTH KEEPING CLEAR: fly ash, slag and silica fume are MINERAL admixtures used in tens of per cent by weight of cement, replacing part of it.**

> **Chemical admixtures are used in fractions of a per cent and change the paste's behaviour without contributing material.**

> **The two are often discussed together and act quite differently, and a mix using both — a high-slag cement with a polycarboxylate superplasticiser, say — is exploiting two independent mechanisms rather than one.**

> **One caution worth carrying: a superplasticiser's effect is not permanent. Slump loss with a naphthalene-based product can be rapid, so the dose must be timed to the placing rather than to the batching — and re-dosing at the site, rather than adding water, is the correct remedy for a load that has stiffened in transit.**

examTip.trick: **15-30 % water reduction by dispersing flocculated cement particles** and releasing the water trapped inside the flocs. Plasticisers manage only 5-12 %.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is a retarder, (c) an air entrainer, (d) an accelerator.** Air entrainment costs about 5 % strength per 1 % air, accepted for freeze-thaw resistance only.
examTip.mnemonic: **It breaks the link between workability and water** — the conflict every pre-admixture concrete had to compromise. Re-dose at site rather than adding water to a stiffened load.

questions.stem: PLASTIC SHRINKAGE cracking of a concrete slab is distinguished from DRYING SHRINKAGE cracking in that plastic shrinkage cracking:
options: Occurs only in concrete containing no reinforcement
Occurs within the FIRST FEW HOURS
Occurs only after the concrete has reached its full design strength
Is caused by the chemical reaction of the cement rather than by moisture loss
questions.solution:
**It occurs within the FIRST FEW HOURS, while the concrete is still plastic**, when the rate of evaporation from the surface exceeds the rate at which bleed water rises to replace it.

**The forms of shrinkage, which occur at quite different times:**

| Type | When | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| **PLASTIC (early) shrinkage** ← | **First 1 to 8 HOURS, before setting** ← | **Rapid surface EVAPORATION outpacing bleeding — this question** ← |
| **AUTOGENOUS shrinkage** ← | **Days to weeks** | **The hydration reaction's products occupying LESS volume than the reactants — self-desiccation; significant only in low-w/c, rich mixes** ← |
| **DRYING shrinkage** ← | **Months to YEARS** ← | **Loss of adsorbed water from the gel to the atmosphere** ← |
| **CARBONATION shrinkage** | **Long term, at the surface** | **CO₂ reacting with the hydration products** ← |
| **THERMAL contraction** | **Days, in thick members** | **Cooling from the hydration peak** ← |

> **THE TIME COLUMN IS THE WHOLE BASIS OF DIAGNOSIS AND IT IS THE PRACTICAL VALUE OF THIS TABLE: a crack's timing identifies its cause more reliably than its appearance does.**

> **A crack present when the finishers leave the slab is plastic shrinkage.**

> **A crack that appears over the following weeks in a thick element is thermal.**

> **A crack that develops slowly over months and years is drying shrinkage.**

> **So the first question about any crack is WHEN it appeared, and a site record of that is worth more than any amount of subsequent speculation.**

**The appearance and character of plastic shrinkage cracks:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **SHORT, discontinuous, roughly PARALLEL cracks** ← | **Often diagonal to the slab's edges, sometimes in a random map pattern** ← |
| **They do not extend to the slab's edges** ← | **Unlike structural cracks, which run to a free edge or between supports** ← |
| **Shallow — usually 20 to 50 mm deep** ← | **Rarely through the slab** ← |
| **Wide at the surface, tapering rapidly** ← | ← |
| **They can be CLOSED by re-vibration if caught while still plastic** ← | **Which is the immediate remedy** ← |

> **THE CONDITIONS THAT CAUSE IT ARE ENTIRELY PREDICTABLE, WHICH MEANS IT IS AN ENTIRELY PREVENTABLE DEFECT:**

| Condition | Effect |
|---|---|
| **HIGH air temperature** ← | **Raises the evaporation rate** ← |
| **LOW relative humidity** ← | **Raises it further** ← |
| **WIND across the surface** ← | **The single most influential factor — a light breeze can multiply the evaporation rate several times** ← |
| **HIGH concrete temperature** ← | **Warm concrete gives up water faster** ← |
| **Large exposed SURFACE relative to volume** ← | **Which is why SLABS suffer and columns do not** ← |
| **Low-bleed mixes** ← | **A rich or a silica fume mix bleeds little, so there is no water rising to replace what evaporates — such mixes are MORE prone, not less** ← |

> **THE WIND IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE FACTOR MOST UNDERESTIMATED ON SITE AND IT IS THE EASIEST TO REMEDY: wind removes the saturated air layer immediately above the surface, so evaporation proceeds at its maximum rate instead of being self-limiting.**

> **A windbreak of sheeting around a slab being placed on an exposed site is a trivial provision that addresses the dominant cause.**

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE COUNTER-INTUITIVE ONE AND IT CATCHES DESIGNERS OUT: a high-quality, low-water, silica-fume mix is MORE vulnerable to plastic shrinkage than an ordinary one.**

> **Bleeding, which is a defect in most respects, happens to protect the surface during the first hours by continuously replenishing the water that evaporates.**

> **A mix that does not bleed has no such replenishment, so its surface dries almost immediately and cracks readily.**

> **This is why high-performance concrete requires curing to begin sooner and more aggressively than ordinary concrete — fogging or an evaporation retarder applied within minutes of screeding, rather than the following morning — and why an excellent mix badly protected can perform worse than a modest mix well protected.**

The concrete is still plastic, when the rate of EVAPORATION from the surface exceeds the rate at which bleed water rises to replace it.

examTip.trick: **First few hours, while still plastic** — evaporation outruns bleeding. Short, discontinuous, parallel cracks that do not reach the edges, and closable by re-vibration.
examTip.trap: **Low-bleed, low-w/c, silica-fume mixes are MORE prone** — bleeding happens to protect the surface, and a mix that does not bleed has nothing replenishing what evaporates.
examTip.mnemonic: **Diagnose a crack by WHEN it appeared**: hours = plastic, weeks in a thick member = thermal, months to years = drying shrinkage. And WIND is the dominant cause — put up a windbreak.

questions.stem: CREEP of concrete is:
options: The instantaneous elastic deformation on first loading
The contraction of the concrete as it loses moisture to the atmosphere, independent of any load
The gradual increase in STRAIN under a SUSTAINED load, continuing for years and reaching two to three times the initial elastic strain
The reduction in strength of concrete under repeated cycles of loading
questions.solution:
**The gradual increase in STRAIN under a SUSTAINED load**, continuing for years and reaching two to three times the initial elastic strain.

**The distinction from the other time-dependent effects:**

| Effect | Depends on load? | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **ELASTIC strain** ← | **Yes** | **INSTANTANEOUS, recoverable on unloading** ← (option a) |
| **CREEP** ← | **YES — proportional to the sustained stress** ← | **Gradual, largely irrecoverable** ← |
| **SHRINKAGE** ← | **NO — occurs in an unloaded specimen** ← | **Gradual, from moisture loss** ← (option b) |
| **FATIGUE** | **Yes, cyclic** | **Progressive damage under repeated loading** ← (option d) |

> **THE LOAD DEPENDENCE IN THE SECOND COLUMN IS THE DEFINING TEST AND IT IS HOW THE TWO ARE SEPARATED EXPERIMENTALLY: creep needs stress and shrinkage does not.**

> **A loaded specimen and an identical unloaded companion are kept side by side in the same environment; the unloaded one's strain is shrinkage, and the difference between them is creep.**

> **In a real structure the two occur together and both cause the same thing — increasing deformation with time — so they are often lumped together in practice, but they respond to different remedies and must be understood separately.**

**The magnitude, which is what makes creep matter:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Ultimate creep strain is typically 2 to 3 times the initial ELASTIC strain** ← | **So a member's long-term deflection is several times its immediate deflection** ← |
| **About HALF the ultimate creep occurs in the first 2 to 3 months** ← | **The rest over years, at a decreasing rate** ← |
| **The CREEP COEFFICIENT in IS 456 is 2.2 at 7 days of loading, 1.6 at 28 days and 1.1 at one year** ← | **Loading YOUNGER concrete produces MORE creep** ← |
| **The long-term elastic modulus is taken as E_c/(1 + θ)** ← | **The effective modulus method, which is how creep enters a deflection calculation** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW HAS A DIRECT CONSTRUCTION CONSEQUENCE AND IT IS ONE OF THE FEW PLACES WHERE THE PROGRAMME AFFECTS THE STRUCTURE'S LONG-TERM BEHAVIOUR: concrete loaded early creeps more.**

> **So striking props too soon and loading a young slab does not merely risk immediate damage — it commits the member to a permanently larger deflection, because the creep coefficient at 7 days is twice that at one year.**

> **A slab propped for a month and then loaded will deflect noticeably less over its life than the same slab loaded at a week, and no subsequent care can undo that.**

> **This is a real argument against the pressure to strike formwork early on a fast programme, and it is an argument about serviceability that a strength check will never reveal.**

**Where creep is harmful and where it helps, which is worth balancing:**

| Harmful | Beneficial |
|---|---|
| **Long-term DEFLECTION of beams and slabs increases substantially** ← | **RELIEVES stress concentrations, redistributing them by flow** ← |
| **PRESTRESS LOSS — the concrete shortens, so the tendon relaxes** ← | **Reduces SHRINKAGE and TEMPERATURE stresses, which relax over time instead of cracking the member** ← |
| **Increased deflection can crack partitions and finishes** ← | **Softens differential SETTLEMENT effects — a slowly settling foundation is accommodated by creep** ← |
| **Buckling capacity of slender columns is reduced** ← | **Assists moment redistribution in continuous members** ← |
| **Composite members REDISTRIBUTE load from concrete to steel** | **Which can be beneficial or not, depending on the design** ← |

> **THE SECOND BENEFICIAL ROW IS AN IMPORTANT ONE AND IT EXPLAINS WHY CONCRETE STRUCTURES ARE MORE TOLERANT THAN THEIR CALCULATED STRESSES SUGGEST: a restrained concrete member subject to shrinkage or a temperature drop develops tension, and tension cracks concrete.**

> **But creep allows that tension to relax over time, so a stress that would crack the member if applied instantly may be substantially dissipated if it develops slowly.**

> **This is why long walls and slabs survive restraint conditions that an elastic calculation says should crack them, and why the rate at which a strain is imposed matters as much as its magnitude.**

> **The prestress loss in the second harmful row is the mirror image of the same mechanism: creep relaxes the concrete's stress, and in a prestressed member the concrete's stress is the whole point — so what is a blessing in a restrained slab is a straightforward loss in a prestressed beam, and must be computed and allowed for in the initial tensioning.**

examTip.trick: **Strain increasing under SUSTAINED load**, reaching 2-3 times the elastic strain. Creep needs stress; shrinkage does not — that is how the two are separated.
examTip.trap: **Creep coefficient 2.2 at 7 days, 1.6 at 28 days, 1.1 at one year** — loading young concrete permanently commits the member to a larger deflection. An argument against early stripping.
examTip.mnemonic: **Creep also RELAXES restraint stresses**, which is why long walls survive shrinkage that an elastic calculation says should crack them — and why prestress is lost in a prestressed beam.

questions.stem: The REBOUND HAMMER test on hardened concrete in a structure:
options: Measures the concrete's compressive strength directly and definitively
Measures the depth of carbonation of the cover concrete
Determines the position and diameter of the reinforcement
Measures the SURFACE HARDNESS of the concrete, from which strength is inferred only APPROXIMATELY through a correlation
questions.solution:
**It measures the SURFACE HARDNESS of the concrete**, from which strength is inferred only approximately through a correlation — making it a tool for comparing and screening areas rather than for establishing strength.

**What the test does and what limits it:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A spring-driven mass strikes the surface and the REBOUND distance is measured** ← | **Reported as a rebound number** ← |
| **The rebound depends on the surface's ELASTIC properties and hardness** ← | **Which correlate with strength, but only loosely** ← |
| **It interrogates only the outer 30 mm or so** ← | **So it says nothing about the concrete deeper in the member** ← |
| **CARBONATION of the surface raises the reading substantially** ← | **An old carbonated surface can read as much stronger than it is** ← |
| **Surface MOISTURE, texture, and the presence of aggregate or a void just below the point all affect it** ← | **Which is why many readings are averaged and outliers discarded** ← |
| **The hammer's ORIENTATION affects the reading** ← | **Horizontal, upward and downward each need a different correction** ← |
| **Correlation must be established for the PARTICULAR concrete** ← | **A manufacturer's generic curve can be far out for a different aggregate or mix** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MOST SERIOUS SYSTEMATIC ERROR AND IT MATTERS MOST WHERE THE TEST IS MOST OFTEN USED: assessing OLD structures.**

> **Carbonation hardens the surface layer, so an old concrete reads high — and an old structure is precisely the one whose strength is in doubt.**

> **So the rebound hammer flatters exactly the concrete it is called upon to judge, and a favourable reading on a forty-year-old building is close to meaningless without a core to calibrate against.**

**The non-destructive methods and what each is good for:**

| Method | Measures | Best used for |
|---|---|---|
| **REBOUND HAMMER** ← | **Surface hardness** ← | **COMPARING areas, screening for weak zones, mapping uniformity** ← |
| **ULTRASONIC PULSE VELOCITY (UPV)** ← | **The velocity of a sound pulse THROUGH the member** ← | **Detecting internal VOIDS, cracks, honeycombing and assessing overall quality; it interrogates the full thickness** ← |
| **CORE test** ← | **Actual compressive strength of extracted concrete** ← | **The DEFINITIVE strength measure — semi-destructive** ← |
| **COVER METER (rebar locator)** ← | **Position, depth and approximate diameter of bars** ← (option c) | **Verifying cover and locating steel before coring** ← |
| **CARBONATION depth (phenolphthalein)** ← | **How far the alkalinity has been lost** ← (option b) | **Assessing corrosion risk** ← |
| **HALF-CELL POTENTIAL** | **Electrochemical potential of the steel** | **Detecting ACTIVE corrosion** ← |
| **Chloride content, by sampling and titration** | **Chloride at various depths** | **Assessing chloride-induced corrosion risk** ← |

> **THE COMBINATION OF THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS THE STANDARD PRACTICE AND IT IS BETTER THAN EITHER ALONE, which is worth knowing as a method rather than as a fact:**

> **The rebound hammer is quick, so it can cover a whole structure and identify which areas are anomalous.**

> **UPV then examines those areas through their full thickness, distinguishing genuinely poor concrete from a merely poor surface.**

> **Cores are then cut at the few locations that matter, calibrating the indirect measurements and settling the question.**

> **That sequence — screen broadly, investigate selectively, confirm definitively — costs a fraction of coring everywhere and gives a better picture than coring at arbitrary points, since the cores go where the screening said to look.**

> **THE UNDERLYING PRINCIPLE IS WORTH STATING GENERALLY: no non-destructive test measures strength.**

> **Each measures some other property — hardness, pulse velocity, resonance — that correlates with strength through a relationship depending on the aggregate, the mix, the age, the moisture and the carbonation.**

> **So a non-destructive result quoted as a strength in newtons per square millimetre, without a core correlation for that concrete, is an inference presented as a measurement — and it is the commonest misuse of these instruments in practice.**

examTip.trick: **Surface hardness only, over the outer 30 mm** — a comparative and screening tool, not a strength measurement. Option (b) is carbonation depth, (c) a cover meter.
examTip.trap: **Carbonation HARDENS the surface, so old concrete reads high** — the hammer flatters exactly the old structures it is called on to judge. Useless without a core to calibrate against.
examTip.mnemonic: **Screen with the hammer, investigate with UPV, confirm with cores.** No NDT method measures strength — each measures something that correlates with it for that particular concrete.

questions.stem: CARBONATION of concrete leads to corrosion of the reinforcement because it:
options: Reduces the pH of the pore solution from about 13 to below 9
Dissolves the reinforcement chemically
Increases the concrete's permeability so that water reaches the steel
Causes the concrete to expand and spall, exposing the bars directly
questions.solution:
**It reduces the pH of the pore solution from about 13 to below 9, DESTROYING the PASSIVE oxide film that protects the steel in alkaline surroundings.**

**The mechanism:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
