| **Fresh concrete's pore water is highly ALKALINE, pH about 12.5 to 13.5** ← | **From the calcium hydroxide released by cement hydration** ← |
| **At that pH, steel forms a stable PASSIVE film of iron oxide** ← | **A few nanometres thick, and it stops corrosion completely** ← |
| **Atmospheric CO₂ diffuses into the concrete and reacts with the calcium hydroxide** ← | **Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O** ← |
| **This CONSUMES the alkalinity, dropping the pH below about 9** ← | **The carbonation FRONT advancing inward from the surface** ← |
| **Below pH 9 the passive film is no longer stable and DEPASSIVATES** ← | **The steel is now free to corrode wherever oxygen and moisture reach it** ← |
| **Corrosion products occupy 2 to 6 times the volume of the steel consumed** ← | **Which cracks and spalls the cover — the visible symptom, and option (d) confuses it with the cause** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE FACT ON WHICH ALL REINFORCED CONCRETE DEPENDS AND IT DESERVES TO BE STATED AS SUCH: steel embedded in concrete does not corrode, not because the concrete keeps water out, but because the concrete's ALKALINITY keeps the steel passive.**

> **A bar in wet alkaline concrete is safe; a bar in dry carbonated concrete is at risk.**

> **So the cover's job is chemical as much as physical — it maintains an alkaline environment around the steel, and its thickness determines how many years the carbonation front takes to arrive.**

> **This is why cover is specified by EXPOSURE rather than by structural need, and why a reduction in cover on site is a reduction in the structure's service life rather than in its strength.**

**The rate of carbonation:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The depth advances roughly as the SQUARE ROOT of time: d = k√t** ← | **So it slows as it deepens, the CO₂ having further to diffuse** ← |
| **k depends on the concrete's PERMEABILITY above all** ← | **A dense low-w/c concrete may carbonate 5 mm in 50 years; a porous one 25 mm in 10** ← |
| **Carbonation is FASTEST at intermediate humidity, around 50 to 70 per cent** ← | **Not in the wettest conditions** ← |
| **In SATURATED concrete it nearly stops** ← | **CO₂ cannot diffuse through water-filled pores** ← |
| **In BONE DRY concrete it also nearly stops** ← | **The reaction needs water to proceed** ← |

> **THE THIRD TO FIFTH ROWS CONTAIN A GENUINELY SURPRISING RESULT AND IT IS WORTH FOLLOWING THROUGH: carbonation is worst in moderately humid conditions, not in wet ones.**

> **The reaction needs water, so a bone-dry concrete does not carbonate; the CO₂ needs air-filled pores to diffuse through, so a saturated concrete does not carbonate either.**

> **Both conditions must be partly satisfied, and that happens around 50 to 70 per cent relative humidity — which is ordinary sheltered interior and exterior air.**

> **A permanently submerged element therefore carbonates hardly at all, and a sheltered soffit under a bridge deck carbonates readily.**

> **The most damaging condition of all is ALTERNATE wetting and drying, which lets the CO₂ in during the dry phase and supplies the water for corrosion during the wet — which is why splash zones, rain-exposed soffits and the underside of leaking joints are where corrosion is always found first.**

**Carbonation compared with the other durability attacks, to place it:**

| Attack | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **CARBONATION-induced corrosion** ← | **pH drop depassivates the steel — this question; GENERAL corrosion over a wide area** ← |
| **CHLORIDE-induced corrosion** ← | **Chlorides break the passive film LOCALLY even at high pH — PITTING, which is more dangerous because it is concentrated and hidden** ← |
| **SULPHATE attack** ← | **Sulphates react with hydrated C₃A to form expansive ettringite, disrupting the paste** ← |
| **ALKALI-AGGREGATE reaction** ← | **Reactive silica in the aggregate reacts with the cement's alkalis, forming an expansive gel — map cracking** ← |
| **FREEZE-THAW** | **Water expanding on freezing in the pores, spalling the surface** ← |

> **The contrast in the second row is worth carrying: carbonation produces general corrosion that announces itself by rust staining and spalling over an area, while chloride attack produces deep local pits that can substantially reduce a bar's section with very little surface evidence.**

> **So a chloride-affected structure can be considerably more damaged than it looks, and the assessment of one requires chloride profiling and half-cell survey rather than a visual inspection.**

examTip.trick: **pH falls from about 13 to below 9, and the passive oxide film depassivates.** Option (d) is the consequence — spalling from expansive rust — not the cause.
examTip.trap: **Carbonation is FASTEST at 50-70 % RH, not in the wettest conditions** — saturated concrete blocks CO₂ diffusion and bone-dry concrete lacks the water. Alternate wetting and drying is worst.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cover is CHEMICAL protection, not just a barrier** — it keeps the steel alkaline, and d = k√t sets how long that lasts. Reducing cover cuts service life, not strength.

questions.stem: The essential difference between the WORKING STRESS method and the LIMIT STATE method of design is that:
options: The working stress method uses higher grades of concrete
The limit state method ignores the serviceability of the structure
The working stress method keeps stresses within a permissible fraction of the material strength under SERVICE loads using a SINGLE factor of safety
The limit state method applies only to steel structures and the working stress method only to concrete
questions.solution:
**The working stress method keeps stresses within a permissible fraction of the material strength under SERVICE loads using a SINGLE factor of safety, while the limit state method checks the structure against EACH limit state separately using SEPARATE partial factors on loads and on materials.**

**The two methods compared:**

| Aspect | Working stress | Limit state |
|---|---|---|
| **Loads used** | **SERVICE (unfactored) loads** ← | **FACTORED loads for strength; service loads for serviceability** ← |
| **Material behaviour assumed** | **Linear ELASTIC throughout** ← | **The ACTUAL non-linear stress-strain curve up to failure** ← |
| **Safety provided by** | **ONE factor of safety, applied to the material stress** ← | **SEPARATE partial factors: γ_f on each load, γ_m on each material** ← |
| **Concrete permissible stress** | **About f_ck/3** ← | **0.67 f_ck / 1.5 = 0.446 f_ck at the ultimate state** ← |
| **Steel permissible stress** | **About 0.55 f_y** ← | **0.87 f_y** ← |
| **What is checked** | **Stresses only** ← | **Collapse, deflection, cracking, durability, vibration — each as a separate limit state** ← |
| **Economy** | **Conservative and uneconomical** ← | **More economical, using the material's real capacity** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE CONCEPTUAL ADVANCE AND IT IS WORTH SEEING WHY IT MATTERS SO MUCH: a single factor of safety must cover every uncertainty at once.**

> **The uncertainty in the dead load is small — a concrete beam's weight is known within a few per cent. The uncertainty in the imposed load is much larger. The uncertainty in concrete strength is larger than in steel strength, steel being a manufactured product with tight control.**

> **A single factor cannot reflect any of that. It must be large enough for the worst uncertainty, which makes it wastefully large for the best.**

> **Partial factors allow each uncertainty to be covered in proportion: 1.5 on imposed load but 0.9 where dead load is favourable; 1.5 on concrete but only 1.15 on steel.**

> **That is why the limit state method is both safer and more economical than the working stress method — it is not a relaxation of safety but a better-targeted application of it.**

**THE SIXTH ROW IS THE OTHER MAJOR ADVANCE AND IT ADDRESSES A REAL DEFICIENCY OF THE OLDER METHOD:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The working stress method checks STRESSES and infers everything else** ← | **On the assumption that a lightly stressed structure will also be adequately stiff and will not crack** ← |
| **That assumption is unreliable** ← | **A high-strength steel used at its permissible stress gives large strains, hence large deflections and wide cracks, while the stress check passes** ← |
| **The limit state method asks each question DIRECTLY** ← | **Will it collapse? Will it deflect too much? Will it crack too widely? Will it last?** ← |
| **Which is the honest structure of the problem** ← | **Since these are genuinely different requirements with different governing parameters** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW EXPLAINS WHY THE CHANGE BECAME NECESSARY RATHER THAN MERELY DESIRABLE: as higher strength steels came into use, the working stress method's implicit link between stress and serviceability broke down.**

> **With mild steel at a permissible stress of 140 N/mm², strains were small and deflections were rarely a problem, so checking stress happened to protect serviceability as well.**

> **With Fe 415 or Fe 500 at a permissible stress of 230 N/mm² or more, the strains are much larger and deflection and cracking can be excessive in a member whose stresses are perfectly acceptable.**

> **So a method that inferred serviceability from strength stopped working, and the limit state method's separation of the two became unavoidable.**

**Where the working stress method survives, which is worth knowing:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **LIQUID RETAINING structures** ← | **Where crack width is critical, and a low permissible stress in the steel is a direct and simple way to limit it — IS 3370 uses it** ← |
| **Assessment of OLDER structures designed by it** ← | **Comparing like with like** ← |
| **As a check on limit state designs in some circumstances** | ← |

> **The first row is the interesting survival and its logic is sound: in a water tank, the governing requirement is that the concrete should not crack enough to leak, and crack width follows from steel STRESS.**

> **Limiting that stress directly is therefore a more transparent route to the objective than designing for collapse and then checking crack width — so the older method persists precisely where serviceability rather than strength is the real design criterion.**

examTip.trick: **Working stress: service loads, elastic behaviour, ONE factor on material stress. Limit state: factored loads, real stress-strain curve, SEPARATE γ_f and γ_m, each limit state checked.**
examTip.trap: **A single factor must cover the worst uncertainty, so it is wasteful for the best** — dead load is known within a few per cent while imposed load is not, and steel is better controlled than concrete.
examTip.mnemonic: **High-strength steel broke the old method** — at 230 N/mm² the strains give excessive deflection and cracking while the stress check passes. Working stress survives in IS 3370 water tanks.

questions.stem: In the limit state design of a singly reinforced rectangular beam to IS 456, the total compressive force in the concrete and the distance of its centroid from the extreme compression fibre are taken as:
options: 0.446 f_ck b x_u, acting at 0.5 x_u
0.67 f_ck b x_u, acting at 0.5 x_u
0.36 f_ck b x_u, acting at 0.5 x_u
0.36 f_ck b x_u, acting at 0.42 x_u from the extreme compression fibre
questions.solution:
**0.36 f_ck b x_u, acting at 0.42 x_u from the extreme compression fibre.**

**Where the two coefficients come from:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **The design stress block is a PARABOLA up to a strain of 0.002, then a RECTANGLE up to 0.0035** ← | **The idealisation IS 456 adopts** ← |
| **Its peak stress is 0.67 f_ck / 1.5 = 0.446 f_ck** ← | **0.67 converts cube strength to the strength of concrete in a flexural member, and 1.5 is γ_m** ← |
| **The AREA of that combined shape, integrated, is 0.36 f_ck x_u per unit width** ← | **So C = 0.36 f_ck b x_u** ← |
| **Its CENTROID lies 0.42 x_u from the extreme compression fibre** ← | **Computed from the areas of the parabolic and rectangular portions** ← |
| **The LEVER ARM is therefore d − 0.42 x_u** ← | **Which is what enters the moment expression** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN 0.446 AND 0.36 IS THE POINT ON WHICH THE OPTIONS TURN, AND IT IS WORTH BEING CLEAR: 0.446 f_ck is the PEAK STRESS in the block, and 0.36 f_ck is the AVERAGE stress over the depth x_u.**

> **The ratio 0.36/0.446 = 0.81 is simply the shape factor of the parabolic-rectangular block — the fraction of the enclosing rectangle that the actual block fills.**

> **So a candidate who remembers 0.446 has remembered a real number in the wrong role, and the resulting force is 24 per cent too large.**

> **Similarly the centroid at 0.42 x_u rather than 0.5 x_u reflects the block's shape: a rectangle's centroid would be at 0.5, and the parabolic portion near the neutral axis pulls the centroid toward the compression face.**

**The design equations that follow:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Compression in concrete** | **C = 0.36 f_ck b x_u** ← |
| **Tension in steel** | **T = 0.87 f_y A_st** ← |
| **Equilibrium, C = T, gives the neutral axis depth** ← | **x_u = 0.87 f_y A_st / (0.36 f_ck b)** ← |
| **Moment of resistance about the steel** ← | **M_u = 0.36 f_ck b x_u (d − 0.42 x_u)** ← |
| **Or equivalently about the concrete** | **M_u = 0.87 f_y A_st (d − 0.42 x_u)** ← |

> **THE TWO EXPRESSIONS FOR M_u IN THE LAST TWO ROWS ARE IDENTICAL IN VALUE AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING WHY, because the choice between them saves work: taking moments about the steel eliminates T, and taking them about the concrete's centroid eliminates C.**

> **Both give the same answer once x_u is known from equilibrium, so the second is generally the quicker for an analysis problem where A_st is given.**

> **For a DESIGN problem, where M_u is given and A_st is required, the second expression is used with x_u expressed in terms of A_st, giving a quadratic — or the design is done from tables of M_u/bd² against the percentage of steel, which is how it is normally done in practice.**

**AND THE 0.67 IN THE SECOND ROW OF THE FIRST TABLE DESERVES A NOTE, BECAUSE IT IS OFTEN TAKEN FOR A SAFETY FACTOR AND IS NOT ONE:**

> **It accounts for the difference between the strength of a concrete CUBE tested in a few minutes and the strength of concrete in a real member under a sustained load.**

> **Two effects combine in it: the cube's platen restraint flatters its strength, as discussed for the cube-cylinder comparison, and a sustained load reduces concrete's strength by roughly 15 per cent below its short-term value.**

> **So 0.67 is a conversion between a test result and a material property, and γ_m = 1.5 is the safety factor applied afterwards.**

> **Keeping the two separate matters when reading other codes, which may partition the same total reduction differently between a conversion coefficient and a material factor — and comparing a single number between codes without checking what it includes is a reliable route to error.**

examTip.trick: **C = 0.36 f_ck b x_u at 0.42 x_u from the top; lever arm d − 0.42 x_u.** Then M_u = 0.87 f_y A_st (d − 0.42 x_u).
examTip.trap: **0.446 f_ck is the PEAK stress, 0.36 f_ck the AVERAGE** — their ratio 0.81 is the block's shape factor. Using 0.446 as the average overstates the force by 24 %.
examTip.mnemonic: **0.67 is not a safety factor** — it converts cube strength to in-member sustained strength (platen restraint plus about 15 % sustained-load loss). γ_m = 1.5 comes after it.

questions.stem: For a beam reinforced with Fe 415 steel, IS 456 limits the depth of the neutral axis at the ultimate limit state to:
options: x_u,max = 0.48 d
x_u,max = 0.53 d
x_u,max = 0.46 d
x_u,max = 0.36 d
questions.solution:
**x_u,max = 0.48 d.**

**The limits for the three grades:**

| Steel grade | x_u,max / d |
|---|---|
| **Fe 250 (mild steel)** ← | **0.53** ← (option b) |
| **Fe 415** ← | **0.48** ← |
| **Fe 500** ← | **0.46** ← (option c) |

> **THE VALUES FALL AS THE STEEL GRADE RISES, AND THE REASON IS WORTH DERIVING RATHER THAN MEMORISING, because the derivation makes all three recoverable:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The limit is set by requiring the STEEL to have YIELDED at failure** ← | **Which is what makes the failure ductile** ← |
| **The concrete's strain at the compression face is fixed at 0.0035** ← | **The code's assumed ultimate strain** ← |
| **The steel must have reached its yield strain, 0.87 f_y/E_s plus 0.002** ← | **For Fe 415: 0.87 × 415/200,000 + 0.002 = 0.0018 + 0.002 = 0.0038** ← |
| **By similar triangles across the section, x_u,max/d = 0.0035/(0.0035 + ε_y)** ← | **= 0.0035/0.0073 = 0.48 for Fe 415** ← |
| **A HIGHER grade steel has a LARGER yield strain, so the neutral axis must be HIGHER** ← | **Which is why the limit falls from 0.53 to 0.48 to 0.46** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE ESSENTIAL LOGIC AND IT IS A GEOMETRIC ARGUMENT ABOUT STRAINS: high-strength steel needs to stretch further before it yields.**

> **For it to stretch that far while the concrete's strain is capped at 0.0035, the neutral axis must sit closer to the compression face — leaving more of the depth in tension, and more strain available at the steel's level.**

> **So the limit on x_u is not an arbitrary code rule but a direct consequence of insisting that the steel yields first.**

**Which is exactly the classification of sections:**

| Section | Condition | Failure |
|---|---|---|
| **UNDER-reinforced** ← | **x_u < x_u,max** ← | **Steel yields FIRST, the section deflects and cracks visibly, then the concrete crushes — DUCTILE and with warning** ← |
| **BALANCED** ← | **x_u = x_u,max** ← | **Steel reaches yield exactly as the concrete reaches 0.0035 — the theoretical boundary** ← |
| **OVER-reinforced** ← | **x_u > x_u,max** ← | **CONCRETE crushes while the steel is still elastic — SUDDEN, brittle, without warning** ← |

> **THE CODE PERMITS ONLY THE FIRST OF THESE, AND THE PROHIBITION OF THE THIRD IS THE WHOLE PURPOSE OF THE x_u,max LIMIT.**

> **An over-reinforced section is not weak — it may carry a large moment — but it fails without warning, which is unacceptable in a structure that people occupy.**

> **An under-reinforced beam gives warning: it deflects, its cracks widen visibly, and the deflection continues to grow while the load is held.**

> **That warning is what allows a building to be evacuated, and it is why ductility is valued above efficiency in structural design.**

**And what to do when a section calculates as over-reinforced, which is the practical follow-through:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **INCREASE the section's depth** ← | **The best answer, and usually the cheapest — it reduces x_u/d directly** ← |
| **Increase the concrete GRADE** ← | **A higher f_ck raises the compression capacity, so a smaller x_u carries the same force** ← |
| **Provide COMPRESSION reinforcement — a doubly reinforced section** ← | **The steel in compression takes the excess, so the concrete's compression zone need not deepen** ← |
| **Widen the beam** | **Less effective than deepening, since the moment capacity goes with d²** ← |

> **The last row is worth noting for the ratio it implies: moment capacity depends on the width to the first power and on the depth roughly to the second, so 50 mm of extra depth is worth far more than 50 mm of extra width.**

> **A designer constrained on depth by headroom or by floor-to-floor height — which is the usual constraint — is therefore driven to compression steel or a higher grade, and that is why doubly reinforced beams are so common in buildings and comparatively rare in bridges, where depth is available.**

examTip.trick: **Fe 250: 0.53, Fe 415: 0.48, Fe 500: 0.46.** Falling as the grade rises, because a stronger steel needs a larger strain to yield.
examTip.trap: **Derive it: x_u,max/d = 0.0035/(0.0035 + ε_y)**, with ε_y = 0.87f_y/E_s + 0.002. That recovers all three values and explains the trend.
examTip.mnemonic: **The limit exists to force the STEEL to yield first** — an over-reinforced beam is not weak, it is brittle, and gives no warning. Warning is what lets a building be evacuated.

questions.stem: IS 456 requires the MINIMUM area of tension reinforcement in a beam to be:
options: 0.12 per cent of the gross cross-sectional area
A_st/(b d) = 0.85/f_y, that is about 0.205 per cent for Fe 415
1.0 per cent of the effective area
0.04 per cent of the gross area
questions.solution:
**A_st/(b d) = 0.85/f_y, that is about 0.205 per cent for Fe 415.**

**The reinforcement limits for a beam:**

| Limit | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **MINIMUM tension steel** ← | **A_st/(bd) = 0.85/f_y — about 0.205 % for Fe 415, 0.34 % for Fe 250, 0.17 % for Fe 500** ← |
| **MAXIMUM tension steel** ← | **0.04 b D, that is 4 per cent of the GROSS area** ← |
| **Maximum compression steel** ← | **Also 4 per cent of the gross area** ← |
| **Minimum steel in a SLAB (distribution and main)** ← | **0.15 % of gross area for mild steel, 0.12 % for deformed bars** ← (option a is the slab figure) |

> **OPTION (a) IS THE SLAB MINIMUM RATHER THAN THE BEAM MINIMUM, AND THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE TWO PROVISIONS IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING because they exist for different reasons:**

> **The SLAB minimum of 0.12 per cent is a SHRINKAGE AND TEMPERATURE requirement — enough steel to distribute cracking, applied to the gross area and independent of the steel's strength in the same way.**

> **The BEAM minimum of 0.85/f_y is a DUCTILITY requirement, and it depends on f_y because that is what determines the steel's contribution.**

**WHY A MINIMUM IS NEEDED AT ALL IS THE INTERESTING PART, AND THE REASONING IS NOT OBVIOUS:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A beam with VERY LITTLE steel has a moment capacity LESS than its own CRACKING moment** ← | **The plain concrete section, before it cracks, resists more than the cracked reinforced section can** ← |
| **So the first crack causes IMMEDIATE failure** ← | **At the instant the concrete cracks, the tension it was carrying transfers to the steel, which cannot take it and yields or fractures at once** ← |
| **The failure is therefore SUDDEN and occurs at the cracking load** ← | **Which is the very brittle behaviour that reinforcement is meant to prevent** ← |
| **The minimum steel ensures the cracked section can carry MORE than the cracking moment** ← | **So the beam cracks, redistributes to the steel, and continues to carry load with warning** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW DESCRIBES A GENUINELY DANGEROUS CONDITION AND IT IS WORTH DWELLING ON, because it is counter-intuitive: an under-steeled beam is more brittle than a plain concrete one.**

> **A plain concrete beam fails when it cracks, and everyone expects that.**

> **A lightly reinforced beam looks like a reinforced beam, is expected to behave like one, and fails at the cracking load without the ductile phase that reinforcement exists to provide.**

> **So the minimum steel requirement is not about strength — a lightly loaded lintel might be strong enough with less — it is about ensuring the member behaves as reinforced concrete rather than as cracked plain concrete.**

**And the MAXIMUM of 4 per cent, which has quite different reasons:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **PLACING and COMPACTING become impossible** ← | **Congested steel prevents concrete reaching the bottom of the beam, giving honeycombing exactly where the tension steel needs its bond** ← |
| **BOND cannot be developed with so many bars** ← | **The perimeter available for bond does not keep pace with the area of steel** ← |
| **The section becomes over-reinforced and brittle in any case** ← | **So the 4 per cent limit and the x_u,max limit tend to bite together** ← |
| **It is uneconomic** ← | **A section needing 4 per cent steel should be larger** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL LIMIT IN REALITY AND IT USUALLY BINDS BEFORE THE CODE'S 4 PER CENT DOES: long before a beam reaches 4 per cent steel, the bars are too closely spaced for the concrete's aggregate to pass between them.**

> **IS 456 accordingly requires a clear horizontal spacing of at least the greater of the bar diameter or the maximum aggregate size plus 5 mm, and a vertical spacing between layers of at least 15 mm or two-thirds the aggregate size.**

> **Those spacing rules, applied to a beam of realistic width, generally cap the steel well below 4 per cent — and a designer who satisfies the area limit while violating the spacing rules has produced a drawing that cannot be built.**

examTip.trick: **A_st/(bd) = 0.85/f_y** — about 0.205 % for Fe 415. Option (a), 0.12 %, is the SLAB minimum, which is a shrinkage requirement rather than a ductility one.
examTip.trap: **An under-steeled beam is MORE brittle than a plain one** — its cracked capacity is below its cracking moment, so the first crack fails it immediately, while it looks like a reinforced beam.
examTip.mnemonic: **Maximum is 4 % of the GROSS area, but BAR SPACING binds first** — clear spacing of at least the bar diameter or aggregate size + 5 mm. Meeting the area limit while breaking the spacing rules is unbuildable.

questions.stem: The EFFECTIVE SPAN of a simply supported beam or slab, as defined by IS 456, is taken as:
options: The clear span between the faces of the supports in all cases
The centre-to-centre distance between the supports in all cases
The CLEAR SPAN plus the EFFECTIVE DEPTH, or the centre-to-centre distance between supports, whichever is LESS
The clear span plus the full width of both supports
questions.solution:
**The CLEAR SPAN plus the EFFECTIVE DEPTH, or the centre-to-centre distance between supports, whichever is LESS.**

**The effective span in the various cases:**

| Case | Effective span |
|---|---|
| **SIMPLY SUPPORTED beam or slab** ← | **The LESSER of (clear span + effective depth) and (centre to centre of supports)** ← |
| **CONTINUOUS beam, support width ≤ 1/12 of clear span** ← | **The lesser of (clear span + d) and (centre to centre)** ← |
| **Continuous beam, WIDER support, with one end fixed** | **Clear span** ← |
| **Continuous beam, wider support, both ends continuous** | **Clear span** ← |
| **CANTILEVER** ← | **Clear projection PLUS half the effective depth — but measured to the face of the support where it forms part of a continuous beam** ← |
| **FRAMES** | **Centre to centre of the members** ← |

> **THE 'WHICHEVER IS LESS' PROVISION IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE PART THAT REQUIRES THOUGHT AND IT IS EASILY MISAPPLIED, so it is worth seeing what it is doing.**

> **The clear span plus the effective depth is a recognition that the reaction is not concentrated at the support's face — it spreads into the support, so the effective point of support lies inboard of the face by roughly half the depth at each end.**

> **The centre-to-centre distance is the conservative limit: however wide the support, the reaction cannot act beyond its centre.**

> **So for a NARROW support the centre-to-centre distance is smaller and governs, and for a WIDE support the clear span plus d is smaller and governs.**

> **Taking the lesser of the two is therefore not an arbitrary rule but the smaller of two upper bounds, and it happens to give the sensible answer in both extremes.**

**THE EFFECTIVE DEPTH d, WHICH APPEARS IN ALL OF THIS, MUST ALSO BE DEFINED CAREFULLY:**

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Overall depth D** ← | **The full depth of the member** ← |
| **EFFECTIVE depth d** ← | **From the extreme COMPRESSION fibre to the CENTROID of the TENSION reinforcement** ← |
| **Clear cover** ← | **From the concrete surface to the nearest surface of the reinforcement — including the stirrup** ← |
| **So d = D − cover − stirrup diameter − half the main bar diameter** ← | **For a single layer of bars** ← |
| **With TWO layers, d is measured to the centroid of the group** ← | **Which is deeper into the section, so d is smaller than for one layer** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS AN ARITHMETIC STEP THAT IS ROUTINELY GOT WRONG IN EXAMINATIONS AND OCCASIONALLY ON DRAWINGS: the cover is measured to the STIRRUP, not to the main bar.**

> **For a beam of 450 mm overall depth with 25 mm cover, 8 mm stirrups and 20 mm main bars, d = 450 − 25 − 8 − 10 = 407 mm, not 450 − 25 = 425 mm.**

> **The 18 mm difference is small in itself but it enters the moment capacity through the lever arm and through d² in the deflection check, and a habit of omitting the stirrup and the half-bar allowance produces a consistent over-estimate.**

> **THE TWO-LAYER CASE IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE MORE SIGNIFICANT ERROR AND IT ARISES WHENEVER A BEAM IS HEAVILY REINFORCED: bars in two layers have their centroid well above the bottom layer, so the effective depth is materially reduced.**

> **A designer who computes the steel required using a single-layer d, finds it will not fit in one layer, and then places it in two without recomputing has reduced the lever arm without reducing the demand — and the beam is under-designed by whatever the change in d amounts to.**

> **The correct sequence is to assume a d, compute the steel, arrange the bars, recompute d from the actual arrangement, and check the capacity again — an iteration that is short but must not be skipped.**

examTip.trick: **The LESSER of (clear span + d) and (centre to centre).** Narrow supports: centre-to-centre governs. Wide supports: clear span + d governs.
examTip.trap: **Cover is measured to the STIRRUP** — d = D − cover − stirrup dia − half the bar dia. Not D − cover.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two layers of bars put the centroid higher, reducing d** — so recompute d from the actual bar arrangement and recheck. Assuming, arranging and never rechecking under-designs the beam.

questions.stem: In the WORKING STRESS method of design, the MODULAR RATIO m is taken as:
options: E_s / E_c, computed from the actual moduli of the two materials
A constant value of 13.33 for all grades of concrete
The ratio of the permissible steel stress to the permissible concrete stress
280 / (3 σ_cbc), which builds in an allowance for the long-term CREEP of the concrete and therefore gives a value HIGHER than the ratio of the short-term elastic moduli
questions.solution:
**280 / (3 σ_cbc)** — which builds in an allowance for the long-term CREEP of the concrete and therefore gives a value higher than the ratio of the short-term elastic moduli.

**The values that result:**

| Grade | σ_cbc (N/mm²) | m = 280/(3σ_cbc) |
|---|---|---|
| **M15** | **5.0** | **18.67** ← |
| **M20** | **7.0** | **13.33** ← |
| **M25** | **8.5** | **10.98** ← |
| **M30** | **10.0** | **9.33** ← |

> **OPTION (b) IS THE M20 VALUE, WHICH IS SO WIDELY USED THAT IT IS OFTEN MISTAKEN FOR A UNIVERSAL CONSTANT — AND IT IS NOT: m falls as the concrete grade rises, because a stronger concrete is stiffer and the steel is therefore relatively less dominant.**

**Why the code's value differs from E_s/E_c, which is the substance of the question:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The short-term ratio would be E_s/E_c = 200,000 / 5,000√f_ck** ← | **For M20 that is 200,000/22,360 = 8.9** ← |
| **The code's value for M20 is 13.33 — half again as large** ← | **A deliberate difference, not an approximation** ← |
| **The difference accounts for CREEP** ← | **Under sustained load the concrete's effective modulus falls, so the steel takes a progressively larger share of the compression** ← |
| **A larger m models exactly that redistribution** ← | **The transformed section places more emphasis on the steel** ← |
| **Using the short-term ratio would UNDER-estimate the steel's long-term stress** ← | **Which is the unsafe direction** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS ARE THE ESSENTIAL POINT AND IT IS A GOOD ILLUSTRATION OF WHAT A DESIGN CONSTANT DOES: m is not a material property, it is a modelling parameter chosen so that an elastic analysis predicts the long-term stresses correctly.**

> **The real concrete creeps; the elastic analysis does not know how to creep; so the modular ratio is inflated to make the elastic answer come out where the creeping answer would.**

> **This is the same device as the effective modulus method used for creep deflections in limit state design — E_c/(1 + θ) — approached from the other end.**

> **Recognising both as the same idea is useful, and it removes the puzzle of why the working stress method's m looks wrong when checked against the moduli.**

**How m is used, for completeness:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **The TRANSFORMED SECTION** ← | **Steel of area A_s is replaced by an equivalent concrete area of m·A_s, so a single homogeneous elastic section can be analysed** ← |
| **In the COMPRESSION zone, the equivalent area is (m − 1)A_sc** ← | **The −1 avoiding double-counting the concrete the bar displaces** ← |
| **The neutral axis is found from the transformed section's centroid** ← | **First moments of area equated about it** ← |
| **Stresses are then computed elastically and compared with the permissible values** ← | **σ_cbc for concrete, σ_st for steel** ← |

> **THE (m − 1) IN THE SECOND ROW IS A DETAIL WORTH KEEPING STRAIGHT AND IT DISTINGUISHES THE TWO ZONES: in the TENSION zone the concrete is assumed cracked and to carry nothing, so the steel's transformed area is the full m·A_st — there is no concrete there to double-count.**

> **In the COMPRESSION zone the concrete is intact and is already included in the gross area, so the bar's contribution is only the EXCESS over the concrete it replaces, hence (m − 1).**

> **Using m instead of (m − 1) in the compression zone counts the displaced concrete twice, which over-estimates the section slightly — a small error, but a conceptual one that indicates the transformed section has not been properly understood.**

examTip.trick: **m = 280/(3σ_cbc)** — 18.67 for M15, 13.33 for M20, 10.98 for M25. Option (b) is the M20 value mistaken for a constant.
examTip.trap: **It is deliberately HIGHER than E_s/E_c (13.33 against 8.9 for M20)** — the excess models CREEP, under which the steel progressively takes more of the compression.
examTip.mnemonic: **Transformed area is m·A_st in tension but (m − 1)·A_sc in compression** — the −1 avoids double-counting the concrete the bar displaces, since that zone is uncracked.

questions.stem: The NOMINAL SHEAR STRESS τ_v in a reinforced concrete beam of rectangular section is computed as:
options: V_u / (b D), using the overall depth
V_u / (b d), using the effective depth
1.5 V_u / (b d), the maximum value of the parabolic distribution
questions.solution:
**V_u / (b d), using the effective depth.**

**The definition and what it is not:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **τ_v = V_u / (b d)** ← | **The factored shear force divided by the width times the EFFECTIVE depth** ← |
| **It is a NOMINAL stress, not the actual maximum shear stress** ← | **The real distribution over a cracked reinforced section is nothing like uniform** ← |
| **The factor 1.5 for a parabolic distribution is NOT applied** ← | **That belongs to an uncracked homogeneous elastic section** ← (option c) |
| **The EFFECTIVE depth is used, not the overall depth** ← | ← (option a) |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE CONCEPTUAL POINT AND IT MATTERS FOR HOW THE WHOLE SHEAR PROVISION IS READ: τ_v is a convenient index rather than a physical stress.**

> **The actual state of stress near a shear crack in a reinforced beam involves aggregate interlock across the crack, dowel action of the longitudinal bars, the compression zone's shear capacity and arch action — none of which is captured by a single stress figure.**

> **So τ_v is defined simply and consistently, and the permissible value τ_c is derived EMPIRICALLY from tests on beams — the two being calibrated together.**

> **This is why τ_c is given in a table against the concrete grade and the percentage of tension steel rather than by a formula from first principles: the whole provision is a curve-fit to test results, expressed in terms of a nominal stress.**

**The design procedure:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Compute τ_v = V_u/(bd)** ← | ← |
| **2. Find τ_c from Table 19, by grade and by the percentage of TENSION steel** ← | **More tension steel gives a higher τ_c — because the bars restrain the crack and provide dowel action** ← |
| **3. Check τ_v against τ_c,max** ← | **The absolute ceiling, 2.8 N/mm² for M20 and 3.1 for M25 — if exceeded, the SECTION must be enlarged; no amount of stirrups will do** ← |
| **4. If τ_v ≤ τ_c** | **Provide MINIMUM shear reinforcement only** ← |
| **5. If τ_c < τ_v ≤ τ_c,max** | **Design stirrups for the EXCESS shear, V_us = V_u − τ_c b d** ← |

> **THE CEILING IN STEP 3 IS THE PROVISION MOST WORTH UNDERSTANDING, BECAUSE IT IS ABSOLUTE AND CANNOT BE DESIGNED AROUND: above τ_c,max the concrete itself fails by crushing of the web, in DIAGONAL COMPRESSION.**

> **Stirrups resist the diagonal TENSION across a shear crack. They do nothing whatever about the diagonal COMPRESSION in the strut between cracks.**

> **So a beam whose τ_v exceeds τ_c,max cannot be rescued with more stirrups — the concrete web is the limiting element and it must be made larger or of higher grade.**

> **A design that responds to a high shear stress by adding stirrups without checking the ceiling has misunderstood the failure mode it is guarding against, and the beam will crush its web regardless of how much steel surrounds it.**

**AND THE DEPENDENCE OF τ_c ON THE TENSION STEEL IN STEP 2 IS WORTH A NOTE, since it surprises people:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **τ_c rises with the percentage of LONGITUDINAL tension steel** ← | **From about 0.28 N/mm² at 0.15 % to 0.82 N/mm² at 3 % for M20** ← |
| **Because the longitudinal bars cross the inclined crack** ← | **Providing dowel action and restraining the crack's width** ← |
| **A narrower crack transmits more shear by AGGREGATE INTERLOCK** ← | **Which is a major component of a beam's shear capacity** ← |
| **So tension steel provided for BENDING also improves SHEAR capacity** ← | **The two are not independent** ← |
| **Which means CURTAILING the tension steel reduces τ_c at the curtailment point** ← | **A place where the shear is often high, since curtailment happens toward the supports** ← |

> **The last row is a real design trap: bars are curtailed where the moment falls, which is toward the support, and the shear is greatest at the support.**

> **So the section just beyond a curtailment can have a reduced τ_c and a near-maximum shear at once — which is why IS 456 requires additional shear reinforcement at curtailment points in the tension zone, and why the curtailment detail is checked for shear and not only for moment.**

examTip.trick: **τ_v = V_u/(bd)** — effective depth, and no 1.5 factor. It is a nominal index calibrated against an empirical τ_c, not a real stress.
examTip.trap: **τ_c,max (2.8 for M20, 3.1 for M25) is absolute** — above it the web crushes in diagonal COMPRESSION, and stirrups only resist diagonal TENSION. Enlarge the section.
examTip.mnemonic: **τ_c rises with the LONGITUDINAL steel** (dowel action and aggregate interlock) — so curtailing bars cuts τ_c near the support where shear is greatest. Hence extra stirrups at curtailment.

questions.stem: VERTICAL STIRRUPS resist shear in a reinforced concrete beam by:
options: CROSSING the inclined shear crack and carrying the DIAGONAL TENSION across it in the manner of the tension members of a truss
Increasing the beam's effective depth
Preventing the longitudinal bars from buckling
Confining the concrete so that its compressive strength is increased
questions.solution:
**By CROSSING the inclined shear crack and carrying the DIAGONAL TENSION across it in the manner of the tension members of a truss** — while the concrete between cracks acts as the compression diagonals.

**The truss analogy, which is how shear in a reinforced beam is properly understood:**

| Element of the analogy | Corresponding part of the beam |
|---|---|
| **The top CHORD in compression** ← | **The concrete compression zone** ← |
| **The bottom CHORD in tension** ← | **The longitudinal tension reinforcement** ← |
| **The DIAGONAL members in compression** ← | **The concrete struts between the inclined cracks** ← |
| **The VERTICAL members in tension** ← | **The STIRRUPS** ← |

> **THE ANALOGY EXPLAINS BOTH WHY STIRRUPS WORK AND WHERE THEIR LIMIT LIES, AND IT ACCOUNTS FOR SEVERAL PROVISIONS AT ONCE:**

> **Shear in a beam produces DIAGONAL TENSION at roughly 45 degrees, and concrete is weak in tension — so it cracks along the perpendicular to that tension, giving the characteristic inclined shear crack.**

> **A vertical stirrup crosses such a crack and holds the two faces together, carrying the tension the concrete could not.**

> **The concrete between adjacent cracks is then in COMPRESSION as a diagonal strut, which it can sustain — being strong in compression.**

> **So the cracked beam functions as a truss, and its capacity is limited either by the stirrups yielding (a tension failure, which is ductile and which the design controls) or by the struts crushing (the τ_c,max ceiling, which is brittle and which no stirrup can prevent).**

**Why INCLINED stirrups or bent-up bars are theoretically better, and why vertical stirrups are used anyway:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A stirrup inclined at 45 degrees is PERPENDICULAR to the crack** ← | **So it is loaded axially and used most efficiently** ← |
| **A vertical stirrup crosses the crack obliquely** ← | **So only its vertical component resists, which is less efficient** ← |
| **But vertical stirrups are FAR easier to fabricate, place and fix** ← | **And they work for shear of EITHER sign, which matters under reversing load** ← |
| **Inclined bars work in one direction only** ← | **So they are useless if the shear reverses — as it does under earthquake or wind** ← |
| **Hence vertical stirrups are standard, and bent-up bars are now rare** ← | **Bent-up bars were common when steel was expensive and labour cheap** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE DECISIVE OBJECTION TO INCLINED SHEAR REINFORCEMENT IN A SEISMIC REGION AND IT SETTLES THE MATTER: an earthquake reverses the shear in every member many times.**

> **A bent-up bar inclined to suit one direction of shear is a diagonal in the wrong direction when the load reverses, and it contributes nothing.**

> **So the modest theoretical efficiency of inclined reinforcement is worthless where the load reverses, and vertical stirrups — which are symmetric and therefore indifferent to the direction — are the only sensible choice.**

> **IS 13920 accordingly requires closed stirrups with 135-degree hooks in ductile detailing, and dispenses with bent-up bars altogether.**

**And options (c) and (d) are worth acknowledging, because stirrups do both those things as well:**

| Secondary function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Holding the longitudinal bars in position during concreting** ← | **A practical necessity, and the reason stirrups appear even where shear is negligible** ← |
| **Preventing BUCKLING of compression bars** ← | **Which is the primary function of LATERAL TIES in a COLUMN** ← (option c) |
| **CONFINING the concrete, raising its strain capacity** ← | **Which is the purpose of closely spaced closed stirrups in a PLASTIC HINGE zone** ← (option d) |
| **Resisting TORSION, in combination with longitudinal steel** ← | ← |

> **The third row is genuinely important in its own right even though it is not the answer here: confinement is why IS 13920 demands stirrup spacing as close as d/4 within a distance of 2d from the face of a beam-column joint.**

> **In that zone the stirrups' job is no longer principally to carry shear but to confine the concrete core so that it can sustain large compressive strains without disintegrating — which is what allows the plastic hinge to rotate rather than crush.**

> **So the same bar serves as a shear member along the span and as confinement at the ends, and the spacing rules for the two duties are quite different.**

examTip.trick: **The truss analogy: compression zone and tension steel are the chords, concrete struts the compression diagonals, stirrups the tension verticals.**
examTip.trap: **Bent-up bars work for shear of ONE SIGN only** — useless when an earthquake reverses it. Which is why vertical closed stirrups are standard and IS 13920 drops bent-up bars.
examTip.mnemonic: **Stirrups yielding is ductile; struts crushing is the τ_c,max ceiling and no stirrup helps.** And near a joint their job becomes CONFINEMENT, at d/4 spacing — a different duty, different rule.

questions.stem: IS 456 requires MINIMUM shear reinforcement to be provided in a beam even where the nominal shear stress τ_v is less than τ_c, principally because:
options: It is needed to hold the longitudinal bars in place and nothing more
It guards against a SUDDEN diagonal tension failure should the shear exceed the calculated value
The code requires it only for beams deeper than 750 mm
It increases the beam's flexural capacity
questions.solution:
**It guards against a SUDDEN diagonal tension failure should the shear exceed the calculated value, holds the longitudinal bars in position, resists any unforeseen torsion, and improves the ductility of the member.**

**The reasons, each of which is real:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **A shear failure without stirrups is SUDDEN and BRITTLE** ← | **The diagonal crack opens and the beam fails with no warning — quite unlike a flexural failure** ← |
| **τ_c is an EMPIRICAL value with real scatter** ← | **A section computed as just adequate may not be** ← |
| **The actual shear may EXCEED the calculated value** ← | **Unforeseen loading, settlement, a load applied where none was assumed** ← |
| **Incidental TORSION is almost always present** ← | **An eccentric load, a slab on one side only, a continuity moment from a transverse beam** ← |
| **The stirrups hold the longitudinal bars in position while concreting** ← | **Which is a practical necessity in itself** ← |
| **They confine the concrete slightly, improving ductility** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE REASON THAT JUSTIFIES THE OTHERS AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: shear failure is the failure mode a designer least wants, because it gives no warning at all.**

> **A beam failing in flexure sags visibly, cracks widely at the soffit, and does so over a period — the classic ductile behaviour that the whole limit state philosophy is arranged to secure.**

> **A beam failing in shear without stirrups splits diagonally and drops. There is no deflection to observe and no time to react.**

> **So the consequence of being slightly wrong about shear is far worse than the consequence of being slightly wrong about moment, and the code's response is to require a minimum provision everywhere rather than to rely on the calculation being right.**

**The minimum requirement itself:**

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| **A_sv/(b s_v) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f_y)** ← | **The minimum area of shear reinforcement per unit length** ← |
| **Equivalently, A_sv ≥ 0.4 b s_v /(0.87 f_y)** ← | ← |
| **MAXIMUM spacing: the LEAST of 0.75 d, or 300 mm** ← | **For vertical stirrups** ← |
| **And for inclined stirrups at 45 degrees: the least of d or 300 mm** | ← |

> **THE MAXIMUM SPACING IN THE THIRD ROW IS AS IMPORTANT AS THE AREA REQUIREMENT AND IT IS THE ONE MORE OFTEN VIOLATED, so it is worth understanding what governs it.**

> **A stirrup only resists shear if the crack actually crosses it.**

> **An inclined crack at roughly 45 degrees extends across a horizontal distance of about d, so a spacing greater than about d admits the possibility of a crack passing BETWEEN two stirrups without crossing either.**

> **The limit of 0.75 d ensures at least one and generally two stirrups cross every potential crack, which is why the limit is expressed as a fraction of the depth rather than as an absolute distance.**

> **The 300 mm cap then applies to deep beams, where 0.75 d would be a very wide spacing in absolute terms.**

> **THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE IS THAT THE CENTRAL REGION OF A SIMPLY SUPPORTED BEAM — WHERE THE SHEAR IS NEAR ZERO AND THE MOMENT IS GREATEST — STILL CARRIES STIRRUPS AT NO MORE THAN 0.75 d SPACING.**

> **A drawing that shows closely spaced stirrups near the supports and none at all at midspan is wrong, and a common enough error to be worth recognising: the requirement is a minimum everywhere along the beam, not a provision that lapses where the shear calculation permits.**

examTip.trick: **Shear failure is SUDDEN and gives no warning** — so a minimum is required everywhere rather than relying on the calculation. Plus bar positioning, incidental torsion and ductility.
examTip.trap: **A_sv/(b s_v) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f_y), and spacing ≤ the LEAST of 0.75d or 300 mm** — the spacing limit is violated more often than the area requirement.
examTip.mnemonic: **0.75d exists so a 45° crack cannot pass BETWEEN two stirrups** — which is why it is a fraction of the depth. Stirrups are needed at midspan too, where shear is near zero.

questions.stem: The BASIC span to effective depth ratios given by IS 456 for controlling the deflection of beams and slabs are:
options: 10 for cantilevers, 25 for simply supported and 30 for continuous members
5 for cantilevers, 15 for simply supported and 20 for continuous members
7 for CANTILEVERS, 20 for SIMPLY SUPPORTED and 26 for CONTINUOUS members
12 for cantilevers, 24 for simply supported and 32 for continuous members
questions.solution:
**7 for CANTILEVERS, 20 for SIMPLY SUPPORTED and 26 for CONTINUOUS members.**

**The ratios and the reason they differ:**

| Support condition | Basic span/d | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **CANTILEVER** ← | **7** ← | **No support at the free end, so a given span deflects far more; the deflection of a cantilever under uniform load is 48 times that of a simply supported beam of the same span** ← |
| **SIMPLY SUPPORTED** ← | **20** ← | **The reference case** ← |
| **CONTINUOUS** ← | **26** ← | **End restraint reduces the midspan deflection, so a slenderer member is acceptable** ← |

> **THE 48-FOLD FIGURE IN THE FIRST ROW IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT SHOWS WHY THE CANTILEVER RATIO IS SO MUCH SMALLER: the deflection of a uniformly loaded cantilever is wL⁴/8EI against 5wL⁴/384EI for a simply supported span.**

> **The ratio of the two is 48/5, that is 9.6 — and per unit of span the cantilever is very much worse.**

> **So a cantilever must be far stockier than a simply supported member for the same deflection, which is exactly what a ratio of 7 against 20 expresses.**

> **The practical consequence is that cantilevers are DEEP: a 2 m balcony cantilever needs about 285 mm of effective depth, whereas a 2 m simply supported slab would need only 100 mm.**

**The MODIFICATION FACTORS applied to the basic ratio, which is where the method's real content lies:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **For spans over 10 m** ← | **MULTIPLY by 10/span (for simply supported and continuous members) — because deflection grows faster than the code's simple ratio allows** ← |
| **For the percentage and grade of TENSION steel** ← | **A modification factor from Fig. 4; MORE tension steel or LOWER grade steel means a LARGER factor** ← |
| **For COMPRESSION steel** ← | **A factor from Fig. 5; compression steel reduces long-term deflection by restraining creep, so it increases the permissible ratio** ← |
| **For FLANGED sections** ← | **A reduction factor from Fig. 6, based on the web-to-flange width ratio** ← |

> **THE TENSION STEEL FACTOR IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD, AND ITS LOGIC RUNS THROUGH STEEL STRESS RATHER THAN STEEL AREA: what actually governs deflection is the STRAIN in the steel at service load.**

> **A section with generous tension steel works at a lower stress, so its strains and hence its curvatures and deflections are smaller — and it may therefore be more slender.**

> **A section with high-grade steel used efficiently works at a high stress, with larger strains, so it must be less slender.**

> **This is the same phenomenon met in the comparison of the working stress and limit state methods: strength and stiffness are separate properties, and using a stronger steel more efficiently buys strength at the cost of stiffness.**

> **Which is why the span/depth ratio depends on f_y and on the percentage of steel, and why the ratio 20 is a starting point rather than an answer.**

**AND THE PURPOSE OF THE WHOLE PROVISION IS WORTH STATING, since it is easily mistaken for a rule of thumb:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is a DEEMED-TO-SATISFY provision** ← | **A member complying with it need not have its deflection calculated at all** ← |
| **The limits it stands in for are span/250 for total deflection** ← | **And span/350 or 20 mm, whichever is less, for the deflection occurring after partitions and finishes are built** ← |
| **A member failing the ratio is not thereby unacceptable** ← | **It simply must have its deflection COMPUTED and shown to meet those limits** ← |
| **The computation is laborious, involving cracked section properties, creep and shrinkage** ← | **Which is why the deemed-to-satisfy route is used for almost all ordinary work** ← |

> **The third row is the point that matters in practice: exceeding the span/depth ratio is a trigger for calculation, not a violation.**

> **A slender member with generous compression steel and a modest load may compute perfectly well, and there is no obligation to deepen it merely to satisfy a ratio that exists as a shortcut.**

> **What is not acceptable is to exceed the ratio and do neither — which is the commonest way in which deflection provisions are actually breached, since nothing visible goes wrong until the partitions crack.**

examTip.trick: **7 cantilever, 20 simply supported, 26 continuous.** A uniformly loaded cantilever deflects 9.6 times as much as a simply supported span of equal length.
examTip.trap: **The basic ratio is only a starting point** — multiply by 10/span above 10 m, and apply factors for tension steel, compression steel and flanged sections.
examTip.mnemonic: **It is a DEEMED-TO-SATISFY route standing in for span/250 and span/350** — exceeding it triggers a calculation, not a violation. Doing neither is the real breach.

questions.stem: A rectangular slab supported on all four sides is designed as a ONE-WAY slab when:
options: It is supported on beams rather than on walls
Its thickness exceeds 150 mm
It carries a concentrated load at its centre
The ratio of its LONGER span to its SHORTER span EXCEEDS 2
questions.solution:
**When the ratio of its LONGER span to its SHORTER span EXCEEDS 2** — so that almost all the load is carried by bending in the shorter direction.

**The distinction:**

| Ratio L_y/L_x | Behaviour | Design as |
|---|---|---|
| **Up to 2** ← | **The slab bends in BOTH directions and shares the load between them** ← | **TWO-WAY slab** ← |
| **Greater than 2** ← | **The long direction contributes so little that it may be ignored** ← | **ONE-WAY slab, spanning the short direction** ← |

> **WHY THE THRESHOLD SITS AT 2 IS WORTH DERIVING, BECAUSE IT MAKES THE RULE INTELLIGIBLE RATHER THAN ARBITRARY:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Consider two orthogonal strips through the slab's centre, of spans L_x and L_y** ← | **Each carrying a share of the load, w_x and w_y** ← |
| **At the centre both strips must have the SAME deflection** ← | **They are the same piece of slab** ← |
| **Deflection goes as w L⁴, so w_x L_x⁴ = w_y L_y⁴** ← | ← |
| **Therefore w_x/w_y = (L_y/L_x)⁴** ← | **The load divides as the FOURTH POWER of the span ratio** ← |
| **At a ratio of 2, that gives w_x/w_y = 16** ← | **The short span carries 16 parts and the long span 1 — about 94 per cent against 6 per cent** ← |

> **THE FOURTH POWER IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE REASON THE THRESHOLD IS SO LOW, and it is a strikingly strong dependence: doubling the span ratio makes the load share sixteen times more lopsided.**

> **Even at a ratio of 1.5 the split is 5:1, so the long span already carries only about 17 per cent.**

> **By a ratio of 2 the long direction's contribution is a few per cent, which is within the accuracy of the whole calculation — so ignoring it costs nothing and simplifies the design greatly.**

> **Being able to reconstruct that from the equal-deflection condition is far more useful than remembering the number 2, and it also explains why the two-way action is worth exploiting at all: a square panel splits the load 50:50 and therefore needs roughly half the moment capacity in each direction.**

**The design consequences:**

| Aspect | One-way slab | Two-way slab |
|---|---|---|
| **MAIN steel** | **In the SHORT direction only** ← | **In BOTH directions, both being main steel** ← |
| **The other direction** | **DISTRIBUTION steel — a nominal minimum** ← | **Main steel, designed** ← |
| **Moments** | **From simple beam analysis of a 1 m wide strip** ← | **From coefficients in IS 456 Tables 26 and 27, by panel type and ratio** ← |
| **Economy** | **Thicker for the same span** ← | **Thinner and lighter — two-way action is efficient** ← |
| **CORNER reinforcement** | **Not required** | **REQUIRED at corners where the slab is restrained but not held down, against uplift and torsion** ← |

> **THE CORNER PROVISION IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN MISSED ON DRAWINGS AND IT ADDRESSES A REAL EFFECT: a two-way slab restrained along its edges tends to LIFT at its corners as it deflects.**

> **The corners are subject to twisting moments, and if the slab is held down there — by a wall above, or by continuity — that restraint generates torsion that cracks the corner diagonally on both faces.**

> **IS 456 accordingly requires torsion reinforcement at such corners: a mesh in the top and bottom over a fifth of the shorter span each way, at three-quarters of the midspan area.**

> **Its omission produces the diagonal corner cracks visible on the soffit of many two-way slabs, which are unsightly and admit water to the reinforcement but are seldom structurally serious — a defect of detailing rather than of design, and entirely avoidable.**

verification.notes: Equal central deflection gives w_x/w_y = (L_y/L_x)^4; at a ratio of 2 that is 16:1, about 94% to 6%.

examTip.trick: **Long span / short span greater than 2.** Then the long direction carries only a few per cent and can be ignored.
examTip.trap: **Derive it from equal central deflection: w_x/w_y = (L_y/L_x)⁴** — the load divides as the FOURTH power, so a ratio of 2 gives a 16:1 split, and even 1.5 gives 5:1.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two-way slabs need CORNER torsion reinforcement** where the edges are restrained but not held down — a mesh top and bottom over L_x/5, at 0.75 of the midspan steel. Routinely omitted.

questions.stem: For a deformed bar of Fe 415 steel in M20 concrete, the DEVELOPMENT LENGTH required in tension, taking the design bond stress for plain bars in M20 as 1.2 N/mm² and the 60 per cent increase permitted for deformed bars, is approximately:
options: 47 times the bar diameter
30 times the bar diameter
56 times the bar diameter
38 times the bar diameter
questions.solution:
**About 47 times the bar diameter.**

**The derivation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Design bond stress for M20, plain bars** | **τ_bd = 1.2 N/mm²** ← |
| **Increased 60 per cent for DEFORMED bars** ← | **τ_bd = 1.2 × 1.6 = 1.92 N/mm²** ← |
| **Design stress in the steel** | **σ_s = 0.87 f_y = 0.87 × 415 = 361.05 N/mm²** ← |
| **The development length formula** | **L_d = φ σ_s / (4 τ_bd)** ← |
| **Substituting** | **= φ × 361.05 / (4 × 1.92) = φ × 361.05 / 7.68** ← |
| **Evaluating** | **= 47.0 φ** ← |

> **So L_d ≈ 47 φ, which for a 16 mm bar is about 750 mm.**

**WHERE THE FORMULA ITSELF COMES FROM IS A ONE-LINE EQUILIBRIUM AND IS WORTH SEEING, since it makes the expression impossible to forget:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The FORCE the bar must develop is its area times its stress** ← | **(πφ²/4) × σ_s** ← |
| **The bond RESISTANCE is the bar's surface area times the bond stress** ← | **(π φ L_d) × τ_bd** ← |
| **Equating them: (πφ²/4)σ_s = πφ L_d τ_bd** ← | ← |
| **Cancelling πφ gives L_d = φ σ_s /(4 τ_bd)** ← | **The 4 comes from the area formula, not from anywhere mysterious** ← |

> **THE STRUCTURE OF THE RESULT IS INFORMATIVE: L_d is proportional to the bar DIAMETER, because a bar's area grows as φ² while its perimeter grows only as φ.**

> **So a thicker bar needs proportionately more length to develop its force — and a bundle of small bars develops in less length than one large bar of the same total area.**

> **This is why large-diameter bars are awkward in shallow members and why the code requires the development length of a bundle to be increased by 10, 20 or 33 per cent for two, three or four bars, the bundle's effective perimeter being less than the sum of its bars'.**

**The values to have to hand:**

| Concrete | τ_bd, plain | τ_bd, deformed | L_d for Fe 415 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **M20** | **1.2** | **1.92** | **47 φ** ← |
| **M25** | **1.4** | **2.24** | **40 φ** ← |
| **M30** | **1.5** | **2.40** | **38 φ** ← |
| **M35** | **1.7** | **2.72** | **33 φ** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION SHOWS THAT A HIGHER GRADE CONCRETE SHORTENS THE DEVELOPMENT LENGTH SUBSTANTIALLY, which is a real design lever: raising M20 to M30 cuts L_d by nearly a fifth.**

> **That can be the difference between a lap that fits within a member and one that does not — a consideration in short cantilevers, in narrow columns and at the ends of beams framing into slender supports.**

> **Note also that for a bar in COMPRESSION the design bond stress is increased by a further 25 per cent, so a compression lap is shorter than a tension lap — because a compression bar bears on the concrete at its end as well as bonding along its length.**

> **AND THE MOST COMMON PRACTICAL FAILURE RELATED TO ALL THIS IS NOT A CALCULATION ERROR BUT A DETAILING ONE: the length is available on the drawing and not on site, because the bar has been cut short or the lap has been positioned where the member is not deep enough.**

> **A development length that runs past the end of the member is not a development length, and the check that matters is whether the bar's full L_d lies inside concrete measured from the section where the full stress is required.**

examTip.trap: **Apply the 60 % deformed-bar increase to τ_bd before dividing** — forgetting it gives 75φ, which is a large over-estimate.
examTip.mnemonic: **Derive it by equilibrium: area × stress = perimeter × bond × length.** Area grows as φ² and perimeter as φ, which is why L_d is proportional to diameter and why bundles need extra.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, the ANCHORAGE VALUE of a standard 90-degree BEND in a reinforcing bar is taken as:
options: 16 times the bar diameter
8 times the bar diameter for each bend
4 times the bar diameter
The bend contributes no anchorage value at all
questions.solution:
**8 times the bar diameter for each bend, subject to a maximum of 24 times the diameter for the whole bar.**

**The anchorage values:**

| Detail | Anchorage value |
|---|---|
| **A standard 90-degree BEND** ← | **8 φ per bend** ← |
| **A standard U-TYPE HOOK (180 degrees)** ← | **16 φ** ← (option a is the hook, not the bend) |
| **The MAXIMUM total credit from bends in one bar** ← | **24 φ** ← |
| **A straight length** | **Its actual length** ← |

> **THE 24 φ CEILING IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE PROVISION MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND IT PREVENTS AN OBVIOUS ABUSE: a bar cannot be given unlimited anchorage by putting more and more bends in it.**

> **Three 90-degree bends would nominally give 24 φ, and a fourth adds nothing.**

> **The reason is physical rather than administrative — each bend anchors by bearing the bar against the concrete on the inside of the curve, and the bearing stresses from successive bends overlap and interact.**

> **Beyond a certain amount, adding bends simply concentrates bearing stress in a small volume of concrete which then splits, rather than mobilising more anchorage.**

**How a bend actually anchors, which explains the geometry rules:**

| Mechanism | Note |
|---|---|
| **The bar bears radially against the concrete around the INSIDE of the bend** ← | **Developing a large radial bearing pressure** ← |
| **That pressure must be resisted by the surrounding concrete** ← | **Which is why the bend must be inside a confined region, not near a free surface** ← |
| **Too TIGHT a bend concentrates the pressure and SPLITS the concrete** ← | **Hence a minimum internal radius** ← |
| **Too tight a bend also damages the STEEL** ← | **Cold bending to a small radius work-hardens and can crack high-strength bar** ← |
| **The minimum internal radius is 2 φ for a standard bend, and 4 φ for the hook of a stirrup in mild steel** ← | **With larger radii for high-strength steel** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE PRACTICAL CONSTRAINT THAT DETERMINES WHERE A BEND MAY BE PLACED AND IT IS FREQUENTLY IGNORED: a bend near a free face or in a thin cover has nothing to bear against.**

> **The radial pressure then simply spalls the cover off, and the anchorage is lost at the moment it is needed.**

> **So an anchorage bend must be located within the body of the member — turned INTO the concrete, not toward the surface — which is why the standard detail for a beam bar anchoring into a column turns DOWN into the column rather than out toward its face.**

> **A bend detailed the wrong way round is a common drawing error and is worth checking for, because it looks tidy on paper and provides no anchorage in fact.**

**WHERE ANCHORAGE VALUE IS ACTUALLY USED, WHICH IS ITS PRACTICAL IMPORTANCE:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **At a SIMPLE SUPPORT, where the available length is short** ← | **The bar must develop its stress within the support's width, and a straight length seldom suffices** ← |
| **At an EXTERNAL beam-column joint** ← | **The beam's top bars must anchor into the column, and the column is not wide enough for a straight L_d** ← |
| **STIRRUP hooks** ← | **Which must anchor in the compression zone, and in seismic detailing must be bent 135 degrees into the core** ← |
| **Column bars at a foundation** | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CARRIES A SEISMIC REQUIREMENT WORTH KNOWING: an ordinary stirrup is closed with a 90-degree hook, and IS 13920 requires 135 degrees with an extension of at least 10 φ (or 75 mm) turned INTO the concrete core.**

> **The reason is that under severe cyclic loading the cover concrete spalls off, and a 90-degree hook anchored in the cover then opens out and the stirrup unwraps — losing both its shear capacity and, more importantly, its confinement of the core exactly when the core is relying on it.**

> **A 135-degree hook engages the core itself and holds after the cover has gone, which is a small detailing difference with a decisive effect on how a member behaves in the plastic hinge zone.**

examTip.trick: **8φ per 90° bend, 16φ for a U-hook, maximum 24φ total from bends.** Option (a) is the hook value, not the bend value.
examTip.trap: **A bend anchors by RADIAL BEARING on the concrete inside the curve** — so it must turn INTO the member, not toward a free face, or the cover spalls and the anchorage is lost.
examTip.mnemonic: **IS 13920 requires 135° stirrup hooks with a 10φ extension into the core** — a 90° hook anchored in the cover unwraps when the cover spalls, losing shear and confinement together.

questions.stem: When tension reinforcement in a beam is CURTAILED, IS 456 requires that the bar extend beyond the point at which it is no longer required for flexure by a distance of:
options: The full development length, in every case
The effective depth only
The EFFECTIVE DEPTH or 12 times the bar diameter, whichever is GREATER
Half the effective depth
questions.solution:
**The EFFECTIVE DEPTH or 12 times the bar diameter, whichever is GREATER** — and additionally, the bar must extend the full development length beyond the point of maximum moment it was designed for.

**The two requirements, both of which apply:**

| Requirement | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Extend d or 12 φ beyond the theoretical cut-off point** ← | **Covers the SHIFT in the moment diagram caused by shear cracking, and any inaccuracy in the assumed loading** ← |
| **Provide the full L_d beyond the section of maximum moment** ← | **So that the bar can actually DEVELOP the stress it was designed to carry** ← |

> **THE FIRST REQUIREMENT ADDRESSES SOMETHING SUBTLE THAT IS WORTH EXPLAINING, because 'the moment diagram shifts' sounds like a fudge and is not:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **In an UNCRACKED beam, the tension at a section corresponds to the moment at that section** ← | ← |
| **In a beam cracked in SHEAR, the crack is INCLINED** ← | **Crossing the beam at roughly 45 degrees** ← |
| **So the tension in the bar at the crack's BOTTOM corresponds to the moment at the crack's TOP** ← | **Which is a section further along the beam, with a HIGHER moment** ← |
| **The tension demand on the bar is therefore GREATER than the local moment suggests** ← | **Effectively the tension diagram is shifted toward the support by roughly the effective depth** ← |
| **Hence the extension of d beyond the theoretical cut-off** ← | **It is not a margin of ignorance but a correction for a known effect** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MECHANISM AND IT REPAYS PICTURING: a diagonal crack means the bar and the compression zone that balance a given moment are at different positions along the span.**

> **Once that is seen, the extension requirement follows necessarily, and its magnitude — about one effective depth, the horizontal reach of a 45-degree crack — is exactly what the geometry implies.**

**THE ADDITIONAL SHEAR REQUIREMENTS AT A CURTAILMENT IN THE TENSION ZONE, WHICH ARE OFTEN OMITTED:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Curtailment in a tension zone is permitted only if one of three conditions is met** ← | ← |
| **Either the shear at the cut-off does not exceed TWO-THIRDS of the permitted value** ← | ← |
| **Or EXCESS STIRRUPS are provided over a distance of 0.75 d from the cut-off** ← | **Of area at least 0.4 b s/f_y, at a spacing not exceeding d/(8 β_b)** ← |
| **Or, for bars of 36 mm and smaller, the continuing bars provide at least TWICE the area required for flexure there** ← | ← |

> **THE REASON FOR THESE IS THE POINT MADE EARLIER ABOUT τ_c: the design shear strength of concrete DEPENDS on the percentage of tension steel, so cutting a bar REDUCES τ_c at that section.**

> **And curtailment happens toward the supports, where the shear is greatest — so the reduction occurs precisely where the shear demand is highest.**

> **A cut-off in a high-shear region is therefore a genuine weak point, and the code's three alternative conditions are three different ways of ensuring it is not.**

> **A drawing showing bars neatly curtailed at their theoretical cut-off points, with uniform stirrups throughout, has satisfied the flexural requirement and ignored the shear one — and it is one of the commoner detailing deficiencies, precisely because the flexural logic is so tidy and the shear consequence so easy to miss.**

**A related provision worth noting alongside it:**

> **At a SIMPLE SUPPORT, at least one-third of the positive moment reinforcement must continue INTO the support for a length of L_d/3.**

> **This guards against the beam lifting, against an unforeseen negative moment at a support assumed to be simple, and against the loss of anchorage if the support settles or rotates — and it is the reason bottom bars are always shown running into the support rather than stopping at its face.**

examTip.trick: **d or 12φ beyond the theoretical cut-off, AND the full L_d beyond the point of maximum moment.** Two separate requirements.
examTip.trap: **The d extension corrects for the INCLINED shear crack** — the bar's tension at the crack's bottom matches the moment at the crack's top, a section further along with a higher moment.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cutting a bar reduces τ_c where the shear is greatest** — hence three alternative conditions for curtailing in a tension zone. And a third of the bottom steel must run into a simple support.

questions.stem: The EFFECTIVE WIDTH of the flange of a T-beam is limited by IS 456 because:
options: The flange is not strong enough to carry the compression over a greater width
Only the portion of the flange directly above the web is reinforced
The slab's own reinforcement runs in the wrong direction beyond a certain distance
The longitudinal compressive stress in the flange DIMINISHES with distance from the web, so beyond a certain width the slab contributes very little
questions.solution:
**The longitudinal compressive stress in the flange DIMINISHES with distance from the web**, so beyond a certain width the slab contributes very little — and the effective width is the width of an equivalent flange carrying uniform stress.

**The concept:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **In a real T-beam, the compressive stress in the flange is HIGHEST over the web and falls off sideways** ← | **Because the flange is loaded by shear transferred from the web at its junction, and that shear takes distance to spread** ← |
| **The true stress distribution is a curve, not a rectangle** ← | ← |
| **Analysis with a varying stress would be laborious** ← | ← |
| **So an EQUIVALENT width is defined, over which the PEAK stress is assumed UNIFORM** ← | **Chosen so the total force is the same as under the real distribution** ← |
| **That equivalent width is the EFFECTIVE FLANGE WIDTH** ← | **A modelling device, exactly like the nominal shear stress and the modular ratio** ← |

> **THE PHENOMENON UNDERLYING THIS IS CALLED SHEAR LAG, AND RECOGNISING IT BY NAME IS USEFUL BECAUSE IT APPEARS ELSEWHERE: the same effect limits the effective width of the deck acting with a bridge girder, the effective width of a plate acting with a stiffener in a steel structure, and the flange width of a box girder.**

> **In every case a wide plate attached to a stiff rib cannot be fully mobilised, because the force must travel sideways through the plate's own shear stiffness and it diminishes as it goes.**

> **So the effective width concept is not a peculiarity of T-beams but a general treatment of a general problem, and its form is always the same: replace a varying stress over the true width with a uniform stress over a reduced width.**

**The limits IS 456 gives:**

| Beam | Effective flange width b_f is the LEAST of |
|---|---|
| **T-BEAM** ← | **(i) b_w + 6 D_f + L_0/6, (ii) the actual width available — that is, the centre-to-centre distance to the adjacent beams** ← |
| **ISOLATED T-beam** ← | **L_0/(L_0/b + 4) + b_w** ← |
| **L-BEAM** ← | **(i) b_w + 3 D_f + L_0/12, (ii) b_w plus half the clear distance to the next beam** ← |
| **Where L_0 is** ← | **The distance between points of ZERO MOMENT — which for a continuous beam is 0.7 times the effective span, NOT the full span** ← |

> **THE DEFINITION OF L_0 IN THE LAST ROW IS THE DETAIL MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG AND IT MATTERS BECAUSE IT REDUCES THE FLANGE WIDTH BY NEARLY A THIRD IN CONTINUOUS BEAMS: L_0 is the distance between points of zero moment, not the span.**

> **For a simply supported beam those coincide, and L_0 equals the effective span.**

> **For a continuous beam the points of contraflexure are inboard of the supports, and the code permits L_0 to be taken as 0.7 times the effective span.**

> **Using the full span for a continuous beam over-estimates the effective flange width, and therefore over-estimates the compression capacity — an error in the unsafe direction.**

**AND THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL LIMITATION OF T-BEAM ACTION IS ONE OF SIGN, WHICH IS WORTH CLOSING ON:**

| Situation | Flange in |
|---|---|
| **MIDSPAN of a beam, sagging moment** ← | **COMPRESSION — the flange is fully effective, and the T-beam is very efficient** ← |
| **Over a SUPPORT of a continuous beam, hogging moment** ← | **TENSION — the flange is CRACKED and contributes NOTHING to the compression** ← |
| **So the section over a support must be designed as a RECTANGULAR beam of width b_w** ← | **Much weaker than the T-section at midspan** ← |
| **And the tension steel there must be spread across the flange** ← | **Within the effective width, so that the slab's cracking is controlled** ← |

> **The second and third rows explain why the support region of a continuous T-beam is so often the critical section despite the flange being present: the flange is on the wrong side.**

> **A designer who takes advantage of the T-section throughout, without recognising that the support section is a narrow rectangle, has over-estimated the capacity exactly where the moment is greatest — and the support of a continuous beam is where the largest moment usually occurs.**

examTip.trick: **Shear lag: flange stress falls off sideways from the web**, so an equivalent width carrying uniform stress replaces the true varying distribution.
examTip.trap: **L_0 is the distance between points of ZERO MOMENT — 0.7 × effective span for a continuous beam**, not the full span. Using the span over-estimates the flange, which is unsafe.
examTip.mnemonic: **Over a support the flange is in TENSION and contributes nothing** — design that section as a rectangle of width b_w. And that is usually where the largest moment is.

questions.stem: The DISTRIBUTION (secondary) reinforcement placed perpendicular to the main steel in a one-way slab serves to:
options: DISTRIBUTE any concentrated load across several strips of the slab
Carry the principal bending moment in the long direction
Provide shear resistance in the slab
Increase the slab's effective depth
questions.solution:
**To DISTRIBUTE any concentrated load across several strips of the slab, resist SHRINKAGE and TEMPERATURE stresses in that direction, and hold the main bars in position during concreting.**

**The three functions, each independently sufficient reason for it:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **DISTRIBUTING concentrated loads** ← | **A load on one strip is shared with the neighbouring strips through this steel, so no single 1 m strip has to carry it alone** ← |
| **Resisting SHRINKAGE and TEMPERATURE stresses** ← | **The slab shrinks in BOTH directions, and the long direction has no main steel to control the resulting cracking** ← |
| **Holding the main bars in POSITION** ← | **The main bars are tied to the distribution bars, which fixes their spacing and keeps them at the correct level during concreting** ← |

> **THE SECOND FUNCTION IS THE ONE THAT FIXES THE QUANTITY REQUIRED AND IT IS WHY THE MINIMUM IS EXPRESSED AS A PERCENTAGE OF THE GROSS AREA: shrinkage acts on the whole section, uncracked, so the steel needed to control it is proportional to the concrete's area rather than to any bending moment.**

> **Hence the requirement of 0.15 per cent of the gross area for mild steel and 0.12 per cent for high-strength deformed bars — a figure independent of the span, the load and the slab's structural action.**

> **This is a different logic from every other reinforcement requirement in the chapter, all of which follow from an action, and it is worth recognising as such.**

**The spacing rules, which matter as much as the area:**

| Steel | Maximum spacing |
|---|---|
| **MAIN reinforcement in a slab** ← | **The LESSER of 3 d or 300 mm** ← |
| **DISTRIBUTION reinforcement** ← | **The LESSER of 5 d or 450 mm** ← |

> **THE SPACING LIMIT ON DISTRIBUTION STEEL IS THE PROVISION MOST OFTEN BREACHED IN PRACTICE AND ITS PURPOSE IS CRACK CONTROL RATHER THAN STRENGTH: widely spaced bars, even of adequate total area, allow wide cracks to form between them.**
