> **The area requirement determines how much total restraint the steel offers; the spacing requirement determines whether that restraint is distributed finely enough to keep individual cracks narrow.**

> **Both are needed, and satisfying one does not satisfy the other — 8 mm bars at 400 mm centres and 6 mm bars at 225 mm centres provide almost the same area with quite different crack control, and only the second is acceptable in a 150 mm slab.**

> **The general principle is that for controlling cracking, MANY SMALL bars are better than FEW LARGE ones of the same total area — because crack width depends on the spacing of the restraint as well as its magnitude.**

**WHERE THE DISTRIBUTION STEEL IS PLACED IS ALSO WORTH GETTING RIGHT, AND IT IS A COMMON SITE ERROR:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The MAIN steel goes in the OUTER layer, nearest the tension face** ← | **To give it the greatest effective depth** ← |
| **The DISTRIBUTION steel sits INSIDE it** ← | **Losing one bar diameter of depth, which does not matter for its purpose** ← |
| **Reversing them reduces the main steel's effective depth** ← | **By 8 to 12 mm, which in a 100 mm slab is a real fraction of d** ← |
| **In a slab spanning the SHORT way, the main steel therefore runs the SHORT way and lies at the bottom** ← | **Which is easy to get wrong on a rectangular panel** ← |

> **The third row quantifies why this is not a pedantic distinction: in a 100 mm slab with 15 mm cover and 10 mm bars, the correct d is 80 mm and the reversed d is 70 mm.**

> **That is a 12 per cent reduction in effective depth and therefore in the lever arm, so the slab's moment capacity falls by about the same proportion — from a detail that costs nothing to get right and is invisible once the concrete is poured.**

> **It is worth checking on site during the steel inspection rather than afterwards, since it cannot be corrected later and there is no way to tell from the finished slab which layer was on top.**

examTip.trick: **Distributes concentrated loads, resists shrinkage and temperature, and holds the main bars in place.** It does not carry the principal moment (b).
examTip.trap: **Minimum 0.12 % (deformed) or 0.15 % (mild) of GROSS area** — a shrinkage requirement, independent of span and load, which is why it is a percentage of the section and not of anything structural.
examTip.mnemonic: **MAIN steel outermost, distribution steel inside it** — reversing them costs 10 mm of d in a 100 mm slab, about 12 % of the capacity. And spacing ≤ 5d or 450 mm: many small bars beat few large.

questions.stem: In reinforced concrete, FLEXURAL bond stress differs from ANCHORAGE (local) bond stress in that flexural bond stress:
options: Acts only on plain bars, anchorage bond only on deformed bars
Arises from the RATE OF CHANGE of the bar's force along its length
Is always larger than the anchorage bond stress
Is measured in a pull-out test, whereas anchorage bond is measured in a beam test
questions.solution:
**It arises from the RATE OF CHANGE of the bar's force along its length** — and is therefore greatest where the SHEAR is greatest, while anchorage bond arises from the need to develop a bar's full force over a finite length at its end.

**The two kinds of bond:**

| Type | Origin | Greatest where |
|---|---|---|
| **FLEXURAL (local) bond** ← | **The bar's force CHANGES along the span because the moment changes, and bond must transfer that change** ← | **Where the moment changes fastest — that is, where the SHEAR is greatest, near the supports** ← |
| **ANCHORAGE (development) bond** ← | **A bar must build up its full force from zero over a finite length at its END** ← | **At bar ends, laps, and cut-off points** ← |

> **THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN FLEXURAL BOND AND SHEAR IS WORTH DERIVING, BECAUSE IT IS A ONE-LINE ARGUMENT THAT MAKES THE WHOLE DISTINCTION CLEAR:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The bar's force is T = M / (lever arm)** ← | ← |
| **So dT/dx = (dM/dx) / (lever arm) = V / (lever arm)** ← | **Since dM/dx = V** ← |
| **The bond stress required is dT/dx divided by the bar's perimeter** ← | ← |
| **Therefore flexural bond stress is proportional to the SHEAR** ← | **Not to the moment** ← |

> **THAT RESULT IS SLIGHTLY SURPRISING AND IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION: bond stress in a beam follows the SHEAR diagram, not the moment diagram.**

> **Where the moment is greatest — at midspan of a simply supported beam — the shear is zero and the flexural bond stress is nil, because the bar's force is not changing there.**

> **Where the shear is greatest — at the supports — the bar's force is changing fastest and the bond demand is highest.**

> **So the critical sections for bond and for moment are at opposite ends of the beam, and a bar is most at risk of bond failure where it carries the least force.**

**Why modern codes give development length rather than checking flexural bond:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **IS 456 does not require a routine flexural bond check** ← | **It is deemed satisfied if the development length and curtailment rules are followed** ← |
| **Because bond does not fail locally in the way the elastic theory implies** ← | **Slip redistributes the bond stress along the bar, so a local peak is relieved rather than causing failure** ← |
| **What actually fails is the anchorage as a whole** ← | **The bar pulls out, or the cover SPLITS along the bar** ← |
| **So the code controls the TOTAL length available rather than the local stress** ← | **Which is a more realistic model of the failure** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW NAMES THE REAL FAILURE MODE AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING BECAUSE IT DETERMINES THE DETAILING RULES: bond failure in practice is usually SPLITTING, not pull-out.**

> **A deformed bar's ribs bear against the concrete and generate RADIAL bursting forces, like a wedge — and those forces split the cover along the line of the bar.**

> **Once the cover splits, the bar's confinement is lost and the bond fails suddenly along its whole length.**

> **Which is why bond capacity depends so strongly on the COVER, on the bar SPACING, and on TRANSVERSE reinforcement crossing the potential splitting plane — all of which confine the concrete around the bar.**

> **A bar with generous cover and stirrups around it develops far more bond than the same bar near a free edge with nothing crossing the splitting plane, even though the code's τ_bd makes no distinction between them.**

> **THE PRACTICAL LESSONS FOLLOW DIRECTLY, and they are the ones to carry away:**

> **Never reduce cover to fit reinforcement in — it costs bond as well as durability.**

> **Keep bars adequately spaced rather than grouped, so that splitting planes do not join up between adjacent bars.**

> **Provide stirrups through lap zones, where the bursting forces of two bars act together.**

> **And place laps in regions of LOW stress where the choice exists, since a lap in a high-moment region is asking the most of the mechanism most likely to fail.**

examTip.trick: **Flexural bond comes from dT/dx = V/(lever arm), so it follows the SHEAR diagram** — nil at midspan where the moment is greatest, maximum at the supports.
examTip.trap: **IS 456 does not require a routine flexural bond check** — slip redistributes local peaks. It controls the total development length instead, which models the real failure better.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bond fails by SPLITTING, not pull-out** — the ribs act as wedges and burst the cover radially. So cover, bar spacing and transverse steel govern bond in practice.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, a compression member is treated as a SHORT column when the ratio of its effective length to its least lateral dimension:
options: Exceeds 12 in either direction
Is less than 3
Exceeds 30
Is LESS than 12 in BOTH directions
questions.solution:
**When the ratio of effective length to least lateral dimension is LESS than 12 in BOTH directions.**

**The classification:**

| Condition | Column |
|---|---|
| **l_ex/D < 12 AND l_ey/b < 12** ← | **SHORT — designed for the axial load and the primary moments only** ← |
| **Either ratio ≥ 12** ← | **SLENDER — additional moments from the lateral deflection must be included** ← |
| **l_e/least dimension > 60, or > 100 b²/D for a cantilever column** ← | **NOT PERMITTED at all** ← |

> **THE REQUIREMENT THAT BOTH DIRECTIONS SATISFY THE LIMIT IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE POINT THE QUESTION TURNS ON, and it is worth stating why: a column can be short about one axis and slender about the other.**

> **A rectangular column 600 mm by 250 mm in a frame braced in one direction and unbraced in the other may have quite different effective lengths and quite different lateral dimensions in the two directions.**

> **If it is slender in either, it must be treated as slender — the additional moments arise about whichever axis the slenderness permits it to buckle about, and being stocky in the other direction does not help.**

> **So the check is made separately for each axis and the more onerous conclusion governs.**

**Why 12, and what the distinction actually means physically:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A SHORT column fails by CRUSHING of the material** ← | **Its capacity is the material's capacity, and its length is irrelevant** ← |
| **A SLENDER column deflects laterally under load, and that deflection creates an ADDITIONAL moment P·Δ** ← | **Which increases the deflection further — the second-order or P-delta effect** ← |
| **The additional moment reduces the capacity below the material's value** ← | **Increasingly so as the slenderness grows** ← |
| **Below a ratio of about 12 the effect is small enough to neglect** ← | **Within the accuracy of the rest of the calculation** ← |
| **Above it the additional moment must be computed and added** ← | ← |

> **THE SELF-REINFORCING CHARACTER OF THE SECOND ROW IS WHAT MAKES SLENDERNESS DANGEROUS AND IT IS WORTH SEEING CLEARLY: the deflection creates a moment, which increases the deflection, which increases the moment.**

> **For a stocky column that loop converges quickly and the increase is trivial.**

> **For a very slender one it may not converge at all, which is buckling — and the failure is sudden, occurring at a load well below the material's crushing capacity.**

> **This is why the code sets an absolute ceiling of 60 in the third row of the first table: beyond that the behaviour is dominated by stability rather than strength, and the empirical additional-moment provisions cease to be reliable.**

**AND THE MINIMUM ECCENTRICITY REQUIREMENT, WHICH APPLIES TO EVERY COLUMN INCLUDING A SHORT ONE:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **e_min = l/500 + D/30, subject to a minimum of 20 mm** ← | **In each direction** ← |
| **No column is designed as PURELY axially loaded** ← | **Because no column is ever purely axially loaded in reality** ← |
| **Construction tolerances, unequal spans, accidental loads and frame action all introduce moment** ← | **Even where the analysis shows none** ← |
| **If the actual eccentricity exceeds e_min, the actual value is used** ← | **e_min is a floor, not a substitute** ← |
| **Where e_min does not exceed 0.05 D, the simple axial formula may be used** ← | **Which is the condition for using P_u = 0.4 f_ck A_c + 0.67 f_y A_sc** ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS ARE THE JUSTIFICATION AND THEY DESERVE A MOMENT'S THOUGHT, because the provision is sometimes dismissed as a formality: a column built exactly where the drawing shows it, carrying exactly the loads the analysis assumed, would indeed be axially loaded.**

> **No column is. It is built a few millimetres out of plumb, its beams frame in at slightly different levels, the slab on one side is loaded and the other is not, and the frame sways slightly under wind.**

> **Each of those introduces a small moment, and a column designed for pure axial load has no capacity allocated to resist any of them.**

> **The minimum eccentricity requirement reserves a modest capacity for the moments that certainly exist and cannot be calculated — which is a different kind of provision from a safety factor, and a sensible one.**

examTip.trick: **Less than 12 in BOTH directions.** A column short about one axis and slender about the other must be designed as slender.
examTip.trap: **Every column, short or slender, needs e_min = l/500 + D/30 ≥ 20 mm** — no column is ever truly axially loaded, because of out-of-plumb, unequal spans and frame action.
examTip.mnemonic: **Short columns CRUSH; slender ones deflect, and P·Δ feeds back on itself.** Above a ratio of 60 the column is not permitted at all — stability dominates and the empirical rules fail.

questions.stem: IS 456 requires the longitudinal reinforcement in a column to lie between:
options: 0.8 per cent and 6 per cent of the GROSS cross-sectional area
0.15 per cent and 2 per cent of the gross area
0.4 per cent and 8 per cent of the gross area
0.12 per cent and 4 per cent of the gross area
questions.solution:
**Between 0.8 per cent and 6 per cent of the GROSS cross-sectional area**, with 4 per cent the practical upper limit where bars are lapped.

**The provisions and the reason for each:**

| Provision | Reason |
|---|---|
| **MINIMUM 0.8 per cent of the gross area** ← | **To resist the moments certainly present but not calculated, to provide some ductility, and to control creep and shrinkage effects in a heavily loaded member** ← |
| **MAXIMUM 6 per cent** ← | **The absolute ceiling — beyond it the section cannot be concreted** ← |
| **4 per cent is the practical maximum** ← | **Because at a LAP the steel DOUBLES locally, so 4 per cent becomes 8 per cent in the lap zone, which is unbuildable** ← |
| **Minimum bar diameter 12 mm** ← | **Smaller bars are too flexible to stand and to be fixed accurately** ← |
| **Minimum FOUR bars in a rectangular column, SIX in a circular one** ← | **One in each corner; six for a helically reinforced column** ← |
| **Maximum spacing of longitudinal bars 300 mm along each face** ← | **So that intermediate bars are tied, and none is left unrestrained** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CONTAINS THE PRACTICAL POINT AND IT IS THE PART MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED IN DESIGN: the limit that matters is 4 per cent, not 6.**

> **Column bars are lapped just above each floor, and in the lap zone two bars occupy the space of one.**

> **So a column with 4 per cent steel has 8 per cent in the lap region, which is already at the limit of what can be concreted.**

> **A column designed at 6 per cent simply cannot be built with laps, and the only way to realise it is to use couplers or to weld — which is expensive and normally means the column should have been made larger instead.**

> **The general rule to carry is that a column needing more than 4 per cent steel is a column of insufficient size, and enlarging the section or raising the concrete grade is almost always cheaper than the congestion.**

**WHY THE MINIMUM IS SO MUCH HIGHER THAN A SLAB'S 0.12 PER CENT IS WORTH ADDRESSING, since the contrast is striking:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A slab's minimum steel controls SHRINKAGE cracking in a lightly stressed member** ← | **A small quantity suffices** ← |
| **A column carries a large SUSTAINED compressive load** ← | ← |
| **Concrete CREEPS under that load, and the creep transfers stress progressively to the steel** ← | **The steel does not creep** ← |
| **With too little steel, that transferred stress can yield the bars over time** ← | **And the column's behaviour becomes dependent on the concrete alone** ← |
| **The 0.8 per cent minimum ensures enough steel to absorb the transfer** ← | **And provides real reserve if the concrete is locally deficient** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS DESCRIBE A LONG-TERM REDISTRIBUTION THAT IS OFTEN NOT APPRECIATED: the steel in a column carries a larger share of the load after ten years than it did on the day the props were struck.**

> **Creep shortens the concrete; the steel, bonded to it, must shorten equally; so the steel's strain and hence its stress increase while the concrete's stress falls.**

> **In a lightly reinforced column that transfer can be substantial, and it is one of the reasons the axial capacity formula's coefficients — 0.4 for concrete and 0.67 for steel — are lower than the materials' design strengths would suggest.**

> **Both are reduced from the values used in bending, and the reduction accounts partly for the minimum eccentricity that every column must be assumed to carry and partly for this long-term redistribution.**

4 per cent being the practical upper limit where bars are lapped.

examTip.trick: **0.8 % to 6 % of the GROSS area** — with a minimum of 12 mm bars, four in a rectangular column and six in a circular one.
examTip.trap: **4 % is the real limit, because bars DOUBLE at a lap** — 4 % becomes 8 % in the lap zone. A column needing more than 4 % is too small; enlarge it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Creep transfers load from concrete to steel over years** — the steel carries more at ten years than at stripping. Hence a high minimum, and the reduced 0.4/0.67 coefficients.

questions.stem: The PITCH of the lateral ties in a reinforced concrete column must not exceed the LEAST of:
options: 300 mm, 12 times the tie diameter, or half the column dimension
The LEAST lateral dimension of the column, 16 times the smallest longitudinal bar diameter, or 300 mm
The effective depth, 20 times the tie diameter, or 450 mm
48 times the tie diameter or 600 mm
questions.solution:
**The LEAST of: the least lateral dimension of the column, 16 times the smallest longitudinal bar diameter, or 300 mm.**

**The requirements for lateral ties:**

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| **PITCH — the least of three limits** ← | **The column's least lateral dimension; 16 × the smallest longitudinal bar diameter; 300 mm** ← |
| **DIAMETER — the greater of two limits** ← | **One quarter of the largest longitudinal bar diameter; and 6 mm** ← |
| **Arrangement** ← | **Every corner and alternate bar must be held by the corner of a tie; no bar may be further than 75 mm from such a restrained bar** ← |

> **THE 16 φ LIMIT IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE ONE THAT USUALLY GOVERNS, AND IT IS THE ONE WHOSE PURPOSE MATTERS MOST: it prevents the longitudinal bars from BUCKLING between ties.**

> **A column bar in compression is a slender strut, and its unsupported length is the tie spacing.**

> **If the ties are too far apart, the bar buckles outward between them, bursts the cover, and the column fails locally even though the concrete is not overloaded.**

> **Limiting the spacing to 16 bar diameters keeps each bar's slenderness low enough that it cannot buckle before the concrete crushes — so the two materials fail together rather than the steel first.**

**The THREE functions of lateral ties, all of which matter:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Preventing BUCKLING of the longitudinal bars** ← | **The primary function, as above** ← |
| **CONFINING the concrete core** ← | **Restraining its lateral expansion so it can sustain higher strains — the basis of ductility** ← |
| **Resisting SHEAR** ← | **Columns carry shear too, particularly under lateral load** ← |
| **And holding the cage together during construction** | ← |

> **THE CONFINEMENT FUNCTION IN THE SECOND ROW IS WHAT SEISMIC DETAILING EXPLOITS, AND IS 13920'S REQUIREMENTS GO WELL BEYOND IS 456'S:**

| Provision | IS 13920 requirement |
|---|---|
| **Special CONFINING reinforcement over a length l_o at each end of the column** ← | **l_o being the greater of the larger column dimension, one-sixth of the clear height, or 450 mm** ← |
| **Spacing within l_o** ← | **Not more than one-quarter of the minimum column dimension, and not less than 75 mm nor more than 100 mm** ← |
| **Hooks bent at 135 degrees with a 10 φ extension into the core** ← | **So the tie holds after the cover spalls** ← |
| **Closed ties, or a single continuous spiral** ← | **Never open ties or ties closed only by a lap in the cover** ← |
| **Confining reinforcement through the JOINT as well** ← | **Which is the part most often omitted, the joint being congested and awkward** ← |

> **THE SPACING OF 75 TO 100 MM IN THE SECOND ROW IS FOUR OR FIVE TIMES CLOSER THAN THE ORDINARY REQUIREMENT, AND THAT IS THE MEASURE OF WHAT CONFINEMENT DEMANDS: a seismically detailed column end is a dense cage, not a column with a few extra ties.**

> **The purpose is to hold the concrete core together after the cover has spalled off, so that the core continues to carry the axial load while the column rotates through large drifts.**

> **Unconfined concrete crushes at a strain of about 0.0035; well-confined concrete can reach several times that before losing capacity.**

> **That extra strain capacity is the ductility on which the whole response-reduction bargain rests — so the confining steel at a column end is not a detail but the physical mechanism by which R = 5 is earned.**

> **THE JOINT PROVISION IN THE LAST ROW DESERVES ITS EMPHASIS BECAUSE ITS OMISSION IS SO COMMON AND SO CONSEQUENTIAL: the beam-column joint is the most congested region of a frame, with beam bars from two or four directions passing through it, and fixing ties inside it is genuinely difficult.**

> **It is therefore frequently left out, and the joint becomes the weakest part of a frame that is otherwise well detailed — failing before either the beam or the column can develop its capacity, and defeating the strong-column-weak-beam hierarchy entirely.**

examTip.trick: **Least of: least lateral dimension, 16 × smallest longitudinal bar diameter, 300 mm.** Tie diameter is the greater of φ/4 and 6 mm.
examTip.trap: **The 16φ limit prevents the longitudinal bars BUCKLING between ties** — their unsupported length is the tie spacing. Too wide and the bar bursts the cover before the concrete crushes.
examTip.mnemonic: **IS 13920 demands 75-100 mm spacing over l_o at each end** — four or five times closer, to confine the core after the cover spalls. That confinement is how R = 5 is earned.

questions.stem: A short axially loaded column of 400 mm × 400 mm section in M25 concrete is reinforced with eight 16 mm bars of Fe 415 steel (total area 1,608 mm²). Its ultimate axial load capacity, from P_u = 0.4 f_ck A_c + 0.67 f_y A_sc, is about:
questions.solution:
**About 2,031 kN.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Gross area** | **400 × 400 = 160,000 mm²** ← |
| **Steel area A_sc** | **1,608 mm²** ← |
| **NET concrete area A_c** ← | **160,000 − 1,608 = 158,392 mm² — the steel's area must be DEDUCTED** ← |
| **Concrete contribution** | **0.4 × 25 × 158,392 = 1,583,920 N** ← |
| **Steel contribution** | **0.67 × 415 × 1,608 = 447,104 N** ← |
| **Total P_u** | **= 2,031,024 N = 2,031 kN** ← |

> **So the capacity is about 2,031 kN.**

**THE DISTRACTORS EACH CORRESPOND TO A SPECIFIC ERROR AND ARE WORTH IDENTIFYING:**

| Option | Error |
|---|---|
| **1,584 kN** ← | **The CONCRETE contribution alone — the steel's contribution omitted entirely** ← |
| **1,600 kN** ← | **Using the GROSS area for concrete (0.4 × 25 × 160,000) and forgetting the steel** ← |
| **2,600 kN** ← | **Using the full design strengths 0.446 f_ck and 0.87 f_y instead of the reduced 0.4 and 0.67** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE CONCEPTUAL ERROR RATHER THAN AN ARITHMETIC ONE, AND IT IS WORTH BEING CLEAR ABOUT WHY THE COEFFICIENTS ARE REDUCED: 0.4 and 0.67 are NOT the design strengths of the two materials.**

| Comparison | Bending | Axial column |
|---|---|---|
| **Concrete** | **0.446 f_ck peak, 0.36 f_ck average** ← | **0.4 f_ck** ← |
| **Steel** | **0.87 f_y** ← | **0.67 f_y** ← |

> **The reduction in the column formula allows for the MINIMUM ECCENTRICITY that every column must be presumed to carry — up to 0.05 D — without requiring it to be calculated explicitly.**

> **So the formula is not 'the material capacities added up'; it is the capacity of a column carrying a small unavoidable moment, expressed as a purely axial expression for convenience.**

> **Which is exactly why the formula may be used ONLY when the actual eccentricity does not exceed 0.05 D — beyond that, the allowance built into the coefficients is used up and the column must be designed for combined axial load and moment.**

**THE DEDUCTION OF THE STEEL AREA IN THE THIRD ROW OF THE CALCULATION IS A SMALL POINT WORTH GETTING RIGHT, and it is the same idea as the (m − 1) in the transformed section:**

> **The steel occupies space that would otherwise be concrete, so counting the full gross area as concrete AND adding the steel's contribution counts that region twice.**

> **In this example the double-counting would be 0.4 × 25 × 1,608 = 16,080 N, that is 16 kN out of 2,031 — under one per cent, and negligible.**

> **At 4 per cent steel in a large column it would matter more, and the habit of deducting is worth keeping since it costs nothing and is always correct.**

> **A useful check on any such calculation is to note the SPLIT between the two contributions: here the concrete provides 78 per cent and the steel 22 per cent of the capacity from 1 per cent of the area.**

> **That ratio — steel contributing several times its area share — is what makes reinforcement worthwhile, and a result in which the proportions come out wildly different from this is worth re-examining before it is trusted.**

examTip.trick: **P_u = 0.4 f_ck A_c + 0.67 f_y A_sc = 1,584 + 447 = 2,031 kN.** Deduct the steel area from the gross to get A_c.
examTip.trap: **0.4 and 0.67 are NOT the design strengths (0.446 and 0.87)** — the reduction covers the minimum eccentricity every column must be presumed to carry. Hence the 0.05D limit on using the formula.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check the split: concrete 78 %, steel 22 % from 1 % of the area.** Steel contributing several times its area share is what makes reinforcement worth having.

questions.stem: IS 456 permits the axial load capacity of a column with HELICAL (spiral) reinforcement to be taken as 1.05 times that of a similar column with lateral ties, because the helix:
options: Provides a larger area of steel for the same weight
Is easier to place accurately and therefore has less variability
Resists shear more effectively than rectangular ties
CONFINES the concrete core CONTINUOUSLY
questions.solution:
**Because the helix CONFINES the concrete core CONTINUOUSLY**, restraining its lateral expansion and so raising both its strength and its strain capacity.

**The mechanism of confinement:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Concrete under axial compression tries to expand LATERALLY** ← | **By the Poisson effect, and increasingly so as it approaches failure and microcracks open** ← |
| **A helix wrapped around it resists that expansion in HOOP TENSION** ← | ← |
| **The concrete core is thus placed in TRIAXIAL compression** ← | **Axial compression plus radial confinement** ← |
| **Triaxially confined concrete is both STRONGER and far more DUCTILE** ← | **Its strength rises with the confining pressure, and its ultimate strain can be several times the unconfined value** ← |
| **A helix does this CONTINUOUSLY along the column's length** ← | **Whereas rectangular ties confine only at discrete levels** ← |

> **THE CONTINUITY IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE REASON THE HELIX EARNS ITS 5 PER CENT AND RECTANGULAR TIES DO NOT, and the geometry matters as much as the continuity:**

| Aspect | Helix | Rectangular ties |
|---|---|---|
| **Along the length** | **CONTINUOUS confinement** ← | **Confinement only at each tie, arching between them** ← |
| **In cross-section** | **CIRCULAR — pure hoop tension, uniform pressure all round** ← | **The tie's straight sides BEND outward, so confinement is effective only near the corners** ← |
| **Effectiveness** | **High** | **Much lower, unless intermediate cross-ties are provided** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MORE IMPORTANT DIFFERENCE AND IT IS PURELY GEOMETRIC: a circle under internal pressure carries it entirely in hoop tension, with no bending at all.**

> **A rectangle under internal pressure must carry it in BENDING of its straight sides, and a thin tie bar bends very readily — so it bows outward and the confinement over the middle of each face is largely lost.**

> **The effectively confined region of a tied column is therefore a set of arches springing from the corners, not the whole core, and this is why cross-ties and intermediate bars improve confinement so markedly: each one provides another point from which the arch can spring.**

> **That is exactly why IS 13920 requires no bar to be more than 75 mm from a laterally restrained bar in a confining zone, and why a large column needs internal cross-ties rather than merely a perimeter tie.**

**Where the helical column's other advantage lies, which is the more valuable one:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **5 per cent higher axial capacity** ← | **The provision in this question — modest** ← |
| **Very much greater DUCTILITY and toughness** ← | **The real benefit: a spirally reinforced column deforms greatly before losing capacity** ← |
| **A GRADUAL failure rather than a sudden one** ← | **The cover spalls, the helix takes over, and the core continues to carry load at large strains** ← |
| **Which is why bridge PIERS and columns in seismic regions are so often spirally reinforced** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW DESCRIBES THE BEHAVIOUR THAT MAKES SPIRALS VALUABLE AND IT IS WORTH PICTURING: a tied column at failure spalls its cover, its bars buckle between ties, and it collapses.**

> **A spirally reinforced column spalls its cover and then keeps going — the exposed helix continues to confine the core, and the column can sustain its load through very large axial strains before the helix itself yields and the core disintegrates.**

> **That gives warning, and it gives a structure time to redistribute, which is worth far more than 5 per cent of capacity.**

> **IS 456's condition for claiming the 1.05 factor reflects this: the volume of the helical reinforcement must satisfy a minimum ratio related to the core and gross areas, ensuring the helix is substantial enough to take over when the cover goes — a spiral too light to do that earns no increase.**

examTip.trick: **Continuous circular confinement puts the core in triaxial compression** — stronger and much more ductile than unconfined concrete.
examTip.trap: **A circle carries internal pressure in pure HOOP TENSION; a rectangle must carry it in BENDING of its sides**, which bow outward, so tied confinement works only near the corners.
examTip.mnemonic: **The 5 % capacity gain is the minor benefit; the DUCTILITY is the real one** — the helix keeps confining after the cover spalls, which is why bridge piers are spirally reinforced.

questions.stem: In the design of a SLENDER column, the ADDITIONAL MOMENTS that must be considered arise because:
options: The concrete's strength is reduced in a long member
The reinforcement must be lapped more frequently over the greater height
The column DEFLECTS laterally under load
The wind load on a taller column is greater
questions.solution:
**Because the column DEFLECTS laterally under load, and the axial force acting through that deflection produces a moment P·Δ which further increases the deflection.**

**The mechanism, and why it is called a second-order effect:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The column carries an axial load P and bends slightly** ← | **From the primary moments, from imperfections, or from sway** ← |
| **Its mid-height therefore moves laterally by Δ** ← | ← |
| **The axial force P now acts at an eccentricity Δ from the column's ends** ← | **Producing an additional moment P·Δ** ← |
| **That additional moment increases the bending, hence increases Δ** ← | **Which increases the additional moment again** ← |
| **The process converges for a stocky column and diverges for a very slender one** ← | **Divergence being buckling** ← |
| **It is 'second order' because the equilibrium must be written on the DEFORMED geometry** ← | **A first-order analysis, on the undeformed geometry, does not see it at all** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST USEFUL WAY TO UNDERSTAND THE WHOLE CLASS OF EFFECTS, AND IT GENERALISES BEYOND COLUMNS: a first-order analysis assumes the structure's geometry does not change under load.**

> **For most structures at working loads that is an excellent assumption, and it is why linear analysis works.**

> **For slender compression members it is not, because the geometry change itself generates the actions that matter.**

> **The same reasoning applies to a whole FRAME that sways: the frame's lateral deflection multiplied by the total vertical load on it produces an additional overturning moment, the P-Delta effect at building scale — and a tall flexible building must be checked for it just as a slender column must.**

**How IS 456 handles it:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **Additional moment M_ax = P_u D (l_ex/D)² / 2000** ← | **About the major axis, and similarly with b and l_ey for the minor axis** ← |
| **The form shows the moment growing with the SQUARE of the slenderness** ← | **Which is why the effect is negligible at a ratio of 12 and dominant at 50** ← |
| **A reduction factor k may be applied where the axial load is low** ← | **Since the P·Δ effect is proportional to P, a lightly loaded slender column suffers less** ← |
| **The additional moment is ADDED to the primary moment from the frame analysis** ← | **And the column designed for the combination** ← |
| **The EFFECTIVE LENGTH must be established first** ← | **From the end conditions, and this is the step most open to error** ← |

> **THE SQUARE DEPENDENCE IN THE SECOND ROW IS WHAT MAKES SLENDERNESS SO CONSEQUENTIAL AND IT IS WORTH QUANTIFYING: doubling the slenderness ratio QUADRUPLES the additional moment.**

> **A column at a ratio of 12 has an additional moment of P_u D × 144/2000 = 0.072 P_u D, which is comparable with the minimum eccentricity and is why 12 is the threshold.**

> **At a ratio of 40 it is 0.8 P_u D — over ten times as large, and quite capable of governing the design entirely.**

> **So slenderness is not a gradual penalty but an accelerating one, and a modest increase in a column's unsupported height can have a disproportionate effect on the steel it needs.**

**THE EFFECTIVE LENGTH IN THE LAST ROW DESERVES A CLOSING WARNING, BECAUSE IT IS WHERE SLENDER COLUMN DESIGN GOES WRONG IN PRACTICE:**

| Condition | Effective length |
|---|---|
| **Both ends effectively held in position AND restrained against rotation** ← | **0.65 l** ← |
| **Both ends held in position, one end restrained against rotation** | **0.80 l** ← |
| **Both ends held in position, neither restrained against rotation** ← | **1.00 l** ← |
| **One end held in position and restrained against rotation, the other entirely free** ← | **2.00 l — the cantilever column** ← |
| **Ends NOT held in position — an UNBRACED frame** ← | **1.2 l to 2.0 l and beyond, depending on the restraint** ← |

> **The last row is the one that catches designers out: 'held in position' means prevented from moving SIDEWAYS, which requires a bracing system, a shear wall or a stiff frame — not merely a beam framing into the column.**

> **A column in an unbraced frame has an effective length exceeding its actual height, sometimes by a factor of two, and treating it as 1.0 l because beams frame into both ends can under-estimate its slenderness ratio by a factor of two and its additional moment by a factor of four.**

examTip.trick: **P acting through the lateral deflection Δ gives P·Δ, which increases Δ again.** A second-order effect: equilibrium on the DEFORMED geometry.
examTip.trap: **M_ax = P_u D (l_ex/D)²/2000 — the SQUARE of the slenderness.** Doubling the ratio quadruples the additional moment, so slenderness is an accelerating penalty.
examTip.mnemonic: **'Held in position' means braced against SWAY, not merely having beams framing in** — an unbraced column's effective length can be 2l, quadrupling the additional moment.

questions.stem: The INTERACTION DIAGRAM of a reinforced concrete column is a plot of:
options: The axial load capacity P_u against the moment capacity M_u
The stress against the strain in the concrete at the extreme fibre
The axial load against the column's lateral deflection
The bending moment against the curvature of the section
questions.solution:
**A plot of the axial load capacity P_u against the moment capacity M_u**, every point on the curve representing a combination at which the section just reaches its ultimate limit state.

**How to read the diagram:**

| Feature | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **The point on the P axis (M = 0)** ← | **PURE AXIAL capacity — the maximum load with no moment** ← |
| **The point on the M axis (P = 0)** ← | **PURE BENDING capacity — the section acting as a beam** ← |
| **Any point INSIDE the curve** ← | **A SAFE combination of P and M** ← |
| **Any point OUTSIDE the curve** ← | **UNSAFE — the section cannot carry that combination** ← |
| **Any point ON the curve** ← | **Exactly at capacity** ← |
| **The BALANCED point, at the curve's outermost bulge** ← | **Where the concrete reaches 0.0035 exactly as the tension steel reaches yield** ← |

> **THE MOST STRIKING FEATURE OF THE CURVE IS ONE THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE AND IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING PROPERLY: over the upper part of the diagram, ADDING axial load INCREASES the moment capacity.**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The curve does not fall monotonically from the P axis to the M axis** ← | **It bulges outward, reaching its maximum moment at the balanced point** ← |
| **Above the balanced point, the section is COMPRESSION controlled** ← | **The concrete crushes before the steel yields** ← |
| **There, axial compression HELPS resist moment** ← | **Because it delays the onset of tension on the far face** ← |
| **Below the balanced point, the section is TENSION controlled** ← | **The steel yields first, and additional axial load then REDUCES the moment capacity** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE COUNTER-INTUITIVE PART AND THE EXPLANATION IS SIMPLE ONCE SEEN: a section in pure bending cracks on its tension face and its capacity is limited by that.**

> **Add axial compression and the tension is partly cancelled, so the section can carry more moment before it cracks and before the steel yields.**

> **Push the axial load higher and the compression face becomes the limitation instead, and from there on more axial load reduces the moment capacity.**

> **Hence the bulge, and hence a design consequence that matters: the WORST load case for a column is not necessarily the one with the largest axial load.**

> **A column may be perfectly safe under maximum axial load with its accompanying moment, and unsafe under a smaller axial load with a larger moment — which is exactly the situation under wind or earthquake, where the windward column's axial load is REDUCED while its moment is greatest.**

**WHICH IS WHY ALL THE LOAD COMBINATIONS MUST BE PLOTTED, NOT MERELY THE LARGEST:**

| Combination | Note |
|---|---|
| **1.5(DL + LL)** ← | **Usually maximum P with modest M** ← |
| **1.2(DL + LL ± EL)** ← | **Moderate P, large M** ← |
| **0.9 DL ± 1.5 EL** ← | **MINIMUM P with large M — often the critical point on the diagram, and the one most often overlooked** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE CASE THE INTERACTION DIAGRAM EXISTS TO CATCH: the combination with reduced dead load and full seismic load gives the least axial compression together with the greatest moment.**

> **On the tension-controlled part of the curve, that is the least favourable place to be — and a column checked only under maximum axial load will never reveal it.**

> **Plotting every combination as a point and confirming that all lie inside the curve is therefore not a formality but the whole purpose of the method, and it is why interaction diagrams (or the equivalent SP-16 charts) are used rather than a single formula: the capacity is a curve, and the demand is a scatter of points that must all fall within it.**

examTip.trick: **P_u against M_u — inside is safe, outside is not.** The curve bulges outward, its maximum moment at the balanced point.
examTip.trap: **Above the balanced point, MORE axial load INCREASES the moment capacity** — compression delays tension on the far face. Below it, more axial load reduces capacity.
examTip.mnemonic: **0.9DL ± 1.5EL is often the critical point** — least axial load with the greatest moment, on the tension-controlled branch. Checking only maximum P never finds it.

questions.stem: In the design of an isolated column footing, ONE-WAY shear and TWO-WAY (punching) shear differ in that punching shear is checked:
options: Only in footings supporting circular columns
On a PERIMETER surrounding the column at a distance of d/2 from its face
At the edge of the footing rather than near the column
Only where the footing is reinforced in one direction
questions.solution:
**On a PERIMETER surrounding the column at a distance of d/2 from its face**, the footing tending to fail by the column punching through it — whereas one-way shear is checked on a vertical section across the full width of the footing.

**The two checks compared:**

| Aspect | ONE-WAY shear | TWO-WAY (punching) shear |
|---|---|---|
| **Critical section** | **A vertical plane at a distance d from the column face, across the FULL WIDTH** ← | **A PERIMETER at d/2 from the column face, all round** ← |
| **Failure imagined** | **The footing shearing off as a beam** ← | **The column PUNCHING a plug through the footing** ← |
| **Area resisting** | **Footing width × d** ← | **Perimeter × d** ← |
| **Permissible stress** | **τ_c from Table 19, by grade and steel percentage** ← | **k_s × 0.25 √f_ck** ← |
| **Which usually governs** | **Wide, shallow footings** ← | **Small footings under heavily loaded columns** ← |

> **THE PUNCHING CHECK IS THE MORE DANGEROUS OF THE TWO AND IT DESERVES THE MORE CARE, for a reason worth stating: a punching failure is sudden, brittle and gives no warning.**

> **The column simply drives a truncated pyramid of concrete through the footing, and there is no ductile phase at all.**

> **It is the same mechanism as a flat slab failing around a column — and progressive punching failures in flat slab buildings, where one column's punching overloads the next, have caused some of the worst structural collapses on record.**

> **So a footing or a flat slab must be comfortably safe in punching, and the check should not be passed by a narrow margin.**

**The permissible punching stress and the k_s factor:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **Permissible stress = k_s × 0.25 √f_ck** ← | ← |
| **k_s = 0.5 + β_c, subject to a MAXIMUM of 1.0** ← | **β_c being the ratio of the column's SHORTER side to its longer side** ← |
| **For a SQUARE column, β_c = 1, so k_s = 1.5 which is capped at 1.0** ← | **Full permissible stress** ← |
| **For a very ELONGATED column, β_c is small, so k_s falls toward 0.5** ← | **Halving the permissible stress** ← |

> **THE PENALTY FOR AN ELONGATED COLUMN IN THE FOURTH ROW HAS A CLEAR PHYSICAL BASIS AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING WHY: the shear stress around a punching perimeter is NOT uniform.**

> **Around a square column it is nearly uniform, and every part of the perimeter contributes.**

> **Around a long thin column the stress concentrates at the ends and along the short faces, while the long faces are less effectively engaged — so the nominal average stress computed over the full perimeter understates the peak.**

> **The k_s factor corrects for that concentration, and it is why a long thin wall-like column requires more footing depth than a square column carrying the same load.**

**AND WHAT TO DO WHEN THE PUNCHING CHECK FAILS, since the options are limited:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **INCREASE the footing DEPTH** ← | **The primary remedy — depth enters the resisting area directly and also increases the perimeter at d/2** ← |
| **Raise the concrete GRADE** ← | **The permissible stress goes as √f_ck, so the gain is modest** ← |
| **Provide SHEAR reinforcement** ← | **Possible but awkward in a footing, and generally avoided** ← |
| **Use a PEDESTAL or a column CAPITAL to enlarge the loaded area** ← | **Which increases the punching perimeter substantially** ← |
| **Never simply add flexural steel** ← | **Punching capacity depends hardly at all on the bottom reinforcement** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE MISTAKE TO AVOID AND IT IS AN EASY ONE TO MAKE, because adding steel is the instinctive response to any deficiency: the punching capacity of a footing is essentially a function of its DEPTH, its concrete grade and the loaded perimeter.**

> **Flexural reinforcement in the bottom of the footing does very little for it, because the punching failure surface is inclined and passes through the concrete rather than along the reinforcement.**

> **So a footing failing in punching must be made DEEPER, and no amount of additional bottom steel will substitute — which is why the punching check is normally done early in the design, since it usually determines the footing's thickness before the flexural steel is calculated at all.**

examTip.trick: **Punching: a perimeter at d/2 all round the column. One-way: a plane at d from the face across the full width.** Different sections, different permissible stresses.
examTip.trap: **Permissible punching = k_s × 0.25√f_ck, with k_s = 0.5 + β_c ≤ 1.0** — an elongated column halves it, because the shear concentrates at the short faces.
examTip.mnemonic: **Punching capacity depends on DEPTH, not on bottom steel** — the failure surface passes through the concrete. So a failing check means a deeper footing, and it is checked first.

questions.stem: The PLAN AREA of an isolated footing is determined using:
options: The factored (ultimate) column load divided by the ultimate bearing capacity of the soil
The factored column load divided by the safe bearing capacity
The SERVICE (unfactored) column load, increased by an allowance for the footing's own weight and the soil above it, divided by the SAFE BEARING CAPACITY of the soil
The service load divided by the ultimate bearing capacity
questions.solution:
**The SERVICE (unfactored) column load, increased by an allowance for the footing's own weight and the soil above it, divided by the SAFE BEARING CAPACITY of the soil.**

**The two-stage nature of footing design, which is the point of the question:**

| Stage | Loads used | Determines |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Sizing the PLAN AREA** ← | **SERVICE loads** ← | **The footing's length and breadth, from the safe bearing capacity** ← |
| **2. Designing the SECTION — depth and reinforcement** ← | **FACTORED loads** ← | **The thickness, the flexural steel, and the shear checks** ← |

> **THE REASON FOR THE SPLIT IS THAT THE TWO STAGES ARE GOVERNED BY DIFFERENT LIMIT STATES, AND MIXING THEM IS THE COMMONEST ERROR IN FOOTING DESIGN:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The PLAN AREA is governed by SETTLEMENT and by soil bearing failure** ← | **Both of which are checked against the SAFE bearing capacity — a value that already includes a factor of safety, usually 2.5 to 3 on shear failure, and is also limited by permissible settlement** ← |
| **So applying factored loads to it would apply a factor of safety TWICE** ← | **Giving a footing perhaps 50 per cent larger than necessary** ← |
| **The SECTION is governed by the concrete's and steel's ultimate strength** ← | **Which requires factored loads, like any other reinforced concrete member** ← |
| **The soil pressure used for the section design is therefore the FACTORED load divided by the area already fixed** ← | **A notional pressure, larger than the real one, used only for the structural design** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE ERROR TO AVOID AND IT IS EXPENSIVE RATHER THAN UNSAFE: the safe bearing capacity is not a characteristic value awaiting a partial factor, it is already a working value with its own factor of safety embedded.**

> **Dividing a factored load by it therefore applies about 1.5 on top of about 2.5, giving an effective factor near 4 — and the footing is oversized by half.**

> **On a building with a hundred footings that is a substantial and entirely wasted quantity of concrete and excavation.**

> **THE FOURTH ROW DESCRIBES THE STEP THAT LOOKS INCONSISTENT AND IS NOT: having sized the footing on service loads, the designer computes an upward soil pressure from the FACTORED load over that same area and designs the concrete for it.**

> **That pressure will never actually occur — the soil will never be loaded to it, because the loads will never be factored in reality.**

> **It is a device for arriving at the correct factored bending moments and shears in the footing slab, and it is the standard approach.**

**THE SELF-WEIGHT ALLOWANCE IN THE ANSWER IS THE DETAIL MOST OFTEN OMITTED:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The footing and the soil above it also bear on the soil beneath** ← | **So they consume part of the bearing capacity** ← |
| **An allowance of 10 to 15 per cent of the column load is customary** ← | **Refined once the footing's dimensions are known, if it matters** ← |
| **For a LIGHTLY loaded footing at a considerable depth, the allowance can be a large fraction of the total** ← | **A footing 2 m deep in soil at 18 kN/m³ imposes 36 kN/m² before the column's load is counted at all** ← |
| **Which for a soil of 100 kN/m² safe bearing capacity is over a third of the available pressure** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS SHOW WHY THE CUSTOMARY 10 PER CENT IS NOT ALWAYS ADEQUATE AND THE ALLOWANCE SHOULD BE COMPUTED WHERE IT MATTERS: a deep footing on a weak soil can have a large part of its capacity consumed by the overburden it carries.**

> **In such cases the NET bearing capacity — the safe capacity less the pressure from the footing and its backfill — is what is actually available for the column, and using the gross figure over-estimates it substantially.**

> **This is also the reason a BUOYANT or compensated foundation works: excavating soil and replacing it with a lighter structure can impose no net additional pressure at all, which is how heavy buildings are founded on soft ground without excessive settlement.**

examTip.trick: **Service loads plus about 10 % for self weight, divided by the SAFE bearing capacity.** Then factored loads for the depth and reinforcement.
examTip.trap: **The safe bearing capacity already contains its own factor of 2.5-3** — using factored loads applies safety twice and oversizes the footing by about half.
examTip.mnemonic: **Area from service loads, section from factored loads.** The factored soil pressure is a notional device for getting the right moments — it will never actually occur.

questions.stem: A COMBINED footing, carrying two or more columns on a single base, is adopted principally when:
options: The soil's bearing capacity is unusually high
The columns carry equal loads
A single large footing is always cheaper than two separate ones
The columns are so CLOSE that their individual footings would OVERLAP
questions.solution:
**When the columns are so CLOSE that their individual footings would OVERLAP, or a column stands so near a PROPERTY LINE that a symmetrical footing cannot be built under it.**

**The circumstances that call for a combined footing:**

| Circumstance | Note |
|---|---|
| **Columns CLOSE together, so isolated footings would overlap** ← | **Which happens with closely spaced columns on weak soil, where each footing must be large** ← |
| **A column near a PROPERTY LINE or an existing building** ← | **A symmetrical footing would trespass, so the footing must be eccentric to the column — and combining it with an interior column balances the eccentricity** ← |
| **Weak soil requiring large footings generally** ← | **The larger the footings, the sooner they meet** ← |
| **Columns of very unequal load close together** ← | **Where separate footings would settle differentially** ← |
| **To reduce DIFFERENTIAL settlement between two columns** ← | **A common base settles as one** ← |

> **THE PROPERTY LINE CASE IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE CLASSIC PROBLEM AND IT IS WORTH SEEING WHY IT NEEDS A SOLUTION AT ALL: a footing must be concentric with its column's load, or the soil pressure is non-uniform and the footing tilts.**

> **A boundary column cannot have a concentric footing, because half of it would be on the neighbour's land.**

> **An eccentric footing under it alone would rotate, so the column would tilt and its moment would have to be resisted by the frame above.**

> **Combining it with the next interior column puts the two loads on one base whose centroid can be made to coincide with the resultant of the two loads — so the pressure is uniform and nothing tilts.**

**The forms available:**

| Form | Suited to |
|---|---|
| **RECTANGULAR combined footing** ← | **Two columns of roughly EQUAL load — the resultant falls near the middle** ← |
| **TRAPEZOIDAL combined footing** ← | **Two columns of UNEQUAL load, where the resultant is closer to the heavier column — the footing is made wider under it** ← |
| **STRAP (cantilever) footing** ← | **Two separate footings joined by a rigid beam that transfers moment — used where the columns are far apart and a full combined slab would be wasteful** ← |
| **RAFT (mat) footing** ← | **All columns on one slab — for very weak soil or very heavy structures** ← |

> **THE TRAPEZOIDAL FORM IN THE SECOND ROW EXISTS FOR A SPECIFIC GEOMETRIC REASON AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: the footing's CENTROID must coincide with the RESULTANT of the column loads, so that the pressure is uniform.**

> **With equal loads the resultant is midway between the columns, and a rectangle's centroid is also midway — so a rectangle serves.**

> **With unequal loads the resultant shifts toward the heavier column, and a rectangle's centroid cannot be moved without extending the footing beyond the light column, which may not be possible or may be wasteful.**

> **A trapezoid, being wider at one end, has its centroid displaced toward that end — so the widths can be chosen to place the centroid exactly under the resultant while the overall length stays within the space available.**

> **That is the whole reason for the shape, and it also sets the limit of its usefulness: a trapezoid's centroid can be moved only between one-third and one-half of its length, so if the resultant lies outside that band a trapezoid cannot be made to work and a strap footing is needed instead.**

**THE STRAP FOOTING IN THE THIRD ROW DESERVES A NOTE BECAUSE ITS ACTION IS DIFFERENT IN KIND:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The two footings remain SEPARATE and bear on the soil independently** ← | ← |
| **A rigid STRAP BEAM connects the columns above them** ← | **And the beam must be stiff enough not to deflect appreciably** ← |
| **The strap carries the MOMENT needed to make the boundary footing's pressure uniform** ← | **Transferring it to the interior footing** ← |
| **The strap itself does NOT bear on the soil** ← | **It is deliberately kept clear of the ground, or the soil beneath it is loosened, so that it acts purely as a beam** ← |

> **The last row is a detail that must be got right or the mechanism fails: if the strap bears on the soil, it picks up an upward pressure that was never in the analysis, and the moment transfer it was built to provide is disturbed.**

> **Hence the drawing note requiring the ground beneath a strap beam to be excavated slightly and backfilled loose, or a compressible layer placed under it — a small provision that is essential to the design's logic and easily overlooked on site.**

examTip.trick: **Overlapping footings, or a column at a property line where a concentric footing cannot be built.** Not about the soil being strong or the loads being equal.
examTip.trap: **The footing's CENTROID must coincide with the RESULTANT of the loads** — which is why unequal loads need a trapezoid, whose centroid is displaced toward the wider end.
examTip.mnemonic: **A strap beam must NOT bear on the soil** — excavate slightly beneath it, or it picks up pressure that was never in the analysis and defeats the moment transfer.

questions.stem: The column bars projecting into a footing (starter or dowel bars) must extend into it far enough to:
options: DEVELOP their full design stress within the footing
Reach the bottom reinforcement mat, and no further
Extend at least 300 mm below the top of the footing in every case
Reach the mid-depth of the footing
questions.solution:
**To DEVELOP their full design stress within the footing** — that is, at least the development length below the top of the footing, which frequently governs the footing's minimum thickness.

**The requirement and its consequence:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The column's load is transferred to the footing partly by BEARING and partly through the BARS** ← | ← |
| **A column bar in compression must develop its stress by bond within the footing** ← | **Over a compression development length, which is L_d/1.25 — 25 per cent shorter than the tension value** ← |
| **Where the column carries MOMENT, some bars are in TENSION** ← | **And must develop the full tension L_d** ← |
| **So the footing's thickness must accommodate that length, plus the cover** ← | **Which often makes the footing thicker than either the flexural or the shear check requires** ← |
| **A standard 90-degree bend at the bar's foot contributes 8 φ of anchorage** ← | **Which helps, and is why starter bars are always shown with a foot turned outward along the bottom mat** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE PRACTICAL POINT AND IT IS ONE OF SEVERAL SEPARATE CHECKS THAT CAN GOVERN A FOOTING'S DEPTH — which is worth listing together:**

| Check | Note |
|---|---|
| **PUNCHING shear** ← | **Usually the governing check for a heavily loaded column** ← |
| **One-way shear** ← | **Governs wide footings** ← |
| **Flexure** ← | **Rarely governs, footings being thick** ← |
| **DEVELOPMENT LENGTH of the column bars** ← | **Governs where the column has large-diameter bars and a modest load** ← |
| **A minimum practical thickness** | **150 mm at the edge of a sloped footing, and enough for two mats plus cover** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW OF THIS TABLE IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN FORGOTTEN AND IT CATCHES DESIGNERS OUT ON LIGHTLY LOADED COLUMNS WITH LARGE BARS: a column with 25 mm bars in M20 concrete needs 47 × 25 = 1,175 mm of tension development length.**

> **No ordinary footing is that thick. So the bar must be anchored by a bend — and even with the 8 φ credit and the compression reduction the requirement is substantial.**

> **The usual resolution is that the compression length applies (L_d/1.25 = 940 mm for that bar), a bend contributes, and the footing is made as thick as it must be — or a PEDESTAL is introduced between the column and the footing, giving the extra depth without thickening the whole base.**

**THE LOAD TRANSFER AT THE COLUMN-FOOTING INTERFACE IS WORTH SETTING OUT PROPERLY, since it is a separate check in its own right:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **The permissible BEARING stress at the interface is 0.45 f_ck** ← | **Which may be increased by a factor of √(A₁/A₂), up to 2, to allow for the confinement the surrounding footing provides** ← |
| **A₁ being the supporting area and A₂ the loaded area** ← | **The enhancement recognising that a small loaded area on a large block is confined** ← |
| **Any load in excess of the permissible bearing must be carried by DOWELS or by the extended column bars** ← | ← |
| **The dowel area must be at least 0.5 per cent of the column's area** ← | **With a minimum of four bars** ← |

> **THE √(A₁/A₂) ENHANCEMENT IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS THE SAME CONFINEMENT PRINCIPLE MET IN THE HELICAL COLUMN AND IN THE CUBE-CYLINDER COMPARISON, and recognising it as such is useful: concrete loaded over a small area on a large mass is laterally supported by the surrounding material and can carry a much higher stress than its uniaxial strength.**

> **It is the same reason a nail can be driven into hardwood without crushing, and the same reason a cube tested between platens reads high.**

> **In a footing it is a genuine and usable benefit — a column bearing on a footing many times its own area may take up to twice the ordinary permissible stress — and it is why bearing at a column base is rarely the governing consideration despite the stresses appearing alarming when computed on the plain area.**

examTip.trick: **Full development length below the top of the footing** — which frequently dictates the footing's thickness, ahead of flexure and sometimes ahead of shear.
examTip.trap: **A 25 mm bar in M20 needs 1,175 mm in tension** — no ordinary footing is that thick. Compression reduces it by 25 %, a bend adds 8φ, and a PEDESTAL is the usual resolution.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bearing at the interface is 0.45f_ck, enhanced by √(A₁/A₂) up to 2** — the same confinement effect as the helix and the test cube. Small area on a large mass takes more.

questions.stem: PRE-TENSIONING differs from POST-TENSIONING in that in pre-tensioning the:
options: Tendons are tensioned after the concrete has hardened, and anchored at the ends
TENDONS are tensioned FIRST, against external abutments, and the concrete is then cast around them
Concrete is compressed by jacking against the abutments directly
Tendons are left unbonded throughout the member's life
questions.solution:
**The TENDONS are tensioned FIRST, against external abutments, and the concrete is then cast around them** — the prestress being transferred by BOND when the tendons are released.

**The two methods:**

| Aspect | PRE-TENSIONING | POST-TENSIONING |
|---|---|---|
| **Order of operations** | **TENSION the tendons, cast the concrete, release** ← | **CAST the concrete with ducts, then tension and anchor** ← (option a) |
| **Prestress transferred by** | **BOND along the tendon** ← | **END ANCHORAGES bearing on the concrete** ← |
| **Where it is done** | **In a FACTORY, against permanent abutments or a stressing bed** ← | **On SITE, or in a factory** ← |
| **Tendon profile** | **Usually STRAIGHT (can be deflected with hold-downs)** ← | **Any CURVED profile, following the moment diagram** ← |
| **Suited to** | **Repetitive PRECAST units — sleepers, piles, planks, beams** ← | **Large, long-span, in-situ or segmental structures — bridges, silos, long-span floors** ← |
| **Grouting** | **Not applicable, the tendon is in direct contact with concrete** ← | **Ducts are GROUTED after stressing, for bond and corrosion protection** ← |

> **THE TENDON PROFILE IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE DECISIVE PRACTICAL DIFFERENCE AND IT EXPLAINS THE DIVISION OF APPLICATIONS: post-tensioning allows the tendon to be CURVED.**

> **A curved tendon can be placed low at midspan where the sagging moment is greatest and high over the supports where the moment reverses — so the prestress follows the moment diagram and is efficient at every section.**

> **A straight pre-tensioned tendon gives the same eccentricity everywhere, which is right at midspan and wrong at the ends, where it produces a hogging moment the member does not need.**

> **That is manageable in a simply supported precast unit and unacceptable in a long continuous bridge — which is why bridges are post-tensioned and railway sleepers are pre-tensioned.**

> **The curved tendon also provides a VERTICAL component of force that acts against the applied load, which is the basis of the load-balancing method of design.**

**AND THE TRANSFER MECHANISM IN THE SECOND ROW HAS AN IMPORTANT CONSEQUENCE AT THE ENDS OF A PRE-TENSIONED MEMBER:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The prestress builds up from ZERO at the member's end over the TRANSMISSION LENGTH** ← | **Because bond needs distance to develop the force** ← |
| **The transmission length is of the order of 50 to 100 tendon diameters** ← | **Depending on the concrete strength, the tendon type and its surface** ← |
| **So the end region of a pre-tensioned beam is NOT fully prestressed** ← | **Which must be allowed for if the beam is short or if loads act near its end** ← |
| **A post-tensioned member, by contrast, has its full force applied at the anchorage immediately** ← | **But then suffers intense local BURSTING stresses there instead** ← |

> **THE CONTRAST IN THE LAST ROW IS INSTRUCTIVE AND IT SHOWS THAT NEITHER METHOD ESCAPES THE END PROBLEM, only relocates it:**

> **Pre-tensioning distributes the transfer over a length, so the stresses are gentle but the end region is under-stressed.**

> **Post-tensioning concentrates the transfer at a point, so the full prestress is available immediately but the anchorage zone must be heavily reinforced against splitting and bursting.**

> **The end block of a post-tensioned beam accordingly carries a dense cage of spirals, links or a grid, designed specifically for the transverse tensile stresses that a concentrated force produces as it spreads into the section.**

> **This is one of the places where prestressed concrete design is genuinely different in character from ordinary reinforced concrete: the highest and most awkward stresses occur where there is no bending moment at all, and the reinforcement there resists nothing that appears in the member's global analysis.**

examTip.trick: **Pre-tension: stress the tendons, cast, release — transfer by BOND. Post-tension: cast with ducts, then stress — transfer by ANCHORAGES.**
examTip.trap: **Post-tensioning allows a CURVED tendon following the moment diagram** — which is why bridges are post-tensioned and sleepers pre-tensioned. A straight tendon is wrong at the ends.
examTip.mnemonic: **Neither escapes the end problem, it just moves** — pre-tensioning has a transmission length of 50-100 diameters where prestress is incomplete; post-tensioning has bursting stresses at the anchorage.

questions.stem: Among the losses of prestress, those that occur IMMEDIATELY (at transfer) rather than over time are:
options: Creep of concrete, shrinkage of concrete and relaxation of steel
Friction only
ELASTIC SHORTENING of the concrete, FRICTION along the tendon, and ANCHORAGE SLIP
Shrinkage of concrete and anchorage slip
questions.solution:
**ELASTIC SHORTENING of the concrete, FRICTION along the tendon, and ANCHORAGE SLIP.**

**The losses, separated by when they occur:**

| Loss | When | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **ELASTIC SHORTENING of concrete** ← | **IMMEDIATE** ← | **The concrete shortens as the prestress is applied, so the bonded tendon shortens with it and loses stress** ← |
| **FRICTION (in post-tensioning)** ← | **IMMEDIATE** ← | **Along the duct — both CURVATURE friction and WOBBLE (unintentional deviation) friction** ← |
| **ANCHORAGE SLIP (draw-in)** ← | **IMMEDIATE** ← | **The wedges seat themselves a few millimetres as the jack is released** ← |
| **CREEP of concrete** ← | **TIME-DEPENDENT** ← | **The largest of the long-term losses** ← (option a groups all three long-term losses) |
| **SHRINKAGE of concrete** ← | **TIME-DEPENDENT** ← | ← |
| **RELAXATION of steel** ← | **TIME-DEPENDENT** ← | **The tendon loses stress at constant strain** ← |

> **THE TOTAL LOSS AMOUNTS TO ROUGHLY 15 TO 20 PER CENT IN PRE-TENSIONING AND 20 TO 25 PER CENT IN POST-TENSIONING, AND ITS MAGNITUDE IS THE WHOLE REASON PRESTRESSED CONCRETE NEEDS HIGH-STRENGTH STEEL, which is worth following through.**

**THE ANCHORAGE SLIP IN THE THIRD ROW HAS A PROPERTY THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE AND MATTERS GREATLY IN SHORT MEMBERS:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The slip is a fixed DISTANCE — typically 3 to 6 mm, set by the anchorage system** ← | **Not a fixed percentage** ← |
| **The strain loss is that distance divided by the TENDON LENGTH** ← | ← |
| **So the same 5 mm slip is trivial in a 50 m tendon and severe in a 5 m one** ← | **5/50,000 = 0.01 % against 5/5,000 = 0.1 % — ten times worse** ← |
| **In a short member the loss can be a large fraction of the total prestress** ← | **Which is why post-tensioning short members is inefficient and pre-tensioning is preferred for them** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE PRACTICAL CONCLUSION AND IT EXPLAINS A DESIGN PREFERENCE THAT OTHERWISE LOOKS ARBITRARY: post-tensioning is for LONG members, and not merely because long members are large.**

> **A 4 m post-tensioned lintel loses so much prestress to anchorage slip that the method is barely worth using, whereas a 40 m bridge girder loses a tenth as much proportionally.**

> **So the choice of method follows from the member's length as well as from its shape and its production setting.**

**THE FRICTION LOSS IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE ONE THAT REQUIRES ACTIVE MANAGEMENT ON SITE:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Curvature friction depends on the total ANGLE turned through** ← | **Not on the length — a sharply curved tendon loses more** ← |
| **Wobble friction depends on the LENGTH, and on how accurately the duct was held in line** ← | **A badly supported duct that snakes between its supports has a large unintended angle change** ← |
| **The loss is measured on site by comparing the JACK pressure with the tendon ELONGATION** ← | **The two must agree within a few per cent, or something is wrong** ← |
| **Stressing from BOTH ends halves the maximum friction loss** ← | **Standard practice for long tendons** ← |
| **The duct may be flushed with water or lubricant before stressing** | ← |

> **THE ELONGATION CHECK IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT QUALITY CONTROL MEASURE IN POST-TENSIONING AND IT DESERVES ITS PROMINENCE: the jack's pressure gauge says what force is being applied at the anchorage, and the measured extension says what force the tendon has actually experienced along its length.**

> **If the extension is much LESS than predicted, friction is higher than assumed — perhaps the duct is blocked, kinked, or full of grout from a leak.**

> **If it is much MORE, the tendon may be slipping, or a wire may have broken.**

> **Either discrepancy must be resolved before the tendon is accepted, because once the duct is grouted nothing can be inspected or corrected — and a tendon stressed to the wrong force is a defect permanently sealed inside the member.**

examTip.trick: **Immediate: elastic shortening, friction, anchorage slip. Time-dependent: creep, shrinkage, relaxation.** Total 15-20 % pre-tensioned, 20-25 % post-tensioned.
examTip.trap: **Anchorage slip is a fixed DISTANCE (3-6 mm), not a percentage** — so it is ten times worse proportionally in a 5 m tendon than a 50 m one. Hence post-tensioning suits long members.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check jack pressure against measured ELONGATION** — a discrepancy means blocked duct, kink or broken wire. After grouting nothing can be inspected or corrected.

questions.stem: HIGH-STRENGTH steel is essential in prestressed concrete, rather than ordinary mild steel, because:
options: Mild steel cannot be bent to the required tendon profiles
High-strength steel bonds better to concrete
Mild steel corrodes faster inside a duct
The LOSSES of prestress consume a roughly FIXED STRAIN
questions.solution:
**Because the LOSSES of prestress consume a roughly FIXED STRAIN**, so a low initial stress would be almost entirely lost — a high initial stress is needed for a useful residual prestress to remain.

**The argument, worked through with numbers:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The total loss from creep, shrinkage, elastic shortening and relaxation is a STRAIN of roughly 0.0006 to 0.0008** ← | **Largely set by the concrete's shrinkage and creep, which do not care what steel is used** ← |
| **A strain loss of 0.0007 in steel of E = 200 GPa is a STRESS loss of about 140 N/mm²** ← | **0.0007 × 200,000** ← |
| **MILD steel prestressed to its working stress of about 140 N/mm² would lose ALL of it** ← | **Nothing whatever would remain** ← |
| **High-strength wire stressed to 1,200 N/mm² loses the same 140** ← | **Retaining about 1,060 — some 88 per cent** ← |
| **So the SAME absolute loss is ruinous at low stress and modest at high stress** ← | **Which is the entire reason for high-strength steel** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE HISTORICAL FACT THAT DELAYED PRESTRESSED CONCRETE BY DECADES AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: early attempts at prestressing in the nineteenth century failed, and nobody could explain why.**

> **They used ordinary steel at ordinary stresses, and the prestress simply disappeared over the following months.**

> **Freyssinet identified the cause in the 1920s — creep and shrinkage of the concrete — and drew the correct conclusion: prestressing requires steel stressed far higher than structural practice then allowed, which in turn requires high-strength steel.**

> **So prestressed concrete was not merely an idea awaiting invention but an idea awaiting a MATERIAL, and it became possible only when high-strength wire could be made reliably.**

**HIGH-STRENGTH CONCRETE IS EQUALLY NECESSARY, AND FOR SEVERAL SEPARATE REASONS:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **The prestress must be RESISTED — the concrete carries the full force in compression** ← | **Often 12 to 20 N/mm², applied at transfer when the concrete is young** ← |
| **Higher strength concrete CREEPS and SHRINKS less** ← | **Reducing the very losses that made high-strength steel necessary** ← |
| **It has a higher modulus, so the elastic shortening loss is smaller** ← | ← |
| **BEARING stresses at the anchorages are intense** ← | **And must be carried locally** ← |
| **Bond and transmission length in pre-tensioning improve with strength** ← | **Shortening the under-stressed end region** ← |
| **IS 1343 requires a minimum of M30 for post-tensioned and M40 for pre-tensioned work** ← | **Pre-tensioning being the more demanding, since transfer relies on bond** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW SHOWS A PLEASING CIRCULARITY IN THE DESIGN LOGIC AND IT IS WORTH NOTING: high-strength concrete reduces the losses, which reduces the demand on the steel — so the two high-strength materials are not two independent requirements but a mutually reinforcing pair.**

> **A prestressed member in weak concrete would suffer larger creep and shrinkage losses, needing an even higher initial steel stress, which would need still stronger concrete to carry it.**

> **The technology therefore only works at the upper end of both materials' ranges, which is why prestressed concrete is inseparable from good quality control — it is not a technique that can be executed carelessly with ordinary materials at a slightly higher stress.**

> **This is also why prestressing is executed by specialist subcontractors with their own equipment and procedures, and why the tendon force, the concrete strength at transfer and the grouting are all subject to hold points that must be witnessed rather than merely recorded.**

verification.notes: Strain loss 0.0007 x E 200000 = 140 N/mm2 stress loss, which equals mild steel's whole working stress but is 12% of 1200.

examTip.trick: **The loss is a fixed STRAIN of about 0.0007, that is 140 N/mm² of stress** — the whole of mild steel's working stress, but only 12 % of a 1,200 N/mm² tendon.
examTip.trap: **Early prestressing attempts failed for exactly this reason** and nobody knew why until Freyssinet identified creep and shrinkage. It was an idea awaiting a MATERIAL.
examTip.mnemonic: **High-strength concrete reduces the very losses that demand high-strength steel** — the two reinforce each other. IS 1343: M30 post-tensioned, M40 pre-tensioned.

questions.stem: In the LOAD BALANCING approach to prestressed concrete design, a parabolic tendon is chosen so that:
options: The UPWARD force the curved tendon exerts on the concrete balances a chosen part of the applied load
The tendon's length is minimised
The friction losses along the duct are minimised
The tendon lies wholly within the section's kern
questions.solution:
**So that the UPWARD force the curved tendon exerts on the concrete balances a chosen part of the applied load** — so that under that load the member has no deflection and carries only uniform axial compression.

**The mechanism:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A tendon under tension T, forced to follow a CURVE, presses against the concrete** ← | **Just as a bent bowstring presses on the bow** ← |
| **For a parabolic tendon of sag h over a span L, that pressure is an equivalent UPWARD uniform load** ← | **w_p = 8 T h / L²** ← |
| **If the applied downward load equals w_p, the two cancel exactly** ← | ← |
| **The member then has NO transverse load at all** ← | **No bending moment, no shear, no deflection** ← |
| **All that remains is the AXIAL compression T, uniformly distributed over the section** ← | **A member in pure uniform compression** ← |

> **THE RESULT IN THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS IS ELEGANT AND IT IS THE WHOLE APPEAL OF THE METHOD: a beam under its balanced load behaves as though it were not a beam at all.**

> **It is simply a prism in uniform compression — perfectly flat, uncracked, with a uniform stress across every section.**

> **Deflection under the balanced load is zero, so the long-term creep deflection is also zero, because there is no bending to creep under.**

> **That last consequence is the practically valuable one: a conventionally reinforced long-span floor sags progressively for years, while a load-balanced prestressed floor does not.**

**HOW THE METHOD IS USED IN PRACTICE:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Choose the load to be BALANCED — usually the DEAD load, or dead plus a part of the imposed load** ← | **Balancing the dead load means the member is flat under permanent load, which is what matters for finishes** ← |
| **From w_p = 8Th/L², choose T and h to suit** ← | **h being limited by the section's depth and the cover** ← |
| **The member is then analysed for the UNBALANCED remainder only** ← | **A much smaller load, giving small moments and deflections** ← |
| **Stresses are checked at transfer and at service** ← | **Since at transfer the full prestress acts with only the self weight, which is the critical case for the top fibre** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WHERE THE METHOD SAVES SO MUCH WORK AND IT IS WHY IT BECAME STANDARD FOR PRESTRESSED FLAT SLABS: an indeterminate prestressed structure is awkward to analyse directly, because the prestress induces secondary moments through the restraint of the supports.**

> **Load balancing sidesteps that: the prestress is replaced by an equivalent upward load, the structure is analysed for the NET load by ordinary elastic methods, and the secondary moments emerge automatically because the equivalent loads are applied to the real indeterminate structure.**

> **So a complicated prestressing problem becomes an ordinary load case on a familiar frame — which is why the method, introduced by T Y Lin, transformed the design of prestressed floors and made continuous prestressed construction routine.**

**AND THE CRITICAL CASE IN THE FOURTH ROW DESERVES ITS EMPHASIS, BECAUSE IT IS PECULIAR TO PRESTRESSING:**

| Stage | Condition |
|---|---|
| **AT TRANSFER** ← | **FULL prestress acts, but only the SELF WEIGHT resists it — so the member HOGS, and the BOTTOM fibre is in maximum compression while the TOP may go into TENSION** ← |
| **AT SERVICE** ← | **Reduced prestress after losses, with the full imposed load — the conventional case** ← |

> **The transfer condition is often the more severe, and it is the reverse of the service condition in sign — which means a prestressed member must be checked for two nearly opposite states.**

> **A member adequate at service may crack at its top at transfer, particularly if it is stressed early while the concrete is young and the imposed load is absent.**

> **This is why the concrete strength at transfer is a specified hold point, and why the sequence and timing of stressing are part of the design rather than a matter for the contractor.**
