examTip.trick: **w_p = 8Th/L² upward from a parabolic tendon.** Balance the load and the member has no moment, no shear and no deflection — only uniform axial compression.
examTip.trap: **The transfer condition is often more severe and is OPPOSITE in sign** — full prestress with only self weight makes the member hog, putting the TOP fibre into tension.
examTip.mnemonic: **Replacing prestress with an equivalent load turns an indeterminate prestressing problem into an ordinary load case** — and the secondary moments come out automatically. T Y Lin's method.

questions.stem: In the classification of prestressed concrete members by IS 1343, a member of TYPE 2 is one in which:
options: No tensile stress is permitted in the concrete at any stage
TENSILE stress is PERMITTED at service load, but no VISIBLE CRACKING is allowed
Cracking is permitted, with the crack width limited to a specified value
The tendons are left unbonded
questions.solution:
**One in which TENSILE stress is PERMITTED at service load, but no VISIBLE CRACKING is allowed.**

**The three types:**

| Type | Permitted at service load | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **TYPE 1 — FULL prestressing** ← | **NO tensile stress at all** ← (option a) | **The section remains wholly in compression** ← |
| **TYPE 2 — LIMITED prestressing** ← | **Tensile stress permitted, but NO visible cracking** ← | **Tension up to the concrete's flexural strength — this question** ← |
| **TYPE 3 — PARTIAL prestressing** ← | **CRACKING permitted, with the width limited to 0.1 or 0.2 mm by exposure** ← (option c) | **Untensioned reinforcement usually added to control the cracks** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION FROM TYPE 1 TO TYPE 3 IS A PROGRESSION IN HOW MUCH PRESTRESS IS APPLIED, AND THE TRADE-OFF IS WORTH SETTING OUT, because the intuitive assumption that more prestress is better is wrong:**

| Consideration | Full prestressing (Type 1) | Partial prestressing (Type 3) |
|---|---|---|
| **Prestress required** | **HIGH** ← | **LOWER** ← |
| **Cost of tendons and anchorages** | **High** | **Lower** ← |
| **Behaviour under service load** | **Uncracked, very stiff** ← | **Cracked, less stiff** ← |
| **CAMBER (upward deflection) under permanent load** | **LARGE, and it grows with creep** ← | **Modest** ← |
| **Behaviour at OVERLOAD** ← | **Can be brittle, with little warning** ← | **More ductile, with visible cracking as warning** ← |
| **Suited to** | **Water-retaining and gas-tight structures, severe exposure** ← | **Buildings, ordinary bridges, most structures** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS CONTAIN THE ARGUMENT FOR PARTIAL PRESTRESSING AND THEY EXPLAIN WHY IT IS NOW THE NORMAL PRACTICE RATHER THAN A COMPROMISE:**

> **A fully prestressed member is heavily compressed, so it CAMBERS upward under permanent load, and creep amplifies that camber over years — which can be visually objectionable in a floor and can crack partitions just as sagging does.**

> **It is also stiff and highly stressed, so at overload it has little reserve deformation and fails with less warning.**

> **A partially prestressed member with some untensioned reinforcement cracks visibly before it fails, deflects noticeably, and cambers less — behaving much more like ordinary reinforced concrete in its warning of distress, while retaining most of prestressing's benefits under service load.**

> **So partial prestressing is not a cheapened version of full prestressing but a deliberate design choice, and Type 3 members are the majority of prestressed construction.**

**WHERE TYPE 1 IS GENUINELY REQUIRED, WHICH IS THE OTHER SIDE OF THE ARGUMENT:**

| Application | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Water and liquid RETAINING structures** ← | **A crack leaks, so no crack is acceptable at all** ← |
| **Gas-tight and pressure containments** ← | **Same reasoning** ← |
| **Structures in SEVERE or marine exposure** ← | **A crack admits chlorides to a tendon, and a prestressing tendon is far more vulnerable to corrosion than a reinforcing bar** ← |
| **Members subject to heavy fatigue loading** | **Cracks propagate under cycling** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CONTAINS THE MOST IMPORTANT DURABILITY CONSIDERATION IN PRESTRESSED CONCRETE AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: a prestressing tendon cannot tolerate the corrosion that a reinforcing bar can.**

> **A tendon is a thin, highly stressed, high-carbon wire, and it is susceptible to STRESS CORROSION and to hydrogen embrittlement — mechanisms that can fracture it with very little section loss and no external warning.**

> **Worse, a tendon's failure is not local: it releases the prestress over a whole length of the member, so one broken tendon can affect a span rather than a section.**

> **This is why grouting of post-tensioning ducts is treated as a structural operation rather than a finishing one, why voids in grout are a serious defect, and why several major bridge failures and demolitions have followed from tendon corrosion in inadequately grouted ducts.**

examTip.trick: **Type 1: no tension. Type 2: tension but no visible cracking. Type 3: cracking limited to 0.1-0.2 mm.**
examTip.trap: **More prestress is not better** — full prestressing cambers upward, creep amplifies it, and it fails with less warning. Partial prestressing is the normal choice, not a compromise.
examTip.mnemonic: **A tendon cannot tolerate what a rebar can** — stress corrosion fractures it with little section loss, and its failure releases prestress over a whole span. Hence Type 1 in severe exposure.

questions.stem: The END BLOCK of a post-tensioned member requires heavy transverse reinforcement (spirals, links or a grid) because:
options: The concrete there is cast later and is therefore weaker
The tendon must be developed by bond over that length
The concentrated anchorage force SPREADS into the section over a transition length
The end of the member is subject to the largest bending moment
questions.solution:
**Because the concentrated anchorage force SPREADS into the section over a transition length, and that spreading generates TRANSVERSE TENSILE (bursting) stresses** which the concrete cannot resist unaided.

**The mechanism:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The anchorage applies a very large force over a very SMALL area** ← | **The anchor plate being a fraction of the section** ← |
| **That force must spread out to become a uniform stress across the whole section** ← | **Which it does over a distance roughly equal to the member's depth** ← |
| **The spreading STRESS TRAJECTORIES bow outward** ← | **Like the flow lines of a fluid emerging from a nozzle into a wide pipe** ← |
| **Curved compression trajectories require TRANSVERSE TENSION to hold them in equilibrium** ← | **Exactly as a curved tendon presses sideways on the concrete** ← |
| **That transverse tension is the BURSTING force, and concrete is weak in tension** ← | **So it splits, longitudinally, along the line of the tendon** ← |
| **Reinforcement must therefore carry the bursting force** ← | **Spirals immediately behind the anchor, plus links or a grid through the end block** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE KEY IDEA AND IT GENERALISES USEFULLY: whenever compressive stress trajectories CURVE, transverse forces are needed to keep them in equilibrium — and if the curvature spreads them apart, those forces are tensile.**

> **This is the same principle as the bursting force on the inside of a curved tendon, as the splitting force around a deformed bar's ribs, and as the tension in the flange of a spreading footing.**

> **Recognising it as one mechanism appearing in four places is more valuable than treating each as a separate rule, because it means the reinforcement's direction and location can be worked out from the geometry rather than recalled.**

> **The rule is simply this: the steel must cross the plane along which the concrete would split, and that plane lies where the trajectories are diverging.**

**THE ST VENANT PRINCIPLE, WHICH SETS THE EXTENT OF THE PROBLEM:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The disturbed region extends about one SECTION DEPTH from the anchorage** ← | **Beyond that the stress is essentially uniform and ordinary beam theory applies** ← |
| **So the END BLOCK is taken as a length equal to the depth** ← | **And it is designed separately from the rest of the member** ← |
| **Within it, ordinary bending theory does NOT apply** ← | **The stress distribution is genuinely two- or three-dimensional** ← |
| **Hence the use of STRUT AND TIE models, or the code's empirical bursting tension formulae** ← | **Rather than a flexural calculation** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE REASON END BLOCK DESIGN FEELS DIFFERENT FROM THE REST OF STRUCTURAL DESIGN AND IT IS WORTH BEING EXPLICIT ABOUT: the assumptions that underlie beam theory — plane sections remaining plane, stress proportional to distance from the neutral axis — are simply not valid there.**

> **A designer who computes an end block's stresses with the flexural formula gets an answer that bears no relation to reality, and the error is not one of accuracy but of applicability.**

> **The strut-and-tie method is the honest alternative: idealise the flow of force as a truss of concrete struts and steel ties, satisfy equilibrium, and provide steel for every tie.**

> **That method also handles deep beams, corbels, pile caps, openings in walls and beam-column joints — every situation where a region is too short or too disturbed for beam theory — and it is worth learning as a general tool rather than as a prestressing technique.**

**AND THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCES AT THE END OF A POST-TENSIONED MEMBER ARE WORTH LISTING, since this is where prestressing goes wrong on site:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The end block is CONGESTED — anchorages, spirals, links, ordinary reinforcement and ducts all together** ← | **And concrete must still be compacted through it** ← |
| **Honeycombing behind an anchorage is a serious defect** ← | **The anchorage bears on voids, and it can punch through** ← |
| **The concrete must have reached its specified TRANSFER strength before stressing** ← | **Verified by cubes, not assumed from the calendar** ← |
| **Stressing a member whose end block concrete is deficient can burst it explosively** ← | **Which is a genuine safety hazard, and why nobody stands in line with a tendon being stressed** ← |

> **The last row is worth taking literally: a tendon under stress stores an enormous quantity of elastic energy, and an anchorage failure releases it instantly.**

> **The area behind a stressing jack is kept clear for that reason, and it is one of the few operations in ordinary construction where the immediate hazard to the operators is bound up directly with the correctness of the design and the quality of the concrete.**

examTip.trick: **A concentrated force spreading into a section makes its compression trajectories CURVE, and curved trajectories need transverse TENSION** — the bursting force, which splits concrete.
examTip.trap: **Beam theory does not apply within one section depth of the anchorage** — plane sections do not remain plane. Use strut-and-tie or the code's bursting formulae, not the flexural formula.
examTip.mnemonic: **Same mechanism as curved tendons, rebar ribs and spreading footings** — the steel must cross the plane where trajectories diverge. And never stress before the transfer cubes confirm the strength.

questions.stem: In the Indian designation of rolled steel sections, ISMB 400 denotes:
options: An Indian Standard MEDIUM WEIGHT BEAM of 400 mm overall DEPTH
An Indian Standard beam of 400 mm flange width
An Indian Standard beam weighing 400 N per metre
An Indian Standard beam of 400 mm² cross-sectional area
questions.solution:
**An Indian Standard MEDIUM WEIGHT BEAM of 400 mm overall DEPTH.**

**The designation system:**

| Prefix | Section |
|---|---|
| **ISMB** ← | **Indian Standard MEDIUM weight BEAM — the commonest structural beam** ← |
| **ISLB** | **Indian Standard LIGHT weight beam — same depth, lighter, less strong** ← |
| **ISHB** ← | **Indian Standard HEAVY weight beam — wider flanges, much used for COLUMNS** ← |
| **ISWB** | **Indian Standard WIDE flange beam** ← |
| **ISJB** | **Indian Standard JUNIOR beam — the lightest** ← |
| **ISA** ← | **Indian Standard ANGLE — designated by leg lengths and thickness, e.g. ISA 75×75×6** ← |
| **ISMC** ← | **Indian Standard medium weight CHANNEL** ← |
| **ISNT / ISST** | **Normal and deep legged TEE sections** ← |
| **ISSC** | **Indian Standard COLUMN section** ← |

> **THE NUMBER IS ALWAYS THE DEPTH IN MILLIMETRES FOR BEAMS AND CHANNELS, WHICH MAKES THE SYSTEM EASY TO READ ONCE THAT IS FIXED — and it is worth noting that sections of the SAME depth but different series are NOT interchangeable.**

> **An ISLB 400 and an ISMB 400 are both 400 mm deep and will both fit the same opening, but the ISMB is substantially heavier and stronger.**

> **So a substitution made on site because 'the depth is the same' can materially reduce a beam's capacity, and it is a real and easily made procurement error.**

**THE ISHB SERIES IN THE THIRD ROW DESERVES A NOTE BECAUSE ITS PURPOSE IS SPECIFIC AND EXPLAINS A DESIGN PRACTICE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A BEAM needs a large section modulus about one axis only** ← | **So a deep narrow shape is efficient — that is what an ISMB is** ← |
| **A COLUMN may buckle about EITHER axis, so it needs strength in both** ← | **Which wants a section whose two radii of gyration are more nearly equal** ← |
| **An ISMB has r_yy far smaller than r_xx** ← | **Perhaps a quarter of it, so it buckles readily about the weak axis** ← |
| **An ISHB, being wider in the flange, has a much better ratio** ← | **Making it far more suitable as a column** ← |
| **Even so, a single I-section is rarely ideal for a column** ← | **Which is why built-up sections and box sections are used for heavy columns** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE REASON A BEAM SECTION MAKES A POOR COLUMN AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL THING IN THIS ANSWER: an I-section is an optimisation for bending about one axis, and a column is not a bending problem about one axis.**

> **Using an ISMB as a column means its capacity is governed entirely by weak-axis buckling, and the large strong-axis properties that make it an excellent beam contribute nothing.**

> **So the section is being paid for and not used, and an ISHB or a built-up section of the same weight would carry considerably more.**

> **The general principle — that the efficient shape follows from the ACTION rather than from the member's name — recurs throughout steel design: a tension member wants area regardless of shape, a beam wants depth, a column wants a large radius of gyration in both directions, and a torsion member wants a closed section.**

**THE SECTION TABLES THEMSELVES ARE WORTH KNOWING HOW TO READ, since almost every steel calculation begins there:**

| Property | Use |
|---|---|
| **Area A** | **Tension and compression capacity** ← |
| **Moment of inertia I_xx, I_yy** | **Bending stiffness and deflection** ← |
| **Section modulus Z_xx, Z_yy** | **Elastic bending capacity** ← |
| **Plastic section modulus Z_pxx** ← | **PLASTIC bending capacity, used in IS 800:2007 limit state design** ← |
| **Radius of gyration r_xx, r_yy** ← | **Buckling — the smaller value governs** ← |
| **Flange and web thickness** | **Section classification, and local buckling checks** ← |

> **The plastic modulus in the fourth row is the property that the 2007 limit state code brought into routine use: the older working stress code used Z, the elastic modulus, while limit state design uses Z_p, which for an I-section is roughly 1.14 times Z.**

> **That shape factor is the extra capacity available once the section is allowed to yield fully rather than only at its extreme fibre — and capturing it is one of the direct economies of limit state design in steel.**

examTip.trick: **The number is the DEPTH in mm.** ISMB medium beam, ISLB light, ISHB heavy (wide flanges, for columns), ISMC channel, ISA angle by leg × leg × thickness.
examTip.trap: **Same depth does NOT mean interchangeable** — an ISLB 400 fits where an ISMB 400 does and is substantially weaker. A real procurement error.
examTip.mnemonic: **An I-section is optimised for bending about ONE axis, so it makes a poor column** — its capacity is set by weak-axis buckling and the strong-axis properties go unused.

questions.stem: IS 800:2007 replaced the working stress approach of the earlier code with LIMIT STATE design. The partial safety factors it prescribes for the material are:
options: 1.5 for yielding and 1.5 for ultimate rupture
1.0 for both yielding and rupture, safety being provided on the loads alone
γ_m0 = 1.10 for YIELDING (and buckling), and γ_m1 = 1.25 for ULTIMATE RUPTURE of a section in tension
1.15 for yielding and 1.0 for rupture
questions.solution:
**γ_m0 = 1.10 for YIELDING (and buckling), and γ_m1 = 1.25 for ULTIMATE RUPTURE of a section in tension.**

**The material partial factors of IS 800:2007:**

| Factor | Applies to | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **γ_m0** ← | **Resistance governed by YIELDING or by BUCKLING** ← | **1.10** ← |
| **γ_m1** ← | **Resistance governed by ULTIMATE RUPTURE** ← | **1.25** ← |
| **γ_mb** ← | **BOLTS — bearing type, in shear or bearing** ← | **1.25** ← |
| **γ_mf** | **Friction type (HSFG) bolts at slip** | **1.25 (or 1.10 for slip at service load)** ← |
| **γ_mw** ← | **WELDS — shop welding 1.25, SITE welding 1.50** ← | **1.25 / 1.50** ← |

> **THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN γ_m0 AND γ_m1 IS THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE FEATURE OF THE SET AND IT REFLECTS A REAL DIFFERENCE IN CONSEQUENCE, which is worth stating:**

> **YIELDING is a DUCTILE limit state. A member that yields deforms, redistributes, gives warning, and does not separate. So a modest factor of 1.10 suffices.**

> **RUPTURE is a BRITTLE limit state. A section that reaches its ultimate tensile strength FRACTURES, suddenly and completely. So a larger factor of 1.25 is applied.**

> **The code is therefore treating the two failure modes according to how dangerous each is rather than applying one factor to the material — the same logic that gives concrete 1.5 and steel 1.15 in IS 456, applied within a single material to two of its limit states.**

**THE SITE WELDING FACTOR IN THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST PRACTICALLY SIGNIFICANT AND IT IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **γ_mw = 1.25 for SHOP welds, 1.50 for SITE welds** ← | **A 20 per cent penalty on a site weld's capacity** ← |
| **The reason is entirely about CONTROL** ← | **A shop weld is made in a fixed position, by a qualified welder, with good access, controlled conditions and systematic inspection** ← |
| **A site weld may be overhead, in wind or rain, on a scaffold, with poor access and cursory inspection** ← | ← |
| **So the same weld specification produces a less reliable weld on site** ← | **And the code prices that difference explicitly** ← |

> **THE PENALTY IS A GENUINE DESIGN INCENTIVE AND IT SHAPES HOW STEELWORK IS DETAILED: it is one of the reasons steel structures are designed with SHOP-WELDED and SITE-BOLTED connections wherever possible.**

> **A fabricator welds the plates, cleats and stiffeners onto each member in the shop, under controlled conditions and with full inspection.**

> **The erector then bolts the members together on site, because a bolt's capacity does not depend on the weather or on the position it was installed in.**

> **This is the standard arrangement in steel construction and it follows from exactly this consideration — a bolt is a manufactured item whose quality is established before it arrives, whereas a weld is manufactured in place and its quality is established by the circumstances of its making.**

**AND THE LOAD FACTORS FOR COMPLETENESS, since they differ from those in IS 456:**

| Combination | Factors |
|---|---|
| **DL + LL** | **1.5 DL + 1.5 LL** ← |
| **DL + LL + WL/EL** | **1.2 DL + 1.2 LL + 1.2 WL** ← |
| **DL + WL/EL** | **1.5 DL + 1.5 WL** ← |
| **DL opposing WL/EL** | **0.9 DL + 1.5 WL** ← |
| **SERVICEABILITY (deflection)** | **1.0 DL + 1.0 LL** ← |

> **These follow the same pattern as IS 456, which is deliberate — the two codes were harmonised on load combinations so that a composite or a mixed structure can be designed consistently.**

> **The 0.9 DL case in the fourth row matters particularly in steel, because steel structures are LIGHT: a light roof has little dead load to resist wind uplift, so the uplift case governs far more often in steel than in concrete, and it is where the 0.9 factor does its real work.**

examTip.trick: **γ_m0 = 1.10 for yielding and buckling; γ_m1 = 1.25 for ultimate rupture.** Bolts 1.25; welds 1.25 shop, 1.50 site.
examTip.trap: **Yielding is ductile (1.10) and rupture is brittle (1.25)** — two limit states of one material, factored by how dangerous each failure is.
examTip.mnemonic: **Site welds carry a 20 % penalty**, which is why steelwork is SHOP-WELDED and SITE-BOLTED. A bolt's quality arrives with it; a weld's is made where it is made.

questions.stem: A HIGH STRENGTH FRICTION GRIP (HSFG) bolted connection differs fundamentally from an ordinary BEARING type bolted connection in that the HSFG connection:
options: Uses bolts of larger diameter for the same load
Requires the holes to be drilled rather than punched, and nothing more
Can only be used in tension, not in shear
Transfers shear by FRICTION between the clamped plate faces, developed by the bolt's high PRETENSION
questions.solution:
**It transfers shear by FRICTION between the clamped plate faces, developed by the bolt's high PRETENSION** — so the bolt itself carries no shear and the plates do not slip.

**The two mechanisms compared:**

| Aspect | BEARING type | FRICTION type (HSFG) |
|---|---|---|
| **Load transfer** | **The plates SLIP until they bear on the bolt, which then carries SHEAR** ← | **FRICTION between the faying surfaces; no slip at all** ← |
| **Bolt condition** | **Snug tightened** ← | **PRETENSIONED to a high proportion of its proof load** ← |
| **Bolt loaded in** | **SHEAR and the plate in BEARING** ← | **TENSION only** ← |
| **Slip** | **Occurs, of the order of the hole clearance** ← | **NONE, up to the slip load** ← |
| **Stiffness of the joint** | **Lower — the slip is a real movement** ← | **HIGH — the joint is rigid until slip** ← |
| **Behaviour under FATIGUE and reversal** | **POOR — the slip works back and forth, wearing the hole** ← | **EXCELLENT — nothing moves** ← |
| **Cost and control** | **Cheap, simple** ← | **Dearer; the tension must be CONTROLLED and verified, and the surfaces prepared** ← |

> **THE SIXTH ROW IS WHERE HSFG BOLTS EARN THEIR COST AND IT IS THE REASON THEY EXIST: a bearing-type joint under reversing load slips one way and then the other, every cycle.**

> **That movement wears the hole, loosens the joint, and initiates fatigue cracks at the hole's edge — so a bearing joint is unsuitable wherever the load reverses or cycles many times.**

> **An HSFG joint does not move at all, so there is nothing to wear and no relative displacement to concentrate strain.**

> **This is why bridge girders, crane gantries, machine supports and any structure subject to repeated loading use friction-grip connections, while ordinary building frames — loaded essentially statically — use bearing-type bolts.**

**WHAT MAKES AN HSFG CONNECTION WORK IN PRACTICE, AND THEREFORE WHAT CAN DEFEAT IT:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The BOLT TENSION must be achieved and verifiable** ← | **By torque wrench, by turn-of-nut, or by load-indicating washers — and torque is the least reliable of the three** ← |
| **The FAYING SURFACES must be clean and unpainted, or coated only with an approved friction coating** ← | **Paint, oil, grease, mill scale and loose rust all reduce the slip factor** ← |
| **The SLIP FACTOR μ is specified — typically 0.2 to 0.5** ← | **0.2 for untreated surfaces, up to 0.5 for grit-blasted** ← |
| **The plies must be in close CONTACT** ← | **A gap means the clamping force is spent bending the plates rather than clamping them** ← |
| **The tension must not RELAX** ← | **Which is why HSFG bolts must not be used through soft packing, gaskets or long grips without care** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE REQUIREMENT MOST OFTEN VIOLATED ON SITE AND IT IS AN INSTRUCTIVE PARADOX: an HSFG connection must NOT be painted on its contact surfaces.**

> **Everything else about steelwork is painted for protection, so the instruction to leave a specific area bare runs against the grain of normal practice — and a painter who coats the whole member before erection has silently reduced the joint's capacity, perhaps by half.**

> **The defect is invisible once the joint is assembled and it is not detectable by any subsequent inspection.**

> **So the masking of faying surfaces before painting is a hold point on any project using friction-grip connections, and it is one of the clearest examples in construction of a quality requirement that is obvious to the designer, counter-intuitive to the tradesman, and undetectable afterwards.**

> **The first row's warning about torque is worth carrying too: torque relates to tension only through a friction coefficient at the thread, which varies with lubrication, thread condition and washer type — so a torque wrench can be substantially out. Turn-of-nut and direct-tension-indicating washers measure the extension itself and are more dependable.**

examTip.trick: **Friction between clamped faces, from bolt PRETENSION — the bolt is in TENSION only and nothing slips.** Bearing type: the plates slip and the bolt takes shear.
examTip.trap: **HSFG faying surfaces must NOT be painted** — paint, oil or mill scale wrecks the slip factor. Invisible once assembled and undetectable afterwards.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bearing joints slip back and forth under reversal, wearing the hole** — so bridges, cranes and anything cyclic use HSFG. And torque is the least reliable way to verify tension.

questions.stem: BLOCK SHEAR failure of a bolted connection is the mode in which:
options: The bolt shears across its shank on one or more planes
A BLOCK of the connected plate TEARS OUT, failing in TENSION on one plane and in SHEAR on another perpendicular to it
The plate crushes locally where the bolt bears against the hole
The bolt is pulled out of the plate in tension
questions.solution:
**A BLOCK of the connected plate TEARS OUT, failing in TENSION on one plane and in SHEAR on another perpendicular to it.**

**The failure modes of a bolted connection, all of which must be checked:**

| Mode | Description |
|---|---|
| **BOLT SHEAR** ← | **The bolt shears across its shank — on one plane in a single-shear joint, two in double shear** ← (option a) |
| **BEARING on the plate** ← | **The plate crushes and elongates where the bolt presses against the hole** ← (option c) |
| **BEARING on the bolt** | **The bolt's shank deforms** ← |
| **TENSION rupture of the plate at the net section** ← | **The plate tears across the line of holes** ← |
| **BLOCK SHEAR** ← | **A block tears out, tension on one plane and shear on the other — this question** ← |
| **BOLT TENSION** ← | **The bolt fails in tension, in a moment connection or under prying** ← (option d) |
| **Plate TEAR-OUT at the edge** | **Insufficient end distance, so the bolt splits out through the plate's edge** ← |

> **BLOCK SHEAR IS THE MODE MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND IT WAS NOT EVEN IN THE OLDER CODE, so it deserves particular attention:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **It requires a group of bolts near the END of a member** ← | **A single bolt cannot produce a block** ← |
| **The failure surface has TWO parts at right angles** ← | **A tension plane across the last row of bolts, and shear planes running out to the member's end** ← |
| **Neither part alone would fail — it is the COMBINATION** ← | **Which is why checking net-section tension and bolt shear separately does not catch it** ← |
| **It is a common failure in ANGLE and GUSSET connections** ← | **Where a small number of bolts is used near the end of a thin member** ← |
| **IS 800:2007 gives it an explicit check** ← | **T_db, taking the lesser of two expressions combining gross shear with net tension and net shear with gross tension** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WHY THE MODE ESCAPED ATTENTION FOR SO LONG AND IT IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION: block shear is not a failure of the bolts and it is not a failure of the net section.**

> **A connection can have ample bolt shear capacity and ample net-section tension capacity and still tear a block out, because the block's boundary passes through neither of those critical sections in the way the individual checks assume.**

> **So it is a genuinely separate limit state and must be checked as one, and the fact that connections designed under the old code sometimes failed this way is exactly why the 2007 code introduced the check.**

**THE PRACTICAL REMEDIES ARE ALL GEOMETRIC, WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **INCREASE the END DISTANCE** ← | **Lengthening the shear planes, which is the most effective single measure** ← |
| **Use MORE bolts in more rows** ← | **Distributing the load over a larger block boundary** ← |
| **Increase the PLATE thickness** ← | **The failure surfaces are proportional to thickness** ← |
| **Increase the GAUGE (transverse spacing)** ← | **Widening the tension plane** ← |
| **Not simply using LARGER bolts** ← | **Which increases bolt shear capacity and does little for block shear — and larger holes actually reduce the net tension plane** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE INSTINCTIVE WRONG ANSWER AND IT IS WORTH BEING EXPLICIT ABOUT: when a connection is short of capacity, the natural response is to use bigger bolts.**

> **For bolt shear that works. For block shear it barely helps and can hurt, because a bigger bolt needs a bigger hole, which removes more of the tension plane.**

> **The correct response is to lengthen the connection — more end distance, more rows — which is why a properly detailed gusset connection is longer than it first appears necessary, and why compressing a connection to fit a tight space is a real risk to its capacity rather than a mere inconvenience.**

examTip.trick: **A block tears out — TENSION on one plane, SHEAR on the perpendicular ones.** Option (a) is bolt shear, (c) bearing, (d) bolt tension.
examTip.trap: **Adequate bolt shear AND adequate net-section tension does not prevent it** — the block's boundary passes through neither critical section as those checks assume. A separate limit state.
examTip.mnemonic: **The remedy is geometric: more END DISTANCE and more rows, not bigger bolts** — a bigger bolt needs a bigger hole, which removes more of the tension plane.

questions.stem: As per IS 800:2007, the MINIMUM PITCH (centre-to-centre spacing along the line of force) of bolts is:
options: 2.5 times the nominal bolt DIAMETER
1.5 times the bolt diameter
The hole diameter plus 5 mm
5 times the bolt diameter
questions.solution:
**2.5 times the nominal bolt DIAMETER.**

**The spacing and edge distance rules:**

| Requirement | Limit |
|---|---|
| **MINIMUM pitch** ← | **2.5 d** ← |
| **MAXIMUM pitch, in a compression or tension member** ← | **The lesser of 16 t or 200 mm (t being the thinner plate)** ← |
| **Maximum pitch in a member exposed to weather (unpainted)** ← | **The lesser of 12 t or 200 mm — tighter, to prevent moisture entering between the plates** ← |
| **Minimum EDGE / END distance, MACHINE flame cut or drilled edge** ← | **1.5 × the HOLE diameter** ← |
| **Minimum edge / end distance, HAND flame cut or sheared edge** ← | **1.7 × the hole diameter — larger, because a rough edge has notches from which a tear can start** ← |
| **Maximum edge distance** ← | **12 t ε, where ε = √(250/f_y); and 40 mm + 4t for exposed conditions** ← |

> **THE MINIMUM PITCH OF 2.5 d EXISTS FOR THREE SEPARATE REASONS, AND EACH IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **To leave enough NET SECTION between holes** ← | **Closely spaced holes remove too much of the plate** ← |
| **To allow the bolt's BEARING stresses to spread without overlapping** ← | **Adjacent bolts each crush a region of plate, and those regions must not merge** ← |
| **To allow physical ACCESS for the spanner or the impact wrench** ← | **A practical constraint that governs surprisingly often** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE THAT DECIDES THE LAYOUT IN REALITY AND IT IS WORTH RESPECTING: a bolt that cannot be reached with a wrench cannot be tightened.**

> **The socket of an impact wrench for a 20 mm bolt is a substantial object, and it must be able to sit squarely on the nut with room to turn.**

> **Connections detailed to the minimum code spacing are sometimes impossible to assemble in practice, particularly inside a channel, near a flange, or in a corner — and the error is discovered by the erector rather than by the checker.**

> **A detailer therefore works to the fabricator's standard gauges and spacings rather than to the code minima, and those standard values embed the access requirement.**

**THE MAXIMUM LIMITS ARE LESS OBVIOUS AND EACH ADDRESSES A DIFFERENT PROBLEM:**

| Limit | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Maximum PITCH of 16 t** ← | **Prevents the plate BUCKLING between bolts when in compression, and prevents the plies separating** ← |
| **Maximum pitch of 12 t in exposed conditions** ← | **Keeps the plies pressed together tightly enough to exclude moisture — corrosion between plates is insidious** ← |
| **Maximum EDGE distance** ← | **Same reasoning — a wide unstitched edge lifts, letting water in** ← |

> **THE CORROSION REASONING IN THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS IS WORTH DWELLING ON BECAUSE THE MECHANISM IS PARTICULARLY DAMAGING: water drawn by capillary action between two plates cannot dry out.**

> **The rust that forms there occupies several times the volume of the steel consumed, so it forces the plates apart — which opens the gap, admits more water, and accelerates the process.**

> **This is called PACK RUST or crevice corrosion, and it can prise a riveted or bolted connection apart, distort members and shear fasteners.**

> **It has been a major cause of deterioration in old riveted bridges and trusses, and the tighter maximum pitch in exposed conditions is the code's response: keep the plies clamped closely enough that water never gets in, because once it does the process is self-driving and effectively unstoppable without dismantling the joint.**

examTip.trick: **Minimum pitch 2.5d.** Edge distance 1.5 × hole diameter for a machine-cut edge, 1.7 × for a sheared or hand-cut one.
examTip.trap: **Maximum pitch tightens from 16t to 12t in exposed conditions** — to clamp the plies against moisture. Corrosion between plates, not buckling, is the reason.
examTip.mnemonic: **Wrench ACCESS governs in practice** — a connection at the code minimum may be impossible to assemble. And PACK RUST prises joints apart once water gets between the plies.

questions.stem: A 6 mm fillet weld is made in the shop with electrodes and parent metal of ultimate tensile strength 410 N/mm². Taking γ_mw = 1.25, the design strength of the weld per millimetre of effective length is about:
options: 0.55 kN/mm
1.13 kN/mm
0.66 kN/mm
0.80 kN/mm
questions.solution:
**About 0.80 kN per mm.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Effective THROAT thickness** ← | **t_t = K × size = 0.7 × 6 = 4.2 mm (K = 0.7 for a 90-degree fillet)** ← |
| **Design strength of the weld metal** ← | **f_wd = f_u / (√3 γ_mw) = 410 / (1.732 × 1.25)** ← |
| **Evaluating** | **= 410 / 2.165 = 189.4 N/mm²** ← |
| **Capacity per mm of length** | **= 4.2 × 189.4 = 795.5 N/mm** ← |
| **In kN/mm** | **= 0.795, about 0.80 kN/mm** ← |

> **So the weld carries roughly 0.8 kN for every millimetre of effective length.**

**THE TWO COEFFICIENTS IN THE CALCULATION BOTH DESERVE EXPLANATION:**

| Coefficient | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **0.7 for the THROAT** ← | **A fillet weld's cross-section is a right triangle of legs equal to the size; its shortest dimension — the THROAT — is the leg times cos 45°, that is 0.707** ← |
| **√3 in the denominator** ← | **The von Mises relation: a material's shear strength is its tensile strength divided by √3, and a fillet weld is designed as though it fails in SHEAR on the throat plane** ← |

> **THE THROAT IS WHERE A FILLET WELD FAILS AND THAT IS WHY IT IS THE DIMENSION USED, which is worth picturing: the weld's triangular section is thinnest along the line from the root to the outer face, and any failure plane takes the shortest path.**

> **So the weld's capacity is governed by the throat and not by the leg length, and the useful rule follows that a fillet weld's capacity is about 0.7 of what its nominal size might suggest.**

> **The assumption that failure is in SHEAR on that plane is a simplification — a fillet weld loaded transversely is actually stronger than one loaded longitudinally — but the code adopts the conservative shear treatment for all directions, which keeps the calculation simple at a modest cost in economy.**

**THE PRACTICAL RULES FOR FILLET WELDS, WHICH THE CALCULATION SITS INSIDE:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **MINIMUM size depends on the THICKER plate** ← | **3 mm for plates to 10 mm, 5 mm to 20 mm, 6 mm to 32 mm, 8 mm above** ← |
| **The minimum exists to prevent CRACKING from rapid cooling** ← | **A small weld on a thick plate cools too fast, since the plate draws the heat away — so it hardens, becomes brittle and cracks** ← |
| **MAXIMUM size along a rounded toe of a section** | **Three-quarters of the section's thickness at the toe** ← |
| **EFFECTIVE LENGTH = actual length − 2 × the weld size** ← | **Deducting the incomplete craters at the start and the stop** ← |
| **Minimum effective length: 4 times the weld size** ← | **A shorter weld is mostly craters** ← |
| **END RETURNS of twice the weld size are required round corners** ← | **Where a weld ends at a free edge under tension** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS A GENUINELY COUNTER-INTUITIVE REQUIREMENT AND IT IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN QUESTIONED ON SITE: the MINIMUM weld size grows with the plate's thickness.**

> **The instinct is that a thick plate needs a big weld for strength, and that is true but is not the reason for the rule.**

> **The reason is THERMAL: a thick plate is a large heat sink, and a small bead of molten metal deposited on it loses its heat very rapidly into the surrounding steel.**

> **Rapid cooling of steel through its transformation range produces a hard, brittle martensitic structure, and the weld cracks — sometimes days later, from hydrogen.**

> **A larger weld deposits more heat, cools more slowly, and forms a sound tough structure. Preheating the plate achieves the same thing by another route, which is why preheat is specified for thick sections and in cold weather.**

> **So the minimum size rule is about metallurgy rather than strength, and complying with it while thinking it is about strength leads a fabricator to economise in exactly the wrong place.**

examTip.trick: **Throat = 0.7 × size; strength = f_u/(√3 γ_mw).** 4.2 × 189.4 = 795 N/mm ≈ **0.80 kN/mm**.
examTip.trap: **The 0.7 is cos 45° — the throat is the SHORTEST path through the weld**, and that is where it fails. So capacity is 0.7 of what the nominal size suggests.
examTip.mnemonic: **Minimum weld size grows with plate thickness for METALLURGICAL reasons** — a thick plate is a heat sink, the small bead cools too fast, hardens and cracks. Preheat does the same job.

questions.stem: The weld defect known as LACK OF PENETRATION (incomplete penetration) is:
options: A cavity in the weld caused by trapped gas
A groove melted into the parent metal alongside the weld, left unfilled
A region at the weld ROOT where the weld metal has FAILED TO FUSE with the parent metal, leaving an unbonded crack-like discontinuity
Slag left between successive passes of a multi-pass weld
questions.solution:
**A region at the weld ROOT where the weld metal has FAILED TO FUSE with the parent metal**, leaving an unbonded crack-like discontinuity.

**The principal weld defects:**

| Defect | Description |
|---|---|
| **LACK OF PENETRATION** ← | **The weld does not reach the root, leaving an unfused gap — this question** ← |
| **LACK OF FUSION** ← | **The weld metal fails to fuse with the parent metal or with a previous pass, at a side wall** ← |
| **POROSITY / blowholes** ← | **Cavities from trapped gas — usually from damp electrodes, oil, or a wet surface** ← (option a) |
| **SLAG INCLUSION** ← | **Slag from one pass not cleaned off before the next, trapped inside** ← (option d) |
| **UNDERCUT** ← | **A groove melted into the parent metal beside the weld and left unfilled — reducing the plate's section** ← (option b) |
| **CRACKS — hot, cold, and hydrogen-induced** ← | **The most serious class** ← |
| **OVERLAP / cold lap** | **Weld metal spilling onto unfused parent metal at the toe** ← |
| **EXCESS convexity, or insufficient throat** | **Geometric defects** ← |
| **DISTORTION** | **Not a defect in the weld itself, but a consequence of its shrinkage** ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ARE THE MOST DANGEROUS OF THE NON-CRACK DEFECTS AND IT IS WORTH SAYING WHY: an unfused region is a CRACK in every mechanical sense.**

> **A pore is a rounded cavity, and a rounded cavity concentrates stress only mildly — a weld with scattered porosity may lose little strength.**

> **An unfused root or side wall is a flat discontinuity with a sharp edge, which is a stress raiser of the most severe kind and a ready-made site for a fatigue crack to start and propagate.**

> **So porosity is generally tolerated within limits, and lack of fusion or penetration is generally not — which is why the acceptance criteria for the two are quite different rather than a single quality threshold.**

**THE INSPECTION METHODS, AND WHAT EACH CAN FIND:**

| Method | Finds |
|---|---|
| **VISUAL inspection** ← | **Surface defects, profile, undercut, size — and it is the most cost-effective of all, catching the majority of defects** ← |
| **DYE PENETRANT (liquid penetrant)** ← | **Surface-breaking cracks only** ← |
| **MAGNETIC PARTICLE** ← | **Surface and slightly sub-surface defects in ferromagnetic material** ← |
| **ULTRASONIC (UT)** ← | **INTERNAL defects, and it is particularly good at detecting PLANAR defects such as lack of fusion — the method of choice for butt welds in thick plate** ← |
| **RADIOGRAPHY (X-ray or gamma)** ← | **Internal defects, giving a permanent image — good for POROSITY and slag, but POOR at planar defects lying parallel to the beam** ← |

> **THE CONTRAST BETWEEN THE LAST TWO ROWS IS THE MOST USEFUL PRACTICAL POINT IN THIS ANSWER AND IT IS OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD: radiography and ultrasonics are not interchangeable.**

> **Radiography detects a defect by the change in absorption along the beam's path — so a rounded pore shows clearly, while a tight planar crack lying edge-on to the beam may absorb almost nothing extra and be invisible.**

> **Ultrasonics detects a defect by reflecting sound off its surface — so a flat crack presenting its face to the beam is a strong reflector and is found readily, while a rounded pore scatters the sound and shows less distinctly.**

> **So the two methods are strong exactly where the other is weak, and the choice depends on which defects matter.**

> **Since lack of fusion and cracks are the dangerous defects and porosity is the tolerable one, ULTRASONIC testing is generally the more appropriate for structural welds — a conclusion that follows directly from the physics and is worth being able to justify rather than merely assert.**

> **The visual inspection in the first row is worth its emphasis too: it is the cheapest method, it requires no equipment, and a competent visual inspection of fit-up before welding and of profile afterwards eliminates a large share of defects before any instrument is brought out.**

examTip.trick: **Unfused metal at the ROOT.** Option (a) is porosity, (b) undercut, (d) slag inclusion.
examTip.trap: **An unfused region is mechanically a CRACK — a flat, sharp-edged stress raiser** — while porosity is rounded and mild. That is why their acceptance criteria differ so much.
examTip.mnemonic: **Radiography finds ROUNDED defects; ultrasonics finds PLANAR ones** — each is weak where the other is strong. Since cracks matter most, UT suits structural welds.

questions.stem: When a single ANGLE is used as a tension member and connected through ONE LEG only, its design strength must be reduced to account for:
options: The reduced yield strength of rolled angles
SHEAR LAG
The greater corrosion of an angle's inner surfaces
The eccentricity of the bolt holes from the angle's heel
questions.solution:
**SHEAR LAG** — the stress being unable to distribute uniformly into the unconnected leg, so that the outstanding leg is not fully effective.

**The mechanism:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The load enters the angle only through the CONNECTED leg** ← | ← |
| **To reach the outstanding leg, it must travel round the heel by SHEAR** ← | ← |
| **That transfer takes DISTANCE, and near the connection it is incomplete** ← | **So the outstanding leg is under-stressed there while the connected leg is over-stressed** ← |
| **The stress distribution across the section is therefore NON-UNIFORM near the joint** ← | **And rupture is initiated in the connected leg before the whole section reaches its strength** ← |
| **The effect is called SHEAR LAG, and the design strength is reduced accordingly** ← | ← |

> **THIS IS THE SAME PHENOMENON MET IN THE EFFECTIVE FLANGE WIDTH OF A T-BEAM, AND RECOGNISING THAT IS USEFUL: in both cases a stiff loaded element must share its force sideways with an attached element through shear, and the sharing is incomplete over a transition length.**

> **In the T-beam the consequence is a reduced effective flange width; in the angle it is a reduced effective net area.**

> **The remedy in both cases is the same in principle — the longer the transition available, the more complete the transfer — which is why a LONGER connection reduces the shear lag penalty in an angle.**

**HOW IS 800:2007 TREATS IT:**

| Expression | Note |
|---|---|
| **T_dn = 0.9 A_nc f_u / γ_m1 + β A_go f_y / γ_m0** ← | **The connected leg's NET area at ultimate, plus the outstanding leg's GROSS area at yield, reduced by β** ← |
| **β = 1.4 − 0.076 (w/t)(f_y/f_u)(b_s/L_c)** ← | **Subject to limits; it falls as the connection gets SHORTER relative to the section's width** ← |
| **L_c being the LENGTH of the connection** ← | **A longer connection gives a larger β and a higher strength** ← |

> **THE DEPENDENCE ON L_c IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE DESIGN LEVER AND IT IS THE POINT WORTH TAKING AWAY: shear lag is mitigated by LENGTHENING the connection.**

> **A single angle bolted with two bolts suffers a substantial penalty; the same angle with four bolts in a longer line suffers much less, because the force has more distance over which to migrate into the outstanding leg.**

> **So a tension connection should be made long rather than compact, which is the opposite of the instinct to keep connections neat — and it is the same conclusion reached for block shear, arrived at from a different direction.**

**THE THREE LIMIT STATES OF A TENSION MEMBER, WHICH THIS SITS WITHIN:**

| Limit state | Expression | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **YIELDING of the GROSS section** ← | **T_dg = A_g f_y / γ_m0** ← | **DUCTILE — the member stretches, so γ_m0 = 1.10 suffices** ← |
| **RUPTURE of the NET section** ← | **T_dn, as above, at the holes** ← | **BRITTLE — so γ_m1 = 1.25** ← |
| **BLOCK SHEAR** ← | **T_db, tearing out a block** ← | **BRITTLE** ← |
| **The design strength is the LEAST of the three** ← | ← | ← |

> **THE COMPARISON BETWEEN THE FIRST TWO ROWS EXPLAINS SOMETHING THAT LOOKS ODD AT FIRST SIGHT: yielding of the gross section is treated as a limit state at all, even though a yielded member has not broken.**

> **The reason is that once the whole gross length yields, the member elongates greatly and continuously — it has effectively lost its function as a tie even though it remains in one piece.**

> **A structure whose tension members have yielded along their length has deformed beyond use.**

> **Net section rupture, by contrast, is an actual fracture and is confined to a short region — which is why it carries the larger factor despite involving the higher material strength f_u.**

> **A well-proportioned tension member is one in which gross yielding governs, so that any overload announces itself by stretching rather than by breaking — and achieving that is a matter of making the connection strong enough relative to the member, which is again an argument for a generous connection.**

examTip.trick: **Shear lag: the load enters one leg and must travel round the heel by shear**, which is incomplete near the joint. The same phenomenon as a T-beam's effective flange width.
examTip.trap: **β improves with a LONGER connection (L_c)** — so lengthen the connection rather than compacting it. The same conclusion as for block shear, reached differently.
examTip.mnemonic: **Three limit states: gross yielding (1.10, ductile), net rupture (1.25, brittle), block shear (brittle) — take the LEAST.** A good tie is one where gross yielding governs.

questions.stem: In a plate with bolt holes arranged in a STAGGERED pattern, the NET AREA available to resist tension is found by:
options: Deducting all the holes in the plate, whatever their arrangement
Deducting only the holes in the single row containing the most holes
Using the gross area, since staggering eliminates the reduction entirely
Examining every possible ZIGZAG failure path and taking the one giving the LEAST net area
questions.solution:
**By examining every possible ZIGZAG failure path and taking the one giving the LEAST net area** — each staggered step being credited with an addition of p_s²/(4g) to compensate for its inclination.

**The rule:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **A failure path may run straight across, or ZIGZAG from hole to hole** ← | **Whichever gives the least remaining material** ← |
| **A zigzag path is LONGER than a straight one** ← | **So it has more material along it, other things being equal** ← |
| **But it is inclined, so it is not purely in tension — it carries shear too** ← | ← |
| **The empirical allowance p_s²/(4g) accounts for that** ← | **p_s being the STAGGER (pitch measured along the direction of force) and g the GAUGE (transverse spacing)** ← |
| **Every credible path must be checked and the SMALLEST net area used** ← | **Which for a many-holed plate means several trials** ← |

> **THE FORM OF THE CORRECTION IS WORTH READING FOR WHAT IT IMPLIES, since it explains when staggering is worth doing:**

| Observation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **The credit p_s²/(4g) grows with the SQUARE of the stagger** ← | **So a small stagger achieves very little, and a generous one achieves a great deal** ← |
| **It falls as the gauge g increases** ← | **Widely separated rows benefit less from staggering** ← |
| **A stagger large enough makes the zigzag path stronger than the straight path** ← | **At which point the straight path across a single row governs, and the staggering has done all it can** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW EXPLAINS A COMMON DETAILING ERROR AND IT IS WORTH BEING EXPLICIT ABOUT: a token stagger is worse than useless.**

> **Offsetting alternate holes by a small amount produces a zigzag path that is barely longer than the straight one, while adding the complication of having to check it — and the net area is scarcely improved.**

> **A stagger worth having is a substantial one, comparable with the gauge, and the purpose of staggering is precisely to prevent all the holes lying on one transverse plane.**

> **So the detailer's choice is to stagger properly or not at all, and half-measures gain nothing.**

**WHY THE HOLE DEDUCTION IS LARGER THAN THE BOLT, WHICH IS A DETAIL WORTH GETTING RIGHT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The deduction uses the HOLE diameter, not the bolt diameter** ← | **Since it is the hole that removes material** ← |
| **The hole is larger than the bolt by the clearance** ← | **1 mm for bolts up to 14 mm, 2 mm for 16 to 24 mm, 3 mm above 24 mm** ← |
| **For PUNCHED holes, a further 2 mm is added** ← | **Because punching damages and work-hardens the metal around the hole, leaving a brittle rim** ← |
| **So a 20 mm bolt in a punched hole deducts 20 + 2 + 2 = 24 mm** ← | **Twenty per cent more than the bolt's own diameter** ← |

> **THE PUNCHING PENALTY IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE PROVISION MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND IT REFLECTS REAL METALLURGICAL DAMAGE: punching a hole through steel plate tears the material rather than cutting it.**

> **The rim of the hole is cold-worked, hardened and left with small tears — a condition that reduces its ductility and provides crack initiation sites.**

> **For static loading the effect is modest and the 2 mm allowance covers it. For fatigue loading or for low-temperature service it is more serious, which is why punched holes are prohibited in bridges and in dynamically loaded structures, and holes are drilled or punched undersize and then reamed.**

> **This is a good instance of a fabrication method affecting the design value: the same bolt in the same plate has a different net area depending on how the hole was made, and the drawing must therefore say which method is permitted rather than leaving it to the fabricator.**

examTip.trick: **Check every zigzag path, credit p_s²/(4g) per stagger, and take the LEAST net area.**
examTip.trap: **The credit grows with the SQUARE of the stagger** — a token offset gains nothing while adding a check. Stagger generously or not at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **Deduct the HOLE, not the bolt: bolt + clearance (1/2/3 mm) + another 2 mm if PUNCHED.** Punching tears and work-hardens the rim, so it is barred in bridges and fatigue work.

questions.stem: IS 800:2007 assigns a steel compression member to one of four BUCKLING CLASSES (a, b, c, d) according to its cross-sectional shape, its thickness and its axis of buckling. The purpose of the classification is to account for:
options: The differing magnitudes of RESIDUAL STRESSES from rolling or welding and of geometric imperfections in different section types
The differing yield strengths of different sections
The variation in the modulus of elasticity between hot-rolled and welded sections
The different corrosion allowances required for different shapes
questions.solution:
**The differing magnitudes of RESIDUAL STRESSES from rolling or welding and of geometric imperfections in different section types** — which cause real columns to buckle at loads below the Euler value by differing amounts.

**Why a real column falls short of the Euler load:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **RESIDUAL stresses from uneven cooling after rolling or welding** ← | **Parts of the section are already in compression before any load is applied, so they yield early** ← |
| **Initial CROOKEDNESS of the member** ← | **A member is never perfectly straight, so bending begins at once rather than at a critical load** ← |
| **Eccentricity of the applied load** ← | ← |
| **Variation of yield strength across the section** ← | ← |
| **The Euler formula assumes a perfectly straight, perfectly elastic, concentrically loaded member** ← | **None of which is true** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE DOMINANT CAUSE AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING HOW IT ARISES, because the mechanism is not obvious:**

> **When a hot-rolled section cools, its thin extremities — the flange tips and the web centre — cool FIRST and contract while the thicker junctions are still hot and plastic.**

> **When the junctions later cool and contract, the already-solid extremities restrain them.**

> **The result is a self-balancing pattern of stress locked into the section: the flange tips end up in COMPRESSION and the web-flange junctions in TENSION, typically to a substantial fraction of the yield stress.**

> **A column so stressed begins to yield at its flange tips as soon as the applied compression is added to the residual compression there — and yielded material contributes no stiffness, so the section's effective moment of inertia falls progressively and it buckles early.**

> **A WELDED section has larger residual stresses still, because welding applies intense local heating, so welded sections fall into a lower buckling class than comparable rolled ones.**

**The classes and what they mean:**

| Class | Imperfection factor α | Typical sections |
|---|---|---|
| **a** ← | **0.21 — the LEAST imperfection, the highest capacity** ← | **Hot-rolled hollow sections** ← |
| **b** | **0.34** | **Rolled I-sections buckling about the strong axis; welded box sections** ← |
| **c** | **0.49** | **Rolled I-sections about the WEAK axis; channels; angles; tees** ← |
| **d** ← | **0.76 — the MOST imperfection, the lowest capacity** ← | **Thick welded sections, and I-sections with very thick flanges about the weak axis** ← |

> **THE POSITION OF ROLLED I-SECTIONS IN CLASSES b AND c IS THE MOST USEFUL PRACTICAL POINT AND IT REWARDS ATTENTION: the SAME section belongs to a different class depending on WHICH AXIS it buckles about.**

> **About the strong axis the flange tips' residual compression is close to the neutral axis and matters less; about the weak axis those same flange tips are the extreme fibres and their early yielding is directly damaging.**

> **So the weak axis suffers both the smaller radius of gyration AND the worse buckling class — a double penalty, which is why an I-section used as a column is so much weaker than its area suggests.**

> **The hollow section in class a is correspondingly favoured: a tube cools evenly, has small residual stresses, has the same radius of gyration in every direction, and is the same class about every axis — which is why circular and square hollow sections are the most efficient compression members available and are used wherever their connection difficulties can be accommodated.**

> **That last qualification is the practical catch: a hollow section is hard to bolt to, because there is no access to the inside for a nut — so connections must be welded, or made with special blind fasteners, or the tube must be slotted and a plate inserted.**

> **The structural efficiency of the tube is therefore bought at the price of more difficult and more expensive connections, and the balance between the two decides whether tubes or open sections are used on a particular job.**

examTip.trick: **Residual stresses and initial imperfections** — which differ by section type and by axis, so real columns fall below Euler by differing amounts.
examTip.trap: **The SAME I-section is class b about the strong axis and class c about the weak one** — so the weak axis suffers both a smaller r and a worse class. A double penalty.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rolling leaves flange TIPS in compression** — they yield first, lose stiffness and precipitate buckling. Welded sections are worse; even-cooling hollow sections are class a.

questions.stem: For a compression member with one end FIXED and the other end FREE (a flagpole or cantilever column), the effective length is:
options: 0.5 times the actual length
0.7 times the actual length
2.0 times the actual length
1.0 times the actual length
questions.solution:
**2.0 times the actual length.**

**The effective lengths for the ideal end conditions:**

| End conditions | Effective length | Euler load relative to pinned |
|---|---|---|
| **Both ends FIXED (in position and direction)** ← | **0.5 L** ← | **4 times** ← |
| **One end fixed, one end pinned** ← | **0.7 L** ← | **About 2 times** ← |
| **Both ends PINNED (held in position, free to rotate)** ← | **1.0 L** ← | **1 — the reference case** ← |
| **One end FIXED, one end FREE** ← | **2.0 L** ← | **One QUARTER** ← |
| **Both ends fixed in direction but one free to SWAY** ← | **1.0 L to 1.2 L** ← | ← |

> **THE RANGE FROM 0.5 L TO 2.0 L IS A FACTOR OF FOUR IN LENGTH AND THEREFORE A FACTOR OF SIXTEEN IN BUCKLING LOAD, and that is the measure of how much the end conditions matter:**

> **The Euler load is π²EI/l_e², so it varies as the INVERSE SQUARE of the effective length.**

> **A fixed-fixed column carries sixteen times the load of a fixed-free column of the same section and the same actual length.**

> **No other single decision in compression member design has that leverage, which is why establishing the restraint conditions honestly is more important than refining the section.**

**WHAT THE EFFECTIVE LENGTH PHYSICALLY MEANS, WHICH MAKES THE VALUES RECOVERABLE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The effective length is the distance between POINTS OF INFLECTION in the buckled shape** ← | **That is, the length of the equivalent PINNED column** ← |
| **A pinned-pinned column buckles in a single half sine wave over its whole length** ← | **So l_e = L** ← |
| **A fixed-fixed column has inflection points at the quarter points** ← | **The middle half is the equivalent pinned column, so l_e = 0.5 L** ← |
| **A fixed-free column's buckled shape is a QUARTER wave** ← | **Its mirror image about the fixed base completes a half wave of total length 2L — hence l_e = 2 L** ← |

> **THE MIRROR-IMAGE CONSTRUCTION IN THE LAST ROW IS THE EASIEST WAY TO SEE WHY THE ANSWER IS 2 AND NOT SOMETHING SMALLER, and it is worth carrying because it makes the value derivable rather than remembered.**

> **A cantilever column deflecting sideways at the top, reflected downward about its base, traces exactly the shape of a pinned column of twice the height.**

> **So a 5 m flagpole buckles as a 10 m pinned strut would — which is why cantilever columns are so inefficient and why they must be made much stouter than their height suggests.**

**AND THE PRACTICAL WARNING, WHICH IS WHERE REAL DESIGN DEPARTS FROM THIS TABLE:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A truly FIXED end requires a connection stiff enough to prevent rotation entirely** ← | **Which a bolted cleat does not do, and even a substantial base plate on a footing rarely does completely** ← |
| **A truly PINNED end requires the position to be held absolutely** ← | **Which requires a bracing system, not merely a beam framing in** ← |
| **IS 800 gives values for realistic PARTIAL restraint** ← | **1.2 L, 1.5 L, 2.0 L and more for sway conditions, which are the values that apply to real frames** ← |
| **Assuming more restraint than exists is the commonest and most dangerous error** ← | **It under-estimates the effective length, hence the slenderness, hence the buckling load** ← |
| **Where in doubt, the CONSERVATIVE assumption is the LONGER effective length** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE POINT TO CARRY INTO PRACTICE AND IT CONNECTS TO THE SLENDER COLUMN QUESTION IN CONCRETE: 'fixed' and 'pinned' are idealisations, and real connections fall between them.**

> **A designer who assumes fixity because a base plate has four bolts, or assumes a braced condition because beams frame in on both sides, has taken a benefit the structure may not provide.**

> **Since the buckling load varies as the inverse square of the effective length, a factor-of-two error in the assumption is a factor-of-four error in the capacity — and unlike most design errors it produces no warning, because buckling is sudden.**

examTip.trick: **Fixed-fixed 0.5L, fixed-pinned 0.7L, pinned-pinned 1.0L, fixed-free 2.0L.** A factor of 4 in length, hence 16 in buckling load.
examTip.trap: **Reflect the cantilever's quarter-wave about its base** — it traces a half wave of length 2L, so a 5 m flagpole buckles like a 10 m pinned strut. That is why 2.0 and not less.
examTip.mnemonic: **Assuming more restraint than exists is the dangerous error** — P_cr goes as 1/l_e², so a factor-of-2 mistake is a factor-of-4 loss, and buckling gives no warning.

questions.stem: For a given cross-sectional AREA, the most efficient shape for a long compression member is one that:
options: Concentrates the material near the centroid, minimising the radius of gyration
DISTRIBUTES the material as FAR from the centroid as possible and EQUALLY about both axes — maximising the least radius of gyration
Is solid rather than hollow, to avoid local buckling
Has the greatest possible depth in one direction only
questions.solution:
**One that DISTRIBUTES the material as FAR from the centroid as possible and EQUALLY about both axes** — maximising the LEAST radius of gyration.

**The reasoning:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The buckling load depends on I, and I = A r²** ← | **So for a fixed area, the capacity depends on r²** ← |
| **r = √(I/A) measures how far the material sits from the centroid** ← | **Material at a distance contributes to I as the square of that distance** ← |
| **So pushing material OUTWARD raises r and raises the capacity, for no extra weight** ← | ← |
| **But a column buckles about its WEAKEST axis** ← | **So the LEAST r governs, and there is no benefit in making one axis strong if the other is weak** ← |
| **Hence the ideal is material spread far out and EQUALLY in every direction** ← | **Which is a thin-walled TUBE** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE CONSTRAINT THAT DEFEATS THE I-SECTION AND IT IS THE HEART OF THE QUESTION: a compression member has no strong axis in any useful sense.**

> **Its capacity is set entirely by its weakest direction, so the strong direction's properties are wasted.**

> **A beam can exploit a single strong axis because the bending is about a known axis, fixed by how the beam is loaded and supported.**

> **A column can buckle in any direction it likes, and it will choose the easiest — so any asymmetry in the section is a pure loss.**

> **This is why the ideal compression section is one for which every direction is equally strong: a circular hollow section, and after it a square hollow section.**

**The comparison, for equal area:**

| Section | Efficiency as a strut |
|---|---|
| **CIRCULAR HOLLOW section** ← | **The BEST — r is identical in every direction, and the material is all at the maximum radius** ← |
| **SQUARE hollow section** ← | **Nearly as good, and much easier to connect and to fit into a rectangular frame** ← |
| **Built-up section of four angles laced apart** ← | **Excellent for very long struts — the material is spread very far out** ← |
| **I-section (ISHB)** ← | **Moderate — r_yy is perhaps half r_xx** ← |
| **I-section (ISMB)** ← | **Poor — r_yy may be a quarter of r_xx** ← |
| **Single ANGLE** ← | **The worst common section — unsymmetrical, and it buckles about a diagonal axis with a small r** ← |
| **SOLID round or square bar** ← | **Very poor — all the material is close to the centroid** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WORTH NOTING BECAUSE IT CONTRADICTS AN INSTINCT AND ANSWERS OPTION (c): a solid bar is a bad column, not a good one.**

> **A solid 100 mm round bar and a 200 mm tube of the same area have radii of gyration of 25 mm and about 70 mm respectively, so the tube carries nearly eight times the buckling load from the same steel.**

> **The solid section's material near the centre contributes almost nothing to I while weighing exactly as much as material at the perimeter would.**

> **So hollowness is an advantage in compression, not a liability — and the limit on how thin the wall may be made is set by LOCAL buckling of the wall itself, which is a separate check and the reason section classification exists.**

> **THE BUILT-UP SECTION IN THE THIRD ROW TAKES THE PRINCIPLE TO ITS CONCLUSION AND IS WORTH KNOWING FOR LONG MEMBERS: four angles at the corners of a large square, joined by light lacing, place all the material at a great radius.**

> **The lacing carries almost no axial load — its job is to make the four angles act as one member rather than four independent struts — and it therefore weighs very little.**

> **The result is a strut of enormous radius of gyration for its weight, which is why transmission towers, crane booms, and long bracing members are built this way rather than from rolled sections.**

examTip.trick: **Material far from the centroid and equal about both axes** — because I = Ar² and the LEAST r governs. That means a thin-walled tube.
examTip.trap: **A column has no useful strong axis** — it buckles whichever way is easiest, so any asymmetry is a pure loss. This is why an ISMB makes a poor column and an ISHB a better one.
examTip.mnemonic: **A SOLID bar is a bad column** — a tube of the same area carries several times the load. Hollowness helps; only LOCAL buckling of the wall limits how thin it can go.

questions.stem: A GUSSETED base is used in preference to a SLAB base for a steel column when:
options: The column is a hollow section
The concrete pedestal is of high strength
The column is short
The load is LARGE
questions.solution:
**When the load is LARGE, so that a slab base would require an impracticably THICK plate** — the gussets stiffening the plate and spreading the load over a wider area.

**The two types compared:**

| Aspect | SLAB base | GUSSETED base |
|---|---|---|
| **Construction** | **A single thick plate, the column bearing directly on it** ← | **A thinner base plate stiffened by gusset plates and angles welded or bolted to the column** ← |
| **Load transfer** | **Directly through the plate in BENDING** ← | **Through the gussets into the plate, which then spans between them** ← |
| **Suited to** | **Light and moderate loads** ← | **HEAVY loads, and columns with significant moment** ← |
| **Plate thickness** | **Grows rapidly with load, since the plate cantilevers from the column's perimeter** ← | **Much less, the gussets reducing the spans** ← |
| **Cost** | **Cheap — one plate, minimal fabrication** ← | **Dearer — more plates, more welding, more fitting** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW EXPLAINS WHY THE SLAB BASE RUNS OUT OF CAPACITY SO ABRUPTLY AND IT IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION: a slab base plate acts as a CANTILEVER projecting from the column's outline, carrying the upward bearing pressure from the concrete.**

> **Its bending moment therefore grows as the SQUARE of the projection, and the plate's thickness must grow roughly as the square root of that moment.**

> **So a heavily loaded column, needing a large base area to spread its load onto the concrete, has a large projection and needs a very thick plate — 60, 80 or 100 mm, which is expensive, hard to obtain, and hard to drill and handle.**

> **Gussets solve the problem by dividing that large projection into several short spans, so the plate's moments fall dramatically and a much thinner plate suffices.**

> **It is the same device as putting stiffeners in any wide plate: reduce the span rather than increase the thickness.**

**The design of a column base, in outline:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. The base AREA from the concrete's bearing capacity** ← | **Area = factored load ÷ 0.6 f_ck for the concrete of the pedestal** ← |
| **2. The plate THICKNESS from its bending as a cantilever** ← | **Or as a plate spanning between gussets** ← |
| **3. HOLDING DOWN bolts** ← | **For uplift and moment; two bolts for a nominally pinned base, four or more for a moment base** ← |
| **4. The connection of the column to the plate** ← | **Weld or bolts, and for a fully bearing column a machined contact face can transfer much of the load directly** ← |
| **5. GROUT beneath the plate** ← | **A non-shrink cement grout filling the gap between the plate and the concrete, so the bearing is uniform** ← |

> **THE GROUT IN THE LAST ROW IS THE STEP MOST OFTEN NEGLECTED ON SITE AND ITS OMISSION DEFEATS THE WHOLE DESIGN: a base plate is set on levelling nuts or shims, standing clear of the concrete, so that the column can be plumbed.**

> **In that condition the entire load passes through a few small shims — a bearing area of perhaps a few thousand square millimetres instead of the design's hundreds of thousands.**

> **The concrete beneath the shims is loaded to many times its capacity and crushes, and the plate bends around them.**

> **The grout is what converts the temporary arrangement into the designed one, and it must be a NON-SHRINK grout completely filling the space, placed from one side so that air escapes rather than being trapped.**

> **A column left un-grouted, or grouted with an ordinary shrinking mortar that pulls away as it dries, is carrying its load in a manner nobody designed — and since the defect is entirely concealed beneath the plate, it is not discoverable later without dismantling.**

> **This is why grouting of base plates is a specified hold point on well-run steel erection, and why the grout's specification appears on the drawings rather than being left as a builder's item.**

examTip.trick: **Heavy loads** — a slab base's plate cantilevers from the column outline, so its moment grows as the square of the projection and the plate becomes impracticably thick.
examTip.trap: **Gussets reduce the SPAN rather than increasing the thickness** — the same device as stiffening any wide plate. Cheaper in steel, dearer in fabrication.
examTip.mnemonic: **Un-grouted base plates carry their load on a few shims** — crushing the concrete beneath them. Non-shrink grout, fully filled, placed from one side. A concealed and undiscoverable defect.

questions.stem: In a BUILT-UP compression member consisting of two channels placed apart, the LACING (or battening) that joins them is designed to:
options: Carry a transverse SHEAR of 2.5 per cent of the axial load in the member, so that the two components act as ONE member rather than as two independent struts
Carry half the axial load in the member
Resist the full bending moment in the member
Carry no force at all, being provided only to hold the components together during transport
questions.solution:
**To carry a transverse SHEAR of 2.5 per cent of the axial load in the member**, so that the two components act as ONE member rather than as two independent struts.

**Why the lacing is needed at all:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Two channels placed apart have an enormous combined moment of inertia about the axis between them** ← | **Which is the whole reason for spacing them** ← |
| **But only if they act TOGETHER** ← | ← |
| **Unconnected, each channel would buckle INDEPENDENTLY about its own weak axis** ← | **And the combined capacity would be merely twice one channel's — a fraction of the built-up value** ← |
| **The lacing forces them to deflect together** ← | **So the assembly buckles as a single member with the large combined I** ← |
| **To do that, the lacing must transfer SHEAR between them** ← | **Just as a beam's web transfers shear between its flanges** ← |

> **THE ANALOGY IN THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST USEFUL WAY TO UNDERSTAND LACING AND IT MAKES THE 2.5 PER CENT INTELLIGIBLE: the two channels are the FLANGES of a very deep open-web beam, and the lacing is its WEB.**

> **A buckling column bends, and a bending member carries shear.**

> **The lacing's duty is therefore exactly a web's duty — to carry the shear associated with the bending of the assembly — and the 2.5 per cent figure is the code's estimate of the transverse shear that the member's initial crookedness and the P-delta effect generate.**

> **So the lacing carries no axial load, which is why it can be light, and it carries a definite and calculable shear, which is why it cannot be omitted or made nominal.**

**The rules for lacing:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Designed for a transverse shear of 2.5 per cent of the axial load** ← | **Divided among the lacing systems on the two faces** ← |
| **Lacing bars inclined at 40 to 70 degrees to the member's axis** ← | **Outside that range they are inefficient** ← |
| **The SLENDERNESS of a lacing bar must not exceed 145** ← | **It is itself a strut and must not buckle** ← |
| **The slenderness of each individual COMPONENT between lacing connections must not exceed 50, or 0.7 times the whole member's slenderness** ← | **Whichever is less — so the components cannot buckle locally between panel points** ← |
| **Lacing on opposite faces should be a MIRROR image, not a repeat** ← | **Or the member is put into torsion** ← |
| **TIE PLATES are required at the ends of the lacing system** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE PROVISION THAT DECIDES THE LACING SPACING AND IT IS THE ESSENTIAL CHECK: each channel between two lacing connections is itself a little strut.**

> **If the lacing panels are too long, an individual channel buckles between panel points before the assembly buckles as a whole — a local failure that the built-up analysis never contemplated.**

> **Requiring the component's local slenderness to be no more than 0.7 of the overall slenderness ensures the whole-member mode governs, so the built-up section's capacity can actually be realised.**

> **THE MIRROR-IMAGE REQUIREMENT IN THE FIFTH ROW IS A SUBTLE ONE WORTH KNOWING: if the lacing on the front face slopes one way and the lacing on the back face slopes the same way, the shear paths on the two faces are offset and the member twists.**

> **Making the two faces mirror images puts the shear paths in balance, so the transverse shear is carried without inducing torsion.**

> **It is a detailing point invisible in any calculation, discoverable only by thinking about the load path in three dimensions — and it is one of a number of such points which is why built-up members are detailed to standard arrangements rather than improvised.**

**AND THE ALTERNATIVE, BATTENING, DIFFERS IN CHARACTER:**

> **BATTENS are solid plates connecting the components, and they act in BENDING rather than as a triangulated system — so a battened member behaves as a Vierendeel frame, its battens carrying moment and shear.**

> **Battening is therefore less efficient than lacing for a given weight, and IS 800 requires battens to be designed for both the shear and the accompanying moment, with the battens' spacing and depth prescribed.**

> **Its advantage is simplicity of fabrication, and it is preferred where the member also carries transverse load or where lacing's many small welds are undesirable.**

examTip.trick: **Transverse shear of 2.5 % of the axial load.** The channels are the FLANGES of a deep open-web beam and the lacing is its WEB — a buckling column bends, and bending carries shear.
examTip.trap: **Each component's local slenderness between panel points must not exceed 50 or 0.7 × the overall value** — otherwise a single channel buckles locally and the built-up capacity is never realised.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lacing on opposite faces must MIRROR, not repeat** — same-way slopes offset the shear paths and twist the member. Invisible in any calculation.

questions.stem: IS 800:2007 classifies steel cross-sections as PLASTIC, COMPACT, SEMI-COMPACT or SLENDER according to the width-to-thickness ratios of their elements. The purpose is to establish:
options: The corrosion protection required
The grade of steel that may be used
Whether the section can develop its full PLASTIC moment and sustain the rotation needed for redistribution
The weld size required at the flange-web junction
questions.solution:
**Whether the section can develop its full PLASTIC moment and sustain the rotation needed for redistribution, or whether LOCAL BUCKLING of its flange or web will limit it to the yield moment or less.**

**The four classes:**

| Class | Can develop | Rotation capacity | Design moment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PLASTIC (class 1)** ← | **The full plastic moment M_p** ← | **SUFFICIENT for a plastic hinge to form and rotate — so plastic analysis is permitted** ← | **Z_p f_y / γ_m0** ← |
| **COMPACT (class 2)** ← | **The full plastic moment M_p** ← | **LIMITED — the hinge forms but cannot rotate enough for redistribution** ← | **Z_p f_y / γ_m0** ← |
