| **SEMI-COMPACT (class 3)** ← | **Only the YIELD moment M_y — the extreme fibre yields and local buckling follows** ← | **None** ← | **Z_e f_y / γ_m0** ← |
| **SLENDER (class 4)** ← | **LESS than the yield moment — local buckling occurs while still elastic** ← | **None** ← | **Based on an EFFECTIVE reduced section** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN PLASTIC AND COMPACT IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS THE SUBTLEST AND IT IS WORTH GETTING RIGHT, since both develop the same moment:**

> **Both reach M_p, so for a simply supported beam they are equivalent and there is no reason to prefer one.**

> **The difference is ROTATION CAPACITY, and that matters only where MOMENT REDISTRIBUTION is relied upon.**

> **Plastic analysis of a continuous beam or a portal frame assumes that a hinge forms at the most stressed point and then ROTATES while the load increases and further hinges form elsewhere — a collapse mechanism developing progressively.**

> **A compact section's hinge forms and then buckles locally rather than rotating, so the mechanism cannot develop and the frame fails at the first hinge.**

> **So plastic analysis requires PLASTIC sections throughout; compact sections may be designed by elastic analysis using the plastic modulus, which is a lesser but still substantial benefit.**

**THE PHYSICAL MECHANISM BEING GUARDED AGAINST IS LOCAL BUCKLING, AND IT IS WORTH PICTURING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A compression flange is a plate, and a wide thin plate in compression BUCKLES as a plate** ← | **Rippling out of its own plane** ← |
| **This happens independently of the member's overall buckling** ← | **A short stocky beam can suffer local flange buckling with no overall instability at all** ← |
| **Once the flange has buckled it cannot sustain further stress** ← | **So the section's moment capacity is capped at whatever it had reached** ← |
| **The critical stress for plate buckling depends on (b/t)²** ← | **Which is why the classification is by WIDTH TO THICKNESS ratio and by nothing else** ← |
| **The limits are scaled by ε = √(250/f_y)** ← | **Because a higher-strength steel reaches a higher stress before yielding, so it is more prone to buckle first** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW CONTAINS A CONSEQUENCE THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE AND IS PRACTICALLY IMPORTANT: a HIGHER GRADE steel is MORE susceptible to local buckling, not less.**

> **Local buckling is an ELASTIC instability, so it depends on E and on the geometry — and E is the same for all structural steels.**

> **What differs is the stress at which the material yields: a mild steel section yields before its plate slenderness becomes critical, while the same geometry in a high-strength steel is still elastic at that stress and buckles instead.**

> **So substituting a higher grade steel into the same section can move it from compact to semi-compact, REDUCING its design moment despite the stronger material.**

> **The ε factor is exactly this correction, and it means the classification must be redone whenever the grade is changed — which is a genuine trap when a specification is upgraded from Fe 410 to Fe 500 in the belief that stronger can only be better.**

examTip.trick: **Plastic: M_p with rotation. Compact: M_p without rotation. Semi-compact: M_y only. Slender: less than M_y.**
examTip.trap: **Plastic ANALYSIS needs class 1 sections throughout** — a compact section's hinge forms but buckles instead of rotating, so the mechanism never develops.
examTip.mnemonic: **Higher grade steel is MORE prone to local buckling** — E is unchanged, so the stronger steel is still elastic where the milder one would have yielded. Reclassify whenever the grade changes.

questions.stem: LATERAL TORSIONAL BUCKLING of a steel beam is the mode of failure in which the beam:
options: Buckles locally in its compression flange without any overall movement
Deflects SIDEWAYS and TWISTS out of its plane of loading
Fails by shear buckling of the web panel
Yields at its extreme fibre and forms a plastic hinge
questions.solution:
**The beam DEFLECTS SIDEWAYS and TWISTS out of its plane of loading**, the compression flange behaving as a strut restrained by the web and the tension flange.

**The mechanism:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The COMPRESSION flange of a bending beam is in compression along its length** ← | **Just like a column** ← |
| **It therefore wants to buckle SIDEWAYS, out of the plane of bending** ← | **In the direction of least resistance** ← |
| **The TENSION flange, being in tension, resists moving sideways** ← | **Tension stabilises; it does not buckle** ← |
| **So the section TWISTS as well as translating** ← | **The compression flange moves and the tension flange does not, which is a rotation** ← |
| **Hence LATERAL (sideways) TORSIONAL (twisting) buckling** ← | **The two are inseparable, and the name records that** ← |

> **THE PAIRING IN THE FOURTH ROW IS WHAT MAKES THE PHENOMENON DISTINCTIVE AND IT EXPLAINS THE NAME: the beam cannot simply move sideways, because the tension flange holds it; and it cannot simply twist, because that would require the flanges to move oppositely.**

> **What it does instead is a combination — the compression flange swings out while the section rotates about a point near the tension flange.**

> **This is why the resistance depends on both the section's lateral bending stiffness (EI_y) and its TORSIONAL stiffness (GJ and the warping constant), and why open sections such as I-beams are so much more susceptible than closed box sections.**

> **A closed box has an enormous torsional stiffness, so it can hardly twist and therefore hardly buckles laterally — which is one of the strongest arguments for box girders in long spans.**

**What governs the resistance:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **The UNRESTRAINED LENGTH between lateral supports** ← | **The dominant factor — halving it greatly increases the capacity** ← |
| **The section's lateral stiffness I_y** ← | **A wide flange resists better** ← |
| **The section's TORSIONAL stiffness** ← | **Closed sections are nearly immune** ← |
| **The SHAPE of the moment diagram along the unrestrained length** ← | **Uniform moment is the worst case; a varying moment is less severe** ← |
| **The POINT of load application** ← | **A load applied at the TOP flange is DESTABILISING, since it moves sideways with the buckling flange and adds to the twist; a load hung from the bottom flange is stabilising** ← |

> **THE LOAD POSITION EFFECT IN THE LAST ROW IS AN ELEGANT AND PRACTICALLY IMPORTANT POINT AND IT IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED: where the load sits on the beam changes its buckling resistance.**

> **A load resting on the top flange travels sideways with that flange as it buckles, so its line of action moves away from the section's centre and it applies an increasing twisting moment — the buckling feeds on itself.**

> **A load suspended from the bottom flange swings like a pendulum and tends to pull the section back upright — a stabilising effect.**

> **IS 800 accounts for this in the effective length: a beam with a destabilising load has its unrestrained length increased by 20 per cent, which is a substantial penalty for a purely geometric circumstance.**

**AND THE REMEDIES, WHICH ARE MOSTLY ABOUT RESTRAINT RATHER THAN SECTION SIZE:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **Provide LATERAL RESTRAINT to the compression flange at intervals** ← | **A restrained beam has a very short effective length and its full plastic capacity may be available** ← |
| **A concrete slab cast on the beam, or a properly fixed steel deck, restrains it fully** ← | **Which is why composite beams and beams supporting floors need no lateral buckling check at all** ← |
| **Secondary beams and bracing at intervals** ← | ← |
| **Use a section with wider flanges, or a box section** ← | **A more expensive route** ← |
| **Remember that the check applies during CONSTRUCTION too** ← | **A bare steel beam before the slab is cast is unrestrained, and is at its most vulnerable exactly when nobody is checking** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL WARNING THAT MATTERS MOST AND IT HAS CAUSED REAL COLLAPSES: a beam designed as laterally restrained by the finished slab has NO such restraint while the slab is being poured.**

> **At that moment it carries its own weight, the formwork, the wet concrete and the working load of the gang — a substantial load — with its compression flange entirely free.**

> **Temporary bracing during erection and concreting is therefore part of the design's assumptions rather than a contractor's convenience, and its omission has brought down steelwork that would have been perfectly safe once complete.**

examTip.trick: **Sideways deflection plus twist** — the compression flange buckles like a strut while the tension flange holds, which is a rotation. Both together, hence the name.
examTip.trap: **A load on the TOP flange is destabilising** — it moves sideways with the flange and adds twist, so IS 800 lengthens the effective length by 20 %. Bottom-flange loads are stabilising.
examTip.mnemonic: **A beam is unrestrained while the slab is being POURED** — carrying formwork, wet concrete and the gang with a free compression flange. Temporary bracing is a design assumption.

questions.stem: The vertical deflection limit that IS 800:2007 places on a steel floor beam supporting a BRITTLE finish (such as plaster or masonry partitions) under LIVE load is:
options: Span / 180
Span / 240
Span / 300
Span / 360
questions.solution:
**Span / 360.**

**The deflection limits, which vary with what the deflection would damage:**

| Member and situation | Limit (live load) |
|---|---|
| **Floor or roof beam with BRITTLE finish (plaster, masonry)** ← | **Span / 360** ← |
| **Floor or roof beam with ELASTIC (flexible) finish** ← | **Span / 240** ← |
| **CANTILEVER with brittle finish** | **Span / 180** ← |
| **Cantilever with elastic finish** | **Span / 120** ← |
| **Purlins and girts** ← | **Span / 150 for brittle cladding, span / 100 for elastic** ← |
| **Crane gantry girders, manually operated** | **Span / 500** ← |
| **Crane gantry girders, electrically operated up to 50 t** ← | **Span / 750, and span/1000 above 50 t — the tightest limits in the code** ← |
| **Lateral sway of a building** ← | **Height / 300 under wind, or height / 500 for buildings with brittle cladding** ← |

> **THE PRINCIPLE RUNNING THROUGH THE TABLE IS THAT THE LIMIT IS SET BY WHAT THE DEFLECTION WOULD SPOIL, NOT BY THE STEEL — and once that is seen, the whole list becomes reasonable rather than arbitrary:**

> **Plaster and masonry crack at small strains, so a member carrying them is limited tightly.**

> **A flexible finish accommodates movement, so a looser limit serves.**

> **A crane rail must stay very nearly straight or the crane will not run smoothly and its wheels will climb the rail — hence the extraordinary span/750 and span/1000.**

> **The steel itself is nowhere near distress at any of these deflections; the limits protect the building's fabric and its usability.**

**WHY DEFLECTION MATTERS MORE IN STEEL THAN IN CONCRETE, WHICH IS THE POINT WORTH TAKING AWAY:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Steel is STRONG relative to its stiffness** ← | **Its yield stress is high while its E is only three times concrete's** ← |
| **So a steel beam sized for STRENGTH is often too FLEXIBLE** ← | **And the deflection check governs the section rather than the moment check** ← |
| **This becomes more pronounced as the steel grade RISES** ← | **A higher grade permits a smaller section for the same moment, and the smaller section deflects more** ← |
| **E does NOT increase with grade** ← | **All structural steels have E ≈ 200 GPa, so stiffness cannot be bought with strength** ← |
| **Hence long-span steel floors are frequently designed on stiffness, and vibration, rather than on strength** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE FACT THAT GOVERNS THE WHOLE MATTER AND IT DESERVES TO BE STATED PLAINLY: using a higher grade of steel buys strength and buys NO stiffness whatever.**

> **So upgrading from Fe 410 to Fe 500 allows a lighter section for the same moment, and that lighter section deflects proportionately more.**

> **On a deflection-governed member the upgrade is therefore worth nothing at all — the section cannot be reduced, because deflection and not strength is the constraint.**

> **This is a real and frequently misunderstood limitation: high-strength steels pay for themselves in columns and in short heavily loaded members, and not in long-span beams.**

> **THE VIBRATION POINT IN THE LAST ROW IS THE MODERN EXTENSION OF THE SAME ISSUE AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: a long-span light steel floor may satisfy every deflection limit and still be unacceptable because it BOUNCES perceptibly when people walk on it.**

> **Human sensitivity to floor vibration is acute, and the governing parameter is the floor's natural frequency together with its damping — neither of which appears in a deflection check.**

> **A frequency below about 3 to 4 Hz for a floor with normal activity is liable to complaints, and the remedy is stiffness or mass rather than strength.**

> **Composite construction helps greatly, since the concrete slab adds both — which is one reason composite floors have largely displaced bare steel beams with a separate slab in building construction.**
tags: E does not vary with grade

examTip.trick: **Span/360 for brittle finishes, span/240 for elastic ones.** Cantilevers halve those spans' effective severity: /180 and /120.
examTip.trap: **Crane gantries are span/750 electrically operated** — because the crane must run true, not because the steel is at risk. The limit is set by what the deflection would spoil.
examTip.mnemonic: **E is 200 GPa for EVERY grade** — so a higher grade buys strength and no stiffness. On a deflection-governed beam an upgrade to Fe 500 is worth nothing.

questions.stem: In timber, a SHAKE is distinguished from a CHECK in that a shake is:
options: A knot formed where a branch joined the trunk
A separation of the fibres along the grain that occurred in the STANDING TREE or during felling
A twist of the timber out of its plane
A fungal decay of the heartwood
questions.solution:
**A separation of the fibres along the grain that occurred in the STANDING TREE or during felling** — whereas a check is a similar separation caused later, by uneven SEASONING.

**The defects of timber, grouped by their cause:**

| Defect | Cause and description |
|---|---|
| **SHAKE** ← | **A lengthwise separation of fibres, arising in the GROWING tree or at felling — cup shake follows an annual ring, heart shake radiates from the pith, star shake radiates in several directions** ← |
| **CHECK** ← | **A similar separation, but caused by uneven DRYING during seasoning — the surface shrinking faster than the interior** ← |
| **KNOT** ← | **The base of a branch enclosed by the trunk's growth — the grain runs around it, so it is a weak point and a stress raiser** ← (option a) |
| **WARP — bow, cup, twist, spring** ← | **Distortion during seasoning, from uneven shrinkage** ← (option c) |
| **WANE** | **A missing edge where the bark's curve is included in the sawn piece** ← |
| **RIND GALL** | **A swelling where a branch was improperly cut** ← |
| **DRY ROT and WET ROT** ← | **FUNGAL decay — dry rot in unventilated damp conditions, wet rot in alternately wet and dry timber** ← (option d) |
| **UPSET / rupture** | **Fibres crushed transversely by shock, often invisible externally** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN A SHAKE AND A CHECK IS ENTIRELY ONE OF WHEN IT HAPPENED, AND IT MATTERS BECAUSE THE TWO ARE PREVENTABLE BY DIFFERENT MEANS:**

> **A SHAKE is inherent in the log and can only be dealt with by SELECTION — inspecting and rejecting or converting around it.**

> **A CHECK is caused by the seasoning process and is therefore preventable by CONTROLLING that process — drying slowly, protecting end grain, and stacking so that air moves evenly around every piece.**

> **So finding checks in a consignment is evidence of poor seasoning practice, while finding shakes is evidence of poor grading — a useful diagnostic distinction when a delivery is disputed.**

**THE KNOT IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE DEFECT THAT MATTERS MOST STRUCTURALLY AND ITS EFFECT DEPENDS ON POSITION, WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Position | Effect |
|---|---|
| **A knot in the TENSION zone of a beam** ← | **Very damaging — the grain deviates around it, so the tensile stress must cross the grain, where timber is weakest** ← |
| **A knot in the COMPRESSION zone** ← | **Much less harmful — timber carries compression across the grain reasonably well, and the knot itself is dense material** ← |
| **A knot at the EDGE of a beam's tension face** ← | **The worst location of all** ← |
| **A knot in a COLUMN** | **Moderately harmful, reducing the effective section** ← |

> **THE ASYMMETRY BETWEEN THE FIRST TWO ROWS HAS A DIRECT PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE THAT EVERY CARPENTER KNOWS AND THAT IS WORTH STATING AS A RULE: a timber beam should be placed with its BETTER, less knotty face DOWN, in the tension zone.**

> **The same piece of timber can be materially stronger or weaker depending only on which way up it is fixed, and the difference costs nothing to obtain.**

> **It is also why timber grading rules limit knot size much more severely on the tension edge than elsewhere, and why the grade of a piece depends on where its defects are and not merely on how many it has.**

> **This is a general feature of timber as a structural material: it is not homogeneous and its properties are directional and locally variable, so the ORIENTATION and PLACING of each piece is part of the structural design rather than a matter of workmanship alone.**

examTip.trick: **A shake happens in the LIVING tree or at felling; a check happens later during SEASONING.** Both are separations along the grain.
examTip.trap: **Checks indict the seasoning; shakes indict the grading** — a useful diagnostic when a delivery is disputed, since the two are prevented by different means.
examTip.mnemonic: **Put the better, less knotty face DOWN in a beam** — a knot in the tension zone forces tension across the grain, where timber is weakest. The same piece, stronger for nothing.

questions.stem: SEASONING of timber is carried out in order to:
options: REDUCE the moisture content to a level in equilibrium with the timber's service environment
Increase the timber's density
Remove knots and other defects
Make the timber non-combustible
questions.solution:
**To REDUCE the moisture content to a level in equilibrium with the timber's service environment** — so that it does not shrink, warp, split or decay after it has been fixed in place.

**Why it is essential:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Freshly felled (green) timber may hold 60 to 200 per cent moisture, by dry weight** ← | **More water than wood, in some species** ← |
| **Timber SHRINKS as it dries below the FIBRE SATURATION POINT of about 25 to 30 per cent** ← | **Above that point the water is free in the cell cavities and its loss causes no shrinkage; below it the water is bound in the cell walls and its loss shrinks them** ← |
| **Shrinkage is HIGHLY ANISOTROPIC** ← | **Roughly 0.1 per cent along the grain, 4 per cent radially, and 8 per cent tangentially — so a piece distorts as well as shrinking** ← |
| **Timber fixed green will therefore shrink IN PLACE, opening joints, loosening fastenings and splitting** ← | ← |
| **Green timber is also liable to FUNGAL attack** ← | **Fungi need moisture above about 20 per cent, so seasoned timber is largely immune** ← |
| **Strength INCREASES substantially as timber dries** ← | **Roughly doubling between green and 12 per cent moisture** ← |

> **THE ANISOTROPY IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE REASON TIMBER WARPS RATHER THAN MERELY SHRINKING, AND IT EXPLAINS EVERY FORM OF WARP: tangential shrinkage is about twice radial shrinkage.**

> **So a board cut from near the outside of a log, whose growth rings curve across its width, shrinks more along its outer face than its inner one — and it CUPS, curling away from the heart.**

> **A board cut through the centre (quarter-sawn) has its rings running across its thickness, so it shrinks evenly across its width and stays flat.**

> **This is why quarter-sawn timber is more stable and more valuable than plain-sawn, and why the SAWING PATTERN affects the finished timber's behaviour as much as the species does.**

> **The tenfold difference between longitudinal and transverse shrinkage also explains why timber joints are detailed to allow cross-grain movement while restraining along-grain movement, and why a wide timber board should never be rigidly fixed at both edges.**

**The methods of seasoning:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **AIR (natural) seasoning** ← | **Stacked in a covered, ventilated yard on level bearers with spacers between the pieces; SLOW — months to years — but cheap and gentle** ← |
| **KILN seasoning** ← | **In a chamber with controlled temperature, humidity and air circulation; days to weeks, and the moisture content can be brought to any desired value** ← |
| **Water seasoning** | **Immersion to leach out sap, followed by air drying** ← |
| **Boiling and electrical seasoning** | **Rapid, used for small quantities** ← |

> **THE CONTROL OF HUMIDITY IN THE KILN IS THE WHOLE ART OF IT AND IT IS WHY KILN SEASONING IS BETTER RATHER THAN MERELY FASTER: if the surrounding air is too dry, the timber's SURFACE dries and shrinks while its interior is still wet and unshrunk.**

> **The surface is then in tension across the grain, and it CHECKS — which is precisely the defect discussed in the previous question.**

> **A kiln therefore begins with high humidity and low temperature and progresses gradually to low humidity and higher temperature, keeping the moisture gradient through the timber's thickness within safe limits throughout.**

> **The same principle governs air seasoning: the ends of a plank, having exposed end grain, lose moisture many times faster than its faces — so the end grain is sealed or the ends are protected, and the stack is arranged so that air moves but does not blast.**

**AND THE TARGET MOISTURE CONTENT DEPENDS ON WHERE THE TIMBER WILL SERVE, WHICH IS THE POINT MOST OFTEN MISSED:**

| Service condition | Target moisture content |
|---|---|
| **Timber in a heated, air-conditioned interior** ← | **8 to 12 per cent** ← |
| **Timber in an unheated interior or a humid climate** ← | **12 to 16 per cent** ← |
| **Timber in an exposed exterior location** ← | **15 to 20 per cent** ← |

> **Seasoning to a value LOWER than the service condition is as bad as seasoning too little: the timber will absorb moisture in service and SWELL, which jams doors, buckles floors and splits panels just as shrinkage opens them.**

> **So the specification is not 'as dry as possible' but 'in equilibrium with where it is going' — which is why joinery for an air-conditioned building must be drier than joinery for a verandah, and why timber should be delivered and stored in conditions resembling its final service before it is fixed.**

examTip.trick: **Bring the moisture content into EQUILIBRIUM with the service environment** — 8-12 % air-conditioned interior, 12-16 % unheated, 15-20 % exterior.
examTip.trap: **Shrinkage starts only below the fibre saturation point (25-30 %)** and is anisotropic: about 0.1 % along the grain, 4 % radial, 8 % tangential. Hence warping, and hence quarter-sawing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Too dry is as bad as too wet** — timber below its service equilibrium will swell, jamming doors and buckling floors. The kiln's art is controlling HUMIDITY, not just heat.

questions.stem: IS 883 gives the permissible stresses of structural timber for three LOCATIONS of use — inside, outside and wet. The permissible stress is HIGHEST for:
options: Wet locations, since the timber is protected from drying stresses
Outside locations, since the timber is well ventilated
INSIDE locations, where the timber is sheltered and its moisture content stays low and stable
All three are equal, the location affecting only the durability requirement
questions.solution:
**INSIDE locations, where the timber is sheltered and its moisture content stays low and stable.**

**The three locations and their relative permissible stresses:**

| Location | Description | Permissible stress |
|---|---|---|
| **INSIDE** ← | **Continuously protected from rain and wetting; moisture content stays low** ← | **The HIGHEST — the reference values** ← |
| **OUTSIDE** ← | **Exposed to alternate wetting and drying, but not continuously wet** ← | **Reduced — about 5 to 15 per cent lower depending on the stress considered** ← |
| **WET** ← | **Continuously or almost continuously wet, or in contact with water or damp earth** ← | **The LOWEST — reduced most** ← |

> **THE REASON IS THE MOISTURE-STRENGTH RELATIONSHIP MET IN THE PREVIOUS QUESTION AND IT IS DIRECT: timber's strength falls as its moisture content rises.**

> **Water absorbed into the cell walls separates and weakens the cellulose structure, so a wet timber is a weaker timber — and the effect is large, strength roughly HALVING between 12 per cent moisture and the green condition.**

> **Since a timber member's moisture content in service is determined by where it sits, the permissible stress must be too.**

> **So the location classification is a strength provision, not merely a durability one — which is why option (d) is wrong even though durability also depends on location.**

**The other modification factors applied to timber's permissible stresses, which together make timber design distinctive:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **DURATION of load** ← | **Timber is much STRONGER under short-duration load: a 33 per cent increase for a load lasting a week, and 100 per cent (double) for instantaneous load such as impact or earthquake** ← |
| **The reverse also holds — a PERMANENT load is more damaging** ← | **The permissible stress for a load carried for the whole life is lower than the tabulated value** ← |
| **GRADE of the timber** ← | **Select, Grade I and Grade II, by the size and position of defects** ← |
| **Species GROUP** ← | **A, B and C by strength, with a minimum modulus of elasticity for each** ← |
| **FORM factor** | **For sections other than rectangular** ← |
| **SIZE factor** | **Larger members having a slightly lower unit strength** ← |

> **THE DURATION EFFECT IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS PECULIAR TO TIMBER AND IT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO UNDERSTAND ABOUT ITS STRUCTURAL BEHAVIOUR: timber exhibits pronounced CREEP RUPTURE.**

> **A timber member loaded to nearly its short-term strength will eventually fail even though the load never increases, because damage accumulates in the fibres under sustained stress.**

> **Conversely, a load applied for only a moment can be much larger than the sustained capacity, because there is no time for that damage to accumulate.**

> **This has a valuable consequence in earthquake and wind design: timber's permissible stress may be DOUBLED for instantaneous loading, so timber structures are relatively much better at resisting brief extreme loads than their static ratings suggest.**

> **Combined with timber's light weight — which reduces the seismic force at source — this makes timber-framed construction genuinely well suited to seismic regions, and it is one reason traditional timber-framed buildings in the Himalaya have often survived earthquakes that destroyed masonry beside them.**

> **THE CONVERSE IS THE WARNING, AND IT IS LESS WIDELY APPRECIATED: a timber member carrying a heavy PERMANENT load — a long-span roof beam under a heavy tiled roof, or a shoring prop left in place for years — is in the least favourable condition, and the tabulated stresses must be reduced rather than used as they stand.**

> **Failures of old timber roof members under nothing but their own long-carried dead load are a recognised phenomenon and follow directly from this mechanism.**

examTip.trick: **INSIDE is highest, then outside, then wet** — because timber's strength falls as its moisture rises, roughly halving from 12 % moisture to green.
examTip.trap: **It is a STRENGTH provision, not just a durability one** — the location determines the service moisture content, which determines the strength.
examTip.mnemonic: **Timber's permissible stress DOUBLES for instantaneous load** — excellent for earthquake and wind. But a permanent load needs a REDUCTION: creep rupture accumulates damage.

questions.stem: In the design of a timber beam, the check that most often governs at a support and is peculiar to timber's anisotropy is:
options: Bending stress at midspan
Deflection under live load
Buckling of the compression edge
BEARING (compression) PERPENDICULAR to the grain
questions.solution:
**BEARING (compression) PERPENDICULAR to the grain, where the beam sits on its support** — timber's strength across the grain being only a small fraction of that along it.

**Timber's directional strengths, which is the fact behind the answer:**

| Direction and action | Relative strength |
|---|---|
| **Compression PARALLEL to the grain** ← | **Strong — the fibres act as a bundle of columns** ← |
| **Tension parallel to the grain** ← | **Strongest of all** ← |
| **Bending (which combines the two)** ← | **Strong** ← |
| **Compression PERPENDICULAR to the grain** ← | **WEAK — perhaps a fifth to a tenth of the parallel value; the fibres are crushed sideways like a bundle of straws** ← |
| **Shear parallel to the grain** ← | **WEAK — the fibres slide past one another, and a beam can split horizontally** ← |
| **Tension perpendicular to the grain** ← | **The WEAKEST of all — barely any strength, and it must never be relied upon** ← |

> **THE LAST THREE ROWS ARE THE WEAKNESSES THAT GOVERN TIMBER DETAILING, AND EACH PRODUCES A CHARACTERISTIC FAILURE:**

> **Bearing perpendicular to the grain crushes the timber where it rests on a support, so the beam sinks into its bearing and the structure settles.**

> **Shear parallel to the grain splits a beam horizontally along its neutral axis near the supports — a longitudinal split rather than a diagonal crack.**

> **Tension perpendicular to the grain simply tears the timber apart along the grain, and it is the mechanism behind almost every splitting failure at a joint or a fastening.**

**THE BEARING CHECK IN PRACTICE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The bearing stress is the reaction divided by the CONTACT area** ← | **Which is often small, since a joist's end may bear over only 75 or 100 mm** ← |
| **Permissible compression perpendicular to the grain is low** ← | **Of the order of 2 to 6 N/mm² for common species** ← |
| **A BEARING PLATE or a wall plate spreads the reaction** ← | **Which is the standard remedy, and the reason wall plates exist** ← |
| **A longer bearing length also serves** ← | ← |
| **Crushing at a bearing is a SERVICEABILITY failure as much as a strength one** ← | **The beam sinks, the floor slopes, and the finishes crack, without anything breaking** ← |

> **THE WALL PLATE IN THE THIRD ROW IS ONE OF THOSE TRADITIONAL DETAILS WHOSE PURPOSE IS OFTEN FORGOTTEN AND IS PRECISELY THIS: a timber wall plate laid along the top of a masonry wall receives the joists and distributes each reaction over a length of wall.**

> **It also protects the joist ends from the masonry's moisture, provides a level and straight bearing on an uneven wall, and gives something to fix to.**

> **In a seismic context it does more still — a continuous wall plate ties the top of the wall together and distributes the roof's load, functioning as a rudimentary roof band.**

> **So a single traditional member serves four purposes at once, which is characteristic of well-evolved vernacular detailing and a reason to understand such details before simplifying them away.**

**THE SHEAR CHECK DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE, SINCE IT IS THE OTHER SUPPORT-REGION CHECK:**

> **Shear stress in a rectangular timber beam is τ = 1.5 V/(bd), the parabolic maximum at the neutral axis — and unlike reinforced concrete, timber takes no factor-free nominal treatment: the actual maximum is used.**

> **Permissible horizontal shear is low, so shear frequently governs SHORT, heavily loaded timber beams, where the moment is small but the reaction is large.**

> **And notching a beam at its support — a common carpentry expedient to gain headroom — is particularly damaging, because it removes material exactly where the shear is greatest and creates a re-entrant corner from which a longitudinal split propagates.**

> **Notches in the tension face near a support are therefore restricted or prohibited, and where a notch is unavoidable it is kept shallow, given a gradual taper rather than a square corner, and placed as near the support as possible.**

examTip.trick: **Bearing across the grain crushes the fibres sideways** — permissible stress is only a fifth to a tenth of the parallel value, over a small contact area.
examTip.trap: **Tension PERPENDICULAR to the grain is timber's weakest property and must never be relied on** — it is behind almost every splitting failure at a joint or fastening.
examTip.mnemonic: **A wall plate does four jobs**: spreads the bearing, keeps masonry damp off the joist ends, levels an uneven wall, and ties the wall head. Don't detail it away. And never notch at a support.

questions.stem: For the design of a solid timber COLUMN, IS 883 classifies the member as SHORT, INTERMEDIATE or LONG according to the ratio of its unsupported length to its LEAST lateral dimension. A column is classed as LONG when that ratio:
options: EXCEEDS 50
Exceeds 11
Is less than 11
Exceeds 180
questions.solution:
**When that ratio EXCEEDS 50.**

**The three classes:**

| Class | l/d (least dimension) | Behaviour and design |
|---|---|---|
| **SHORT** ← | **LESS than 11** ← | **Fails by CRUSHING; the full permissible compressive stress parallel to the grain applies** ← (option c) |
| **INTERMEDIATE** ← | **11 to 50** ← | **A transition; an empirical (fourth-power parabolic) formula reduces the permissible stress** ← |
| **LONG** ← | **GREATER than 50** ← | **Fails by ELASTIC BUCKLING; an Euler-type formula governs** ← |
| **The absolute maximum permitted** ← | **50 for a load-bearing column; up to 180 for members carrying no load other than wind** ← | ← (option d relates to that upper bound) |

> **THE THREE-CLASS TREATMENT MIRRORS WHAT HAPPENS IN STEEL AND CONCRETE COLUMNS AND IS WORTH SEEING AS THE SAME IDEA IN A THIRD MATERIAL:**

> **A SHORT column's capacity is the material's crushing strength, and its length does not matter.**

> **A LONG column's capacity is the Euler buckling load, and its material strength does not matter — only its stiffness E and its geometry.**

> **An INTERMEDIATE column fails by a combination, yielding partially and then buckling, and no simple theory describes it — so all three materials' codes use an empirical curve fitted between the two extremes.**

> **Recognising this common structure means that a column formula in an unfamiliar material can be read intelligently rather than merely applied: the two ends of the curve are theory and the middle is fitted, in every case.**

**THE FORMULAE, FOR REFERENCE:**

| Class | Permissible compressive stress |
|---|---|
| **SHORT** | **σ_cp — the full tabulated value parallel to the grain** ← |
| **INTERMEDIATE** | **σ_cp [1 − (1/3)(l/(d·K₈))⁴]** ← |
| **LONG** | **0.329 E / (l/d)² — the Euler form, depending on E and not on the timber's strength** ← |

> **THE LONG COLUMN FORMULA'S DEPENDENCE ON E AND NOT ON STRENGTH IN THE THIRD ROW HAS A CONSEQUENCE THAT REPAYS ATTENTION: for a long timber column, using a stronger SPECIES gains nothing.**

> **What matters is the modulus of elasticity, and timber's modulus does not rise in proportion to its strength across species — a dense strong hardwood may have only a modestly higher E than a lighter softwood.**

> **So a slender timber strut should be made STOUTER rather than of better timber, which is the same conclusion reached about high-strength steel in a deflection-governed beam and about steel grade in a buckling-governed column.**

> **The recurring lesson is that STIFFNESS-governed problems are not solved by STRENGTH, and identifying which kind of problem is at hand is more valuable than any formula.**

**AND THE 'LEAST LATERAL DIMENSION' IN THE CLASSIFICATION IS WORTH A NOTE, SINCE IT DIFFERS FROM PRACTICE IN OTHER MATERIALS:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Timber columns are classified by l/d using the LEAST dimension, not by a radius of gyration** ← | **A simplification appropriate to rectangular sections** ← |
| **For a rectangular section, r = d/√12 = 0.289 d** ← | **So l/d of 50 corresponds to a slenderness ratio l/r of about 173** ← |
| **Which is a very slender member indeed** ← | **Comparable with steel's absolute limit of 180 for members carrying wind only** ← |
| **So the timber limit of 50 is not as permissive as the small number suggests** ← | **The units of measurement differ, and comparing the two numbers directly is a mistake** ← |

> **The last row is a genuine trap when codes are compared: a steel column limited to a slenderness of 180 and a timber column limited to l/d of 50 sound wildly different and are in fact closely comparable, because one figure is measured against the radius of gyration and the other against the section's width.**

> **Whenever a slenderness limit is quoted, the dimension it is measured against must be established before the number means anything.**

verification.notes: For a rectangle r = d/sqrt(12) = 0.289d, so l/d = 50 corresponds to l/r = 173.

examTip.trick: **Short below 11, intermediate 11 to 50, long above 50** — measured on the LEAST lateral dimension, not a radius of gyration.
examTip.trap: **A long timber column's capacity depends on E, not on strength** — so a stronger species gains nothing. Make it stouter. The same lesson as steel grade in a buckling problem.
examTip.mnemonic: **l/d = 50 is l/r ≈ 173** for a rectangle — so timber's limit is not as permissive as it sounds. Always establish which dimension a slenderness limit is measured against.

questions.stem: In a bolted timber connection, the timber must be provided with adequate END DISTANCE and the bolt holes must be a close fit, principally because:
options: The bolts would otherwise corrode
Timber is extremely weak in TENSION PERPENDICULAR to the grain
The timber's bending strength would otherwise be reduced
Loose bolts make the connection noisy
questions.solution:
**Because timber is extremely weak in TENSION PERPENDICULAR to the grain, so a bolt too near an end SPLITS the member along the grain** — and an oversized hole concentrates the bearing on too few fibres.

**The failure being guarded against:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A bolt bears against the timber and pushes it toward the member's end** ← | ← |
| **The timber ahead of the bolt is compressed and tends to be forced apart SIDEWAYS** ← | **Wedging the fibres apart** ← |
| **That sideways force is a TENSION across the grain** ← | **Timber's weakest property by a wide margin** ← |
| **So a long SPLIT runs from the bolt hole to the member's end** ← | **And the connection is lost entirely — not weakened, lost** ← |
| **Adequate end distance provides enough material to resist that splitting** ← | ← |

> **THE ABRUPTNESS OF THE FAILURE IN THE FOURTH ROW IS WHY TIMBER CONNECTIONS DEMAND SUCH GENEROUS SPACING AND IT IS THE ESSENTIAL POINT: a split does not reduce the connection's capacity gradually, it removes it.**

> **The split runs to the end of the member in an instant and the bolt then has nothing in front of it.**

> **This is quite unlike a bolted steel connection, where an inadequate end distance leads to progressive tearing and visible deformation before failure.**

> **So timber connection rules are not conservative versions of steel rules — they guard against a different and more sudden failure mode, and they cannot be relaxed on the reasoning that the loads are small.**

**THE SPACING RULES, IN OUTLINE:**

| Requirement | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **End distance in TENSION members** ← | **7 times the bolt diameter — very generous compared with steel's 1.5 to 1.7 times the hole diameter** ← |
| **End distance in COMPRESSION members** ← | **4 diameters — less, because the bolt does not push toward the end** ← |
| **Spacing along the grain** | **4 diameters** ← |
| **Spacing across the grain** | **2.5 diameters** ← |
| **Edge distance** | **1.5 diameters, or half the spacing across the grain** ← |

> **THE CONTRAST BETWEEN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS INSTRUCTIVE AND IT CONFIRMS THAT SPLITTING IS THE CONTROLLING MECHANISM: a compression member's bolt pushes the timber INWARD, away from the end, so no wedging occurs and a much shorter end distance suffices.**

> **A tension member's bolt pushes toward the end and does wedge — hence nearly twice the distance.**

> **If the rule were about bearing or about net section, the two would be the same. That they differ so much shows what is actually being resisted.**

**THE OTHER MEANS OF CONNECTING TIMBER, FOR CONTEXT:**

| Fastening | Note |
|---|---|
| **NAILS** ← | **Cheap and effective in shear for light framing; must not be relied on in withdrawal (pull-out), which is unreliable** ← |
| **SCREWS** | **Better in withdrawal than nails; must be screwed, not hammered** ← |
| **BOLTS** ← | **For structural connections; capacity governed by timber bearing and by splitting, seldom by the bolt** ← |
| **TIMBER CONNECTORS — split rings, shear plates, toothed plates** ← | **Recessed into the timber's face, they spread the load over a much larger area of timber, greatly increasing the capacity per bolt** ← |
| **GLUE — resorcinol and epoxy adhesives** ← | **Stronger than the timber itself when properly made; the basis of glued laminated (glulam) construction** ← |
| **Traditional CARPENTRY joints — mortise and tenon, dovetail, scarf** ← | **Effective, and they rely on bearing rather than on fastenings — but they remove material and are labour-intensive** ← |

> **THE TIMBER CONNECTOR IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE KEY TO EFFICIENT TIMBER CONSTRUCTION AND IT ADDRESSES EXACTLY THE PROBLEM THIS QUESTION IS ABOUT: a bolt's capacity is limited by the small area of timber it bears against.**

> **A split ring or shear plate set into a circular groove around the bolt bears over a much greater area of timber, so it can carry several times the load with the same bolt and the same member.**

> **This is why heavy timber trusses and long-span timber structures use connectors rather than plain bolts, and why a connection detailed with plain bolts may need an impracticable number of them.**

> **The general principle is that in timber, the FASTENING is almost never the limiting element — the TIMBER around it is, and the way to strengthen a timber connection is therefore to spread the load rather than to strengthen the fastener.**

examTip.trick: **The bolt wedges the fibres apart, creating TENSION ACROSS THE GRAIN** — timber's weakest property — and the member splits to its end.
examTip.trap: **End distance is 7d in TENSION but only 4d in COMPRESSION** — proof that splitting, not bearing or net section, is what the rule resists.
examTip.mnemonic: **In timber the FASTENING is never the weak link — the timber around it is.** So spread the load: split rings and shear plates carry several times a plain bolt's capacity.

questions.stem: The PRESSURE (vacuum-pressure) impregnation process is preferred to brushing or dipping for applying a timber preservative because it:
options: Uses a cheaper preservative
Does not require the timber to be seasoned first
Leaves the timber's surface unstained
Forces the preservative DEEP into the timber's cells
questions.solution:
**It forces the preservative DEEP into the timber's cells**, so that later cutting, drilling or surface damage does not expose untreated wood.

**The methods of applying a preservative, in ascending order of effectiveness:**

| Method | Penetration |
|---|---|
| **BRUSHING or SPRAYING** ← | **A surface film only — a millimetre or two at best** ← |
| **DIPPING** ← | **A few millimetres** ← |
| **HOT AND COLD (open tank) process** ← | **Moderate — the timber is heated in the preservative and allowed to cool in it, so the contracting air in the cells draws the liquid in** ← |
| **PRESSURE impregnation (Bethell full-cell, Rueping and Lowry empty-cell)** ← | **DEEP, into the cell structure throughout the sapwood — this question** ← |
| **DIFFUSION (boron, for green timber)** ← | **Deep over time, the salt diffusing through the timber's own moisture** ← |

> **THE CRITICAL WEAKNESS OF THE SURFACE METHODS IS NOT THEIR THINNESS AS SUCH BUT WHAT HAPPENS AFTERWARDS, AND THIS IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A surface-treated member is protected only while its surface is INTACT** ← | ← |
| **Every subsequent CUT, notch, drilled hole or mortise exposes untreated timber** ← | **And those are precisely the places where water collects and decay begins** ← |
| **A cut end is the worst of all** ← | **End grain absorbs water many times faster than a face** ← |
| **So a surface-treated post cut to length on site has an untreated foot** ← | **Standing in the ground, which is the most hostile location it could occupy** ← |
| **Pressure-treated timber has preservative throughout its sapwood** ← | **So a cut exposes treated material** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW DESCRIBES THE COMMONEST FAILURE OF TREATED TIMBER IN PRACTICE AND IT IS ENTIRELY A MATTER OF SEQUENCE: the treatment is applied at the yard and the cutting is done on site.**

> **Even pressure-treated timber has a limit here — the heartwood may take up little preservative, and a deep cut can reach it.**

> **The universal rule is therefore that all cut surfaces must be re-treated on site by brushing or soaking before the member is fixed, and that timber should be cut to length BEFORE treatment wherever the programme permits.**

> **A specification that requires pressure treatment and says nothing about site cuts has left the most vulnerable surfaces unprotected, and it is worth adding the clause.**

**THE PRESERVATIVES THEMSELVES:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **CREOSOTE (tar oil)** ← | **Cheap, very effective, and used for sleepers, poles and marine work — but it stains, smells, cannot be painted over, and is now restricted for health reasons** ← |
| **Water-borne salts — CCA (copper-chrome-arsenic), CCB (copper-chrome-boron), ACQ** ← | **Clean, paintable, odourless; CCA is now restricted in many uses because of its arsenic** ← |
| **Organic solvent types** | **Clean and paintable, good for joinery** ← |
| **BORON compounds** ← | **Low toxicity, applied by diffusion to green timber — but they LEACH OUT in wet conditions, so they suit interior use only** ← |

> **THE LEACHING LIMITATION IN THE LAST ROW IS THE KEY TO SELECTING A PRESERVATIVE AND IT IS THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS MOST: a preservative must be FIXED in the timber if the timber will be wet.**

> **CCA and its relatives react chemically with the wood and become insoluble, so they stay put even in ground contact.**

> **Boron remains soluble, so it washes out of timber exposed to rain or in contact with damp earth — but it is cheap, low in toxicity, penetrates green timber readily, and is excellent against borers and termites indoors.**

> **So the choice is governed by the service condition rather than by which preservative is 'best': boron for roof timbers and joinery, a fixed water-borne salt for exposed and ground-contact work, and creosote or its modern equivalents for the most severe exposures such as poles and marine piles.**

> **And the whole exercise presupposes SEASONED timber, since a preservative cannot penetrate cells already full of water — which is why option (b) is wrong, and why treatment follows seasoning rather than replacing it.**

examTip.trick: **Deep penetration, so later cuts and damage still expose TREATED wood.** Surface methods protect only while the surface is intact.
examTip.trap: **Every site cut exposes untreated timber, and end grain absorbs water fastest** — so a treated post cut to length has an untreated foot in the ground. Re-treat all cuts.
examTip.mnemonic: **Boron LEACHES, so it is for interiors; CCA fixes chemically, so it suits ground contact.** And treatment needs SEASONED timber — a preservative cannot enter water-filled cells.

questions.stem: Compared with cement mortar, MUD MORTAR used in traditional masonry is characterised by:
options: Higher compressive strength and better bond
Greater resistance to water and erosion
VERY LOW strength and NO resistance to water
Setting by hydration, in the same manner as cement
questions.solution:
**VERY LOW strength and NO resistance to water** — but high deformability, allowing the wall to accommodate movement, and it can be repaired with the same material at negligible cost.

**The three mortars compared:**

| Property | MUD | LIME | CEMENT |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Compressive strength** | **Very low, well under 1 N/mm²** ← | **Low to moderate, 0.5 to 2 N/mm²** ← | **High, 3 to 10 N/mm² and above** ← |
| **How it hardens** | **By DRYING only — it does not set chemically and can be re-softened by water** ← | **By CARBONATION, absorbing CO₂ from the air — slow, taking months, and it needs air** ← | **By HYDRATION — a chemical reaction with water, so it sets under water too** ← |
| **Water resistance** | **NONE — it dissolves** ← | **Moderate; hydraulic lime is better** ← | **Good** ← |
| **Deformability** | **HIGH — it accommodates settlement and movement without cracking** ← | **Moderate to high** ← | **LOW — it is rigid and cracks rather than yielding** ← |
| **Bond with units** | **Weak** ← | **GOOD — lime bonds well and is forgiving of irregular units** ← | **Good, but it can be stronger than a weak unit** ← |
| **Repairability** | **Trivial and free** ← | **Straightforward** ← | **Difficult — a cement repair to old work is often worse than the defect** ← |
| **Self-healing** | **No** | **YES — fine cracks re-seal as free lime recrystallises** ← | **No** |

> **THE SELF-HEALING PROPERTY OF LIME IN THE LAST ROW IS GENUINE AND REMARKABLE AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: fine cracks in lime mortar close over time as free lime is dissolved by moisture and redeposited.**

> **This is one reason old lime-mortared buildings survive minor movement so well, and one reason lime is preferred for the repair of historic masonry.**

> **A cement repair to a lime-mortared wall is a well-recognised mistake, and the reason is worth understanding: the cement pointing is HARDER and less permeable than the surrounding masonry.**

> **Moisture that previously evaporated through the joints is then forced to leave through the BRICKS or STONES instead, taking salts with it — and the units spall while the pointing remains perfect.**

> **So the repair destroys the very material it was meant to protect, and the general principle it illustrates is that a repair mortar should be no stronger and no less permeable than what it repairs.**

**MUD MORTAR'S POSITION IN NEPALI CONSTRUCTION DESERVES A HONEST ASSESSMENT, SINCE A GREAT DEAL OF THE COUNTRY'S BUILDING STOCK USES IT:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is essentially FREE, and requires no transport, no cement and no skilled supply chain** ← | **Which is why it is used, and it is a real advantage in remote areas** ← |
| **Its bond and its tensile strength are negligible** ← | **So a mud-mortared wall has almost NO capacity to resist the out-of-plane forces of an earthquake** ← |
| **It softens when wet** ← | **So a wall's base and its parapets, wetted by rain, lose what little strength they had** ← |
| **Mud-mortared stone masonry performed very badly in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake** ← | **It accounts for a large share of the building collapses and the deaths** ← |
| **The NBC's mandatory rules recognise this and require bands and vertical bars** ← | **Which supply the tensile continuity the mortar cannot** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER GIVE THE PRACTICAL CONCLUSION AND IT SHOULD BE STATED WITHOUT EQUIVOCATION: mud-mortared masonry is not made safe by better mortar practice, because the mortar's contribution is inherently negligible.**

> **What makes such a wall survive is the CONTINUITY provided by other elements — horizontal bands at plinth, sill, lintel and roof level, vertical reinforcement at corners and openings, through-stones tying the wall's two faces together, and a light well-tied roof.**

> **Those measures work by holding the masonry together as an assembly once the mortar has failed, which it will.**

> **They are also cheap — a few per cent of the building's cost — and they are the single most valuable intervention available in the Nepali building stock, which is why the NBC's mandatory rules of thumb concentrate on them almost to the exclusion of anything else.**

examTip.trick: **Mud hardens by DRYING only, dissolves in water, and has negligible bond** — but it is free, deformable and trivially repairable.
examTip.trap: **Lime sets by CARBONATION (needs air, takes months); cement by HYDRATION (sets under water).** Mud does not set chemically at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **Never repoint lime work with cement** — the harder pointing forces moisture out through the units, which spall while the pointing stays perfect. Repair mortar must be no stronger than what it repairs.

questions.stem: The compressive strength of a brick MASONRY assembly is:
options: LESS than the strength of the bricks themselves, and it increases only slowly with mortar strength
Equal to the average of the brick strength and the mortar strength
Greater than the strength of the bricks, because the mortar confines them
Determined by the mortar strength alone, the bricks being much stronger
questions.solution:
**LESS than the strength of the bricks themselves, and it increases only slowly with mortar strength** — a stronger mortar beyond a point adding very little.

**The relationship:**

| Observation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Masonry strength is typically 25 to 50 per cent of the BRICK's own crushing strength** ← | **So 10 N/mm² bricks may give masonry of 3 to 4 N/mm²** ← |
| **It rises with brick strength roughly as its SQUARE ROOT** ← | **So doubling the brick strength gains only about 40 per cent in the wall** ← |
| **It rises with mortar strength much more WEAKLY still** ← | **Beyond a moderate mortar strength, further improvement is almost worthless** ← |
| **A very STRONG mortar with WEAK bricks is a poor combination** ← | **The mortar is stiffer than the units, so it does not deform with them and the load concentrates unevenly** ← |

> **WHY THE ASSEMBLY IS WEAKER THAN ITS UNITS IS THE INTERESTING PART AND THE MECHANISM IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING PROPERLY:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The mortar is generally SOFTER and more deformable than the brick** ← | ← |
| **Under vertical compression the mortar tries to squeeze out sideways** ← | **Expanding laterally more than the brick would** ← |
| **But it is bonded to the bricks above and below, which restrain it** ← | ← |
| **So the MORTAR is put into triaxial compression (which strengthens it) and the BRICKS are put into lateral TENSION** ← | **The bricks being pulled outward by the mortar they restrain** ← |
| **Brick is weak in tension, so it splits VERTICALLY** ← | **Which is why masonry prisms fail by vertical splitting, not by crushing of the mortar** ← |
| **Hence the assembly fails below the brick's own crushing strength** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS ARE THE WHOLE EXPLANATION AND THEY ACCOUNT FOR THE CHARACTERISTIC FAILURE PATTERN: a masonry pier under test does not crumble, it splits from top to bottom.**

> **That vertical crack is the brick failing in the lateral tension induced by the mortar's attempt to spread.**

> **It also explains why a THINNER mortar joint gives a STRONGER wall: less mortar means less lateral expansion to restrain, so less tension in the bricks.**

> **A 10 mm joint gives a materially stronger wall than a 20 mm joint with the same materials — which is why joint thickness is specified and why sloppy thick-jointed work is weak work quite apart from its appearance.**

**THE PRACTICAL CONCLUSIONS FROM ALL THIS ARE WORTH DRAWING TOGETHER, BECAUSE THEY RUN AGAINST SEVERAL INSTINCTS:**

| Conclusion | Note |
|---|---|
| **Use the WEAKEST mortar consistent with the strength required** ← | **Not the strongest available — a common misconception** ← |
| **Match the mortar's stiffness to the UNITS' stiffness** ← | **Weak units want weak mortar; strong units can take stronger** ← |
| **Keep the JOINTS THIN and uniform** ← | **10 mm nominal, and full — an unfilled joint is far worse than a thick one** ← |
| **The units' strength matters more than the mortar's** ← | **But only as a square root, so very strong bricks are seldom worth their cost in an ordinary wall** ← |
| **WORKMANSHIP matters as much as either material** ← | **Full joints, bricks wetted but not soaked, uniform courses, correct bond** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE COUNTER-INTUITIVE ONE AND IT IS WORTH BEING EXPLICIT ABOUT: a stronger mortar does not make a stronger wall in proportion, and it makes a worse wall in several other respects.**

> **A rich cement mortar is stiff and brittle, so it cracks rather than accommodating movement; it shrinks more, opening the joints; and it is stronger than a weak brick, so any crack propagates THROUGH the bricks rather than along the joints — which makes the wall unrepairable, since a crack through the units cannot be repointed out.**

> **A mortar weaker than its units confines cracking to the joints, where it can be raked out and repointed indefinitely.**

> **This is the same principle as the repair-mortar rule and it is the reason traditional masonry practice favoured lime: the sacrificial element should be the cheap replaceable one, and that is the mortar.**

examTip.trick: **Masonry is 25-50 % of the brick's strength**, rising as the square root of brick strength and much more weakly with mortar strength.
examTip.trap: **The mortar squeezes sideways and puts the BRICKS into lateral tension** — so the prism splits vertically. Which is why a THIN joint gives a stronger wall.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use the WEAKEST adequate mortar** — a mortar stronger than its units sends cracks THROUGH the bricks, making the wall unrepairable. The mortar should be the sacrificial element.

questions.stem: The SLENDERNESS RATIO of a load-bearing masonry wall is defined as the ratio of its:
options: EFFECTIVE HEIGHT to its EFFECTIVE THICKNESS
Actual height to its actual thickness, in all cases
Height to its length
Length to its thickness only
questions.solution:
**The ratio of its EFFECTIVE HEIGHT to its EFFECTIVE THICKNESS, or of its effective LENGTH to its effective thickness, whichever is LESS.**

**Why the lesser of the two governs:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A wall can buckle in either of two ways** ← | **By bending about a HORIZONTAL axis (over its height) or about a VERTICAL axis (across its length)** ← |
| **Whichever mode is EASIER will occur** ← | **So the smaller slenderness ratio is the relevant one, since it identifies the stiffer direction of restraint** ← |
| **A LONG wall between widely spaced cross-walls has its height governing** ← | **The vertical mode is unrestrained horizontally over a great length** ← |
| **A SHORT wall panel between close cross-walls has its length governing** ← | **The cross-walls restrain it strongly, so the horizontal span is the shorter one** ← |

> **THE 'WHICHEVER IS LESS' PROVISION SOUNDS BACKWARDS UNTIL THE LOGIC IS SEEN AND IT IS WORTH SPELLING OUT: a smaller slenderness ratio means a LESS slender wall and therefore a HIGHER permissible stress.**

> **The wall is being restrained in two directions, and it takes the benefit of the BETTER restraint — because it will be held by whichever support system is more effective.**

> **This is the opposite of the rule for a column, where the WORSE of the two axes governs — and the difference is that a column's two axes are both unbraced along its full length, whereas a wall panel is supported on all four edges and can call on whichever pair of supports is closer.**

> **Getting this the wrong way round is a common error, and the way to keep it straight is to ask which supports the wall will actually lean on.**

**The effective height and thickness:**

| Condition | Effective height |
|---|---|
| **Lateral support at top and bottom, with restraint against rotation** ← | **0.75 H** ← |
| **Lateral support at top and bottom, no rotational restraint** ← | **1.0 H** ← |
| **Lateral support at the bottom only (a parapet or free-standing wall)** ← | **1.5 H or more** ← |

| Wall type | Effective thickness |
|---|---|
| **Solid wall** | **Its actual thickness** ← |
| **Wall stiffened by PIERS or cross-walls** ← | **Actual thickness × a stiffening coefficient greater than 1.0** ← |
| **CAVITY wall** ← | **Two-thirds of the sum of the two leaves' thicknesses, if properly tied** ← |

> **THE LIMITS ON SLENDERNESS, WHICH ARE THE POINT OF COMPUTING IT:**

| Situation | Maximum slenderness ratio |
|---|---|
| **Load-bearing wall in a building up to 2 storeys, in cement mortar** ← | **About 27** ← |
| **Buildings over 2 storeys** ← | **About 27, reducing for lime and mud mortars** ← |
| **Walls in LIME mortar** ← | **Lower limits** ← |
| **Walls in MUD mortar** ← | **Much lower — of the order of 12 to 15** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION DOWN THAT TABLE FOLLOWS FROM THE MORTAR'S CONTRIBUTION AND IT IS INSTRUCTIVE: a slender wall resists buckling by BENDING, and bending a masonry wall requires TENSION across the bed joints.**

> **A cement mortar provides some tensile bond, so the wall has some flexural capacity and can be relatively slender.**

> **A mud mortar provides essentially none, so the wall can only resist lateral force by its own weight acting through the section — a gravity mechanism — and it must therefore be much thicker relative to its height.**

> **This is why traditional mud-mortared walls are so thick: not from ignorance but from necessity, since the only mechanism available to them is self-weight stability.**

> **It also explains why the NBC's slenderness limits for mud-mortared construction are so much tighter, and why increasing a mud wall's height without increasing its thickness — a common alteration when a storey is added to an old house — is a serious and frequently fatal modification.**

examTip.trick: **Effective height/thickness OR effective length/thickness, whichever is LESS** — the wall takes the benefit of whichever pair of supports restrains it better.
examTip.trap: **This is the OPPOSITE of a column, where the worse axis governs** — because a wall panel is supported on all four edges and leans on the closer supports.
examTip.mnemonic: **Mud-mortared walls must be much thicker** — with no tensile bond, their only mechanism is self-weight stability. Adding a storey to an old mud house without thickening is often fatal.

questions.stem: The MANDATORY RULES OF THUMB (MRT) of the Nepal Building Code are intended to:
options: Replace structural design entirely for all buildings
Provide guidance that a designer may follow or disregard at discretion
Give PRESCRIPTIVE, ready-to-use requirements
Apply only to reinforced concrete framed buildings above four storeys
questions.solution:
**To give PRESCRIPTIVE, ready-to-use requirements** — dimensions, reinforcement and detailing — for SMALL, SIMPLE, LOW-RISE buildings, so that they can be built safely WITHOUT a full structural analysis.

**What the MRT approach is, and why it exists:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Most buildings in Nepal are small, simple and built WITHOUT an engineer** ← | **By owners and local masons, often without any drawings at all** ← |
| **Requiring a full analysis for every such building is unenforceable** ← | **There are not enough engineers, and the owners could not pay for them** ← |
| **So the code provides a PRESCRIPTIVE route instead** ← | **Follow these dimensions and these details, and no calculation is needed** ← |
| **The rules are deliberately CONSERVATIVE** ← | **Since they must cover a range of situations without any site-specific assessment** ← |
| **They apply only within stated LIMITS** ← | **On number of storeys, storey height, span, plan size and regularity — outside those limits a design is required** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS DEFINE HOW THE APPROACH SHOULD BE UNDERSTOOD AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: the MRT is not a shortcut for engineers, it is a substitute for engineering where engineering will not otherwise happen.**

> **A designer who applies it to a building outside its stated limits — five storeys, long spans, an irregular plan, a sloping site — has used a tool beyond its validity, and the conservatism built into it does not extend that far.**

> **Conversely an engineer designing a small regular building properly may well arrive at LESS material than the MRT requires, and is entitled to.**

> **So the two routes are alternatives, not a hierarchy: prescriptive compliance for those who cannot design, and analysis for those who can.**

**THE NBC's STRUCTURE, WHICH PLACES THE MRT IN CONTEXT:**

| Level | Document | For |
|---|---|---|
| **1 — International state of the art** ← | **Any recognised international code** ← | **Large, complex or important buildings** ← |
| **2 — Professionally engineered structures** ← | **NBC 000 to 114 series** ← | **Buildings requiring analysis and design** ← |
| **3 — MANDATORY RULES OF THUMB** ← | **NBC 201 (masonry), NBC 205 (RC framed with masonry infill)** ← | **Small buildings within stated limits — this question** ← |
| **4 — GUIDELINES for rural / remote construction** ← | **NBC 202 (low strength masonry), NBC 203 (rural buildings)** ← | **Owner-built rural construction, including mud-mortared and stone masonry** ← |

> **THE FOUR-LEVEL STRUCTURE IS A THOUGHTFUL RESPONSE TO A REAL PROBLEM AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING AS SUCH: a single code written for engineered buildings would be ignored by the great majority of construction, which is not engineered.**

> **By providing four levels, the NBC offers each category of builder something it can actually use — an international code for a hospital, a design code for an apartment block, a rule of thumb for a two-storey house, and a guideline for a village dwelling in stone and mud.**

> **The fourth level is the most socially significant, because it addresses the buildings in which most earthquake deaths occur, and it does so with measures affordable to their builders.**

> **THE PRACTICAL CONTENT OF THE MRT IS ALMOST ENTIRELY DETAILING RATHER THAN SIZING, WHICH IS WORTH NOTING:**

| Typical MRT requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Minimum wall thickness and maximum wall length between cross-walls** ← | ← |
| **Maximum number of storeys and maximum storey height** ← | ← |
| **Horizontal SEISMIC BANDS at plinth, sill, lintel and roof level** ← | **The single most important requirement** ← |
| **VERTICAL reinforcement at corners, junctions and openings** ← | ← |
| **Limits on the SIZE and POSITION of openings** ← | ← |
| **Prescribed column and beam sizes and reinforcement, for NBC 205** ← | **A table by number of storeys and span** ← |

> **The emphasis on detailing rather than on member sizes reflects what the evidence from earthquakes actually shows: buildings of this kind fail from a lack of INTEGRITY — walls separating, corners parting, roofs sliding off — rather than from members being individually undersized.**

> **So the rules concentrate on tying the building together, which is both the most effective intervention and the cheapest.**

examTip.trick: **Prescriptive requirements for small simple buildings, so no analysis is needed** — deliberately conservative, and valid only within stated limits on storeys, spans and regularity.
examTip.trap: **Not a shortcut for engineers but a substitute where engineering will not happen** — and an engineer designing properly may legitimately arrive at less material.
examTip.mnemonic: **NBC has four levels: international, engineered (000-114), MRT (201/205), guidelines (202/203).** The MRT is almost all DETAILING, because these buildings fail from lack of integrity.

questions.stem: The horizontal SEISMIC BANDS required in masonry buildings by the Nepal Building Code function principally to:
options: Support the floor and roof loads, replacing the need for lintels
TIE the walls together into a BOX, providing the TENSILE continuity that masonry lacks
Increase the compressive strength of the masonry below them
Provide a level surface on which to continue building
questions.solution:
**To TIE the walls together into a BOX, providing the TENSILE continuity that masonry lacks** — so that the walls act as one unit and cannot separate at the corners or fall outward.

**The bands and their positions:**

| Band | Position | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **PLINTH band** ← | **At plinth level, just above the ground** ← | **Ties the walls at the base and resists differential settlement; particularly valuable on sloping or poor ground** ← |
| **SILL band** ← | **At window sill level** ← | **Ties the masonry between openings; required in higher seismic zones or where openings are large** ← |
| **LINTEL band** ← | **At the head of the openings, continuous all round** ← | **The MOST IMPORTANT band — it is at the level where walls are weakest, being interrupted by openings** ← |
| **ROOF / EAVES band** ← | **At the top of the walls, at roof level** ← | **Ties the wall heads and connects them to the roof — essential where the roof is light or pitched** ← |
| **GABLE band** ← | **Along the slope of a gable wall** ← | **Gable ends are free-standing triangles of masonry, and they fall outward readily** ← |

> **THE ESSENTIAL PROPERTY OF A BAND IS THAT IT MUST BE CONTINUOUS ALL ROUND THE BUILDING, AND THAT CANNOT BE OVER-EMPHASISED: a band with a gap is not a band.**

> **Its whole function is to form a closed horizontal ring that cannot be pulled apart, so a break — at a doorway, at a junction with a later extension, or where the mason ran out of steel — destroys the mechanism entirely.**

> **The reinforcement must be LAPPED properly at corners and junctions, with the bars bent round the corner rather than merely butted, so that the ring can carry tension continuously through the corner.**

> **A band that stops at each wall and does not turn the corner is the commonest execution failure, and it leaves the building with the appearance of compliance and none of its benefit.**

**WHY THE BOX ACTION MATTERS SO MUCH, WHICH IS THE UNDERLYING MECHANISM:**

| Without bands | With bands |
|---|---|
| **Each wall responds INDEPENDENTLY to the shaking** ← | **All the walls move TOGETHER as a rigid box** ← |
| **A wall perpendicular to the shaking bends OUT OF PLANE** ← | **It is held at top and bottom by the bands, so its span is halved and it is restrained** ← |
| **The corners, where two walls meet, PART** ← | **The bands hold them, so the walls at right angles support one another** ← |
| **Once a corner opens, each wall is a free-standing cantilever and collapses** ← | **The box redistributes the load to the walls PARALLEL to the shaking, which resist it in their strong in-plane direction** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW CONTAINS THE WHOLE VALUE OF BOX ACTION AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL THING TO UNDERSTAND ABOUT MASONRY SEISMIC BEHAVIOUR: a masonry wall is reasonably strong IN ITS OWN PLANE and very weak OUT OF PLANE.**

> **In a building shaken along one axis, the walls parallel to that axis are loaded in their strong direction and the walls perpendicular to it are loaded in their weak direction.**

> **If the building acts as a box, the weak walls' load is transferred through the bands and the floor diaphragm to the strong walls — so the building resists the shaking with the walls that can.**

> **If it does not act as a box, the perpendicular walls must resist the shaking themselves, out of plane, which they cannot — and they fall.**

> **So the bands do not make the masonry stronger; they arrange for the load to be carried by the parts that were already strong enough. That is why they are so effective for so little material, and why they are the single highest-value intervention in low-rise masonry construction.**
tags: plinth sill lintel roof gable bands

examTip.trick: **They supply the TENSILE continuity masonry has none of**, tying the walls into a box so corners cannot part and walls cannot fall outward.
examTip.trap: **A band with a gap is not a band** — the bars must turn the corners and lap properly. Stopping at each wall without turning is the commonest execution failure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Masonry is strong IN plane and weak OUT of plane** — bands transfer the weak walls' load to the strong ones. They do not strengthen the masonry; they redirect the load to what was already adequate.

questions.stem: VERTICAL REINFORCEMENT is required at the corners, wall junctions and the jambs of openings in a masonry building because these locations:
options: Are where the compressive stresses are greatest
Need reinforcement only to support the lintels above
Require reinforcement solely to fix door and window frames
Are where TENSILE stresses CONCENTRATE during shaking
questions.solution:
**Because these locations are where TENSILE stresses CONCENTRATE during shaking** — and a corner or a jamb without vertical steel splits open, after which the walls on either side are no longer connected.

**Why these particular locations:**

| Location | What happens without vertical steel |
|---|---|
| **CORNERS** ← | **The two walls pull apart as the building racks, and a vertical crack opens down the corner — after which each wall is free-standing** ← |
| **Wall JUNCTIONS (T and cross junctions)** ← | **The same, and the cross-wall's restraint of the main wall is lost** ← |
| **JAMBS of openings** ← | **The masonry pier between openings is slender and highly stressed; diagonal cracks radiate from the opening's corners and the jamb splits** ← |
| **Free ENDS of walls** ← | **Unrestrained, and they topple** ← |

> **THE CORNER IS THE MOST CRITICAL LOCATION OF ALL AND THE REASON IS WORTH SEEING GEOMETRICALLY: at a corner, two walls at right angles must remain attached while the building distorts.**

> **Whichever way the ground moves, one of them is being loaded in plane and pulling the corner one way, while the other is being loaded out of plane and pulling it another.**

> **Masonry bonded at a corner resists this only by the tensile bond of the mortar, which is negligible — so the corner opens.**

> **Once it has opened, both walls have lost their end restraint simultaneously: the in-plane wall has lost its return, and the out-of-plane wall has lost its support.**

> **So a single corner crack disables the box action on two sides at once, which is why corner reinforcement is mandatory even in the simplest rules and why corner failures are the signature damage pattern in unreinforced masonry earthquakes.**

**HOW THE VERTICAL REINFORCEMENT WORKS WITH THE BANDS:**

| Element | Duty |
|---|---|
| **HORIZONTAL bands** ← | **Tie the walls together in the horizontal plane, forming closed rings at several levels** ← |
| **VERTICAL bars at corners and jambs** ← | **Tie those rings to one another and to the foundation, so the building is caged in three dimensions** ← |
| **Together they form a CONFINING framework** ← | **Which is why the resulting construction is called CONFINED masonry** ← |
| **The bars must be CONTINUOUS from foundation to roof band** ← | **Lapped properly, and anchored into the foundation and the top band** ← |
| **They are placed in a cavity or a special unit and grouted** ← | **In brickwork, in a pocket formed by the bonding; in blockwork, in the hollow cores** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE EXECUTION REQUIREMENT THAT DECIDES WHETHER ANY OF THIS WORKS AND IT IS ROUTINELY COMPROMISED: a vertical bar must run from the foundation to the roof band without interruption.**

> **A bar that starts at the plinth band and stops at the sill has connected nothing to anything.**

> **A bar that is not anchored into the foundation can be pulled out.**

> **A bar that is not tied into the roof band leaves the top of the wall free.**

> **And a bar placed in a pocket that is never properly grouted is a bar in a void, contributing nothing but the appearance of reinforcement — which is the most insidious of these failures, because it is invisible once the wall is plastered.**

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WORTH DWELLING ON AS A CONCEPT, BECAUSE CONFINED MASONRY IS A GENUINELY GOOD SYSTEM RATHER THAN A COMPROMISE: it is not a frame with infill, and it is not unreinforced masonry with additions.**

> **The masonry is built FIRST and the confining elements are cast against it, so the two are bonded together and act as a composite.**

> **The masonry carries the vertical load and the in-plane shear; the confining elements provide the tensile continuity, hold the masonry together after it cracks, and prevent the cracks from opening.**

> **The result performs very much better in earthquakes than either unreinforced masonry or a frame with masonry infill, at a cost only slightly above the former — and it is the system that the NBC's mandatory rules effectively prescribe.**

examTip.trick: **Tensile stresses concentrate there** — a corner or jamb splits, and the walls on either side are then disconnected and free-standing.
examTip.trap: **One corner crack disables the box on TWO sides at once** — the in-plane wall loses its return and the out-of-plane wall loses its support, simultaneously.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bars must run FOUNDATION to ROOF BAND, continuous, anchored and GROUTED** — an ungrouted pocket is a bar in a void, invisible once plastered. Bands plus bars equals confined masonry.

questions.stem: In an earthquake, the failure of an unreinforced masonry wall loaded OUT OF PLANE (perpendicular to its face) is more dangerous than IN-PLANE failure because:
options: The out-of-plane mechanism causes the WALL TO OVERTURN and COLLAPSE bodily, bringing down whatever it supports
In-plane failure never occurs in practice
Out-of-plane loading produces higher compressive stresses
The out-of-plane direction is where the reinforcement is placed
questions.solution:
**Because the out-of-plane mechanism causes the WALL TO OVERTURN and COLLAPSE bodily**, bringing down whatever it supports — whereas in-plane failure produces diagonal cracking in a wall that generally remains standing.

**The two directions compared:**

| Aspect | IN-PLANE | OUT-OF-PLANE |
|---|---|---|
| **Loading direction** | **Along the wall's length** ← | **Perpendicular to its face** ← |
| **The wall acts as** | **A deep shear panel — strong** ← | **A slender vertical plate spanning between its supports — very weak** ← |
| **Resistance derives from** | **The wall's LENGTH, which is large** ← | **The wall's THICKNESS, which is small** ← |
| **Failure appearance** | **DIAGONAL (X-shaped) cracking, or sliding along a bed joint, or rocking of piers** ← | **Horizontal cracking at mid-height and the wall falling outward as one or two pieces** ← |
| **Consequence** | **Damage, often repairable; the wall usually stands** ← | **COLLAPSE, taking the floor or roof it supported** ← |
| **Warning** | **Cracks appear and widen** ← | **Little — the wall goes** ← |
