> **THE THIRD ROW CONTAINS THE ENTIRE ASYMMETRY AND IT IS THE POINT WORTH FIXING: in plane, the wall's resisting dimension is its LENGTH, which may be several metres; out of plane, it is its THICKNESS, which may be 230 mm.**

> **A wall is therefore something like an order of magnitude weaker in one direction than the other, and its behaviour in an earthquake is dominated by that ratio.**

> **Since an earthquake shakes in all directions, every wall in a building is loaded out of plane at some point during the event — so the weak direction is always exercised.**

> **This is why box action matters so much: it removes the need for any wall to resist out-of-plane load by itself, transferring that load to the walls that are being loaded in plane.**

**THE OTHER CHARACTERISTIC FAILURE MODES OF MASONRY, FOR COMPLETENESS:**

| Mode | Description |
|---|---|
| **DIAGONAL SHEAR (X) cracking** ← | **In-plane, from the reversing shear — the classic diagonal cross on a pier between openings** ← |
| **Bed-joint SLIDING** ← | **In-plane, where the vertical load is low and the mortar bond is weak** ← |
| **Pier ROCKING** ← | **In-plane, a slender pier rocking on its bed joints** ← |
| **OUT-OF-PLANE overturning** ← | **This question** ← |
| **CORNER separation** ← | **Vertical cracking at the corner, as discussed** ← |
| **DELAMINATION of a multi-wythe wall** ← | **The two faces of a thick stone wall separating and the rubble core spilling out — the classic failure of random rubble masonry, and it is why THROUGH STONES matter** ← |
| **GABLE collapse** ← | **The free triangle of masonry at a gable end falling outward** ← |
| **Roof or floor SLIDING off its bearing** ← | **Where the roof is not tied to the walls** ← |

> **THE DELAMINATION MODE IN THE SIXTH ROW IS THE DOMINANT FAILURE OF NEPALI STONE MASONRY AND IT DESERVES ITS OWN EXPLANATION, since it is not obvious:**

> **A random rubble stone wall is commonly built as two outer faces of selected stones with a fill of small stones and mud between them.**

> **Under shaking the two faces separate — there is nothing holding them together — and the loose core runs out like sand from between them.**

> **Each face is then a thin unsupported skin, and the wall collapses.**

> **The remedy is THROUGH STONES: long stones laid across the full wall thickness at regular intervals, typically every 600 mm vertically and 1.2 m horizontally, which stitch the two faces together.**

> **They cost nothing but the trouble of selecting and placing them, and they convert a wall that will delaminate into one that holds together — which is why the NBC's guidelines for stone masonry treat through stones as a mandatory item alongside the bands.**

> **The same reasoning underlies the requirement for bond stones or headers in brickwork, and it is another instance of the general principle that integrity, not strength, is what these buildings lack.**

examTip.trick: **In plane the resisting dimension is the wall's LENGTH; out of plane it is its THICKNESS** — an order of magnitude weaker, and failure means collapse rather than cracking.
examTip.trap: **Every wall is loaded out of plane at some point in an earthquake** — the weak direction is always exercised. Which is exactly what box action removes the need to resist.
examTip.mnemonic: **Random rubble walls DELAMINATE — the two faces part and the core runs out.** THROUGH STONES every 600 mm vertically stitch them together, and cost nothing but care.

questions.stem: In brickwork, ENGLISH BOND is distinguished from FLEMISH BOND in that English bond has:
options: Alternate headers and stretchers in every course
Stretchers only, in every course
ALTERNATE COURSES entirely of headers and entirely of stretchers
Headers only, in every course
questions.solution:
**ALTERNATE COURSES entirely of headers and entirely of stretchers** — whereas Flemish bond alternates headers and stretchers within each course.

**The bonds compared:**

| Bond | Arrangement | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **ENGLISH bond** ← | **One course all HEADERS, the next all STRETCHERS** ← | **The STRONGEST of the common bonds; requires a queen closer next to each corner header** ← |
| **FLEMISH bond** ← | **Headers and stretchers ALTERNATING in every course** ← (option a) | **Better APPEARANCE, slightly weaker, and more wasteful of bats — used for facework** ← |
| **STRETCHER bond** ← | **All stretchers** ← (option b) | **For half-brick walls and for the leaves of a cavity wall; cannot bond a thicker wall** ← |
| **HEADER bond** ← | **All headers** ← (option d) | **For curved walls and for half-brick footings, where the short face suits the curve** ← |
| **Rat-trap bond** ← | **Bricks laid on edge, leaving internal cavities** ← | **Uses about 25 per cent fewer bricks and gives better insulation — genuinely useful, and used in Nepal and India** ← |

> **THE PURPOSE OF ANY BOND IS THE POINT BEHIND THE QUESTION AND IT IS WORTH STATING BEFORE THE PATTERNS: a bond exists to prevent CONTINUOUS VERTICAL JOINTS.**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A continuous vertical joint is a plane of NO strength** ← | **The wall is effectively two separate walls on either side of it** ← |
| **So each course must OVERLAP the one below by at least a quarter of a brick** ← | ← |
| **The overlap distributes a concentrated load sideways as it travels down** ← | **Spreading through the wall at roughly 45 degrees** ← |
| **And it ties the wall's THICKNESS together** ← | **Which is what the HEADERS do — they run across the wall, binding its two faces** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW EXPLAINS WHY ENGLISH BOND IS THE STRONGEST AND CONNECTS DIRECTLY TO THE DELAMINATION PROBLEM: a header course puts a complete layer of bricks running THROUGH the wall's thickness at every second course.**

> **That is the brickwork equivalent of a course of through stones, and it makes the wall behave as one thick element rather than as two skins.**

> **Flemish bond has headers too, but only every other brick in each course, so the transverse tie is less complete.**

> **Stretcher bond has NO headers at all, which is why it cannot bond a wall thicker than half a brick — and why the two leaves of a cavity wall, both in stretcher bond, must be tied with metal wall ties instead.**

**THE PRACTICAL POINTS THAT MATTER MORE THAN THE PATTERN, WHICH IS WORTH SAYING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Bricks must be WETTED before laying — but not soaked** ← | **A dry brick sucks water out of the mortar, which then cannot hydrate; a saturated brick lets the mortar slip and floats** ← |
| **Every joint must be FULL, including the vertical (perpend) joints** ← | **Unfilled perpends are the commonest defect in brickwork, and they destroy both strength and weather resistance** ← |
| **Courses must be LEVEL and the wall PLUMB** ← | **An out-of-plumb wall carries its load eccentrically** ← |
| **Work should rise UNIFORMLY, not in steps of more than about 1 m** ← | **Or the differential settlement of fresh mortar cracks the junction** ← |
| **A maximum of about 1 to 1.5 m of height per day** ← | **Green mortar cannot carry the weight of much more** ← |

> **THE UNFILLED PERPEND IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE DEFECT WORTH LOOKING FOR ON ANY SITE AND IT IS EASY TO CHECK: a bricklayer working quickly butters the bed joint properly and slips the brick sideways against its neighbour, leaving the vertical joint hollow.**

> **The wall looks perfect from the face, since the joint is pointed afterwards, and it has perhaps two-thirds of its intended strength together with a direct path for water through its thickness.**

> **It is checkable only while the work is in progress, by looking at the top of the last course before the next is laid — which is why brickwork inspection has to happen during construction rather than after, and why it is one of the least effectively supervised operations in ordinary building.**

examTip.trick: **English: alternate COURSES of headers and stretchers. Flemish: alternating WITHIN each course.** English is stronger; Flemish looks better.
examTip.trap: **A bond exists to prevent CONTINUOUS VERTICAL JOINTS and to tie the wall's thickness** — headers do the latter, which is why stretcher bond cannot bond a thick wall.
examTip.mnemonic: **A header course is brickwork's THROUGH STONE.** And look for unfilled PERPENDS while the work is in progress — invisible after pointing, and worth a third of the strength.

questions.stem: CONFINED MASONRY differs from a REINFORCED CONCRETE FRAME WITH MASONRY INFILL in that in confined masonry the:
options: Masonry is unreinforced and carries no load
MASONRY is built FIRST and the confining concrete elements are cast against it
Confining elements are made of steel rather than concrete
Masonry panels are separated from the frame by a gap
questions.solution:
**The MASONRY is built FIRST and the confining concrete elements are cast against it** — so the two are bonded and act together, the masonry carrying the vertical load and the in-plane shear.

**The two systems compared:**

| Aspect | CONFINED MASONRY | RC FRAME with INFILL |
|---|---|---|
| **Sequence of construction** | **MASONRY first, then the concrete tie-columns and beams cast against it** ← | **FRAME first, then the masonry built into the openings** ← |
| **Bond between the two** | **GOOD — the concrete is cast against the toothed masonry face, so they interlock** ← | **POOR — the masonry is built up to a hardened frame, and the joint is weak** ← |
| **Who carries the vertical load** | **The MASONRY, principally** ← | **The FRAME; the infill is nominally non-structural** ← |
| **Who carries the lateral load** | **The masonry in shear, CONFINED by the elements** ← | **Nominally the frame — but the stiff infill actually takes most of it, whether intended or not** ← |
| **Size of the concrete elements** | **SMALL — tie-columns of 150 to 230 mm square with four bars** ← | **Substantial beams and columns, designed as a frame** ← |
| **Behaviour in an earthquake** | **GOOD — the masonry cracks but is held together and continues to carry load** ← | **VARIABLE, and often poor, because the infill's real behaviour was not designed for** ← |

> **THE CONSTRUCTION SEQUENCE IN THE FIRST ROW IS NOT A DETAIL BUT THE DEFINING DIFFERENCE, and it produces every other difference in the table:**

> **Casting concrete against masonry that has been left toothed gives a genuine mechanical interlock, so the two materials are composite and share load properly.**

> **Building masonry against a hardened concrete frame gives a butt joint with only mortar adhesion, which cracks at the first movement and leaves the panel loose within its frame.**

> **So the same two materials, in the same geometry, behave quite differently depending only on which was built first — which is a striking illustration that the construction method is part of the structural design.**

**WHY CONFINED MASONRY PERFORMS SO WELL, AND WHY IT IS SO WELL SUITED TO NEPAL:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **It uses the SKILLS and MATERIALS that are already available** ← | **Masons who can lay brick or block, small quantities of concrete and steel — no formwork of consequence and no frame erection** ← |
| **The concrete elements are SMALL and simple** ← | **Cast in narrow forms against the masonry, with four bars and simple links** ← |
| **The masonry does the structural work it is good at** ← | **Carrying compression and in-plane shear** ← |
| **The confinement does what masonry cannot** ← | **Provides tension, holds the cracked masonry together, and prevents out-of-plane collapse** ← |
| **It is only slightly dearer than unreinforced masonry** ← | **A few per cent, against the many times greater cost of a proper RC frame** ← |
| **And it has performed very well in earthquakes worldwide** ← | **In Latin America, Iran, Indonesia and elsewhere** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE DECISIVE PRACTICAL ARGUMENT AND IT IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN MISSED IN DISCUSSIONS OF WHAT NEPAL SHOULD BUILD: a construction system is only as good as the workforce that will actually build it.**

> **An RC frame properly detailed to IS 13920 requires accurate bar bending, congested joint reinforcement, careful formwork, controlled concrete and competent supervision.**

> **Where those are not available — which is most rural construction — the frame that gets built is not the frame that was designed, and a badly built frame with heavy infill is a dangerous building.**

> **Confined masonry asks much less: mostly ordinary masonry, done well, with small simple concrete elements that are hard to get badly wrong.**

> **So it is more likely to be built as designed, and a system that is actually achieved is worth more than a better system that is not — which is a form of engineering judgment that has nothing to do with calculation and everything to do with the realities of where the building is going up.**

examTip.trick: **Masonry FIRST, concrete cast against it** — so they interlock and act together. An infilled frame is built the other way round and the joint is weak.
examTip.trap: **The same two materials behave quite differently depending only on which was built first** — the construction sequence IS part of the structural design here.
examTip.mnemonic: **A system is only as good as the workforce that will build it** — confined masonry asks for good bricklaying and small simple concrete elements, which is what is actually available.

questions.stem: The Nepal Building Code's rules restrict both the SIZE of openings in a masonry wall and their DISTANCE from a corner. The restriction on distance from a corner exists because:
options: Windows near a corner are difficult to construct
The lintel over a corner opening would be difficult to support
Openings near a corner obstruct the view along the wall
The CORNER is where the wall's shear and tensile stresses are highest and where the two walls must remain tied
questions.solution:
**Because the CORNER is where the wall's shear and tensile stresses are highest and where the two walls must remain tied** — so an opening there removes the masonry precisely where it is most needed.

**The rules, in outline:**

| Requirement | Typical limit |
|---|---|
| **Total length of openings in a wall** ← | **Not more than about half the wall's length between cross-walls (less in higher seismic conditions)** ← |
| **Distance of an opening from a CORNER or a wall junction** ← | **At least a quarter of the storey height, and not less than 600 mm** ← |
| **PIER width between two openings** ← | **At least half the height of the shorter opening, and not less than about 600 mm** ← |
| **Vertical distance between two openings, one above the other** ← | **At least 600 mm, or half the width of the smaller opening** ← |
| **Openings should be VERTICALLY ALIGNED from storey to storey** ← | **So that the piers between them are continuous** ← |
| **Where an opening exceeds the limits, VERTICAL reinforcement at its jambs is required** ← | ← |

> **THE CORNER RULE IN THE SECOND ROW FOLLOWS DIRECTLY FROM WHAT THE CORNER DOES, AND ONCE THAT IS SEEN THE RULE NEEDS NO MEMORISING:**

> **The corner is where two walls tie to one another, and that tie is what gives the building its box action.**

> **It is also where the in-plane shear in each wall is transferred into the return wall, so the shear stresses there are at their highest.**

> **Putting a window 200 mm from a corner leaves a slender strip of masonry doing the most demanding job in the wall — and that strip cracks, the corner opens, and the box action is lost.**

> **So the rule is not about buildability or convenience but about preserving the one element whose failure disables the whole system.**

**THE PIER RULE IN THE THIRD ROW ADDRESSES A DIFFERENT AND EQUALLY IMPORTANT MECHANISM:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A wall with openings resists in-plane shear through the PIERS between them** ← | **The openings carry nothing** ← |
| **A slender pier is weak in shear and prone to DIAGONAL cracking** ← | **The X-crack pattern that appears between every pair of windows in a damaged masonry building** ← |
| **A slender pier also ROCKS on its bed joints under reversal** ← | ← |
| **So a wall's shear capacity depends on the WIDTH of its piers, not on its total length** ← | **Which is why the total opening area and the individual pier widths are BOTH limited** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE POINT THAT MAKES THE TWO RULES COMPLEMENTARY RATHER THAN REDUNDANT: limiting only the total opening area would permit one long window with narrow piers, and limiting only the pier width would permit a wall that was almost all openings.**

> **Both are needed, because the wall's capacity depends on how much masonry there is AND on how it is distributed.**

> **THE VERTICAL ALIGNMENT REQUIREMENT IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN SACRIFICED TO ARCHITECTURAL PREFERENCE AND IT IS WORTH DEFENDING: when openings in successive storeys line up, the piers between them line up too, forming continuous vertical strips of masonry from foundation to roof.**

> **Those continuous piers carry the vertical load down a clear path and act as continuous shear elements over the building's height.**

> **When the openings are staggered from storey to storey, a pier in one storey sits over an opening in the storey below — so its load must travel sideways through the lintel and the wall, and the shear path is broken.**

> **The result is local overstress at every offset, and a building whose walls cannot act as continuous elements at all.**

> **This is a case where a modest architectural constraint buys a large structural benefit, and where the cost of ignoring it is not obvious on the drawing but is entirely predictable in an earthquake.**

examTip.trick: **The corner ties the two walls together and carries the highest shear** — an opening there removes the masonry doing the most demanding job in the wall.
examTip.trap: **Total opening area AND individual pier width are both limited** — one rule alone would permit either a single long window or a wall that is nearly all openings.
examTip.mnemonic: **Align openings vertically from storey to storey** — so the piers are continuous from foundation to roof. Staggered openings put a pier over a void and break the shear path.
